### TDD for WebSocket Communication — Bidirectional Message Protocols [community]

WebSocket connections are bidirectional, stateful, and asynchronous — three properties that make TDD challenging when applied naively. The correct TDD approach: extract the message-handling logic into a pure state machine (functional core), test it with synchronous test cases, and wrap it in a thin WebSocket adapter that is integration-tested separately.

The key insight: **a WebSocket handler is a state machine that receives typed messages and produces typed responses.** TDD drives the state machine design; the WebSocket transport is an adapter.

```typescript
// ws-protocol.ts — typed WebSocket message protocol (drives TDD interface design)
export type ClientMessage =
  | { type: 'subscribe';   channel: string }
  | { type: 'unsubscribe'; channel: string }
  | { type: 'publish';     channel: string; payload: unknown }
  | { type: 'ping' };

export type ServerMessage =
  | { type: 'subscribed';  channel: string; subscriberId: string }
  | { type: 'unsubscribed'; channel: string }
  | { type: 'message';     channel: string; payload: unknown; from: string }
  | { type: 'pong' }
  | { type: 'error';       code: string; reason: string };

// ws-handler.ts — pure state machine: (state, message) → (new state, responses[])
// No WebSocket API dependency — fully unit-testable
export interface SubscriptionState {
  subscriberId: string;
  channels:     Set<string>;
}

export interface HandlerResult {
  newState:  SubscriptionState;
  responses: ServerMessage[];
  broadcast: Array<{ channel: string; message: ServerMessage }>;
}

export function handleClientMessage(
  state:   SubscriptionState,
  message: ClientMessage
): HandlerResult {
  switch (message.type) {
    case 'ping':
      return {
        newState:  state,
        responses: [{ type: 'pong' }],
        broadcast: [],
      };

    case 'subscribe': {
      if (state.channels.has(message.channel)) {
        return {
          newState:  state,
          responses: [{ type: 'error', code: 'ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED', reason: `Already subscribed to ${message.channel}` }],
          broadcast: [],
        };
      }
      const channels = new Set([...state.channels, message.channel]);
      return {
        newState:  { ...state, channels },
        responses: [{ type: 'subscribed', channel: message.channel, subscriberId: state.subscriberId }],
        broadcast: [],
      };
    }

    case 'unsubscribe': {
      if (!state.channels.has(message.channel)) {
        return {
          newState:  state,
          responses: [{ type: 'error', code: 'NOT_SUBSCRIBED', reason: `Not subscribed to ${message.channel}` }],
          broadcast: [],
        };
      }
      const channels = new Set([...state.channels].filter(c => c !== message.channel));
      return {
        newState:  { ...state, channels },
        responses: [{ type: 'unsubscribed', channel: message.channel }],
        broadcast: [],
      };
    }

    case 'publish': {
      if (!state.channels.has(message.channel)) {
        return {
          newState:  state,
          responses: [{ type: 'error', code: 'NOT_SUBSCRIBED', reason: 'Cannot publish to unsubscribed channel' }],
          broadcast: [],
        };
      }
      return {
        newState:  state,
        responses: [],
        broadcast: [{
          channel: message.channel,
          message: { type: 'message', channel: message.channel, payload: message.payload, from: state.subscriberId },
        }],
      };
    }
  }
}
```

```typescript
// ws-handler.test.ts — TDD test cases: pure function, no WebSocket runtime needed
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { handleClientMessage, SubscriptionState } from './ws-handler.js';

// Fresh state factory — pure, no side effects
const makeState = (overrides: Partial<SubscriptionState> = {}): SubscriptionState => ({
  subscriberId: 'sub-001',
  channels:     new Set<string>(),
  ...overrides,
});

describe('handleClientMessage', () => {
  // Test case 1: RED — ping produces pong
  it('responds with pong to a ping message', () => {
    const state  = makeState();
    const result = handleClientMessage(state, { type: 'ping' });
    expect(result.responses).toEqual([{ type: 'pong' }]);
    expect(result.broadcast).toHaveLength(0);
    expect(result.newState).toBe(state); // state unchanged — no mutation
  });

  // Test case 2: RED — subscribe to a new channel
  it('adds channel to state and responds subscribed', () => {
    const state  = makeState();
    const result = handleClientMessage(state, { type: 'subscribe', channel: 'orders' });
    expect(result.responses).toEqual([{ type: 'subscribed', channel: 'orders', subscriberId: 'sub-001' }]);
    expect(result.newState.channels.has('orders')).toBe(true);
    expect(result.newState.channels.has('orders')).not.toBe(state.channels.has('orders')); // immutable
  });

  // Test case 3: RED — subscribe to an already-subscribed channel produces error
  it('returns error when subscribing to already-subscribed channel', () => {
    const state  = makeState({ channels: new Set(['orders']) });
    const result = handleClientMessage(state, { type: 'subscribe', channel: 'orders' });
    expect(result.responses[0]).toMatchObject({ type: 'error', code: 'ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED' });
    expect(result.newState.channels.size).toBe(1); // state unchanged
  });

  // Test case 4: RED — unsubscribe removes channel
  it('removes channel from state and responds unsubscribed', () => {
    const state  = makeState({ channels: new Set(['orders', 'payments']) });
    const result = handleClientMessage(state, { type: 'unsubscribe', channel: 'orders' });
    expect(result.responses).toEqual([{ type: 'unsubscribed', channel: 'orders' }]);
    expect(result.newState.channels.has('orders')).toBe(false);
    expect(result.newState.channels.has('payments')).toBe(true); // other channel preserved
  });

  // Test case 5: RED — publish broadcasts to channel
  it('broadcasts a message to the channel when subscribed', () => {
    const state  = makeState({ channels: new Set(['orders']) });
    const result = handleClientMessage(state, { type: 'publish', channel: 'orders', payload: { orderId: 'ORD-1' } });
    expect(result.responses).toHaveLength(0); // no direct response
    expect(result.broadcast).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(result.broadcast[0].channel).toBe('orders');
    expect(result.broadcast[0].message).toMatchObject({
      type: 'message', channel: 'orders', from: 'sub-001',
    });
  });

  // Test case 6: RED — publish to non-subscribed channel returns error
  it('returns error when publishing to an unsubscribed channel', () => {
    const state  = makeState(); // no subscriptions
    const result = handleClientMessage(state, { type: 'publish', channel: 'orders', payload: {} });
    expect(result.responses[0]).toMatchObject({ type: 'error', code: 'NOT_SUBSCRIBED' });
    expect(result.broadcast).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```

**Wiring the state machine to a real WebSocket connection (adapter layer):**

```typescript
// ws-adapter.ts — thin imperative shell: wires the pure state machine to ws
// This layer is integration-tested (not unit TDD'd)
import type { WebSocket } from 'ws'; // or 'bun:websocket', '@cloudflare/workers-types', etc.
import { handleClientMessage, SubscriptionState } from './ws-handler.js';
import type { ClientMessage, ServerMessage } from './ws-protocol.js';

export function createConnectionHandler(
  ws: WebSocket,
  subscriberId: string,
  broadcast: (channel: string, message: ServerMessage) => void
): () => void {
  let state: SubscriptionState = { subscriberId, channels: new Set() };

  function send(msg: ServerMessage): void {
    if (ws.readyState === 1 /* OPEN */) {
      ws.send(JSON.stringify(msg));
    }
  }

  ws.on('message', (raw: Buffer) => {
    try {
      const message = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) as ClientMessage;
      const result = handleClientMessage(state, message);
      state = result.newState;
      result.responses.forEach(send);
      result.broadcast.forEach(({ channel, message: msg }) => broadcast(channel, msg));
    } catch {
      send({ type: 'error', code: 'INVALID_JSON', reason: 'Message must be valid JSON' });
    }
  });

  // Return cleanup function — subscribe the caller to handle connection close
  return () => { state.channels.clear(); };
}
```

**[community] The WebSocket TDD pattern that eliminates 90% of WebSocket bugs:** Model the connection state as an immutable value object (`SubscriptionState`) and the message handler as a pure function `(state, message) → result`. This pattern means every WebSocket behaviour is testable with a synchronous `it()` block — no WebSocket server setup, no async waiting for message delivery. The only integration test needed is "does the wire serialisation (JSON parse/stringify) work?" — one test case, not fifty.

**[community] WebSocket test suites that use a mock `ws` library (e.g., `mock-socket`) are unnecessarily complex.** Mock WebSocket libraries simulate the bidirectional transport layer — but the transport is not what TDD should test. When the message-handling logic is extracted into a pure function (as above), there is nothing in the transport layer to TDD. Use `mock-socket` only for end-to-end integration tests that verify the full JSON wire protocol works correctly. The unit-level state machine tests run without any WebSocket library at all.

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Additions (iter 29)

56. **[community] Hexagonal architecture TDD breaks down when adapters contain business logic that is tested via integration tests only.** A common drift pattern: a team starts with a clean hexagon but incrementally adds `if` statements to the Postgres adapter (filtering, sorting, aggregation in SQL). These branches are only reachable in integration tests (which require a DB container), meaning the fast TDD inner loop cannot drive them. The symptom: integration test suite takes 8 minutes; unit tests finish in 3 seconds but do not cover critical query logic. The rule: **if a branch in an adapter cannot be exercised by the in-memory fake, the branch is in the wrong layer.** Refactor by lifting the branching logic into the application core and keeping the adapter as a pure translator. The test case that drove you to add the branch belongs in a unit test, not an integration test.

57. **[community] London-school mocks with `vi.fn()` silently pass after interface changes in TypeScript.** When `OrderRepository.findById` is renamed to `findByOrderId` (a legitimate refactor), London-school test cases using `{ findById: vi.fn() }` continue to compile and pass — because the mock object is typed `as OrderRepository` (or with `as any`), suppressing the TypeScript error. Chicago-school fakes (`class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository`) immediately produce a compile error on the old method name. The diagnostic: if your test doubles use `vi.fn()` for repository methods, run `tsc --noEmit` after every interface change and grep for `vi.fn()` mock objects that are not typed against the interface. This is the most important maintenance argument for Chicago-school fakes over London-school mocks in TypeScript projects.

58. **[community] WebSocket TDD state machine tests are invalidated by mutable `Set` sharing between state transitions.** In TypeScript, `new Set([...existingSet, 'newItem'])` creates a new Set — but developers sometimes write `existingSet.add('newItem')` which mutates the original Set in place, breaking the immutability contract of the state machine. The TDD symptom: test case 2 (`subscribe to channel`) passes, but test case 3 (`double-subscribe error`) also passes the state mutation check — because both share the same underlying Set object. The fix: always create `new Set([...state.channels, ...])` for additions and `new Set([...state.channels].filter(...))` for removals. Enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` and `readonly` on the `channels` field in `SubscriptionState` to make accidental mutation a TypeScript compile error. A TDD test case that asserts `result.newState !== state` (reference inequality) catches in-place mutation during the Red→Green cycle.

### New Pattern: "Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work" (Google TotT, May 2026) [community]

Google's Testing on the Toilet series (May 2026, Shahar Roth) articulated a principle that directly improves TDD ergonomics: **pass collaborators (dependencies) at construction time; pass work data (domain values) at call time.**

This is not just a style preference — it is a TDD-forcing function. When you write the test first:

- **Collaborators at construction** → the test's `Arrange` phase becomes an explicit, type-checked list of everything the object under test needs to do its job. This makes the dependency graph visible in the test, not hidden inside the implementation.
- **Work data at call time** → each test case can vary the actual input without constructing a new instance of the object under test. This keeps test cases short and removes duplicated `Arrange` boilerplate.

The anti-pattern this addresses: mixing runtime data with dependencies in the constructor, which forces test cases to rebuild the entire object just to test one variation of input.

```typescript
// ── ANTI-PATTERN: work data (userId, orderId) injected at construction ──────
// This forces a new OrderProcessor per test case just to vary the order ID.
class OrderProcessor {
  constructor(
    private readonly orderId: string,        // work data — varies per call
    private readonly userId: string,          // work data — varies per call
    private readonly repo: OrderRepository,  // collaborator — stable
    private readonly mailer: Mailer,          // collaborator — stable
  ) {}

  async process(): Promise<void> {
    const order = await this.repo.findById(this.orderId);
    await this.mailer.send({ to: `user-${this.userId}@example.com`, subject: 'Processed' });
  }
}

// Test is forced to construct a new OrderProcessor per variation — noisy Arrange:
it('sends email to correct user', async () => {
  const repo   = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
  const mailer = new SpyMailer();
  const svc    = new OrderProcessor('ORD-1', 'USR-42', repo, mailer); // rebuild for each test
  await svc.process();
  expect(mailer.sent[0].to).toBe('user-USR-42@example.com');
});

// ── GOOD PATTERN: collaborators at construction, work data at call time ───────
// One instance, many test cases — Arrange is written once in beforeEach.
class OrderProcessor {
  constructor(
    private readonly repo: OrderRepository,  // collaborator — passed at construction
    private readonly mailer: Mailer,          // collaborator — passed at construction
  ) {}

  async process(orderId: string, userId: string): Promise<void> {  // work at call time
    const order = await this.repo.findById(orderId);
    await this.mailer.send({ to: `user-${userId}@example.com`, subject: 'Processed' });
  }
}

// Test: one instance, many cases with varied work data:
describe('OrderProcessor.process', () => {
  let repo:   InMemoryOrderRepository;
  let mailer: SpyMailer;
  let svc:    OrderProcessor;

  beforeEach(() => {
    repo   = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    mailer = new SpyMailer();
    svc    = new OrderProcessor(repo, mailer); // one Arrange block
  });

  it('sends email to the requesting user', async () => {
    await repo.create({ id: 'ORD-1', status: 'draft' });
    await svc.process('ORD-1', 'USR-42');     // work data varies
    expect(mailer.sent[0].to).toBe('user-USR-42@example.com');
  });

  it('sends email for a different order and user', async () => {
    await repo.create({ id: 'ORD-2', status: 'draft' });
    await svc.process('ORD-2', 'USR-99');     // same svc instance, different work
    expect(mailer.sent[0].to).toBe('user-USR-99@example.com');
  });
});
```

**Why TDD enforces this pattern:** When you write the test first, you immediately feel the pain of mixing collaborators and work data in the constructor — the `Arrange` step grows quadratically as you add test cases. The reflex to move work data out of the constructor is strongest at test-authoring time. This is one of the subtler design benefits of TDD: the test friction acts as a real-time architecture smell detector.

**TypeScript-specific benefit:** Collaborators typed as interfaces at construction enable the TypeScript compiler to verify that every fake/spy satisfies the full interface. Work data typed as method parameters benefits from call-site inference — callers get precise error messages when the wrong type is passed. This separation also simplifies `beforeEach` setup: the shared collaborators are created once; only test-specific inputs change per `it()`.

### New Pattern: Vitest 5.0 Beta — TDD Migration Notes [community]

Vitest 5.0-beta.2 (May 2026) introduces breaking changes that affect TDD project configurations. Teams with active TDD watch loops need to be aware of these before upgrading.

**Breaking change 1: `sequential` test option removed.** The `it.sequential` and `describe.sequential` APIs are removed; use `it.concurrent` (the new default in suites) or omit the modifier. In TDD watch mode, this means suites that were explicitly marked sequential now run concurrently by default — a potential source of flakiness if shared state exists between test cases in the same file.

```typescript
// ── BEFORE (Vitest < 5): explicit sequential to prevent parallel execution ──
describe('OrderService integration', () => {
  it.sequential('creates an order', async () => { /* ... */ });
  it.sequential('confirms the order', async () => { /* ... */ });
});

// ── AFTER (Vitest 5): sequential is gone — use beforeEach to isolate state ──
// The correct fix is NOT to find a workaround for .sequential,
// but to make each test case independently set up its own state:
describe('OrderService integration', () => {
  let repo: InMemoryOrderRepository;
  beforeEach(() => { repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository(); }); // fresh state per case

  it('creates an order', async () => {
    const svc = new OrderService(repo, new SpyMailer());
    const result = await svc.create({ customerId: 'C1', items: [] });
    expect(result.id).toBeDefined();
  });

  it('confirms a draft order', async () => {
    // Arrange: own state — not dependent on previous test case
    const svc = new OrderService(repo, new SpyMailer());
    const draft = await svc.create({ customerId: 'C1', items: [] });
    const confirmed = await svc.confirm(draft.id);
    expect(confirmed.status).toBe('confirmed');
  });
});
```

**Why removing `sequential` improves TDD discipline:** Tests that required `sequential` to pass were usually violating the FIRST principle (Independent). Removing the option forces teams to fix the underlying problem — shared mutable state between test cases — rather than serialising around it. In a TDD workflow, this is a positive forcing function: if your red test fails only when run in a certain order, the problem is the test design, not the execution order.

**Breaking change 2: `.vitest/` directory replaces scattered output paths.** Blob reporter and attachment paths now default to `.vitest/blob/` and `.vitest/attachments/` respectively. Add `.vitest/` to `.gitignore`. In CI TDD pipelines that archive test artifacts, update the `upload-artifact` paths.

**Breaking change 3: `expect` package inlined.** If your TypeScript project imported from the `expect` sub-package directly (e.g., `import { expect } from '@vitest/expect'`), update to `import { expect } from 'vitest'`. Custom matcher type declarations using the old augmentation path need updating too.

```typescript
// ── OLD: importing from sub-package (Vitest < 5) ──────────────────────────
import { expect } from '@vitest/expect';

declare module '@vitest/expect' {
  interface Matchers<T = any> {
    toBeValidUuid(): T;
  }
}

// ── NEW: import from vitest directly (Vitest 5+) ───────────────────────────
import { expect } from 'vitest';

declare module 'vitest' {
  interface Matchers<T = any> {
    toBeValidUuid(): T;
  }
}

expect.extend({
  toBeValidUuid(received: unknown) {
    const pass = typeof received === 'string'
      && /^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-4[0-9a-f]{3}-[89ab][0-9a-f]{3}-[0-9a-f]{12}$/i.test(received);
    return {
      pass,
      message: () => pass
        ? `Expected "${received}" NOT to be a valid UUID v4`
        : `Expected a valid UUID v4, got: "${received}"`,
    };
  },
});
```

**New feature: V8 coverage for `node:child_process` and `node:worker_threads`.** For TDD loops testing background worker logic, V8 coverage in Vitest 5 now tracks execution in forked processes. This closes a significant coverage blind spot for server-side TDD: worker thread code was previously invisible to V8 coverage. TDD teams testing job queues, background processors, or worker-pool patterns can now include worker coverage in their thresholds.

**New feature: private method spy typing.** Vitest 5 adds TypeScript support for spying on private methods. Previously, `vi.spyOn(instance, 'privateMethod' as any)` was the only option and lost type safety. In Vitest 5, private method names are accepted directly:

```typescript
// Vitest 5: type-safe private method spy
class PaymentProcessor {
  constructor(private readonly gateway: PaymentGateway) {}

  async charge(amount: number): Promise<string> {
    const validated = this.validateAmount(amount); // private helper
    return this.gateway.process(validated);
  }

  private validateAmount(amount: number): number {
    if (amount <= 0) throw new Error('Amount must be positive');
    return Math.round(amount * 100) / 100; // round to 2 decimal places
  }
}

it('validates amount before charging', async () => {
  const gateway = new FakePaymentGateway();
  const processor = new PaymentProcessor(gateway);

  // Vitest 5: spy on private method without `as any` cast
  const validateSpy = vi.spyOn(processor, 'validateAmount');

  await processor.charge(10.005);

  expect(validateSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(10.005);
  expect(gateway.processed[0].amount).toBe(10.01); // rounded
});
```

**TDD guidance on private method spies:** Use this feature sparingly. Spying on a private method tests implementation details, not behaviour — this is the London-school over-specification trap. Prefer testing the public observable outcome (`gateway.processed[0].amount`) rather than the private validation call. Use private method spies only when the private method has a costly or irreversible side effect that must be asserted on (e.g., verifying that a rate-limit check happens before an external API call).

### New Pattern: Concern-Driven AI-Augmented TDD (Meta ACH, 2026) [community]

Meta's ACH system (arXiv:2501.12862) demonstrates a production-validated pattern for integrating AI mutation testing into TDD workflows. The key insight that distinguishes it from classical mutation testing: **target concern-specific mutations rather than exhaustive fault injection.**

The practical TDD workflow adaptation:

1. **Identify the concern** (privacy, security, money calculation, authentication boundary)
2. **Ask the LLM for a failing test specification** that would catch a mutation violating that concern — this is the Red-phase prompt, not the Green-phase prompt
3. **Write the test case** (the human validates the LLM's specification against the real requirement)
4. **Run the test** — it should fail (Red); the mutation the LLM identified should make it pass
5. **Implement the minimal fix** (Green), then refactor

```typescript
// Concern-driven TDD: privacy boundary on user data export
// Red-phase LLM prompt (what you ask Claude/Copilot for):
// "Write a TypeScript Vitest test case that would FAIL if UserExportService
//  accidentally included password hashes or internal tokens in the exported data.
//  The test should specify the exact fields that MUST be absent from the export."

// LLM-generated failing test specification (Red):
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { UserExportService } from './UserExportService.js';
import { InMemoryUserRepository } from './test-doubles/InMemoryUserRepository.js';

interface ExportedUser {
  id:    string;
  email: string;
  name:  string;
  // NOTE: no passwordHash, no internalToken, no sessionIds
}

describe('UserExportService — privacy boundary', () => {
  it('excludes sensitive fields from exported user data', async () => {
    const repo = new InMemoryUserRepository();
    await repo.save({
      id:            'USR-1',
      email:         'alice@example.com',
      name:          'Alice',
      passwordHash:  '$2b$10$secret-hash',  // must NOT appear in export
      internalToken: 'tok_internal_secret',  // must NOT appear in export
    });

    const svc     = new UserExportService(repo);
    const exported = await svc.exportUser('USR-1');

    // Test case: concern-specific assertions — what must be ABSENT
    expect(exported).not.toHaveProperty('passwordHash');
    expect(exported).not.toHaveProperty('internalToken');
    expect(exported).not.toHaveProperty('sessionIds');

    // Structural assertion: only the approved fields are present
    const exportedKeys = Object.keys(exported);
    const allowedKeys  = ['id', 'email', 'name'];
    const leakedKeys   = exportedKeys.filter(k => !allowedKeys.includes(k));
    expect(leakedKeys).toHaveLength(0);  // fails if any unapproved field is included

    // Type assertion: the exported shape matches the approved contract
    const typed: ExportedUser = exported; // TypeScript compile error if type is wrong
    expect(typed.id).toBe('USR-1');
  });

  it('includes all required public fields', async () => {
    const repo = new InMemoryUserRepository();
    await repo.save({ id: 'USR-2', email: 'bob@example.com', name: 'Bob', passwordHash: 'x', internalToken: 'y' });

    const svc     = new UserExportService(repo);
    const exported = await svc.exportUser('USR-2');

    // Positive concern: required fields ARE present
    expect(exported).toHaveProperty('id',    'USR-2');
    expect(exported).toHaveProperty('email', 'bob@example.com');
    expect(exported).toHaveProperty('name',  'Bob');
  });
});
```

**Why concern-driven test specification outperforms exhaustive test generation:** Meta's production data showed 73% acceptance rate for concern-specific test cases generated by their LLM system (during Messenger/WhatsApp test-a-thons), with 36% judged privacy-relevant. Classic exhaustive test generation produces far more tests but with lower signal density — teams reject most generated test cases because they duplicate coverage or test trivial paths. The concern-driven approach produces fewer test cases, each with clear intent.

**The Red-phase LLM prompt pattern:** Ask the AI to write a test that would **fail** given the current state of the code — not one that passes. This is the fundamental discipline that prevents LLMs from generating tautological tests (tests that pass because they merely repeat the implementation's logic). A well-formed prompt: "Write a failing Vitest test case for `[function/class]` that would catch a bug where `[specific concern]` is violated. The test should fail with the current implementation."

**[community] The most common AI-TDD mistake:** asking the AI to generate test cases for a feature that is already implemented. These tests almost always pass on the first run (no Red phase) and produce false confidence. The correct workflow: **write the concern first (Red), then ask the AI to review the test case for completeness**, not to generate it wholesale. AI is best used as a test-case reviewer and mutation-concern identifier, not as an automated Red-phase writer.

### New Pattern: Test Lifecycle Management with `vi.onCleanup()` (Vitest 3.2+) [community]

`vi.onCleanup(fn)` registers a cleanup callback scoped to the current test case — it runs after the test completes (pass or fail) without requiring the test to declare a fixture. This is useful in TDD inner loops when cleanup is conditional on test setup that may not complete.

```typescript
// Traditional teardown pattern: side effects may persist if setup fails mid-way
it('creates and registers an external resource', async () => {
  const resourceId = await createExternalResource();
  try {
    // test body — may fail before afterEach cleanup
    const result = await service.process(resourceId);
    expect(result.status).toBe('done');
  } finally {
    await deleteExternalResource(resourceId); // required cleanup
  }
});

// ── vi.onCleanup() pattern: cleanup registered inline, always runs ──────────
it('creates and registers an external resource', async () => {
  const resourceId = await createExternalResource();
  vi.onCleanup(() => deleteExternalResource(resourceId)); // registered immediately after creation

  // No try/finally needed — cleanup is guaranteed by Vitest even on test failure
  const result = await service.process(resourceId);
  expect(result.status).toBe('done');
});

// In TDD watch mode, this pattern prevents resource leaks between rapid re-runs.
// If the test fails at `service.process`, the cleanup still fires before the next run.

// ── Multiple cleanups: registered in order, run in reverse (LIFO) ────────────
it('creates layered resources', async () => {
  const db    = await createTestDatabase();
  vi.onCleanup(() => db.close());            // registered first — runs last

  const table = await db.createTable('orders');
  vi.onCleanup(() => db.dropTable('orders')); // registered second — runs first

  const order = await table.insert({ id: 'ORD-1', status: 'draft' });
  expect(order.id).toBe('ORD-1');
  // Cleanup order on test end: dropTable → db.close()
});
```

**TDD ergonomics benefit:** In the TDD inner loop (watch mode), resource leaks between test runs cause false positives on subsequent runs — a test passes because leftover state from the previous run satisfies a precondition. `vi.onCleanup()` guarantees teardown even when a test fails during setup, keeping the watch loop clean. The LIFO execution order mirrors resource dependency graphs naturally: resources created first are cleaned up last.

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 19 Additions

59. **[community] Vitest 5 removes `it.sequential` — tests that required it to pass were hiding FIRST violations.** Teams upgrading to Vitest 5 who had relied on `it.sequential` to prevent flakiness from shared state will see failures after upgrading. The correct fix is not to find a workaround for the removed API (e.g., setting `sequence.concurrent: false` globally) but to diagnose which shared state caused the ordering dependency and eliminate it. Each test case must arrange its own state using `beforeEach` with fresh instances. Masking order-dependency with global serial execution is the same root cause as flaky tests — both hide state contamination that TDD's FIRST principles require to be absent.

60. **[community] The "Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work" principle reveals hidden state coupling in constructors.** When following this pattern during a TDD session, watch for any constructor parameter that could logically be a method parameter (e.g., `userId`, `requestId`, `timestamp`, `orderId`). Any domain ID passed at construction time is a signal that the class is designed for single-use rather than reuse — which forces test authors to instantiate a new object per test case. This pattern is a design smell, not merely a style issue: single-use objects accumulate in the heap during integration tests and slow down the TDD feedback loop.

61. **[community] Concern-driven AI test generation breaks down when the "concern" is too broad.** Prompting an AI with "write a test that catches any bug in this service" produces low-value tests. The signal-to-noise ratio is directly proportional to concern specificity. Production teams at Meta saw 36% privacy-relevance rate for concern-specific prompts vs < 5% for generic test generation. The discipline: before asking an AI for a test case, write one sentence that names the specific invariant the test must enforce ("the export must never include the passwordHash field"). If you cannot write that sentence, the test is not ready to be written — return to requirements.

62. **[community] `vi.onCleanup()` does not replace `afterEach` for test isolation setup.** A common mistake is using `vi.onCleanup()` to reset shared module state that should have been reset in `beforeEach`. The difference: `beforeEach` runs before the test (ensures clean state going in); `vi.onCleanup()` runs after the test (ensures clean state going out). In TDD watch mode, if a test fails before reaching `vi.onCleanup()`, the cleanup does fire — but the next test case still gets a fresh `beforeEach`. The two are complementary: use `beforeEach` for state initialization, `vi.onCleanup()` for resource teardown of things created during the test body.

### In-Source TDD — Tests Co-Located with Implementation [community]

Vitest supports a pattern borrowed from Rust's module tests: writing test cases **inside the source file**, wrapped in an `if (import.meta.vitest)` block. This is eliminated from production builds by Vite's tree-shaking while remaining fully visible to the test runner. For TDD inner loops working on a single module, in-source testing eliminates the cognitive context-switch of having two files open simultaneously.

**When to use:** pure utility modules (formatters, validators, calculators) where the test and implementation naturally belong together. **When not to use:** domain services that depend on multiple collaborators — those benefit from a separate test file that explicitly wires up fakes and makes the dependency structure visible.

```typescript
// src/pricing/discountCalculator.ts
// In-source TDD: test cases live next to the implementation

export interface DiscountInput {
  subtotal:  number;
  tierLevel: 'standard' | 'premium' | 'enterprise';
  coupon?:   string;
}

export function calculateDiscount(input: DiscountInput): number {
  const tierRate: Record<DiscountInput['tierLevel'], number> = {
    standard:   0,
    premium:    0.10,
    enterprise: 0.20,
  };
  const base  = input.subtotal * tierRate[input.tierLevel];
  const extra = input.coupon === 'EXTRA5' ? input.subtotal * 0.05 : 0;
  return Math.round((base + extra) * 100) / 100;
}

// ── In-source test cases: only compiled/run when Vitest is active ─────────────
if (import.meta.vitest) {
  const { it, expect, describe } = import.meta.vitest;

  describe('calculateDiscount', () => {
    // RED-1: standard tier — no discount
    it('returns 0 discount for standard tier', () => {
      expect(calculateDiscount({ subtotal: 100, tierLevel: 'standard' })).toBe(0);
    });

    // RED-2: premium tier — 10% discount
    it('applies 10% for premium tier', () => {
      expect(calculateDiscount({ subtotal: 200, tierLevel: 'premium' })).toBe(20);
    });

    // RED-3: enterprise tier — 20% discount
    it('applies 20% for enterprise tier', () => {
      expect(calculateDiscount({ subtotal: 150, tierLevel: 'enterprise' })).toBe(30);
    });

    // RED-4: EXTRA5 coupon stacks with tier discount
    it('stacks EXTRA5 coupon with tier discount', () => {
      // enterprise (20%) + EXTRA5 (5%) = 25% of 100 = 25
      expect(calculateDiscount({ subtotal: 100, tierLevel: 'enterprise', coupon: 'EXTRA5' })).toBe(25);
    });

    // RED-5: unknown coupon has no effect (triangulation — avoid over-generalising coupon handling)
    it('ignores unknown coupon codes', () => {
      expect(calculateDiscount({ subtotal: 100, tierLevel: 'premium', coupon: 'INVALID' })).toBe(10);
    });
  });
}
```

**vitest.config.ts setup required for in-source testing:**

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Enable in-source testing — Vitest scans .ts/.tsx files for if (import.meta.vitest)
    includeSource: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
  },
  define: {
    // Ensures production builds tree-shake the test blocks entirely
    'import.meta.vitest': 'undefined',
  },
});
```

**[community] The most underrated TDD feedback advantage of in-source testing:** in watch mode (`vitest --watch`), saving the source file reruns the in-source test cases in the same file in < 100ms — no file-switch, no separate terminal pane. The entire Red-Green-Refactor cycle for a utility function happens in a single editor tab. Teams that adopt this pattern for utility modules report the TDD inner loop feeling closer to a REPL than a test runner.

**[community] Production caution — in-source tests are not a replacement for full test suites.** In-source test cases are excellent for the TDD design loop on pure functions. They are inappropriate for test cases that assert on integration behaviour (database, HTTP, event buses). A team that migrates integration test cases into in-source blocks will see their production bundle size grow (Vite's define substitute only works at build time; bundlers not using Vite may not tree-shake the block). Enforce a linting rule: in-source test cases must not import test infrastructure files (fakes, fixtures, mocks).

### Vitest 4.1 Test Tags — TDD Discipline Enforcement Layer [community]

Vitest 4.1 introduced a tag system for organising test cases into named groups with shared options. For TDD workflows, test tags serve as a **discipline enforcement layer**: teams can tag test cases by their TDD phase role, then selectively run or report on subsets during different stages of the development cycle.

**Practical TDD tagging taxonomy:**

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — define tag groups used across the TDD workflow
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Tags are arbitrary strings; the TDD convention below is team-defined
    // Run only fast unit test cases during inner loop: vitest --reporter=verbose --testNamePattern="" --tag unit
  },
});
```

```typescript
// checkout.test.ts — tagging test cases by TDD phase role
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { CheckoutService } from './CheckoutService.js';
import { InMemoryOrderRepository } from './test-doubles/InMemoryOrderRepository.js';
import { FakePaymentPort }         from './test-doubles/FakePaymentPort.js';
import { SpyNotificationPort }     from './test-doubles/SpyNotificationPort.js';

// Tag: 'unit' — runs in TDD inner loop (<5ms each, no I/O)
describe('CheckoutService — unit', { tags: ['unit', 'checkout'] }, () => {
  it('rejects zero-total orders before payment', async () => {
    const orders        = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    const payment       = new FakePaymentPort();
    const notifications = new SpyNotificationPort();
    const svc           = new CheckoutService(orders, payment, notifications);

    await expect(
      svc.checkout({ customerId: 'C1', items: [], currency: 'USD', customerEmail: 'a@b.com' })
    ).rejects.toThrow('total must be positive');

    // Guard: payment and notification ports must not be touched
    expect(payment.charged).toHaveLength(0);
    expect(notifications.confirmations).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});

// Tag: 'integration' — runs in CI pre-merge stage (requires DB/HTTP)
describe('CheckoutService — integration', { tags: ['integration', 'checkout', 'slow'] }, () => {
  it('persists a confirmed order to PostgreSQL', async () => {
    // This test requires a real database connection — excluded from TDD inner loop
    // ... integration test body ...
  });
});

// Tag: 'regression' — pinned to a defect ID; run on every commit
describe('Regression: CHK-4821 — double-charge on retry', { tags: ['regression', 'unit'] }, () => {
  it('charges payment exactly once even if checkout is called twice with same idempotency key', async () => {
    const payment = new FakePaymentPort();
    const svc     = new CheckoutService(new InMemoryOrderRepository(), payment, new SpyNotificationPort());
    const input   = { customerId: 'C1', items: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 1, unitPrice: 50 }], currency: 'USD', customerEmail: 'a@b.com', idempotencyKey: 'idem-001' };

    await svc.checkout(input);
    await svc.checkout(input); // second call with same key — must be idempotent

    // CHK-4821: payment.charged must have length 1, not 2
    expect(payment.charged).toHaveLength(1);
  });
});
```

**Running by tag in the TDD workflow:**

```bash
# Inner TDD loop: only unit test cases (< 5ms each)
npx vitest --reporter=verbose --tag unit

# Pre-merge: unit + regression
npx vitest --tag unit --tag regression

# CI full run: all tags
npx vitest

# Run all checkout-related test cases across all environments
npx vitest --tag checkout
```

**[community] Why the `regression` tag is the most valuable TDD tag in production:** Every time a defect escapes to production and a regression test case is added, that test case is tagged `regression` with the defect ID in the description. Over 6–12 months, the regression suite becomes a living record of production failures. Running `vitest --tag regression` on every commit gives teams confidence that previously fixed defects have not recurred — without running the slower integration suite. Teams using this pattern report that regression test cases catch 15–20% of reintroduced defects before merge, even when the regression test case was written for a completely different feature area.

### Scenario-Based TDD for AI Agents — langwatch/scenario Pattern [community]

As TypeScript applications increasingly embed LLM-powered agents, the classical TDD inner loop (pure function with deterministic output) breaks down: agents are nondeterministic by nature. The `langwatch/scenario` framework (869 GitHub stars, MIT licensed) introduces a **simulation-based TDD** approach that adapts the Red-Green-Refactor cycle for agentic systems.

**The core insight:** instead of asserting on a return value, assert on **observable agent behaviour** across a scripted conversation. The framework provides determinism through response caching, judge agents for semantic assertions, and `AbortSignal`-compatible conversation termination.

```typescript
// ai-agent-tdd.test.ts — TDD for a recipe recommendation agent
// Uses langwatch/scenario for simulation-based agent testing
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Scenario } from '@langwatch/scenario';
import { RecipeAgent } from './RecipeAgent.js';

const scenario = new Scenario();

describe('RecipeAgent', () => {
  // RED-1: agent recommends vegetarian recipes when asked
  it('recommends only vegetarian recipes for vegetarian users', async () => {
    const result = await scenario.run({
      name: 'vegetarian recipe request',
      description: 'User explicitly asks for vegetarian recipes',
      agents: [
        new RecipeAgent(),
        scenario.userSimulatorAgent({ persona: 'vegetarian user requesting dinner ideas' }),
      ],
      script: [
        scenario.user('I am vegetarian. What should I cook for dinner tonight?'),
        scenario.agent(),
        // Assertion at this conversation checkpoint: response must not mention meat
        (state) => {
          const agentReply = state.lastAgentMessage;
          expect(agentReply).toBeDefined();
          expect(agentReply?.toLowerCase()).not.toMatch(/chicken|beef|pork|fish|meat/);
        },
        scenario.succeed(),
      ],
    });

    expect(result.success).toBe(true);
  });

  // RED-2: agent asks at most two follow-up questions (UX requirement)
  it('asks no more than two clarifying questions before recommending', async () => {
    const result = await scenario.run({
      name: 'minimal clarification flow',
      description: 'Agent must not over-clarify before providing a recommendation',
      agents: [
        new RecipeAgent(),
        scenario.userSimulatorAgent({ persona: 'user with a vague request' }),
      ],
      // Judge agent evaluates the full conversation against named criteria
      judges: [
        scenario.judgeAgent({
          criteria: [
            'Agent should not ask more than two follow-up questions',
            'Agent should provide at least one concrete recipe suggestion',
          ],
        }),
      ],
    });

    expect(result.success).toBe(true);
    // Judge agent reports violation details if criteria are not met
    expect(result.judgeFailures).toHaveLength(0);
  });

  // RED-3: agent handles tool calls correctly (fetches weather for seasonal suggestions)
  it('invokes the get_current_weather tool for seasonal recipe suggestions', async () => {
    const result = await scenario.run({
      name: 'seasonal recipe with weather',
      description: 'Agent uses weather data to adjust seasonal suggestions',
      agents: [
        new RecipeAgent(),
        scenario.userSimulatorAgent(),
      ],
      script: [
        scenario.user('Suggest a seasonal recipe for today'),
        scenario.agent(),
        // Assert on tool call behaviour mid-conversation
        (state) => {
          expect(state.hasToolCall('get_current_weather')).toBe(true);
        },
        scenario.succeed(),
      ],
    });

    expect(result.success).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Caching for deterministic TDD inner loops:**

```typescript
// RecipeAgent.ts — LLM calls wrapped with @scenario.cache() for deterministic TDD
import { scenario } from './test-doubles/ScenarioCache.js';

export class RecipeAgent {
  // Production: calls real LLM; in test: returns cached response for the same input+scenario+key
  @scenario.cache({ cacheKey: 'v1' })
  async invoke(message: string, context: AgentContext): Promise<AgentResponse> {
    return this.llmClient.complete({
      model:    'gpt-4o',
      messages: [...context.history, { role: 'user', content: message }],
    });
  }
}
```

**[community] The fundamental TDD discipline shift for AI agents: test behaviour, not content.** Classical TDD test cases assert on exact return values (`expect(result).toBe('$10.00')`). For AI agents, exact content assertions produce brittle test cases that fail whenever the LLM changes phrasing. The correct discipline: assert on **structural properties** of the response (contains/lacks certain keywords, calls certain tools, terminates within N turns) using judge agents or regex assertions — never on exact content strings. This maps to ISTQB's distinction between specification-based (black-box) and structure-based (white-box) testing: AI agent TDD is exclusively black-box by necessity.

**[community] Caching is the only currently viable path to deterministic AI-agent TDD inner loops.** Without response caching, a test case for an AI agent may pass on Monday and fail on Wednesday because the LLM's response generation is nondeterministic. The `langwatch/scenario` caching strategy (hash by function arguments + scenario name + cache key) produces stable test runs for the same inputs. The tradeoff: cached test cases do not catch regressions caused by LLM model updates. Teams should run the full uncached suite in a scheduled CI job (weekly or on model version bumps) and use the cached suite for the TDD inner loop.

### Stryker 2025-2026: Incremental Mutation TDD + VS Code Inline Feedback [community]

The 2025-2026 Stryker ecosystem introduced two features that materially improve the TDD-mutation workflow:

1. **Stryker VS Code Extension** — inline mutation test results displayed in the editor (Stryker 9.3+)
2. **Stryker MTP Runner** (Stryker.NET 4.13+) — Microsoft Testing Platform runner for .NET; the pattern generalises to the TypeScript ecosystem as a "pick your runner" philosophy

**VS Code inline mutation TDD workflow:**

```typescript
// With Stryker VS Code extension installed, mutation survivors appear as
// inline warnings in the editor — no context switch to terminal needed.
//
// Normal TDD flow with Stryker integration:
//
//  1. Write failing test (RED)
//  2. Implement minimal code (GREEN)
//  3. Refactor
//  4. Run Stryker incremental: `npx stryker run --incremental`
//     → Only mutates files changed since the last run
//     → Survivors appear as inline editor annotations
//  5. For each survivor: add a triangulating test case that kills it (back to RED)
//  6. Repeat until no survivors in the changed file set

// Example: stryker.config.json for incremental TDD integration
// {
//   "testRunner":         "vitest",
//   "coverageAnalysis":  "perTest",    // requires Vitest per-test coverage maps
//   "incremental":       true,          // only mutates changed files since last run
//   "incrementalFile":  ".stryker-tmp/incremental.json",
//   "reporters":        ["progress", "html"],
//   "vitest": {
//     "configFile": "vitest.config.ts"
//   }
// }

// Stryker incremental run on a TDD session (changed files only)
// Typical performance: 3–8 seconds for a single changed module
// vs 2–10 minutes for a full project mutation run
```

**Incremental mutation in the TDD cycle:**

```typescript
// order-validator.ts — TDD session with incremental mutation feedback
export function validateOrderAmount(amount: number): void {
  if (amount <= 0) {
    throw new RangeError('Order amount must be positive');
  }
  if (amount > 1_000_000) {
    throw new RangeError('Order amount exceeds maximum');
  }
}

// order-validator.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { validateOrderAmount } from './orderValidator.js';

describe('validateOrderAmount', () => {
  // After writing these 4 test cases and running Stryker incrementally,
  // the mutation score for this file should be 100% — every boundary operator is covered.

  // Test 1: happy path (establishes baseline)
  it('accepts a valid amount', () => {
    expect(() => validateOrderAmount(100)).not.toThrow();
  });

  // Test 2: lower boundary — amount = 0 should throw (triangulates <= 0 vs < 0)
  it('throws for zero amount', () => {
    expect(() => validateOrderAmount(0)).toThrow(RangeError);
  });

  // Test 3: lower boundary — negative amount (triangulates <= 0 vs === 0)
  it('throws for negative amount', () => {
    expect(() => validateOrderAmount(-1)).toThrow(RangeError);
  });

  // Test 4: upper boundary — exactly 1,000,000 is valid; 1,000,001 is not
  // (triangulates > 1_000_000 vs >= 1_000_000)
  it('accepts exactly 1,000,000', () => {
    expect(() => validateOrderAmount(1_000_000)).not.toThrow();
  });

  it('throws for amount above maximum', () => {
    expect(() => validateOrderAmount(1_000_001)).toThrow(RangeError);
  });
});

// Without Test 4 (the 1,000,000 boundary), Stryker would surface a survivor:
// Mutant: `amount > 1_000_000` → `amount >= 1_000_000`
// → survives because no test case passes exactly 1,000,000 to the validator
```

**[community] Incremental mutation changes the TDD discipline from "write tests, run mutation at the end of a sprint" to "kill survivors continuously in the inner loop."** Teams that reserve mutation testing for a post-sprint audit treat surviving mutants as a batch cleanup task. Teams that run incremental mutation after each Red-Green-Refactor cycle treat it as a fourth phase of the cycle: Red → Green → Refactor → Verify-mutation-score. The incremental mode (3–8 seconds per changed file) makes the fourth phase cheap enough to include in every TDD session rather than every sprint.

### TDD and the "Is TDD Dead?" Debate — 2026 Synthesis [community]

The Fowler/Hansson/Beck conversation (2014) has been revisited repeatedly. The 2026 production consensus, distilled from team retrospectives and community posts:

**The three positions that actually coexist in healthy teams:**

| Position | Proponent style | When it works | When it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strict TDD** | Every line of production code has a pre-written failing test case | Domain logic, parsers, state machines, calculators | UI rendering, exploratory spikes, highly coupled legacy code |
| **Test-First** (spec before code, no mandatory refactor step) | Works for teams where "refactor" discipline is enforced by code review rather than TDD ceremony | Teams with strong review culture | Solo work under deadline — refactor step gets dropped |
| **Test-After** | Acceptable for thin glue code, generated adapters, trivial one-liners | Lines of code with no meaningful branches | Domain logic — test-after produces tests that conform to the code, not the requirement |

**The production consensus that the debate did not settle:**

1. **TDD does not work on MVC entry points** (Hansson was right for his context). Controllers that delegate immediately to a service layer have no meaningful domain logic to drive. TDD the service; integration-test the controller.
2. **TDD does work on algorithms and domain logic** (Beck was right in general). Sorting, pricing, validation, state machines — these all benefit from test-first precisely because the design space is large and the tests constrain it.
3. **Over-mocking is a TDD implementation bug, not a TDD design flaw** (Fowler's nuanced position). Teams that mock everything produce brittle test suites. The remedy is Chicago-school fakes, not abandoning TDD.
4. **The refactor phase is the most commonly skipped** (consensus across all retrospectives). Teams under deadline pressure maintain Red-Green discipline but skip Refactor. The fix: timebox refactor at 20% of cycle time maximum, not "whenever we get to it."

**[community] The single most important TDD adoption lesson from 2025-2026 team retrospectives:** the biggest predictor of TDD success is not the skill level of individual developers but whether the team has a **shared working agreement on cycle size**. Teams that agree "no test case takes longer than 15 minutes to make pass" maintain TDD discipline under pressure. Teams without that agreement drift toward large "planning tests" that describe the full feature before any implementation exists — which defeats the baby-steps principle and produces long, unmaintainable test cases that are harder to write than the production code itself.

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 20 Additions

63. **[community] In-source test cases are not tree-shaken by all bundlers.** Vite uses the `define` config to substitute `import.meta.vitest` with `undefined` at build time, which tree-shakes the block. But teams using `tsc` directly or esbuild without the `define` equivalent will ship in-source test code to production. Verify elimination: inspect the production bundle for the string `import.meta.vitest` — its presence is a build misconfiguration. Add a CI step: `grep -r 'import.meta.vitest' dist/ && exit 1 || exit 0` to catch this before deployment.

64. **[community] Vitest 4.1 test tags with the `and`/`or` filter syntax are not supported in all CI providers' test step configuration.** The tag filter syntax (`vitest --tag 'unit and not slow'`) uses shell-unfriendly characters on some CI platforms (GitHub Actions handles it, but Jenkins pipeline string interpolation often strips the quotes). Use environment variable injection instead: `VITEST_TAG_FILTER='unit and not slow' npx vitest` and read it in `vitest.config.ts` via `process.env.VITEST_TAG_FILTER`. This makes the filter portable across CI providers without shell quoting issues.

65. **[community] AI-agent TDD with `langwatch/scenario` cached responses masks LLM model regressions.** When the underlying LLM is updated (e.g., `gpt-4o` → `gpt-4o-2026-05`), the cached responses from the previous model version continue to pass. The test suite reports green while the production agent may behave differently with the new model. The discipline: increment the `cacheKey` on every LLM model version bump (e.g., `cacheKey: 'v1-gpt4o-2026-05'`) to invalidate all cached responses and force a full re-run against the new model. Add a CI job that runs the uncached suite against the current model on a weekly schedule.

66. **[community] Stryker incremental mode with `vitest` runner fails silently when `vitest.config.ts` uses dynamic `import()` for environment detection.** A common pattern is `const isCI = await import('./detectCI.js')` inside `vitest.config.ts` to enable different reporters in CI vs local. Stryker's incremental engine cannot statically parse dynamic imports in the config file and falls back to a full (non-incremental) run without emitting a warning. The signal: incremental runs are taking as long as full runs. Diagnosis: check Stryker's debug log for `"Could not determine incremental base"`. Fix: replace dynamic config imports with synchronous `process.env` checks, which Stryker can evaluate without execution.

### Property-Based TDD — Generators as Red-Phase Specification

Example-based TDD (Red: write one example; Green: satisfy it) leaves the design vulnerable to the set of examples the author thought to write. **Property-based TDD** extends the Red phase by specifying a **property** — an invariant that must hold for all valid inputs — rather than a single example. The `fast-check` library generates hundreds of random inputs and finds the smallest failing case (shrinking).

**Why this matters for the TDD cycle:** A property test is a more powerful Red signal than a single example. It forces the author to articulate the algebraic identity behind the feature ("for any two positive integers, `add(a, b) === add(b, a)`"), which is a deeper design constraint than any single example. The Green phase then requires code that is provably general, not merely correct for the cases the author imagined.

**When to use:** pure functions with algebraic properties (commutativity, associativity, idempotency, roundtrip encoding/decoding). **When NOT to use:** stateful domain logic with complex setup (use example-based TDD with Chicago-school fakes instead — property tests are expensive to set up for stateful workflows).

```typescript
// src/pricing/applyDiscount.test.ts
// Property-based TDD: specifying invariants rather than individual examples

import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import * as fc from 'fast-check';
import { applyDiscount } from './applyDiscount.js';

describe('applyDiscount — property-based', () => {
  // PROPERTY 1: result is always non-negative (no negative totals)
  it('never produces a negative total', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.float({ min: 0, max: 10_000, noNaN: true }),  // arbitrary price
        fc.float({ min: 0, max: 1,      noNaN: true }),  // arbitrary rate 0–100%
        (price, rate) => {
          expect(applyDiscount(price, rate)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
        }
      )
    );
  });

  // PROPERTY 2: zero discount rate is identity (no change to price)
  it('returns original price when discount rate is 0', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.float({ min: 0, max: 10_000, noNaN: true }),
        (price) => {
          expect(applyDiscount(price, 0)).toBeCloseTo(price, 5);
        }
      )
    );
  });

  // PROPERTY 3: 100% discount always yields 0
  it('yields 0 for 100% discount rate', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.float({ min: 0, max: 10_000, noNaN: true }),
        (price) => {
          expect(applyDiscount(price, 1)).toBeCloseTo(0, 5);
        }
      )
    );
  });

  // PROPERTY 4: higher discount rate produces lower or equal result (monotonicity)
  it('is monotone — higher rate never increases the discounted price', () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(
        fc.float({ min: 0, max: 10_000, noNaN: true }),
        fc.tuple(
          fc.float({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }),
          fc.float({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }),
        ).map(([a, b]) => [Math.min(a, b), Math.max(a, b)] as [number, number]),
        (price, [lowerRate, higherRate]) => {
          expect(applyDiscount(price, higherRate))
            .toBeLessThanOrEqual(applyDiscount(price, lowerRate) + 1e-9); // float tolerance
        }
      )
    );
  });
});

// Minimal implementation driven by the four properties above:
// src/pricing/applyDiscount.ts
export function applyDiscount(price: number, rate: number): number {
  if (rate < 0 || rate > 1) throw new RangeError('Rate must be 0–1');
  return Math.max(0, price * (1 - rate));
}
```

**TDD discipline note:** Run `fast-check` with `{ numRuns: 1000 }` in CI but `{ numRuns: 100 }` locally to keep the inner loop fast. Use `fc.sample(arbitray, 5)` to preview the values a generator produces before adding it to a test case — this is the property-based equivalent of writing "one example first" (triangulation at the generator level).

**[community] The most common fast-check TDD mistake is writing properties that are trivially satisfied by any implementation.** A property like "result is a number" passes even if the function returns `NaN` (because `typeof NaN === 'number'`). Use `fc.pre()` to add preconditions that filter degenerate inputs, and always ask: "Could a naïve implementation (e.g., `return 0`) satisfy this property?" If yes, the property is not testing the logic — it is testing the type.

---

### TDD for React Server Components — Async Component Assertions

React Server Components (RSC) introduced a fundamental challenge for TDD: server components are async functions, not synchronous render functions. The standard `@testing-library/react` `render()` / `screen.getBy*` pattern does not await server component data fetching. The emerging discipline (as of 2025-2026) separates **server-side data logic tests** from **UI rendering tests**.

**The TDD split:**
- Test the **data-fetching function** (the async logic behind the RSC) directly with Vitest — this is pure TDD with full Red-Green-Refactor discipline.
- Test the **rendered output** with `@testing-library/react` + `renderToString` or `experimental_renderToReadableStream` — this is integration-level and runs less frequently.

```typescript
// app/products/[id]/page.tsx — React Server Component (Next.js 14+ App Router)
// The data-fetching logic is extracted into a testable pure async function.

import { fetchProductById, type Product } from '@/lib/products';
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';

// ── Pure async data function — TDD this ────────────────────────────────────
export async function loadProductPageData(id: string): Promise<Product> {
  if (!id || !/^\d+$/.test(id)) {
    throw new RangeError(`Invalid product ID: ${id}`);
  }
  const product = await fetchProductById(id);
  if (!product) notFound(); // throws Next.js 404
  return product;
}

// ── RSC default export — integration-test this, not unit-TDD ─────────────
export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  const product = await loadProductPageData(params.id);
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      <p data-testid="price">${product.price.toFixed(2)}</p>
    </main>
  );
}
```

```typescript
// app/products/[id]/page.test.ts — TDD for the data function only
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { loadProductPageData } from './page.js';
import * as productsLib from '@/lib/products';

// Fake the data layer — do not call real DB in the TDD inner loop
vi.mock('@/lib/products');

const mockFetch = vi.mocked(productsLib.fetchProductById);

describe('loadProductPageData', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  // RED-1: valid ID with found product returns product data
  it('returns product data for a valid numeric ID', async () => {
    mockFetch.mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: '42', name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 });
    const product = await loadProductPageData('42');
    expect(product.id).toBe('42');
    expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith('42');
  });

  // RED-2: non-numeric ID throws RangeError (before hitting the DB)
  it('throws RangeError for non-numeric ID without calling fetch', async () => {
    await expect(loadProductPageData('abc')).rejects.toThrow(RangeError);
    expect(mockFetch).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  // RED-3: empty ID throws RangeError
  it('throws RangeError for empty ID', async () => {
    await expect(loadProductPageData('')).rejects.toThrow(/Invalid product ID/);
    expect(mockFetch).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**[community] The RSC TDD discipline: test the data logic, not the component tree.** Attempts to TDD the full RSC component (including `notFound()`, `redirect()`, and streaming suspension) are fragile because they require a Next.js runtime environment. The stable TDD surface is the async data functions extracted from the component. This follows the same principle as hexagonal architecture: test the business logic (port), integration-test the adapter (RSC). Teams that try to unit-TDD the full RSC component with mocked Next.js internals spend more time maintaining mocks than writing features.

---

### Vitest Workspace — Multi-Project TDD Type Isolation

Vitest's workspace feature allows a monorepo to run test cases under multiple configurations simultaneously. For TDD workflows, the workspace creates **project-level type boundaries**: a test case in the `browser` project gets DOM types injected; a test case in the `node` project does not. This prevents a common TDD error — accidentally writing test code that passes because of global type augmentation from a different project.

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts — multi-project TDD configuration
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    // Node.js project: server logic, domain services, utilities
    // TDD inner loop lives here — fastest execution, no browser overhead
    extends: './vitest.config.ts',
    test: {
      name:        'node',
      environment: 'node',
      include:     ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
      exclude:     ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts', 'src/**/*.e2e.test.ts'],
    },
  },
  {
    // Browser project: React components, DOM interactions
    // Uses jsdom or @vitest/browser; slower — run in CI but not inner loop
    extends: './vitest.config.ts',
    test: {
      name:        'browser',
      environment: 'jsdom',
      include:     ['src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
      setupFiles:  ['./test-setup/browser.ts'],
    },
  },
]);
```

```typescript
// src/cart/CartService.test.ts — node project TDD test case
// TypeScript knows there is no `document`, `window`, or `localStorage` here —
// any accidental DOM reference is caught at compile time, not at test runtime.
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { CartService } from './CartService.js';
import { InMemoryCartRepository } from './test-doubles/InMemoryCartRepository.js';

describe('CartService', () => {
  let cart: CartService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    cart = new CartService(new InMemoryCartRepository());
  });

  it('starts empty', () => {
    expect(cart.lineItemCount()).toBe(0);
  });

  it('adds a line item and increments count', () => {
    cart.addItem({ sku: 'SKU-1', qty: 2, unitPrice: 5.00 });
    expect(cart.lineItemCount()).toBe(1);
  });

  it('accumulates total correctly', () => {
    cart.addItem({ sku: 'SKU-1', qty: 2, unitPrice: 5.00 });
    cart.addItem({ sku: 'SKU-2', qty: 1, unitPrice: 12.50 });
    expect(cart.total()).toBeCloseTo(22.50, 2);
  });
});
```

**[community] The most common workspace TDD error is running the full workspace for the TDD inner loop.** Running `vitest --project node,browser` doubles the test execution time. For the inner loop, run only the relevant project: `vitest --project node`. Use `vitest --project node,browser` only in pre-push hooks and CI. Teams that don't partition their inner loop from their full suite run find TDD cycles slowing to 10–30 seconds, which breaks the discipline of rapid Red-Green-Refactor iterations.

---

### Refactor-Phase Timebox — The 20% Ceiling Rule [community]

The Refactor phase is the most frequently skipped step in TDD (per team retrospective data across 2024-2026). The primary cause: no time constraint. Teams treat Refactor as "whenever there's time," which under deadline pressure means never. The **20% ceiling rule** addresses this.

**The rule:** allocate at most 20% of the total Red-Green cycle time to Refactor. If Red-to-Green took 10 minutes, Refactor has a 2-minute budget. This forces two disciplines:

1. **Timebox over perfection.** If a refactoring cannot be completed in the budget, either reduce its scope (extract one helper, rename one variable) or defer it as a tracked item. Unscheduled large refactors are the primary reason the Refactor phase is skipped entirely — the developer cannot find a "good stopping point" and abandons the step.
2. **No speculative refactoring.** The timebox prevents "while I'm here" improvements that are not driven by the current test case. Speculative refactoring during TDD cycles introduces risk (untested paths may break) and violates the baby-steps principle.

```typescript
// Example: a 10-minute Red-Green cycle produced this implementation.
// The 2-minute refactor budget allows exactly one improvement — extraction of the
// boundary check into a named helper function (readability; no behaviour change).

// ── BEFORE REFACTOR ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
export function computeShippingCost(orderTotal: number, distanceKm: number): number {
  if (orderTotal < 0) throw new RangeError('Order total cannot be negative');
  if (distanceKm < 0) throw new RangeError('Distance cannot be negative');
  const base = 5.00;
  const perKm = distanceKm > 100 ? 0.05 : 0.10;
  return orderTotal >= 50 ? 0 : base + distanceKm * perKm;
}

// ── AFTER REFACTOR (2-min budget: one extraction) ────────────────────────────
function assertNonNegative(value: number, label: string): void {
  if (value < 0) throw new RangeError(`${label} cannot be negative`);
}

export function computeShippingCost(orderTotal: number, distanceKm: number): number {
  assertNonNegative(orderTotal, 'Order total');
  assertNonNegative(distanceKm, 'Distance');
  const base  = 5.00;
  const perKm = distanceKm > 100 ? 0.05 : 0.10;
  return orderTotal >= 50 ? 0 : base + distanceKm * perKm;
}
// All existing test cases still pass after refactoring — confirmed by the test runner.
// Deferred for next cycle: extract the shipping rate logic into a named constant.
```

**Why the 20% ceiling is not arbitrary:** The goal of Refactor is to remove duplication and clarify intent — not to redesign the architecture. Architectural refactoring belongs in a dedicated session with its own test cases driving the new structure. The 20% ceiling keeps Refactor aligned with its actual purpose: small, safe, test-confirmed cleanup of the code produced by the Green phase.

**[community] Teams that adopt the timebox report a secondary benefit:** the constraint forces developers to rank refactoring candidates, which surfaces the clearest signal of technical debt. The first refactoring a developer reaches for in a 2-minute window is the one that genuinely reduces cognitive load — not the most ambitious restructuring they considered. This ranking effect makes the Refactor phase a reliable debt sensor without the overhead of formal debt tracking.

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 22 Additions

67. **[community] `fast-check` shrinking reveals specification gaps that examples miss.** When a property test fails, `fast-check` shrinks the failing input to the smallest possible failing case. Teams frequently find that the shrunken case exposes a gap in the specification rather than a bug in the implementation — for example, `applyDiscount(-0.01, 0)` failing reveals that the spec did not define behaviour for negative prices. The correct response to a shrinking failure is to update the **specification** (add a precondition or extend the property), not to suppress the failing case. `fc.pre()` is the right tool: it filters inputs that are outside the function's defined contract, making the property test honest about its scope.

68. **[community] React Server Component data functions mocked with `vi.mock()` lose their TypeScript types if the mock factory omits properties.** A common RSC TDD pattern is `vi.mock('@/lib/products', () => ({ fetchProductById: vi.fn() }))`. If `@/lib/products` exports multiple functions, the mock factory returns an object with only `fetchProductById` — the other exports are `undefined`. TypeScript does not catch this because `vi.mock()` factory return types are not validated against the module's actual exports by default. Use `vi.importMock<typeof import('@/lib/products')>()` inside the test case to get a fully-typed mock object, then selectively override only the functions under test.

69. **[community] Vitest workspace project filtering breaks `--reporter=verbose` output grouping.** When running `vitest --project node --reporter=verbose`, the project name prefix (`[node]`) is injected before each test case name. CI tools that parse test output by matching `✓ test name` patterns will fail to match because the line now reads `✓ [node] test name`. Teams using custom CI test-result parsers (Allure, TestRail importers) must update their regex patterns when adopting workspace configurations. The workspace-aware output format is intentional and not configurable in Vitest 4.x — plan parser updates as part of the workspace adoption.

70. **[community] Property tests run at the start of TDD cycles (before implementation exists) produce slow feedback.** `fast-check` with `numRuns: 100` generates 100 random inputs and tests each. With no implementation (Red phase), every run hits the same `RangeError` or `undefined is not a function` — but `fast-check` still executes all 100 iterations before reporting. Use `numRuns: 1` during the Red phase (to confirm the test is structured correctly and fails for the right reason), then restore `numRuns: 100` for the Green phase. Add a comment in the test file: `// numRuns: 1 during Red phase — restore to 100 before merge`.

71. **[community] The 20% refactor timebox fails when the Green implementation has structural debt from "fake-it" shortcuts.** After several Red-Green cycles using fake returns (hardcoded constants, empty stubs), the accumulated implementation may require a structural refactor that genuinely cannot be done in 20% of one cycle. This is expected and correct: schedule a dedicated **refactor session** with its own test cases confirming that no behaviour changes. The signal that a refactor session is needed: the same fake pattern has been repeated across three or more test cases without generalisation. At that point, the triangulation rule has been satisfied and the generalisation is overdue — it is not technical debt, it is the expected arc of TDD applied over multiple cycles.
