### 5. TDD for Schema Migrations (Data Shape Versioning) [community]

When a persisted data schema changes, a migration function must transform v1 → v2 without data loss. TDD this with one test case per migration path, including the identity case (v2 → v2 is a no-op) and the boundary case (minimal v1 object with only required fields).

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { migrateUserPrefs, UserPrefsV1, UserPrefsV2 } from './migrations/userPrefsV1toV2.js';

describe('migrateUserPrefs v1 → v2', () => {
  it('sets the new colorScheme field to "system" when absent in v1', () => {
    const v1: UserPrefsV1 = { theme: 'dark', language: 'en', notifications: true };
    const result: UserPrefsV2 = migrateUserPrefs(v1);
    expect(result.colorScheme).toBe('system');
  });

  it('preserves all existing fields without modification', () => {
    const v1: UserPrefsV1 = { theme: 'light', language: 'fr', notifications: false };
    const result: UserPrefsV2 = migrateUserPrefs(v1);
    expect(result.theme).toBe('light');
    expect(result.language).toBe('fr');
    expect(result.notifications).toBe(false);
  });

  it('bumps the version field from 1 to 2', () => {
    const v1: UserPrefsV1 = { theme: 'dark', language: 'de', notifications: true };
    const result: UserPrefsV2 = migrateUserPrefs(v1);
    expect(result.version).toBe(2);
  });

  it('maps deprecated theme "light" to colorScheme "light"', () => {
    const v1: UserPrefsV1 = { theme: 'light', language: 'en', notifications: true };
    const result: UserPrefsV2 = migrateUserPrefs(v1);
    expect(result.colorScheme).toBe('light');
  });

  it('migration function does not throw when given a minimally valid v1 object', () => {
    const v1: UserPrefsV1 = { theme: 'dark', language: 'en', notifications: true };
    expect(() => migrateUserPrefs(v1)).not.toThrow();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Schema migration TDD is essential for long-lived applications that store user data persistently (localStorage, IndexedDB, databases, JSON files). Each migration must be idempotent and tested with the boundary case (minimal v1 object). Do NOT skip the version-bump assertion — it is the one assertion that prevents running the migration twice in production. Named alternative: for database migrations, Prisma's migration testing support and Flyway's test runner provide a full migration execution context; TDD the TypeScript migration function in isolation first, then run integration tests with a real DB in CI.

[community]

---

### 6. TDD for Dependency-Injection Containers [community]

When building a DI container or wiring the object graph manually, TDD the container's resolution logic: that dependencies are resolved in the correct order, singletons are shared, and circular dependencies are detected at registration time rather than at call time.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Container, Token } from './Container.js';

const DB_TOKEN   = new Token<Database>('Database');
const REPO_TOKEN = new Token<UserRepository>('UserRepository');
const SVC_TOKEN  = new Token<UserService>('UserService');

describe('Container', () => {
  it('resolves a singleton: same instance returned on every resolve()', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    container.bindSingleton(DB_TOKEN, () => new InMemoryDatabase());
    const db1 = container.resolve(DB_TOKEN);
    const db2 = container.resolve(DB_TOKEN);
    expect(db1).toBe(db2);
  });

  it('resolves a transient: new instance on every resolve()', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    container.bindTransient(REPO_TOKEN, () => new InMemoryUserRepository());
    const r1 = container.resolve(REPO_TOKEN);
    const r2 = container.resolve(REPO_TOKEN);
    expect(r1).not.toBe(r2);
  });

  it('resolves a dependency graph: UserService receives a UserRepository', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    container.bindSingleton(DB_TOKEN,   () => new InMemoryDatabase());
    container.bindSingleton(REPO_TOKEN, c => new InMemoryUserRepository(c.resolve(DB_TOKEN)));
    container.bindSingleton(SVC_TOKEN,  c => new UserService(c.resolve(REPO_TOKEN)));
    const svc = container.resolve(SVC_TOKEN);
    expect(svc).toBeInstanceOf(UserService);
  });

  it('throws at resolution time when a token is unregistered', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    expect(() => container.resolve(DB_TOKEN)).toThrow(/unregistered token: Database/i);
  });

  it('detects a circular dependency and throws a descriptive error', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    const A_TOKEN = new Token<object>('A');
    const B_TOKEN = new Token<object>('B');
    container.bindSingleton(A_TOKEN, c => ({ a: c.resolve(B_TOKEN) }));
    container.bindSingleton(B_TOKEN, c => ({ b: c.resolve(A_TOKEN) }));
    expect(() => container.resolve(A_TOKEN)).toThrow(/circular dependency/i);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD the container only when building a custom DI implementation or extending an existing one. For application-level wiring (composing real services at startup), TDD the individual services with injected fakes and use integration tests to verify the wired graph. The circular dependency test case is critical — most DI containers silently stack overflow without it. Named alternative: `tsyringe` and `inversify` are production-ready DI containers for TypeScript; TDD their usage patterns (token binding, scope, resolution order) using the in-memory fakes pattern rather than testing the container internals.

[community]

---

### 7. TDD for Debounce and Throttle Utilities [community]

Debounce and throttle have time-dependent semantics that are trivially wrong on first implementation. TDD with `vi.useFakeTimers()` and explicit `vi.advanceTimersByTime()` calls makes each boundary condition a failing test before any implementation.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { debounce } from './debounce.js';

describe('debounce', () => {
  afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());

  it('does not call the function before the delay expires', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const fn = vi.fn<[], void>();
    const debounced = debounce(fn, 300);
    debounced();
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(299);
    expect(fn).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  it('calls the function once after the delay expires', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const fn = vi.fn<[], void>();
    const debounced = debounce(fn, 300);
    debounced();
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(300);
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it('resets the timer when called again before the delay expires', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const fn = vi.fn<[], void>();
    const debounced = debounce(fn, 300);
    debounced();
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(200);
    debounced();                   // reset — timer restarts from 0
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(299);   // only 299ms since the second call
    expect(fn).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(1);     // now 300ms since last call
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it('passes the most recent arguments to the delayed call', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const fn = vi.fn<[string], void>();
    const debounced = debounce(fn, 100);
    debounced('first');
    debounced('second');
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(100);
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledWith('second');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD debounce and throttle utilities in isolation using fake timers — this is one of the few cases where pure function extraction + fake timers produces a complete, fast, reliable test suite. The "resets the timer" test case is the most commonly missing in hand-rolled debounce implementations. Do NOT test debounce behaviour through UI interaction tests (fire event → wait → assert) — the timing is non-deterministic in browser environments. Named alternative: `lodash.debounce` is a battle-tested implementation; if you use it, write narrow contract tests (Cycle 28 Pattern 12) documenting exactly the leading/trailing/maxWait behaviours your code depends on.

[community]

---

### 8. TDD for Multi-Step Form Validation [community]

Multi-step form wizards accumulate state across steps and only submit on the final step. TDD drives the validation rules per step, the cross-step invariants, and the submit payload shape — all before building any UI.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import {
  validateStep1, validateStep2, validateStep3,
  buildSubmitPayload, FormState, SubmitPayload,
} from './checkoutFormValidator.js';

describe('CheckoutForm validation', () => {
  it('step 1 rejects an empty email', () => {
    const result = validateStep1({ email: '', fullName: 'Alice' });
    expect(result.success).toBe(false);
    if (!result.success) expect(result.errors.email).toMatch(/required/i);
  });

  it('step 1 accepts a valid email and full name', () => {
    const result = validateStep1({ email: 'alice@example.com', fullName: 'Alice' });
    expect(result.success).toBe(true);
  });

  it('step 2 rejects a card number shorter than 16 digits', () => {
    const result = validateStep2({ cardNumber: '123456789', expiry: '12/27', cvv: '123' });
    expect(result.success).toBe(false);
    if (!result.success) expect(result.errors.cardNumber).toMatch(/16 digits/i);
  });

  it('step 3 rejects a shipping address missing postcode', () => {
    const result = validateStep3({ street: '1 Main St', city: 'London', postcode: '' });
    expect(result.success).toBe(false);
    if (!result.success) expect(result.errors.postcode).toMatch(/required/i);
  });

  it('buildSubmitPayload assembles valid steps into a typed payload', () => {
    const state: FormState = {
      step1: { email: 'alice@example.com', fullName: 'Alice' },
      step2: { cardNumber: '4111111111111111', expiry: '12/27', cvv: '123' },
      step3: { street: '1 Main St', city: 'London', postcode: 'EC1A1' },
    };
    const payload: SubmitPayload = buildSubmitPayload(state);
    expect(payload.contact.email).toBe('alice@example.com');
    expect(payload.payment.last4).toBe('1111');
    expect(payload.shipping.postcode).toBe('EC1A1');
  });

  it('buildSubmitPayload throws if any step is invalid', () => {
    const invalidState: FormState = {
      step1: { email: '', fullName: '' },
      step2: { cardNumber: '4111111111111111', expiry: '12/27', cvv: '123' },
      step3: { street: '1 Main St', city: 'London', postcode: 'EC1A1' },
    };
    expect(() => buildSubmitPayload(invalidState)).toThrow(/step 1 invalid/i);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD the validation logic as pure functions completely separately from the UI components. The `buildSubmitPayload` test is the most important — it ensures the final payload has the correct shape for the server before any component renders. Do NOT co-locate form validation logic inside React components or event handlers — it becomes untestable without rendering. Named alternative: Zod v4 schema-based validation (Cycle 18 patterns) can replace hand-written validation functions; TDD the schema parsing with `z.safeParse()` and `z.input<T>` fixture types to catch the coercion-path gaps described in Gotcha 27.

[community]

---

### 9. TDD for Read-Through Cache [community]

A read-through cache delegates to a data source on cache miss, stores the result, and returns cached results on subsequent reads. TDD drives five key invariants: miss → fetch → cache; hit → no fetch; expired → re-fetch; concurrent misses → single fetch (stampede prevention); separate entries per key.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { ReadThroughCache } from './ReadThroughCache.js';

describe('ReadThroughCache', () => {
  afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());

  it('fetches from the source on cache miss and caches the result', async () => {
    const source = vi.fn<[string], Promise<string>>().mockResolvedValue('fetched');
    const cache = new ReadThroughCache<string, string>(source, { ttlMs: 1000 });
    expect(await cache.get('key1')).toBe('fetched');
    expect(await cache.get('key1')).toBe('fetched');
    expect(source).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });

  it('re-fetches from the source when the cache entry is expired', async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const source = vi.fn<[string], Promise<string>>()
      .mockResolvedValueOnce('first')
      .mockResolvedValueOnce('second');
    const cache = new ReadThroughCache<string, string>(source, { ttlMs: 500 });
    expect(await cache.get('key')).toBe('first');
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(501);
    expect(await cache.get('key')).toBe('second');
    expect(source).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });

  it('prevents stampede: concurrent misses trigger exactly one source fetch', async () => {
    const source = vi.fn<[string], Promise<string>>()
      .mockImplementation(() => Promise.resolve('shared'));
    const cache = new ReadThroughCache<string, string>(source, { ttlMs: 5000 });
    const results = await Promise.all(
      Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => cache.get('stampede-key'))
    );
    expect(results.every(r => r === 'shared')).toBe(true);
    expect(source).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });

  it('uses separate cache entries for different keys', async () => {
    const source = vi.fn<[string], Promise<string>>()
      .mockImplementation(key => Promise.resolve(`value-for-${key}`));
    const cache = new ReadThroughCache<string, string>(source, { ttlMs: 5000 });
    expect(await cache.get('a')).toBe('value-for-a');
    expect(await cache.get('b')).toBe('value-for-b');
    expect(source).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The stampede-prevention test is the most critical and most often missing. Without it, a cache under high concurrency fetches the same resource N times simultaneously, potentially overwhelming the data source. Write the stampede test first — it forces the in-flight request deduplication design into existence. Do NOT use this pattern for mutable data that must reflect writes made through other paths — a write-through or write-around strategy is needed. Named alternative: `lru-cache` (npm) provides a production-grade LRU implementation with TTL support; TDD the wrapping service that calls `lru-cache` rather than building raw cache logic from scratch.

[community]

---

### 10. TDD for Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) Transformations [community]

Code transformation tools (linters, codemods, DSL compilers) operate on ASTs. TDD drives the transformation rules by specifying input AST → output AST for each case. Writing the test first forces the AST node type design before any traversal logic.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { transformImportPaths, ASTImportNode, TransformResult } from './transformImportPaths.js';

describe('transformImportPaths — migrate relative to alias imports', () => {
  it('transforms a relative import inside src/domain/ to an @domain alias', () => {
    const node: ASTImportNode = {
      type: 'ImportDeclaration',
      source: { value: '../../../domain/User.js', raw: "'../../../domain/User.js'" },
      specifiers: [{ local: { name: 'User' }, imported: { name: 'User' } }],
    };
    const result: TransformResult = transformImportPaths(node, {
      rootDir: '/project/src',
      aliases: { '@domain': '/project/src/domain' },
    });
    expect(result.transformed).toBe(true);
    expect(result.node.source.value).toBe('@domain/User.js');
  });

  it('leaves non-matching imports unchanged', () => {
    const node: ASTImportNode = {
      type: 'ImportDeclaration',
      source: { value: 'vitest', raw: "'vitest'" },
      specifiers: [],
    };
    const result = transformImportPaths(node, {
      rootDir: '/project/src',
      aliases: { '@domain': '/project/src/domain' },
    });
    expect(result.transformed).toBe(false);
    expect(result.node.source.value).toBe('vitest');
  });

  it('handles index-file imports: strips /index.js suffix after alias resolution', () => {
    const node: ASTImportNode = {
      type: 'ImportDeclaration',
      source: { value: '../../../domain/cart/index.js', raw: "'../../../domain/cart/index.js'" },
      specifiers: [],
    };
    const result = transformImportPaths(node, {
      rootDir: '/project/src',
      aliases: { '@domain': '/project/src/domain' },
    });
    expect(result.node.source.value).toBe('@domain/cart');
  });

  it('returns transformed: false and does not mutate the original node object', () => {
    const node: ASTImportNode = {
      type: 'ImportDeclaration',
      source: { value: 'vitest', raw: "'vitest'" },
      specifiers: [],
    };
    const original = JSON.stringify(node);
    transformImportPaths(node, { rootDir: '/project/src', aliases: {} });
    expect(JSON.stringify(node)).toBe(original);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** AST transformation TDD works best when the AST node types are typed TypeScript interfaces — writing the test cases first drives the minimal interface surface (only the node properties the transform actually reads). The `TransformResult.transformed: boolean` field is a TDD-forced design decision — without a test asserting "non-matching nodes are not transformed," implementations often silently mutate unrelated nodes. Do NOT use full `@babel/parser` or `ts-morph` AST node types in unit tests — define minimal subset interfaces that contain only the fields the transform function needs. Named alternative: `jscodeshift` provides a higher-level API for writing codemods with a built-in test runner; TDD the transform function in isolation before integrating with the jscodeshift runner.

[community]

---

### 11. TDD for Configuration Validation at Startup [official]

Application configuration loaded from environment variables or JSON files must be validated at startup, not at first use. TDD drives the configuration schema, required vs. optional fields, type coercions, and error messages — before any configuration consumer code exists.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { loadConfig, AppConfig, ConfigValidationError } from './config.js';

describe('loadConfig', () => {
  afterEach(() => vi.unstubAllEnvs());

  it('returns a valid AppConfig from complete environment variables', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('PORT', '3000');
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://localhost/mydb');
    vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'info');
    vi.stubEnv('JWT_SECRET', 'my-secret-key-of-sufficient-length-32');
    const config: AppConfig = loadConfig();
    expect(config.port).toBe(3000);
    expect(config.databaseUrl).toBe('postgres://localhost/mydb');
    expect(config.logLevel).toBe('info');
  });

  it('throws ConfigValidationError when DATABASE_URL is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('PORT', '3000');
    vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'info');
    vi.stubEnv('JWT_SECRET', 'long-enough-secret-minimum-32-chars');
    expect(() => loadConfig()).toThrow(ConfigValidationError);
    expect(() => loadConfig()).toThrow(/DATABASE_URL/);
  });

  it('coerces PORT to a number and rejects non-numeric strings', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('PORT', 'not-a-port');
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://localhost/db');
    vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'info');
    vi.stubEnv('JWT_SECRET', 'long-enough-secret-minimum-32-chars');
    expect(() => loadConfig()).toThrow(/PORT.*must be a number/i);
  });

  it('uses default port 8080 when PORT is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://localhost/db');
    vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'info');
    vi.stubEnv('JWT_SECRET', 'long-enough-secret-minimum-32-chars');
    const config = loadConfig();
    expect(config.port).toBe(8080);
  });

  it('rejects a JWT_SECRET shorter than 32 characters', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('PORT', '3000');
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://localhost/db');
    vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'info');
    vi.stubEnv('JWT_SECRET', 'short');
    expect(() => loadConfig()).toThrow(/JWT_SECRET.*32 characters/i);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Configuration TDD is among the highest-value, lowest-effort TDD applications — configuration bugs (missing env vars, wrong type coercions, security-critical minimums like JWT secret length) are among the most common production outage causes and the easiest to specify as test cases. Using `vi.stubEnv` / `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` (Vitest 3.2+) instead of directly mutating `process.env` ensures environment isolation between test cases. Do NOT validate configuration lazily at first use — the test cases should assert that `loadConfig()` throws at the call site, not when `config.databaseUrl` is first accessed. Named alternative: Zod v4 schema-based env parsing (`z.object({ PORT: z.coerce.number() })`) paired with `vi.stubEnv` produces an identical test structure with less hand-written validation logic.

[official]

---

### 12. TDD with `it.todo` as a Structured Red-Phase Backlog [official]

`it.todo` (Vitest and Jest) is a first-class TDD tool: it marks a planned test case that does not yet have a body, makes it visible in the test report, and keeps the suite green while the Red backlog grows. Using `it.todo` as a structured backlog — rather than comments — keeps planned test cases versioned in the codebase and visible in CI output.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { RateLimiter } from './RateLimiter.js';

// TDD backlog: all planned invariants captured before implementation
describe('RateLimiter', () => {
  // Tests already passing (Green):
  it('allows requests below the rate limit', () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter({ requestsPerSecond: 10 });
    expect(limiter.tryAcquire()).toBe(true);
  });

  // Active Red phase — failing test being implemented now:
  it('denies requests that exceed the rate limit within the window', () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter({ requestsPerSecond: 2 });
    limiter.tryAcquire(); limiter.tryAcquire();
    expect(limiter.tryAcquire()).toBe(false);
  });

  // Backlog — planned Red phase entries (surfaced in CI output as "todo"):
  it.todo('refills tokens after the window resets');
  it.todo('tracks separate windows per clientId when keyed');
  it.todo('emits a rate-limit-exceeded event when a request is denied');
  it.todo('is thread-safe under concurrent tryAcquire() calls (worker_threads test)');
  it.todo('respects a custom window duration beyond the default 1 second');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `it.todo` whenever you identify a test condition during a TDD cycle but are not ready to write the test body yet. The structured backlog prevents "I'll write that test later" from silently disappearing — the todo appears in every CI run until the body is added. In PR reviews, `it.todo` entries are visible as planned coverage gaps, making the review conversation explicit. Do NOT use `it.skip` as a substitute for `it.todo` — a skipped test has a body that is intentionally bypassed (implying "currently broken"), whereas `it.todo` communicates "this test case has not been written yet." Named alternative: GitHub issues for test coverage tracking are less effective because they are detached from the codebase; `it.todo` entries are co-located with the code they specify and are invalidated by the test runner.

[official]

---

### 13. TDD for Builder Pattern Test Fixtures [community]

Test fixture builders provide a fluent API for constructing valid domain objects with overridable defaults. TDD the builder itself first — the builder's test cases document what "valid" means for each domain object.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderBuilder } from '../test-doubles/OrderBuilder.js';
import type { Order } from '../domain/Order.js';

describe('OrderBuilder', () => {
  it('creates a valid default Order', () => {
    const order: Order = new OrderBuilder().build();
    expect(order.id).toMatch(/^ord_/);
    expect(order.status).toBe('pending');
    expect(order.items).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(order.total).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

  it('overrides status via withStatus()', () => {
    const order = new OrderBuilder().withStatus('shipped').build();
    expect(order.status).toBe('shipped');
  });

  it('adds multiple items and recalculates total', () => {
    const order = new OrderBuilder()
      .withItem({ sku: 'A', price: 10, qty: 2 })
      .withItem({ sku: 'B', price: 5,  qty: 3 })
      .build();
    expect(order.items).toHaveLength(2);
    expect(order.total).toBe(35);
  });

  it('each build() call returns an independent object', () => {
    const builder = new OrderBuilder();
    const o1 = builder.build();
    const o2 = builder.build();
    expect(o1).not.toBe(o2);
    expect(o1.id).not.toBe(o2.id);
  });
});

// GREEN: minimal builder implementation driven by the test cases above
// test-doubles/OrderBuilder.ts
export class OrderBuilder {
  #status: Order['status'] = 'pending';
  #items: Array<{ sku: string; price: number; qty: number }> = [
    { sku: 'default-sku', price: 9.99, qty: 1 },
  ];
  #counter = 0;

  withStatus(status: Order['status']): this {
    this.#status = status;
    return this;
  }

  withItem(item: { sku: string; price: number; qty: number }): this {
    this.#items = [...this.#items, item];
    return this;
  }

  build(): Order {
    const id = `ord_${String(++this.#counter).padStart(4, '0')}`;
    const total = this.#items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0);
    return { id, status: this.#status, items: [...this.#items], total };
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD builders pay dividends in test suites with many service-layer tests that each need slightly different domain object configurations. The key rule: every `build()` call must return a valid domain object by default — test cases that need invalid objects should use a separate `buildInvalid()` variant or pass in specific invalid overrides explicitly. Do NOT use `Math.random()` for IDs in test builders — use a deterministic counter (as shown above) so that snapshot-style assertions are stable across runs. Named alternative: the Object Mother pattern (a static factory class with named factory methods per scenario) is simpler when a fixed set of canonical configurations covers all test needs; the Builder pattern is better when the variation space is large.

[community]

---

### 14. TDD for Event Sourcing Aggregates [community]

Event sourcing systems apply a sequence of events to derive current state. TDD drives the aggregate's event-application logic (each event type produces a predictable state transition) before any storage or projection infrastructure exists.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderAggregate, OrderEvent } from './OrderAggregate.js';

describe('OrderAggregate — event sourcing', () => {
  it('starts with empty state when no events are applied', () => {
    const aggregate = OrderAggregate.fromEvents([]);
    expect(aggregate.status).toBe('new');
    expect(aggregate.items).toHaveLength(0);
    expect(aggregate.version).toBe(0);
  });

  it('applies OrderCreated event and sets initial state', () => {
    const events: OrderEvent[] = [
      { type: 'OrderCreated', orderId: 'ORD-1', customerId: 'CUST-1', timestamp: new Date() },
    ];
    const aggregate = OrderAggregate.fromEvents(events);
    expect(aggregate.status).toBe('created');
    expect(aggregate.orderId).toBe('ORD-1');
    expect(aggregate.version).toBe(1);
  });

  it('applies ItemAdded events and accumulates items', () => {
    const events: OrderEvent[] = [
      { type: 'OrderCreated', orderId: 'ORD-1', customerId: 'C1', timestamp: new Date() },
      { type: 'ItemAdded', sku: 'A', price: 10, qty: 2, timestamp: new Date() },
      { type: 'ItemAdded', sku: 'B', price: 5,  qty: 1, timestamp: new Date() },
    ];
    const aggregate = OrderAggregate.fromEvents(events);
    expect(aggregate.items).toHaveLength(2);
    expect(aggregate.total).toBe(25);
    expect(aggregate.version).toBe(3);
  });

  it('rebuilds identical state from the same event sequence (deterministic)', () => {
    const ts = new Date(1000);
    const events: OrderEvent[] = [
      { type: 'OrderCreated', orderId: 'ORD-1', customerId: 'C1', timestamp: ts },
      { type: 'ItemAdded', sku: 'A', price: 10, qty: 2, timestamp: new Date(2000) },
      { type: 'OrderConfirmed', timestamp: new Date(3000) },
    ];
    const a1 = OrderAggregate.fromEvents(events);
    const a2 = OrderAggregate.fromEvents(events);
    expect(a1.status).toBe(a2.status);
    expect(a1.total).toBe(a2.total);
    expect(a1.version).toBe(a2.version);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD event sourcing aggregates from the outside: `fromEvents(eventList)` returns a fully formed aggregate with no mocking needed — this is the purest TDD application in the domain model. The "deterministic rebuilding" test case documents the most important invariant of event sourcing: given the same event history, two separate rebuilds must produce identical state. Do NOT write test cases that test the event store persistence layer in aggregate unit tests — keep the storage concerns in integration tests. Named alternative: for simpler state management needs, the Redux reducer pattern (`(state, action) => newState`) has an identical TDD structure and can be tested without any event sourcing infrastructure.

[community]

---

### 15. TDD for Internationalization (i18n) Message Resolution [community]

Internationalisation logic — locale fallback chains, pluralisation rules, interpolation, missing key handling — has deterministic behaviour that benefits from TDD. Writing the test cases first reveals edge cases in locale fallback chains (e.g., `pt-BR → pt → en`) that are invisible when only testing the happy path.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createI18n, I18nConfig } from './i18n.js';

const config: I18nConfig = {
  defaultLocale: 'en',
  messages: {
    en:      { greeting: 'Hello, {name}!', items: '{count} item | {count} items' },
    fr:      { greeting: 'Bonjour, {name}!', items: '{count} article | {count} articles' },
    'pt-BR': { greeting: 'Olá, {name}!' }, // deliberately missing 'items' key
  },
};

describe('i18n message resolution', () => {
  it('resolves a message for the requested locale', () => {
    const i18n = createI18n(config);
    expect(i18n.t('greeting', { locale: 'fr', params: { name: 'Marie' } }))
      .toBe('Bonjour, Marie!');
  });

  it('falls back to the default locale for a missing key in the requested locale', () => {
    const i18n = createI18n(config);
    expect(i18n.t('items', { locale: 'pt-BR', params: { count: 2 } }))
      .toBe('2 items');
  });

  it('selects the singular form when count is 1', () => {
    const i18n = createI18n(config);
    expect(i18n.t('items', { locale: 'en', params: { count: 1 } })).toBe('1 item');
  });

  it('selects the plural form when count is 0 or greater than 1', () => {
    const i18n = createI18n(config);
    expect(i18n.t('items', { locale: 'en', params: { count: 0 } })).toBe('0 items');
    expect(i18n.t('items', { locale: 'en', params: { count: 5 } })).toBe('5 items');
  });

  it('returns a sentinel when the key is missing from all locales', () => {
    const i18n = createI18n(config);
    const result = i18n.t('nonexistent-key', { locale: 'en', params: {} });
    expect(result).toMatch(/missing key/i);
  });

  it('interpolates multiple named parameters correctly', () => {
    const testConfig: I18nConfig = {
      defaultLocale: 'en',
      messages: { en: { summary: '{count} orders totalling {total}' } },
    };
    const i18n = createI18n(testConfig);
    expect(i18n.t('summary', { locale: 'en', params: { count: 3, total: '$45.00' } }))
      .toBe('3 orders totalling $45.00');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD i18n message resolution as pure functions with an in-memory message registry — never as integration tests against a real CMS or translation service. The locale fallback test case (`pt-BR → en`) is the most commonly missing test in i18n implementations and the most common source of production bugs when new locales are added. Do NOT assert on specific translated strings in application-level tests — assert on the key resolution logic and fallback behaviour, not on specific translated strings. Named alternative: `i18next` and `react-i18next` are production-grade i18n libraries with their own test utilities; TDD the fallback chains against the real `i18next` configuration using `changeLanguage()` in tests.

[community]

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 29 Additions

102. **[community] `vi.useFakeTimers()` without `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach` leaks fake timer state into subsequent test files.** When a test file calls `vi.useFakeTimers()` and a test case within it throws before reaching `afterEach`, the fake timer state persists into the next test file run in the same Vitest worker. Time-dependent test cases in a completely unrelated module start failing with `setTimeout was not called` or silent non-execution of callbacks. WHY this matters: the failure appears in the second file, not in the file that set up fake timers — the debugging trail is completely misleading. Fix: always pair `vi.useFakeTimers()` with `afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers())` in the same `describe` block, never at the module level.

103. **[community] Async `beforeAll` that creates test data without `await` produces silent race conditions.** TypeScript's async/await type system does not enforce that `beforeAll(() => { createTestData(); })` (missing `await`) is incorrect — `createTestData()` returns a `Promise<void>` that is discarded. The test suite begins running before the data exists, and the first test cases see an empty repository. The TypeScript compiler does not warn because `beforeAll` accepts both `() => void` and `() => Promise<void>`. WHY this matters: the race is non-deterministic — on fast machines, the promise may resolve before the first test runs, masking the bug. Fix: use `beforeAll(async () => { await createTestData(); })` and enable the `no-floating-promises` ESLint rule from `typescript-eslint` to catch discarded promises at authoring time.

104. **[community] Typed `it.each` with an object array silently allows extra properties that TypeScript should reject.** `it.each<{a: number, b: number}>([{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }])` does not produce a TypeScript error because TypeScript's excess property checking does not apply to generic type arguments in most contexts — excess properties on inline objects in `it.each` arrays are silently permitted. The `c: 3` column is accessible in the test body without a compiler error, making the test table appear more constrained than it is. WHY this matters: a developer adds a column to the data array expecting the type parameter to enforce it is used, but the test silently ignores unused columns. Fix: use `satisfies` on the array literal: `it.each([{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }] satisfies Array<{a: number, b: number}>)` — this triggers excess property checking and flags undeclared columns.

105. **[community] MSW `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` does NOT reset handlers registered in `beforeAll`.** A common MSW setup pattern registers default handlers in `setupServer(...)` at the module level and overrides them per-test with `server.use(...)` in individual tests. `server.resetHandlers()` only removes the overrides added via `server.use()` — the handlers from the `setupServer(...)` call remain. A test that registers a handler in `beforeAll` and expects `server.resetHandlers()` to remove it will find the handler still active in later test cases. WHY this matters: the test case appears to be fully isolated, but one test's state (a handler for a specific URL) bleeds into subsequent tests, producing unexpected 200 responses where a 404 was expected. Fix: use `server.use()` only for per-test overrides, never in `beforeAll`, and understand that `server.resetHandlers()` reverts overrides to the baseline set passed to `setupServer()`.

106. **[community] Builders that use `Math.random()` for default IDs produce non-deterministic test output that breaks snapshot assertions.** When a fixture builder generates IDs like `ord_${Math.random().toString(36)}`, any `toMatchSnapshot()` or `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` assertion on the full object fails on every run because the ID changes. WHY this matters: the builder pattern (Pattern 13 above) is commonly combined with snapshot assertions for the full payload shape, and non-deterministic IDs silently make snapshot tests useless — they require updating on every run. Fix: use a deterministic counter in the builder: `ord_${String(++this.#counter).padStart(4, '0')}`, or accept an optional `id` parameter. Reserve `Math.random()` for production code that truly needs unpredictable IDs; test infrastructure must be deterministic.

107. **[community] Cursor-based pagination tests that reset the repository in `beforeEach` require re-seeding the full dataset per test case — a common performance trap.** When a pagination test suite seeds 1,000 rows in `beforeAll` but each `beforeEach` clears the repository and re-seeds 1,000 rows, the suite execution time grows by O(n × test-count). WHY this matters: teams observe a 10-test suite that takes 30 seconds and blame "slow I/O" when the real cause is 10 × 1,000 row inserts via an in-memory fake that is artificially reset. Fix: use `beforeAll` to seed shared read-only data (items that tests only read, never mutate), and use `beforeEach` only to reset mutable per-test state. Pagination tests by nature are read-only on the seed data — `beforeAll` seeding with a single `afterAll` cleanup is the correct structure.

### 1. TDD for GraphQL Resolvers — Schema-First with Typed Fakes [community]

GraphQL resolvers are hard to test when wired directly to a real data source. TDD drives the resolver logic through the schema contract before any persistence layer is built, using typed in-memory fakes for every data source dependency.

```typescript
// graphql-resolver.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { buildSchema, graphql } from 'graphql';
import { makeResolvers } from './resolvers.js';
import { InMemoryPostRepository } from './test-doubles/InMemoryPostRepository.js';
import type { PostRepository, Post } from './repositories/PostRepository.js';

const typeDefs = `
  type Post { id: ID! title: String! authorId: String! published: Boolean! }
  type Query { post(id: ID!): Post posts(authorId: String!): [Post!]! }
  type Mutation { publishPost(id: ID!): Post }
`;

const schema = buildSchema(typeDefs);

let repo: PostRepository;

beforeEach(() => { repo = new InMemoryPostRepository(); });

describe('Query.post', () => {
  it('returns null for an unknown post id', async () => {
    const resolvers = makeResolvers({ repo });
    const result = await graphql({ schema, source: '{ post(id: "x") { title } }', rootValue: resolvers });
    expect(result.errors).toBeUndefined();
    expect(result.data?.post).toBeNull();
  });

  it('returns a post that exists', async () => {
    await repo.save({ id: 'p1', title: 'Hello TDD', authorId: 'u1', published: false });
    const resolvers = makeResolvers({ repo });
    const result = await graphql({
      schema, source: '{ post(id: "p1") { title published } }', rootValue: resolvers,
    });
    expect(result.data?.post).toMatchObject<Partial<Post>>({ title: 'Hello TDD', published: false });
  });
});

describe('Mutation.publishPost', () => {
  it('marks the post as published and returns the updated post', async () => {
    await repo.save({ id: 'p2', title: 'Draft', authorId: 'u1', published: false });
    const resolvers = makeResolvers({ repo });
    const result = await graphql({
      schema, source: 'mutation { publishPost(id: "p2") { id published } }', rootValue: resolvers,
    });
    expect(result.data?.publishPost).toMatchObject({ id: 'p2', published: true });
    // Verify the change persisted in the fake repo
    expect((await repo.findById('p2'))?.published).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD GraphQL resolvers by testing against the SDL schema directly — do not generate resolvers from test code. The schema is the contract; the test cases verify that resolver logic satisfies it. Use typed fakes for all data sources. When NOT to use: do not test resolver-level query execution for simple CRUD pass-through resolvers — the resolver calls `repo.findById(args.id)` with zero logic; integration-test the full resolver+DB chain instead. Named alternative: Apollo Server's `ApolloServer.executeOperation` for end-to-end resolver testing when the full Apollo middleware stack must be exercised.

[community]

### 2. TDD for Middleware Pipelines — Function Composition with Context [community]

Express/Hono/tRPC-style middleware chains compose context through a series of functions. TDD each middleware in isolation, then compose them in integration tests. The key: define the typed context object before any middleware implementation.

```typescript
// middleware-pipeline.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { authMiddleware, rateLimitMiddleware, loggingMiddleware } from './middleware.js';

// Typed context shared across the middleware chain
interface RequestContext {
  requestId: string;
  userId?: string;
  rateLimitRemaining?: number;
  log: (msg: string) => void;
}

type Next = () => Promise<void>;
type Middleware = (ctx: RequestContext, next: Next) => Promise<void>;

// Test case 1: RED — authMiddleware sets userId from bearer token
describe('authMiddleware', () => {
  it('extracts userId from a valid Authorization header', async () => {
    const ctx: RequestContext = { requestId: 'r1', log: vi.fn() };
    const headers = new Headers({ Authorization: 'Bearer tok.dXNlci0x' });
    const next = vi.fn<[], Promise<void>>().mockResolvedValue(undefined);

    await authMiddleware(headers)(ctx, next);

    expect(ctx.userId).toBe('user-1');
    expect(next).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it('calls next without setting userId when header is absent', async () => {
    const ctx: RequestContext = { requestId: 'r1', log: vi.fn() };
    const next = vi.fn<[], Promise<void>>().mockResolvedValue(undefined);

    await authMiddleware(new Headers())(ctx, next);

    expect(ctx.userId).toBeUndefined();
    expect(next).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });
});

// Test case 2: RED — rateLimitMiddleware decrements the counter
describe('rateLimitMiddleware', () => {
  it('sets rateLimitRemaining and calls next when under limit', async () => {
    const fakeStore = { remaining: vi.fn<[string], Promise<number>>().mockResolvedValue(10) };
    const ctx: RequestContext = { requestId: 'r1', log: vi.fn() };
    const next = vi.fn<[], Promise<void>>().mockResolvedValue(undefined);

    await rateLimitMiddleware(fakeStore)('client-ip')(ctx, next);

    expect(ctx.rateLimitRemaining).toBe(9); // decremented
    expect(next).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it('does NOT call next when limit is exhausted', async () => {
    const fakeStore = { remaining: vi.fn<[string], Promise<number>>().mockResolvedValue(0) };
    const ctx: RequestContext = { requestId: 'r1', log: vi.fn() };
    const next = vi.fn<[], Promise<void>>().mockResolvedValue(undefined);

    await expect(
      rateLimitMiddleware(fakeStore)('client-ip')(ctx, next)
    ).rejects.toThrow('RateLimitExceeded');
    expect(next).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD each middleware independently against a typed `RequestContext` interface — never against a real `Request`/`Response` object in unit tests. Compose middleware into integration tests only to verify execution order and context propagation. When NOT to use: do not TDD middleware that only delegates to a well-tested library function (e.g., `cors()`, `helmet()`) — test library integration at the HTTP level. Named alternative: for Hono-based projects, use `Hono.request` with `c.get()`/`c.set()` context directly; for tRPC, test procedures directly through the `createCaller` utility.

[community]

### 3. TDD for Typed URL Builders — Compile-Time Safe Routing [community]

Hard-coded URL strings scatter routing knowledge across a codebase. TDD drives a typed URL builder that makes routing changes produce TypeScript compile errors rather than runtime 404s.

```typescript
// url-builder.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildUrl, RouteParams } from './url-builder.js';

// Test case 1: RED — simple route with no params
describe('buildUrl', () => {
  it('builds the dashboard URL with no params', () => {
    const url = buildUrl('dashboard', {});
    expect(url).toBe('/dashboard');
  });

  // Test case 2: RED — route with a required path param
  it('interpolates a required path parameter', () => {
    const url = buildUrl('user.profile', { userId: 'u42' });
    expect(url).toBe('/users/u42/profile');
  });

  // Test case 3: RED — route with query params
  it('appends query parameters when provided', () => {
    const url = buildUrl('products.list', { page: '2', limit: '20' });
    expect(url).toBe('/products?page=2&limit=20');
  });

  // Test case 4: RED — TypeScript enforces required params at compile time
  it('TypeScript error: missing required userId param', () => {
    // This line must fail TypeScript compilation (verified by expectTypeOf):
    // @ts-expect-error userId is required for user.profile
    buildUrl('user.profile', {});
  });
});

// GREEN: typed route registry
// url-builder.ts
const ROUTES = {
  'dashboard':     '/dashboard',
  'user.profile':  '/users/:userId/profile',
  'products.list': '/products',
} as const;

type RouteName = keyof typeof ROUTES;
type ExtractParams<T extends string> = T extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
  ? Param | ExtractParams<`/${Rest}`>
  : T extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
  ? Param
  : never;

export type RouteParams<T extends RouteName> = {
  [K in ExtractParams<(typeof ROUTES)[T]>]: string;
} & Record<string, string | undefined>;

export function buildUrl<T extends RouteName>(
  route: T,
  params: RouteParams<T>
): string {
  let path = ROUTES[route] as string;
  const queryParts: string[] = [];

  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(params)) {
    if (value === undefined) continue;
    if (path.includes(`:${key}`)) {
      path = path.replace(`:${key}`, encodeURIComponent(value));
    } else {
      queryParts.push(`${key}=${encodeURIComponent(value)}`);
    }
  }

  return queryParts.length > 0 ? `${path}?${queryParts.join('&')}` : path;
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD typed URL builders for any codebase with more than 10 routes or where route changes happen frequently. The compile-time param enforcement catches missing path params before testing. When NOT to use: in small projects with 3–5 static routes, a typed builder adds ceremony without proportional value — simple string templates suffice. Named alternative: `next-safe-action` and tRPC's `useUtils().invalidate()` provide type-safe navigation for Next.js and tRPC projects respectively.

[community]

### 4. TDD for Circuit Breaker Patterns — Fault Tolerance State Machine [community]

Circuit breakers protect services from cascading failures by tracking consecutive errors and opening the circuit when a threshold is exceeded. TDD the state machine (closed → open → half-open → closed) before the integration with any real service.

```typescript
// circuit-breaker.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { CircuitBreaker, CircuitState } from './CircuitBreaker.js';

let cb: CircuitBreaker;

beforeEach(() => {
  cb = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 3, recoveryTimeoutMs: 1000 });
});

describe('CircuitBreaker state machine', () => {
  it('starts in CLOSED state', () => {
    expect(cb.state).toBe<CircuitState>('CLOSED');
  });

  it('transitions to OPEN after failureThreshold consecutive failures', async () => {
    const failingFn = vi.fn<[], Promise<never>>().mockRejectedValue(new Error('downstream'));
    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
      await cb.call(failingFn).catch(() => {});
    }
    expect(cb.state).toBe<CircuitState>('OPEN');
  });

  it('throws CircuitOpenError immediately when circuit is OPEN', async () => {
    // Force open state
    const failingFn = vi.fn<[], Promise<never>>().mockRejectedValue(new Error('err'));
    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) await cb.call(failingFn).catch(() => {});

    const spy = vi.fn<[], Promise<void>>().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    await expect(cb.call(spy)).rejects.toThrow('CircuitOpenError');
    expect(spy).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); // not even attempted
  });

  it('transitions to HALF_OPEN after recoveryTimeoutMs elapses', async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const failingFn = vi.fn<[], Promise<never>>().mockRejectedValue(new Error('err'));
    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) await cb.call(failingFn).catch(() => {});

    vi.advanceTimersByTime(1001);
    expect(cb.state).toBe<CircuitState>('HALF_OPEN');
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('closes the circuit on success from HALF_OPEN state', async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const failingFn = vi.fn<[], Promise<never>>().mockRejectedValue(new Error('err'));
    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) await cb.call(failingFn).catch(() => {});
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(1001);

    const successFn = vi.fn<[], Promise<string>>().mockResolvedValue('ok');
    await cb.call(successFn);
    expect(cb.state).toBe<CircuitState>('CLOSED');
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD circuit breakers as pure state machines using fake timers — do not test them against real network calls. The state machine logic is fully deterministic and unit-testable. When NOT to use: do not write unit TDD test cases for the circuit breaker wired to a real HTTP client — that is integration territory. Named alternative: `cockatiel` (npm) provides a production circuit breaker with a well-tested state machine; wrap it with a typed adapter and TDD the adapter's configuration logic only.

[community]

### 5. TDD for CQRS Command and Query Handlers — Separated Write/Read Models [community]

CQRS separates commands (write side, returns void or error) from queries (read side, returns data). TDD the two handler types independently: command handlers assert on emitted domain events and repository state; query handlers assert on read-model projections.

```typescript
// cqrs-handlers.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { PlaceOrderCommandHandler } from './commands/PlaceOrderCommandHandler.js';
import { GetOrderSummaryQueryHandler } from './queries/GetOrderSummaryQueryHandler.js';
import { InMemoryOrderRepository } from './test-doubles/InMemoryOrderRepository.js';
import { InMemoryEventStore } from './test-doubles/InMemoryEventStore.js';

// ── COMMAND HANDLER TESTS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
describe('PlaceOrderCommandHandler', () => {
  let repo: InMemoryOrderRepository;
  let events: InMemoryEventStore;
  let handler: PlaceOrderCommandHandler;

  beforeEach(() => {
    repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    events = new InMemoryEventStore();
    handler = new PlaceOrderCommandHandler(repo, events);
  });

  it('persists a new order and emits OrderPlaced event', async () => {
    const command = {
      customerId: 'cust-1',
      items: [{ sku: 'WIDGET', qty: 2, price: 9.99 }],
    };

    const orderId = await handler.execute(command);

    expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ord-/);
    expect(await repo.findById(orderId)).toMatchObject({ customerId: 'cust-1' });
    expect(events.emitted).toContainEqual(
      expect.objectContaining({ type: 'OrderPlaced', payload: { orderId } })
    );
  });

  it('rejects a command with zero items', async () => {
    await expect(
      handler.execute({ customerId: 'c1', items: [] })
    ).rejects.toThrow('Order must have at least one item');
  });
});

// ── QUERY HANDLER TESTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
describe('GetOrderSummaryQueryHandler', () => {
  it('returns a read-model projection for an existing order', async () => {
    const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    await repo.save({ id: 'ord-1', customerId: 'c1', items: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 1, price: 20 }], status: 'placed' });
    const handler = new GetOrderSummaryQueryHandler(repo);

    const summary = await handler.execute({ orderId: 'ord-1' });

    expect(summary).toMatchObject({
      orderId: 'ord-1',
      total: 20,
      itemCount: 1,
      status: 'placed',
    });
  });

  it('returns null for an unknown order id', async () => {
    const handler = new GetOrderSummaryQueryHandler(new InMemoryOrderRepository());
    const result = await handler.execute({ orderId: 'ghost' });
    expect(result).toBeNull();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD CQRS handlers by keeping commands and queries in separate test files. Command handler tests verify domain invariants and event emission; query handler tests verify read-model shapes. When NOT to use: do not TDD the event store itself with integration tests in the unit test suite — the `InMemoryEventStore` fake is the unit test boundary; test the real event store adapter in a separate integration suite. Named alternative: for simpler domains where CQRS adds over-engineering, a single `OrderService` with clear read/write methods is fully TDD-able without the CQRS ceremony.

[community]

### 6. TDD for Content Negotiation — HTTP Accept Header Routing [community]

Content negotiation logic — choosing a response format based on the `Accept` header — is deterministic decision logic that TDD models as a pure function. Writing test cases first enumerates every supported media type and fallback rule before implementation.

```typescript
// content-negotiation.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { negotiate, MediaType } from './content-negotiation.js';

const SUPPORTED: MediaType[] = ['application/json', 'application/xml', 'text/csv'];

describe('negotiate', () => {
  it('selects json for "*/*"', () => {
    expect(negotiate('*/*', SUPPORTED)).toBe<MediaType>('application/json');
  });

  it('selects the first supported type matching the specific Accept value', () => {
    expect(negotiate('application/xml', SUPPORTED)).toBe<MediaType>('application/xml');
  });

  it('respects quality factors (q=) and picks the highest-quality supported type', () => {
    // application/xml;q=0.9, application/json;q=1.0
    const accept = 'application/xml;q=0.9, application/json;q=1.0';
    expect(negotiate(accept, SUPPORTED)).toBe<MediaType>('application/json');
  });

  it('returns null when no supported type matches', () => {
    expect(negotiate('text/html', SUPPORTED)).toBeNull();
  });

  it('is case-insensitive for media type comparison', () => {
    expect(negotiate('Application/JSON', SUPPORTED)).toBe<MediaType>('application/json');
  });

  it('treats missing Accept header as wildcard', () => {
    expect(negotiate('', SUPPORTED)).toBe<MediaType>('application/json');
  });

  it('ignores unsupported types in multi-value Accept', () => {
    expect(negotiate('text/html, application/csv, application/json', SUPPORTED))
      .toBe<MediaType>('application/json');
  });
});

// GREEN: pure negotiation function
// content-negotiation.ts
export type MediaType = 'application/json' | 'application/xml' | 'text/csv';

export function negotiate(
  accept: string,
  supported: MediaType[]
): MediaType | null {
  if (!accept || accept === '*/*') return supported[0] ?? null;

  const accepted = accept.split(',').map(part => {
    const [type, ...params] = part.trim().split(';');
    const qParam = params.find(p => p.trim().startsWith('q='));
    const q = qParam ? parseFloat(qParam.split('=')[1]) : 1.0;
    return { type: type.trim().toLowerCase(), q };
  }).sort((a, b) => b.q - a.q);

  for (const { type } of accepted) {
    const match = supported.find(s => s.toLowerCase() === type || type === '*/*');
    if (match) return match;
  }
  return null;
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD content negotiation as a pure function — it takes a string and a list of supported types, returns a type or null. Pure functions with enumerable inputs/outputs are ideal TDD subjects. When NOT to use: do not duplicate this in integration tests; verify content negotiation via a single HTTP-level smoke test that confirms the `Content-Type` response header matches the `Accept` request header. Named alternative: the `negotiator` npm package implements RFC 7231 content negotiation fully; wrap it with a typed adapter and TDD only the configuration logic.

[official]

### 7. TDD for Multi-Tenant Context Propagation — AsyncLocalStorage Isolation [community]

Multi-tenant applications must propagate the current tenant context through async call chains without passing it explicitly to every function. TDD the `AsyncLocalStorage`-based context propagation by testing that the context is available downstream and that different tenants never cross-contaminate.

```typescript
// tenant-context.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { TenantContext, runWithTenant, getCurrentTenant } from './TenantContext.js';

describe('TenantContext', () => {
  it('provides the tenant id inside the runWithTenant callback', async () => {
    await runWithTenant({ tenantId: 'acme', plan: 'pro' }, async () => {
      const ctx = getCurrentTenant();
      expect(ctx?.tenantId).toBe('acme');
    });
  });

  it('returns undefined outside a tenant context', () => {
    const ctx = getCurrentTenant();
    expect(ctx).toBeUndefined();
  });

  it('isolates tenant context between concurrent executions', async () => {
    const results: string[] = [];

    await Promise.all([
      runWithTenant({ tenantId: 'tenant-A', plan: 'free' }, async () => {
        await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10)); // yield to interleave with tenant-B
        results.push(getCurrentTenant()?.tenantId ?? 'none');
      }),
      runWithTenant({ tenantId: 'tenant-B', plan: 'pro' }, async () => {
        results.push(getCurrentTenant()?.tenantId ?? 'none');
      }),
    ]);

    expect(results).toContain('tenant-A');
    expect(results).toContain('tenant-B');
    // Neither tenant leaked into the other's context
    expect(results).not.toContain('none');
  });

  it('nested runWithTenant shadows the outer context', async () => {
    await runWithTenant({ tenantId: 'outer', plan: 'free' }, async () => {
      await runWithTenant({ tenantId: 'inner', plan: 'pro' }, async () => {
        expect(getCurrentTenant()?.tenantId).toBe('inner');
      });
      expect(getCurrentTenant()?.tenantId).toBe('outer'); // restored after inner
    });
  });
});

// GREEN: AsyncLocalStorage-backed tenant context
// TenantContext.ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'async_hooks';

export interface TenantContext { tenantId: string; plan: 'free' | 'pro' | 'enterprise'; }

const storage = new AsyncLocalStorage<TenantContext>();

export function runWithTenant<T>(ctx: TenantContext, fn: () => T): T {
  return storage.run(ctx, fn);
}

export function getCurrentTenant(): TenantContext | undefined {
  return storage.getStore();
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD `AsyncLocalStorage` context propagation is essential for multi-tenant SaaS. The concurrent-execution test case (test 3 above) is critical — it proves that tenant A's context does not bleed into tenant B's async chain, which is the most catastrophic multi-tenancy defect. When NOT to use: do not TDD `AsyncLocalStorage` in browser environments (no `async_hooks`); use React Context or a URL-based tenant identifier instead. Named alternative: Cloudflare Workers uses `c.env` via Hono context passing; AWS Lambda uses `context.requestContext` — neither requires `AsyncLocalStorage`.

[community]

---

### 8. TDD for Schema Migration Rollback Safety [community]

Database migrations that are not backward-compatible with the previous application version cause deployment failures when a rollback is needed. TDD migration safety by writing test cases that verify the schema can coexist with both the old and new application code.

```typescript
// migration-safety.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { applyMigration, rollbackMigration, MigrationSchema } from './migrations/v3-add-status.js';
import { InMemorySchemaStore } from './test-doubles/InMemorySchemaStore.js';

// Migration under test: adds nullable `status` column to the `orders` table
const migration: MigrationSchema = {
  version: 3,
  up: `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status TEXT DEFAULT 'pending'`,
  down: `ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN status`,
};

describe('migration v3: add status column', () => {
  let store: InMemorySchemaStore;

  beforeEach(() => { store = new InMemorySchemaStore(); });

  it('adds the status column with a default value', async () => {
    await applyMigration(store, migration);
    const schema = await store.getTableSchema('orders');
    expect(schema.columns).toContainEqual(
      expect.objectContaining({ name: 'status', nullable: true, default: 'pending' })
    );
  });

  it('rollback removes the status column without data loss for other columns', async () => {
    await applyMigration(store, migration);
    await store.insertRow('orders', { id: 'o1', total: 99, status: 'shipped' });
    await rollbackMigration(store, migration);

    const schema = await store.getTableSchema('orders');
    const columnNames = schema.columns.map(c => c.name);
    expect(columnNames).not.toContain('status');
    expect(columnNames).toContain('total'); // existing data unaffected
  });

  it('old application code can write rows that lack the new column (backward compat)', async () => {
    await applyMigration(store, migration);
    // Simulate the pre-migration application INSERT (no status field)
    await store.insertRow('orders', { id: 'o2', total: 50 });
    const row = await store.findRow('orders', 'o2');
    expect(row?.status).toBe('pending'); // default applied by migration
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD migration rollback with an in-memory schema store for fast feedback on migration logic. This catches backwards-compatibility issues (non-nullable columns, dropped defaults) before deploying. When NOT to use: do not skip integration tests against the real database — the in-memory schema store tests the migration logic; a Testcontainers or Neon branch test suite verifies the actual SQL syntax. Named alternative: Flyway and Liquibase have their own test runners; for TypeScript projects using Drizzle or Prisma, shadow-database migration validation (`prisma migrate dev --create-only`) provides automated SQL compatibility checks.

[community]

---

### 9. TDD for Server-Sent Event Streams — Async Iterator Protocol [community]

Server-sent events (SSE) push a sequence of events from server to client. TDD SSE handlers by writing test cases against an async generator interface — the generator is the seam between the SSE infrastructure and the business logic.

```typescript
// sse-stream.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createOrderStatusStream, OrderStatusEvent } from './sse/orderStatusStream.js';
import { InMemoryOrderEventSource } from './test-doubles/InMemoryOrderEventSource.js';

describe('createOrderStatusStream', () => {
  it('emits status events as the order progresses', async () => {
    const source = new InMemoryOrderEventSource('ord-1');
    // Seed events that will be emitted by the fake source
    source.enqueue({ type: 'order:processing', orderId: 'ord-1' });
    source.enqueue({ type: 'order:shipped',    orderId: 'ord-1' });
    source.enqueue({ type: 'order:delivered',  orderId: 'ord-1' });

    const stream = createOrderStatusStream(source);
    const received: OrderStatusEvent[] = [];

    for await (const event of stream) {
      received.push(event);
      if (event.type === 'order:delivered') break; // terminal event
    }

    expect(received.map(e => e.type)).toEqual([
      'order:processing',
      'order:shipped',
      'order:delivered',
    ]);
  });

  it('emits an error event and terminates the stream on downstream failure', async () => {
    const source = new InMemoryOrderEventSource('ord-2');
    source.enqueue({ type: 'order:processing', orderId: 'ord-2' });
    source.enqueueError(new Error('Payment gateway unreachable'));

    const stream = createOrderStatusStream(source);
    const events: OrderStatusEvent[] = [];

    for await (const event of stream) {
      events.push(event);
    }

    expect(events.at(-1)?.type).toBe('order:error');
    expect(events.at(-1)?.message).toMatch(/gateway/i);
  });

  it('stops emitting when the consumer closes the iterator', async () => {
    const source = new InMemoryOrderEventSource('ord-3');
    for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) source.enqueue({ type: 'order:processing', orderId: 'ord-3' });

    const stream = createOrderStatusStream(source);
    let count = 0;

    for await (const _ of stream) {
      count++;
      if (count >= 3) break; // consumer cancels early
    }

    expect(count).toBe(3); // exactly 3 events consumed
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD SSE streams against an async generator interface — the generator can be consumed in test cases with a `for await...of` loop, which mirrors the real client consumption pattern exactly. When NOT to use: do not TDD SSE through the HTTP layer in unit tests; the transport (chunked encoding, `text/event-stream` headers) belongs in integration tests. Named alternative: WebSockets have an analogous pattern (see the WebSocket TDD pattern in earlier iterations); for simpler use cases, `ReadableStream` with `TransformStream` is testable with the same async iterator pattern.

[community]

### 10. TDD for Rate Limiting — Token Bucket Algorithm [community]

Token bucket rate limiters are concurrency-sensitive: they must handle burst consumption correctly while refilling tokens over time. TDD the bucket state machine with fake time.

```typescript
// token-bucket.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { TokenBucket, TokenBucketConfig } from './TokenBucket.js';

const config: TokenBucketConfig = {
  capacity: 5,
  refillRatePerSecond: 2,
};

beforeEach(() => { vi.useFakeTimers(); });
afterEach(() => { vi.useRealTimers(); });

describe('TokenBucket', () => {
  it('starts at full capacity', () => {
    const bucket = new TokenBucket(config);
    expect(bucket.tokens).toBe(5);
  });

  it('allows consumption when tokens are available', () => {
    const bucket = new TokenBucket(config);
    expect(bucket.consume(3)).toBe(true);
    expect(bucket.tokens).toBe(2);
  });

  it('rejects consumption when insufficient tokens remain', () => {
    const bucket = new TokenBucket(config);
    bucket.consume(5); // exhaust
    expect(bucket.consume(1)).toBe(false);
    expect(bucket.tokens).toBe(0);
  });

  it('refills tokens at the configured rate after time passes', () => {
    const bucket = new TokenBucket(config);
    bucket.consume(5); // exhaust
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(1500); // 1.5 seconds × 2/s = 3 tokens refilled
    expect(bucket.tokens).toBe(3);
  });

  it('never exceeds capacity after refilling', () => {
    const bucket = new TokenBucket(config);
    bucket.consume(2); // 3 remaining
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(10_000); // way more than needed to fill
    expect(bucket.tokens).toBe(5); // capped at capacity
  });

  it('supports burst of up to capacity tokens then blocks until refill', () => {
    const bucket = new TokenBucket(config);
    const results = Array.from({ length: 6 }, (_, i) => bucket.consume(1));
    // First 5 succeed, 6th fails
    expect(results).toEqual([true, true, true, true, true, false]);
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(500); // 0.5s × 2 = 1 token refilled
    expect(bucket.consume(1)).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD token buckets with fake timers — real time makes rate-limiter test cases non-deterministic and slow. The burst test (test 6 above) is the most important: it proves the implementation does not allow more than `capacity` tokens to be consumed within a single clock tick. When NOT to use: do not TDD the Redis/Valkey persistence layer for distributed rate limiters in unit tests — use an in-memory bucket for unit TDD and an integration test with a real Redis instance for the distributed case. Named alternative: `limiter` and `rate-limiter-flexible` npm packages provide production rate limiters; TDD only your configuration adapter and the business logic that decides what to rate-limit.

[community]

---

### 11. TDD for Optimistic Concurrency — ETag-Based Conflict Detection [community]

Optimistic concurrency prevents lost updates: before saving, the client presents the version (ETag) it last read. If the stored version has changed, the save is rejected. TDD drives the version-check logic as a pure function.

```typescript
// optimistic-concurrency.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { VersionedOrderRepository } from './VersionedOrderRepository.js';
import { InMemoryVersionedStore } from './test-doubles/InMemoryVersionedStore.js';
import type { VersionedOrder } from './types.js';

let repo: VersionedOrderRepository;

beforeEach(() => {
  repo = new VersionedOrderRepository(new InMemoryVersionedStore());
});

describe('VersionedOrderRepository', () => {
  it('saves a new order and returns version "1"', async () => {
    const order = await repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: 50 });
    expect(order.version).toBe('1');
  });

  it('increments version on each successful update', async () => {
    const v1 = await repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: 50 });
    const v2 = await repo.update(v1.id, { total: 75 }, v1.version);
    expect(v2.version).toBe('2');
  });

  it('rejects an update when the provided version is stale', async () => {
    const v1 = await repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: 50 });
    await repo.update(v1.id, { total: 75 }, v1.version); // advance to v2

    // Attempt to update with the stale v1 version
    await expect(
      repo.update(v1.id, { total: 100 }, v1.version)
    ).rejects.toThrow('ConflictError');
  });

  it('two concurrent readers see the same version before either writes', async () => {
    const created = await repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: 50 });
    const [readA, readB] = await Promise.all([
      repo.findById(created.id),
      repo.findById(created.id),
    ]);
    expect(readA?.version).toBe(readB?.version);
  });

  it('only the first of two concurrent updates succeeds', async () => {
    const v1 = await repo.create({ customerId: 'c1', total: 50 });
    const [result1, result2] = await Promise.allSettled([
      repo.update(v1.id, { total: 75 }, v1.version),
      repo.update(v1.id, { total: 90 }, v1.version),
    ]);
    const succeeded = [result1, result2].filter(r => r.status === 'fulfilled').length;
    const conflicted = [result1, result2].filter(r => r.status === 'rejected').length;
    expect(succeeded).toBe(1);
    expect(conflicted).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD optimistic concurrency with an in-memory versioned store that serialises updates atomically. The concurrent-update test (test 5) is the most important: it proves exactly one update wins without requiring a database lock. When NOT to use: do not rely on in-memory serialisation for a distributed multi-node deployment; the in-memory test proves the algorithm, not the distributed guarantee. Test the actual database-level `WHERE version = :expected` clause in an integration test. Named alternative: pessimistic locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) is an alternative to optimistic concurrency; TDD it differently — test that locked rows cannot be read until the lock is released.

[community]

### 12. TDD for Dependency Injection Containers — Typed Wiring [community]

DI containers wire dependencies at startup. TDD the container configuration to verify that all bindings resolve correctly and that circular dependencies are caught before the application starts.

```typescript
// di-container.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { Container } from './Container.js';
import type { Logger, Database, UserService } from './interfaces.js';

describe('Container', () => {
  it('resolves a registered singleton', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    container.registerSingleton<Logger>('Logger', () => ({ info: () => {}, error: () => {} }));

    const logger1 = container.resolve<Logger>('Logger');
    const logger2 = container.resolve<Logger>('Logger');
    expect(logger1).toBe(logger2); // same instance — singleton
  });

  it('resolves a transient binding as a new instance each time', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    container.registerTransient<{ id: number }>('RequestCtx', () => ({ id: Math.random() }));

    const a = container.resolve<{ id: number }>('RequestCtx');
    const b = container.resolve<{ id: number }>('RequestCtx');
    expect(a).not.toBe(b); // different instances — transient
  });

  it('resolves a dependency graph with multiple levels', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    container.registerSingleton<Database>('Database', () => ({
      query: async () => [],
    }));
    container.registerSingleton<UserService>('UserService', (c) => ({
      findAll: () => c.resolve<Database>('Database').query('SELECT * FROM users'),
    }));

    const svc = container.resolve<UserService>('UserService');
    expect(svc).toBeDefined();
    expect(typeof svc.findAll).toBe('function');
  });

  it('throws a descriptive error for an unregistered token', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    expect(() => container.resolve('UnknownService')).toThrow(
      'No binding registered for token: UnknownService'
    );
  });

  it('detects a circular dependency and throws CircularDependencyError', () => {
    const container = new Container();
    container.registerTransient('A', (c) => c.resolve('B'));
    container.registerTransient('B', (c) => c.resolve('A'));

    expect(() => container.resolve('A')).toThrow('CircularDependencyError');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** TDD the container's own resolution mechanics (singleton, transient, circular detection), not the factories registered in the container. The factory functions themselves are separate units with their own test suites. When NOT to use: do not TDD a DI container for small applications with 5–10 services — constructor injection without a container is simpler and equally testable. Named alternative: `tsyringe`, `inversify`, and `typedi` are production DI containers; use their own test utilities rather than building a custom container, and TDD only your bindings configuration.

[community]
