### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 33 Additions

126. **[community] TypeScript 5.9 `import defer` is silently unsupported when `--module` is set to `commonjs` — no compile error is emitted, the `defer` keyword is stripped and the module body executes eagerly.** If your project uses `--module commonjs` (common in Jest setups with `ts-jest`) and you write `import defer * as ns from "./module"`, TypeScript compiles it to a regular `require()` call, completely defeating the deferred-execution semantics. The test then runs the module body immediately at import time — the deferred evaluation you were testing never occurs. WHY this matters: there is no compiler error or warning; the test passes because the module body ran eagerly, but the production environment (where `--module esnext` or `preserve` is used) correctly defers it, creating a test-production mismatch where the test verifies behavior that does not reflect production. Fix: ensure `tsconfig.json` uses `"module": "esnext"` or `"module": "preserve"` in both the source and test TypeScript configs; add a CI lint rule that bans `import defer` when `module` is set to `commonjs`.

127. **[community] Jest 30's removal of deprecated matcher aliases (`.toBeCalled()`, `.toBeCalledWith()`, `.toReturn()`) causes runtime `TypeError` failures, not TypeScript compile errors — the type definitions were updated at the same time, so `tsc` catches the issue, but `ts-jest` projects using `isolatedModules: true` bypass type checking entirely.** After upgrading to Jest 30, test files that use `ts-jest` with `isolatedModules: true` (which transpiles without type-checking for speed) will compile and load but throw `TypeError: expect(...).toBeCalled is not a function` at runtime when the deprecated method is called. WHY this matters: with `isolatedModules: true`, the Red-phase type-system guardrail is gone — the deprecation is only surfaced at the moment Jest executes the assertion, which may be deep into a long test run. Fix: run `eslint --fix --rule 'jest/no-deprecated-functions: error'` before upgrading to Jest 30 to rename all deprecated aliases; disable `isolatedModules` during the upgrade migration to surface type errors.

128. **[community] Jest 30's `globalsCleanup: 'on'` resets `window.location` between test files, breaking tests that rely on a `window.location.origin` set in `jest.setup.ts` via `Object.defineProperty`.** Teams that configure `Object.defineProperty(window, 'location', { value: { origin: 'https://app.test' } })` in setup files find that subsequent test files see `window.location.origin === 'http://localhost'` instead of the intended `'https://app.test'`. WHY this matters: `window.location`-dependent code (CORS header generation, absolute URL construction, OAuth redirect URIs) behaves differently in the second and later test files, and the failures are highly order-dependent — they are impossible to reproduce when running a single test file in isolation. Fix: call `protectProperties(window.location)` from `jest-util` in `setupFilesAfterEnv` to exempt `window.location` from the cleanup sweep; or use `globalsCleanup: 'soft'` while migrating.

129. **[community] `expect.arrayOf` in Jest 30 short-circuits on the first non-matching element — it does not report all failing elements — making it appear as if the array has only one problem when it may have many.** Developers who expect `arrayOf` to behave like a `toMatchObject` failure (which reports every differing key) are surprised to see "element 0 did not match" with no information about whether elements 1 through N also fail. WHY this matters: when diagnosing why a repository returns malformed records (e.g., a migration left `email` as `null` in 40% of rows), you only see the first bad record — the scope of the data problem is invisible until you run a manual query. Fix: use `results.forEach((element, i) => expect(element, \`element ${i}\`).toEqual(matcher))` when you need exhaustive failure reporting across all elements; use `expect.arrayOf` only when fast-fail on the first non-conforming element is acceptable behavior.

130. **[community] `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` advances by exactly 16ms (integer), not 16.67ms, creating a cumulative drift of ~0.67ms per frame that causes animation tests to exit the animation loop one frame early for animations longer than ~24 frames at 60fps.** An animation controller that tracks elapsed time with `performance.now()` and terminates when `elapsed >= durationMs` will see the clock reach `496ms` after 31 frames (31 × 16ms) instead of reaching the 500ms threshold, leaving `isRunning === true` and causing the completion assertion to fail. WHY this matters: the test appears to be testing a 500ms animation but is actually testing whether the controller completes at or before 496ms — a subtle mismatch that only affects animations longer than about 400ms. Fix: use `jest.advanceTimersByTime(17)` per frame for accurate ~60fps simulation, or write the assertion as `expect(ctrl.currentValue).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(99)` with a generous range to accommodate the drift; document the drift in the test comment.

131. **[community] Migrating from `vitest.workspace.ts` to the unified `projects` array in Vitest 3.2 silently drops any per-package `resolve.alias` or `plugins` entries defined in package-level `vitest.config.ts` files if they are not explicitly re-declared in the `projects` entry.** Teams migrating a monorepo where each package has its own `vitest.config.ts` (with aliases like `@/ → src/`) discover post-migration that aliased imports in tests throw `Cannot find module '@/components/Button'` without any warning about the dropped configuration. WHY this matters: the aliased import error surface looks like a broken path or missing file, not like a missing configuration — developers spend time inspecting `tsconfig.json` paths and directory layouts before realizing the `resolve.alias` key was dropped during migration. Fix: before migrating, run `grep -r "resolve.alias\|plugins:" packages/*/vitest.config.ts` to enumerate all per-project config overrides, then carry each override into the corresponding `projects` entry; run the full test suite immediately after migration to surface any silent drops.

### 1. TDD for Vitest 4.0 `expect.schemaMatching` — Standard Schema Contract Tests [official]

Vitest 4.0 introduced `expect.schemaMatching(schema)` as a new asymmetric matcher that validates values against any Standard Schema v1-compliant schema object (Zod, Valibot, ArkType). In the Red phase, you write a schema assertion to declare the output shape; in the Green phase you implement the data transformation; in Refactor you tighten schema constraints if the implementation drifted toward a looser shape. This approach anchors schema evolution in the test suite: when an API response shape changes, the Red failure on `schemaMatching` is the canonical signal to update the schema and re-discuss the contract before touching any implementation code. Note that `schemaMatching` validates structural shape only and does not evaluate Zod `.refine()` predicates — full Zod validation requires `schema.safeParse(value).success`.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { z } from "zod";

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  createdAt: z.string().datetime(),
  role: z.enum(["admin", "member", "guest"]),
});

// RED: write the schema assertion before the implementation exists
describe("createUser()", () => {
  it("returns a user conforming to UserSchema", async () => {
    const result = await createUser({ email: "test@example.com", role: "member" });
    // schemaMatching performs structural validation, not deep equality
    expect(result).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(UserSchema));
  });

  it("rejects users with invalid roles at schema level", () => {
    const badPayload = { id: "not-uuid", email: "bad", createdAt: "not-date", role: "superadmin" };
    // Negative schema test: confirm invalid shapes fail the matcher
    expect(badPayload).not.toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(UserSchema));
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** the production function's return type is governed by a shared runtime schema (Zod/Valibot) and you want schema evolution to be explicitly tested, not just type-checked.
- **Do NOT use when** the shape is a plain interface with no runtime validation — a `toMatchObject` assertion is simpler and has no schema dependency. Also do NOT rely on it for `.refine()` predicate testing — use `schema.safeParse(payload).success` instead.
- **Alternative:** `expect.objectContaining()` for partial shape checks; `expectTypeOf()` for compile-time-only contract tests.

[official]

---

### 2. TDD for Vitest 4.0 `toMatchScreenshot` — Visual Regression Red Phase [official]

Vitest 4.0 graduated Browser Mode and added `toMatchScreenshot()` as a first-class visual regression assertion. TDD-style visual tests follow the same Red-Green-Refactor loop but at the pixel level: on first run, there is no baseline (Red); the Green phase captures the initial screenshot; the Refactor phase tightens layout or styling. Using `toMatchScreenshot({ threshold: 0.01 })` keeps the Red trigger precise — a 1% pixel deviation is enough to catch accidental CSS changes. Combining this with `page.mark()` annotations lets you annotate what the screenshot covers in the Playwright Trace Viewer for post-mortem analysis. Separate provider packages (`@vitest/browser-playwright`, `@vitest/browser-webdriverio`) must be installed — the browser assertion API is no longer bundled with the core package.

```typescript
import { test, expect, page } from "vitest/browser";

test("ProductCard renders correctly at 375px viewport", async () => {
  // Arrange: configure viewport and render component
  await page.setViewportSize({ width: 375, height: 812 });
  await page.goto("/components/product-card?id=42");
  await page.waitForSelector("[data-testid='product-card']");

  // Annotate for Playwright Trace Viewer
  await page.mark("before-screenshot");

  // Assert visual contract — fails on first run (Red), passes after baseline capture (Green)
  const card = page.locator("[data-testid='product-card']");
  await expect(card).toMatchScreenshot("product-card-375px.png", {
    threshold: 0.01,
    maxDiffPixels: 50,
  });

  await page.mark("after-screenshot");
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** the component has a stable, non-dynamic visual output and you want regression detection across CSS/layout changes.
- **Do NOT use when** the component contains dynamic content (dates, user avatars, ads) that changes between runs — mask volatile regions first with `page.locator().evaluate(el => el.style.visibility = 'hidden')`.
- **Alternative:** `toMatchAriaSnapshot` (Vitest 4.1) for accessibility-contract regression instead of visual pixel comparison.

[official]

---

### 3. TDD for Vitest 4.0 `toBeInViewport` — Visibility Contract Tests [official]

`toBeInViewport()` (Vitest 4.0 Browser Mode) asserts that a locator element is visible within the viewport using the native IntersectionObserver API. This enables TDD for lazy-load triggers, infinite-scroll sentinels, and sticky element behavior — all cases where "visible in viewport" is the core behavioural contract. Writing the `toBeInViewport` assertion first (Red) forces the implementation to include proper intersection observer setup before any scroll logic is written, preventing the common anti-pattern of implementing scroll listeners without testing whether the trigger element is actually visible. The matcher uses `@vitest/browser-playwright` under the hood and requires a real browser environment — it cannot be polyfilled in jsdom.

```typescript
import { test, expect, page } from "vitest/browser";

// RED: sticky nav should remain in viewport after scrolling past hero
test("StickyNav stays in viewport when user scrolls past hero section", async () => {
  await page.goto("/");
  const nav = page.locator("[data-testid='sticky-nav']");
  const hero = page.locator("[data-testid='hero-section']");

  // Verify hero is initially in viewport
  await expect(hero).toBeInViewport();

  // Simulate scrolling past the hero
  await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo({ top: 800, behavior: "instant" }));

  // The nav must remain in viewport after scrolling (sticky behavior)
  await expect(nav).toBeInViewport();

  // Verify hero is now out of viewport
  await expect(hero).not.toBeInViewport();
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** testing a scroll-dependent UI element (sticky headers, lazy images, infinite-scroll triggers) and you need to verify intersection-based behavior.
- **Do NOT use when** testing a server-rendered component that has no scroll interaction — a plain `toBeVisible()` assertion is faster and simpler.
- **Alternative:** `page.evaluate(() => entry.isIntersecting)` via a manually instantiated IntersectionObserver for cases where Vitest's locator API is unavailable.

[official]

---

### 4. TDD for Vitest 4.0 `experimental_parseSpecifications` — Programmatic Test Discovery [official]

Vitest 4.0 exposed `experimental_parseSpecifications()` on the programmatic API, enabling tools to discover and parse test file specifications before running them. In a TDD-at-scale setup, this powers "test routing" pipelines that analyse which test files cover which source modules and route only the relevant subset to each CI agent. The pattern keeps the Red-Green-Refactor cycle fast even in large monorepos: the Green phase only runs tests whose specifications intersect with the changed source files. The API is explicitly marked experimental and may change in minor releases — guard usage behind a Vitest version check.

```typescript
import { createVitest } from "vitest/node";

// Build a test-routing map: source file → test specifications
async function buildTestRoutes(changedFiles: string[]): Promise<string[]> {
  const vitest = await createVitest("test", {
    include: ["**/*.test.ts"],
    watch: false,
  });

  // Parse all specifications without executing any tests
  const allSpecs = await vitest.experimental_parseSpecifications();

  // Filter specs that import any of the changed files
  const affectedSpecs = allSpecs.filter((spec) =>
    spec.moduleGraph?.some((dep) =>
      changedFiles.some((changed) => dep.includes(changed))
    )
  );

  await vitest.close();
  return affectedSpecs.map((s) => s.moduleId);
}

// Usage in CI: run only affected specs
const changedFiles = process.env.CHANGED_FILES?.split(",") ?? [];
const specsToRun = await buildTestRoutes(changedFiles);
console.log(`Running ${specsToRun.length} affected test files`);
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** building a CI orchestration layer that needs to route tests to shards without running all specs first; useful for monorepos with >1000 test files.
- **Do NOT use when** `coverage.changed` (Vitest 4.1) meets the requirement — it is higher-level and requires no custom glue code.
- **Alternative:** `vitest run --changed HEAD~1` (built-in changed-file detection via `git`) for simpler cases where the shard routing logic is not needed.

[official]

---

### 5. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `--detect-async-leaks` — Leak-Driven Red Phase [official]

`--detect-async-leaks` (Vitest 4.1, requires Node.js `async_hooks`) instruments every test with async resource tracking and fails tests that leave behind unresolved promises, leaked timers, or unclosed handles. From a TDD perspective, it transforms the Red phase: writing a test that _should_ clean up a resource now also serves as a leak contract — if the implementation does not tear down correctly, the test turns Red for a second, distinct reason. This catches a common class of flaky-test-causing leaks (uncleared `setInterval`, unclosed `EventEmitter`, unresolved `AbortController`) at the moment they are introduced, not weeks later when CI becomes non-deterministic. Note: `AbortSignal.timeout()` causes false-positive leak reports; use explicit `AbortController` teardown instead.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectAsyncLeaks: true, // enables --detect-async-leaks flag
    setupFiles: ["./test/setup.ts"],
  },
});

// EventBus.test.ts — leak detection in action
import { describe, it, expect, afterEach } from "vitest";
import { EventBus } from "./event-bus";

describe("EventBus", () => {
  let bus: EventBus;

  afterEach(() => {
    // RED (without this line): detectAsyncLeaks reports a leaked subscription handle
    bus.dispose(); // correctly tears down all internal timers and subscriptions
  });

  it("emits events to all subscribers", async () => {
    bus = new EventBus();
    const received: string[] = [];
    bus.on("ping", (msg) => received.push(msg));
    bus.emit("ping", "hello");
    expect(received).toEqual(["hello"]);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** the codebase uses long-lived event emitters, polling intervals, or streamed resource handles that must be explicitly closed.
- **Do NOT use when** the test suite uses third-party libraries that intentionally leave background processes running (e.g., database connection pools) without a teardown path — false-positive rate will be high.
- **Alternative:** `vi.useFakeTimers()` + `vi.clearAllTimers()` as a coarser mechanism that prevents timer leaks without the overhead of `async_hooks` instrumentation.

[official]

---

### 6. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `aroundEach` / `aroundAll` — Transaction Wrapping [official]

`aroundEach` and `aroundAll` hooks (Vitest 4.1) replace the `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pair for cases where the setup and teardown must share scope — most importantly, database transactions. The canonical TDD database pattern is to wrap each test in a transaction, execute it, and roll back regardless of outcome; this previously required a class-level shared `let txn` variable and careful `beforeEach`/`afterEach` coordination. `aroundEach` encodes this as a single generator function, eliminating the coordination boilerplate and making the teardown path unconditional (the `finally` block always runs). Critical: always add a `try/finally` around the post-`yield` code — `test.skip` does not invoke the test body but still resumes the generator, and without `finally` the teardown path is skipped.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, test } from "vitest";
import { db } from "./db";

// Using aroundEach for per-test database transaction rollback
describe("OrderRepository", () => {
  test.extend({
    // aroundEach fixture: wraps each test in a rolled-back transaction
    async txn({}, use) {
      const transaction = await db.beginTransaction();
      try {
        // 'use' runs the test body between the two halves of the fixture
        await use(transaction);
      } finally {
        // Always rolls back regardless of test pass/fail/skip
        await transaction.rollback();
      }
    },
  });

  it("saves an order with line items", async ({ txn }) => {
    const repo = new OrderRepository(txn);
    const orderId = await repo.create({
      userId: "usr_1",
      items: [{ sku: "WIDGET-A", qty: 2 }],
    });
    const saved = await repo.findById(orderId);
    expect(saved.items).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(saved.items[0].sku).toBe("WIDGET-A");
  });

  it("counts orders for a user", async ({ txn }) => {
    const repo = new OrderRepository(txn);
    await repo.create({ userId: "usr_2", items: [] });
    expect(await repo.countForUser("usr_2")).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** the test needs paired setup/teardown that share a resource handle (database transaction, tracing span, OpenTelemetry context) and rollback-on-failure semantics are required.
- **Do NOT use when** the test is unit-testing pure functions with no I/O — the overhead of async hooks is unnecessary.
- **Alternative:** `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pair with a shared `let tx` variable remains viable for simple teardown needs, but loses the guarantee of unconditional cleanup if `afterEach` is accidentally removed.

[official]

---

### 7. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `agent` Reporter — AI Coding Agent TDD Loop [official]

Vitest 4.1 added an `agent` reporter that suppresses passed-test output and emits only failures, warnings, and the final summary — reducing token usage for AI coding agents that drive the Red-Green-Refactor loop via programmatic API or CLI. When an LLM agent is driving TDD (writing the failing test, implementing code, and re-running tests), sending the full verbose output per cycle exceeds context limits. The `agent` reporter emits a minimal, machine-parseable signal: fail count, error messages, and file locations — exactly what the agent needs to decide whether to continue refactoring or declare Green. Pair with `silent: true` to suppress console.log output from production code during the TDD loop.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — configure for AI agent-driven TDD loop
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // 'agent' reporter: only failures + summary, no per-passing-test output
    reporters: process.env.CI_AGENT ? ["agent"] : ["default"],
    // Suppress console.log noise from production code during TDD loop
    silent: !!process.env.CI_AGENT,
    // Run tests sequentially for deterministic agent feedback
    pool: "forks",
    poolOptions: { forks: { singleFork: true } },
  },
});

// Agent-driven TDD loop pattern:
// 1. Agent writes a failing test → RED (agent reporter emits: "1 failed: ...")
// 2. Agent writes minimal implementation → GREEN (agent reporter emits: "0 failed, 1 passed")
// 3. Agent refactors → REFACTOR (agent reporter emits: "0 failed, 1 passed")
// 4. Repeat — each cycle < 2k tokens because 'agent' reporter omits passing-test lines
// Run with: CI_AGENT=1 npx vitest run
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** an LLM agent is in the driver's seat of the TDD loop and token budget per cycle matters (sub-$0.01 per cycle target).
- **Do NOT use when** a human is the primary developer — the suppressed passing-test output removes useful feedback during exploratory debugging.
- **Alternative:** `--reporter=dot` for human-readable brevity; `--reporter=json` for structured machine consumption when the full test result graph is needed.

[official]

---

### 8. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `coverage.changed` — Diff-Scoped Coverage Gate [official]

`coverage.changed` (Vitest 4.1) restricts coverage reporting and thresholds to only the files modified in the current diff (uses `git diff HEAD~1`). In a TDD workflow, this creates a per-PR coverage gate: the Red phase introduces a failing test for the new code; the Green phase must hit the coverage threshold on the changed files specifically; the Refactor phase can improve structure without worrying about incidentally uncovered legacy code inflating the failure. This prevents the common false-negative where a low-coverage legacy module drags the global coverage metric below threshold and blocks a PR that added correctly-tested new code.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      // Only report and gate on files changed since last commit
      changed: true,
      thresholds: {
        // These thresholds apply only to changed files, not the full codebase
        lines: 90,
        branches: 85,
        functions: 90,
        statements: 90,
      },
      include: ["src/**/*.ts"],
      exclude: ["src/**/*.d.ts", "src/**/index.ts"],
    },
  },
});

// CI workflow: run with changed-file coverage gate
// npx vitest run --coverage
// Fails if any file in the diff is below 90% line coverage
// Does NOT fail if legacy files are below threshold
// Gate applies even when adding new test files (they must also be covered)
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** the project has a mix of well-tested new code and legacy code with low coverage, and you want TDD discipline enforced at the PR level without a global coverage blanket.
- **Do NOT use when** the change is a pure refactor of existing code without changing test files — the changed-file gate will flag uncovered lines in refactored files that previously had no tests.
- **Alternative:** Per-file coverage thresholds in `coverage.thresholds` (Vitest's per-file glob pattern support) for more surgical coverage enforcement on specific modules.

[official]

---

### 9. TDD for Jest 30 `jest.unstable_unmockModule` — ESM-Native Mock Restoration [official]

Jest 30 introduced `jest.unstable_unmockModule(modulePath)` for ESM test files. Before this API, unmocking a module in ESM tests required either a full `jest.resetModules()` call (which also cleared every other mock, resetting test isolation too broadly) or restructuring the test file so the mock was never applied. The new API restores a single module to its real implementation mid-test, enabling "mock-then-unmock" patterns where the first assertions cover the mocked path and the second assertions verify real integration. From a TDD perspective, this removes a major friction point in writing tests that span both mocked and real dependency paths in a single describe block.

```typescript
// payment-service.test.ts (ESM)
import { jest, describe, it, expect, beforeAll } from "@jest/globals";

// AUTO-MOCK the stripe module at the top level for fast unit tests
jest.unstable_mockModule("stripe", () => ({
  default: jest.fn().mockImplementation(() => ({
    paymentIntents: {
      create: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: "pi_test_123", status: "requires_payment_method" }),
    },
  })),
}));

describe("PaymentService", () => {
  let PaymentService: typeof import("./payment-service").PaymentService;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    ({ PaymentService } = await import("./payment-service"));
  });

  it("[mocked] creates a payment intent via Stripe mock", async () => {
    const svc = new PaymentService(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!);
    const result = await svc.createIntent({ amount: 1000, currency: "usd" });
    expect(result.id).toBe("pi_test_123");
  });

  it("[real] falls back gracefully when Stripe is unavailable", async () => {
    // Restore the real Stripe module for this assertion block
    jest.unstable_unmockModule("stripe");
    const result = await PaymentService.healthCheck();
    // Real stripe throws on missing key; healthCheck returns "unavailable"
    expect(result).toBe("unavailable");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** a single test file needs to switch between mocked and real implementations for the same module — common in integration boundary tests.
- **Do NOT use when** the test file consistently tests the same boundary; splitting into two test files (one fully mocked, one fully real) is cleaner.
- **Alternative:** `jest.resetModules()` + re-import in a nested `describe` block for CJS test files that cannot use ESM dynamic imports.

[official]

---

### 10. TDD for Google TotT May 2026 "Code Review Responses: Add Context" — Test Comment Discipline [community]

Google's May 2026 TotT post "Code Review Responses: Add Context When It Counts" applies directly to TDD test authorship: a test that needs a reviewer to ask "why is this the expected value?" has failed the communication contract just as much as production code with an unexplained magic number. The pattern is to write test comments that provide the *why*, not the *what* — the assertion already states what is expected; the comment should explain the business rule, edge case, or contract that makes this value correct. In TDD, this discipline belongs in the Red phase: as you write the failing test, write the comment explaining why this failure is the correct failure. This also protects against "test drift" — tests that were correct at write time but whose reasoning is lost, causing them to be updated incorrectly during refactoring.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { calculateRefund } from "./refund-calculator";

describe("calculateRefund()", () => {
  it("applies 85% refund for cancellations within 48h of purchase", () => {
    // Business rule (Payments Policy v3.2, §4.1): full refund minus a 15%
    // processing fee for same-week cancellations. The 15% is non-negotiable
    // — do not change this value without updating the Payments Policy doc.
    const result = calculateRefund({
      purchaseAmount: 100_00, // cents
      cancelledHoursAfterPurchase: 36,
    });
    expect(result.refundAmountCents).toBe(85_00);
    expect(result.feeAmountCents).toBe(15_00);
  });

  it("applies 0% refund for cancellations more than 14 days after purchase", () => {
    // No refund after the 14-day window — this is a hard policy cutoff.
    // Cutoff is strictly >14 days (exclusive): day 14 still gets partial refund.
    // Do NOT change to >= 14 days — that would break the partial-refund window.
    const result = calculateRefund({
      purchaseAmount: 100_00,
      cancelledHoursAfterPurchase: 15 * 24 + 1, // 15 days + 1 hour: past the cutoff
    });
    expect(result.refundAmountCents).toBe(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** the test assertion encodes a non-obvious business rule, a policy boundary, or a contract with an external system — any case where a future reviewer would legitimately ask "why?".
- **Do NOT use when** the assertion is self-documenting (`expect(sum(2, 3)).toBe(5)` needs no comment).
- **Alternative:** Parameterised `test.each` with a `description` column embedding the rule inline, which surfaces the reason in the test name rather than a comment.

[community]

---

### 11. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `page.mark()` / `locator.mark()` — Trace-Annotated TDD [official]

`page.mark(label)` and `locator.mark(label)` (Vitest 4.1 Browser Mode) insert named markers into the Playwright Trace Viewer timeline. In a TDD context, these markers serve as executable documentation of the test's arrange/act/assert boundaries within the trace — when a browser test fails in CI, the trace shows exactly which step (arrange, act, or assert) was active when the failure occurred. Writing `await page.mark("ACT: submit form")` during the Green phase forces you to articulate the test structure inside the trace, making the Red-phase failure message navigable by any teammate without reading the test source. Browser interactions are automatically grouped in the Trace Viewer around mark boundaries.

```typescript
import { test, expect, page } from "vitest/browser";

test("CheckoutForm: submitting with valid card completes the order", async () => {
  // ARRANGE
  await page.mark("ARRANGE: navigate to checkout");
  await page.goto("/checkout");
  await page.waitForSelector("[data-testid='checkout-form']");

  // ACT: fill in credit card form
  await page.mark("ACT: fill card details");
  const form = page.locator("[data-testid='checkout-form']");
  await form.locator("[name='cardNumber']").fill("4242424242424242");
  await form.locator("[name='expiry']").fill("12/28");
  await form.locator("[name='cvv']").fill("123");

  await page.mark("ACT: submit form");
  await form.locator("[type='submit']").click();

  // ASSERT
  await page.mark("ASSERT: confirmation page visible");
  const confirmation = page.locator("[data-testid='order-confirmation']");
  await expect(confirmation).toBeVisible();
  await expect(confirmation.locator("[data-testid='order-id']")).not.toBeEmpty();
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** the test covers a multi-step browser interaction that is difficult to debug from assertion output alone — the trace provides the full timeline.
- **Do NOT use when** the test is a pure unit test with no browser involvement — marks are no-ops outside Browser Mode and add visual noise to the source.
- **Alternative:** `context.annotate(message, options)` (Vitest 3.2) for text-based diagnostic annotations on test results without browser trace integration.

[official]

### 12. TDD for Jest 30 `jest.onGenerateMock` — Realistic Mock Baseline [official]

`jest.onGenerateMock(callback)` (Jest 30) runs a user-supplied callback every time Jest auto-generates a mock for a module, letting you customise the generated mock's return values before any test runs. This changes the TDD auto-mock workflow: instead of writing a `beforeEach` with repeated `mockReturnValue` calls to make auto-mocks realistic, you declare the realistic baseline once in `jest.onGenerateMock` and override per test only for the specific behaviour under test. The Red phase becomes cleaner: the test only states the deviation from the realistic baseline, not the entire mock contract. Register `jest.onGenerateMock` in `jest.setup.ts` via `setupFilesAfterFramework` to ensure it runs before any test file is loaded.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts
import { jest } from "@jest/globals";

// Set realistic baseline for all auto-generated mocks of the HTTP client
jest.onGenerateMock((module, generatedMock) => {
  if (module.includes("http-client")) {
    // Default: all requests return 200 with empty body
    (generatedMock.default as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValue({
      status: 200,
      data: {},
      headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    });
  }
  return generatedMock;
});

// In the test file — only the deviation is stated, not the entire mock
import { jest, it, expect } from "@jest/globals";
jest.mock("./http-client");

it("retries once on 429 Too Many Requests", async () => {
  const { default: httpClient } = await import("./http-client");
  // Override the baseline for this specific test only — baseline handles the 200 case
  (httpClient as jest.Mock)
    .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: 429, retryAfter: 1 })
    .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: 200, data: { id: "obj_1" } });

  const result = await fetchWithRetry("/api/objects/1");
  expect(result.data.id).toBe("obj_1");
  expect(httpClient).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** a module is mocked across many test files and writing the realistic baseline in every `beforeEach` creates duplication.
- **Do NOT use when** only one or two tests mock the module — per-test `mockReturnValue` is more explicit and easier to understand.
- **Alternative:** Shared mock factory functions in `__mocks__/` directories (Jest's manual mock pattern) for complex modules that need deep customisation beyond `onGenerateMock`.

[official]

---

### 13. TDD for Vitest 4.0 `enableCoverage` / `disableCoverage` Programmatic API — Targeted Coverage Measurement [official]

Vitest 4.0 exposed `enableCoverage()` and `disableCoverage()` on the programmatic API, enabling selective coverage collection — only the code paths exercised between the two calls are instrumented. In a TDD context, this allows you to measure coverage of a single Red-Green cycle precisely: wrap the Green-phase test run with `enableCoverage()`/`disableCoverage()` to confirm that the new test actually exercises the new production code. Without this, global coverage numbers include all previously green tests and make it impossible to tell whether a specific new test added meaningful coverage. Important: `waitForTestRunEnd()` resolves before coverage is flushed to disk — always `await getCoverageProvider()?.generateCoverage()` before reading coverage files.

```typescript
import { createVitest } from "vitest/node";

async function measureCycleCoverage(testPattern: string): Promise<void> {
  const vitest = await createVitest("test", {
    include: [testPattern],
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      include: ["src/orders/**/*.ts"],
    },
  });

  // Only collect coverage during this specific test run
  await vitest.enableCoverage();
  await vitest.start();
  await vitest.waitForTestRunEnd();

  // IMPORTANT: must explicitly call generateCoverage() — waitForTestRunEnd()
  // resolves before the coverage provider finishes writing the JSON file
  const coverageResult = await vitest.getCoverageProvider()?.generateCoverage();
  const uncoveredLines = coverageResult?.files.flatMap((f) =>
    f.uncoveredLines.map((l) => `${f.path}:${l}`)
  );

  await vitest.disableCoverage();
  await vitest.close();

  if (uncoveredLines?.length) {
    console.warn("Lines not covered by this TDD cycle:", uncoveredLines);
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** building a TDD CI dashboard that tracks coverage delta per commit — each cycle's contribution to overall coverage becomes auditable.
- **Do NOT use when** running all tests at once; `coverage.changed` (Vitest 4.1) is a simpler higher-level API for the same "only new code needs coverage" goal.
- **Alternative:** Istanbul's `/* istanbul ignore next */` comments to exclude specific code paths from coverage, which is lower-tech but does not provide per-cycle measurement.

[official]

---

### 14. TDD for TypeScript `satisfies` Operator as Red-Phase Type Fixture [official]

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9+, widely adopted in 5.x projects) is a compile-time assertion that a value satisfies a type without widening its inferred type. In TDD, using `satisfies` on test fixtures is a Red-phase technique: the fixture fails to compile if it violates the type contract, surfacing a Red before any runtime assertion. This is stronger than a plain type annotation (which widens literals) and weaker than a full runtime assertion (which executes). The `satisfies` fixture pattern catches type regressions in domain objects at the moment a schema changes — if a required field is added to `Order`, every `satisfies Order` fixture becomes a compile error simultaneously, turning all affected tests Red without any runtime.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";

// Domain types
type OrderStatus = "pending" | "processing" | "shipped" | "cancelled";
interface Order {
  id: string;
  status: OrderStatus;
  lineItems: Array<{ sku: string; qty: number; unitPriceCents: number }>;
  totalCents: number;
}

// 'satisfies Order' — compile-time Red if fixture violates the Order contract
// Literal types are preserved (id is "ord_1", not widened to string)
const pendingOrder = {
  id: "ord_1",
  status: "pending",
  lineItems: [{ sku: "WIDGET-A", qty: 2, unitPriceCents: 500 }],
  totalCents: 1000,
} satisfies Order;

const cancelledOrder = {
  id: "ord_2",
  status: "cancelled",
  lineItems: [],
  totalCents: 0,
} satisfies Order;

describe("OrderRepository", () => {
  it("filters orders by status", () => {
    const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository([pendingOrder, cancelledOrder]);
    const pending = repo.findByStatus("pending");
    // Literal type preserved: pendingOrder.id is "ord_1" (not just string)
    expect(pending).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(pending[0].id).toBe(pendingOrder.id);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** test fixtures are complex domain objects whose type correctness should be verified at compile time before any test runs.
- **Do NOT use when** the fixture is a partial object intended to be spread into a complete object — `satisfies` requires all required fields, which defeats the purpose of a partial fixture factory.
- **Alternative:** `as const satisfies Type` for immutable fixtures where literal-type narrowing of nested properties is also needed.

[official]

---

### 15. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `vi.defineHelper` — Custom Assertion Library Stack Traces [official]

`vi.defineHelper(fn)` (Vitest 4.1) wraps a function so that Vitest removes the helper's own stack frames from error traces and points failures back to the call site in the test file. This is the foundation of a well-crafted custom assertion library built for TDD: when `assertMatchesOrderSchema(result)` fails, the stack trace points to the test line that called `assertMatchesOrderSchema`, not to the internals of the assertion helper. Without `vi.defineHelper`, the Red-phase failure message includes several lines of helper-internal frames that obscure which test triggered the failure. Use `vi.defineHelper` for any shared assertion function that calls `expect()` internally — the improvement in stack trace clarity directly reduces Red-phase debugging time.

```typescript
import { vi, expect } from "vitest";
import type { Order } from "../src/types";

// Custom assertion helper wrapped with vi.defineHelper so stack traces point
// to the test call site, not to the internals of this function
export const assertValidOrder = vi.defineHelper(function assertValidOrder(
  value: unknown
): asserts value is Order {
  expect(value).toMatchObject({
    id: expect.stringMatching(/^ord_/),
    status: expect.stringMatching(/^(pending|processing|shipped|cancelled)$/),
    lineItems: expect.arrayOf(
      expect.objectContaining({
        sku: expect.any(String),
        qty: expect.any(Number),
        unitPriceCents: expect.any(Number),
      })
    ),
    totalCents: expect.any(Number),
  });
});

// In tests — stack trace on failure points to THIS line, not to helper internals
import { assertValidOrder } from "../test/helpers/order-assertions";

it("createOrder returns a valid order object", async () => {
  const result = await createOrder({ userId: "usr_1", items: [] });
  assertValidOrder(result); // <- failure stack trace points here
  expect(result.lineItems).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff note:**
- **Use when** building shared test helper libraries used across many test files — clean stack traces dramatically reduce debugging time in the Red phase.
- **Do NOT use when** the helper is used in only one test file — inline assertions are more readable and the stack trace overhead is not a concern.
- **Alternative:** Vitest's `expect.extend()` for matchers that need to integrate with the `expect` chain (`.toBeValidOrder()` syntax); `vi.defineHelper` is better for standalone assertion functions.

[official]

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 34 Additions

132. **[community] Vitest 4.0's removal of the `basic` reporter breaks CI pipelines that explicitly set `reporters: ['basic']` — the process exits with `Error: Unknown reporter: basic` before any tests run, producing a misleading "zero tests ran" result rather than a test failure.** Teams that pin `reporters: ['basic']` in `vitest.config.ts` to avoid the tree-view output (which clutters CI logs) discover after upgrading to Vitest 4.0 that the `basic` reporter no longer exists and no fallback is applied — the test process crashes on startup, not during test execution. WHY this matters: the error message `Unknown reporter: basic` appears before any test output, so monitoring systems that check for test-failure patterns in stdout see zero failures and report the build as "passed" when it actually never ran — a silent CI bypass. Fix: replace `reporters: ['basic']` with `reporters: ['default']` in your Vitest 4.0+ config; if you need minimal CI output, use `reporters: ['dot']` or `reporters: ['agent']` for AI-optimised minimal output.

133. **[community] Jest 30's `jsdom` upgrade to v26 changes the behaviour of `window.matchMedia` — it now throws `NotImplementedError` instead of returning `undefined`, breaking any test that relied on the old silent-failure mode.** Prior to Jest 30, `window.matchMedia` was simply absent (returned `undefined`) in jsdom, so code that checked `if (typeof window.matchMedia === 'function')` before calling it worked correctly in tests. After the jsdom v26 upgrade, `window.matchMedia` exists but throws `NotImplementedError: window.matchMedia is not implemented` when called, bypassing the `typeof` guard entirely. WHY this matters: the `NotImplementedError` propagates through React responsive-design hooks (e.g., `useMediaQuery`) and turns previously passing tests into runtime errors with a stack trace pointing to jsdom internals — making the root cause opaque. Fix: add `Object.defineProperty(window, 'matchMedia', { value: vi.fn().mockReturnValue({ matches: false, addListener: vi.fn(), removeListener: vi.fn(), dispatchEvent: vi.fn() }) })` in `setupFilesAfterFramework`; or use the `jest-matchmedia-mock` package for a maintained polyfill.

134. **[community] `aroundEach` hooks in Vitest 4.1 are silently not invoked for the test body when the test is skipped with `test.skip` — the generator resumes at the `yield` but the test body function never runs, leaving any commit/commit-path logic after `yield` unreachable unless the generator has a `finally` block.** Teams using `aroundEach` for database transaction rollback discover that `test.skip` tests cause the transaction to be opened but the cleanup path (e.g., `await transaction.commit()`) is placed after `yield` without a `finally` guard, so the transaction is left open. WHY this matters: unclosed transactions hold row-level locks, which cause subsequent non-skipped tests to time out waiting for lock release, creating a cascade of mysterious failures after the first `test.skip` in a suite. Fix: always wrap all post-`yield` code in `aroundEach` inside a `try/finally` block — the `finally` block is the only cleanup path that executes unconditionally regardless of whether the test body ran, was skipped, or threw.

135. **[community] Vitest 4.0's `expect.schemaMatching()` does not evaluate Zod `.refine()` predicates — it validates only the structural shape via Standard Schema v1, producing false-positive Green tests for invalid business-rule data.** A Zod schema with `.refine((user) => user.age >= 18, 'Must be adult')` passes `expect(payload).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(schema))` even when `payload.age` is `16`, because `schemaMatching` runs only the structural parse step. WHY this matters: the TDD contract test appears to enforce the `age >= 18` business rule but is silently ignoring it — the Green test passes for invalid data, creating false confidence that the schema is protecting the domain boundary. Fix: use `expect(schema.safeParse(payload).success).toBe(true)` for full Zod validation including refinements; reserve `expect.schemaMatching()` for structural shape checks where refinement predicates are either absent or tested separately in their own `describe` block.

136. **[community] `--detect-async-leaks` in Vitest 4.1 produces false-positive leak reports for `fetch` requests that internally use `AbortSignal.timeout()` — the Node.js `async_hooks` tracking captures the timeout timer as a leaked resource even when the request completes successfully before the timeout fires.** Code that calls `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })` creates an internal timer in Node.js that is cleaned up by the AbortSignal on completion, but the `async_hooks` instrumentation captures the timer creation before the cleanup and reports it as a "leaked async resource" if the test completes faster than the 5000ms timeout. WHY this matters: tests for fast API calls reliably trigger the false-positive, turning every HTTP-calling test in `--detect-async-leaks` mode into a flaky test — ironically, the leak-detection tool itself causes the flakiness. Fix: replace `AbortSignal.timeout(n)` with an explicitly managed `AbortController` and call `controller.abort()` in the test's `afterEach`/`finally` block; or disable `detectAsyncLeaks` per-file with `// @vitest-environment node\n// detectAsyncLeaks: false` in affected test files until a `ignoreResourceTypes` config option is available.

137. **[community] Vitest 4.0's programmatic `waitForTestRunEnd()` API resolves before the coverage provider has finished writing the coverage JSON file to disk — reading the coverage report immediately after `await vitest.waitForTestRunEnd()` returns a stale or empty file.** Tools that use Vitest's programmatic API to drive TDD loops (running tests, collecting coverage, feeding results to an LLM agent) discover that `fs.readFileSync('./coverage/coverage-final.json')` returns `{}` or throws `ENOENT` because the coverage provider flushes asynchronously after `waitForTestRunEnd` resolves. WHY this matters: the LLM agent receives an empty coverage report and incorrectly concludes that the Green-phase implementation has 0% coverage, triggering unnecessary re-implementation attempts. Fix: always await `vitest.getCoverageProvider()?.generateCoverage()` explicitly after `waitForTestRunEnd()` before reading any coverage files; do not rely on filesystem polling as coverage file write timing is non-deterministic across Vitest versions.

### 1. TDD for TypeScript 5.9 `Uint8Array` / `ArrayBuffer` Hierarchy Break — Binary Protocol Tests [official]

TypeScript 5.9 removed `ArrayBuffer` as a supertype of typed arrays (including Node.js `Buffer`). Before 5.9, `Buffer` was assignable to `ArrayBuffer`, so functions typed as `(data: ArrayBuffer) => void` silently accepted `Buffer` arguments. After 5.9, passing a `Buffer` where `ArrayBuffer` is expected is a compile error — surfaced during the Red phase. TDD for binary protocol handling must now use `Uint8Array` as the canonical type for byte sequences, or explicitly call `.buffer` to extract the underlying `ArrayBuffer`. This is a forced-correct TDD signal: any test fixture that constructs a `Buffer` and passes it to a `process(data: ArrayBuffer)` function will fail to compile, pushing the API toward the explicit and correct type.

```typescript
// binary-processor.test.ts — TypeScript 5.9: typed array hierarchy break
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { processFrame } from "./binary-processor.js";

// RED: define the contract — processFrame must accept Uint8Array
describe("processFrame", () => {
  it("parses a 4-byte header from a Uint8Array", () => {
    // Correct: Uint8Array — NOT Buffer passed directly to ArrayBuffer-typed param
    const frame = new Uint8Array([0x01, 0x02, 0x00, 0x10]);
    const parsed = processFrame(frame);
    expect(parsed.version).toBe(1);
    expect(parsed.type).toBe(2);
    expect(parsed.payloadLength).toBe(16); // bytes 3-4 as big-endian uint16
  });

  it("throws FrameError when payload length exceeds 4096 bytes", () => {
    // Edge case exposed by TypeScript 5.9's stricter Uint8Array typing
    const oversized = new Uint8Array([0x01, 0x02, 0x10, 0x01]); // length = 4097
    expect(() => processFrame(oversized)).toThrow(/FrameError/);
  });

  it("round-trips a Buffer via .buffer property accessor", () => {
    // TypeScript 5.9: Buffer is NOT assignable to ArrayBuffer directly
    // Must use the .buffer accessor to extract the underlying ArrayBuffer
    const nodeBuffer = Buffer.from([0x01, 0x02, 0x00, 0x04]);
    const typed = new Uint8Array(nodeBuffer.buffer, nodeBuffer.byteOffset, nodeBuffer.length);
    const parsed = processFrame(typed);
    expect(parsed.version).toBe(1);
  });
});

// GREEN: implementation with Uint8Array parameter
// binary-processor.ts
export interface FrameHeader { version: number; type: number; payloadLength: number; }
export function processFrame(data: Uint8Array): FrameHeader {
  if (data.length < 4) throw new Error("FrameError: too short");
  const view = new DataView(data.buffer, data.byteOffset, data.byteLength);
  const payloadLength = view.getUint16(2, false); // big-endian
  if (payloadLength > 4096) throw new Error("FrameError: payload too large");
  return { version: data[0]!, type: data[1]!, payloadLength };
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Apply this pattern whenever binary protocol functions accept byte buffers — WebSocket frames, file parsers, crypto functions. The TypeScript 5.9 `lib.d.ts` change makes previously hidden `Buffer`/`ArrayBuffer` confusions into compile-time Red-phase errors. Do NOT update `@types/node` without reading the migration guide first — older `Buffer` usages as `ArrayBuffer` arguments are now type errors. Alternative: abstract the binary input behind a `ByteSource` interface with `.toUint8Array(): Uint8Array` to decouple from both `Buffer` and `ArrayBuffer`.

[official]

### 2. TDD with TypeScript 5.9 Prescriptive `tsc --init` Defaults as Zero-Boilerplate Test Harness [official]

TypeScript 5.9 ships a redesigned `tsc --init` that generates a minimal, prescriptive `tsconfig.json` with `moduleDetection: "force"`, `verbatimModuleSyntax: true`, `isolatedModules: true`, and `types: []` by default. These four options collectively eliminate an entire class of Red-phase phantom errors: `types: []` prevents accidental `@types/jest` leaking into Vitest projects (mixing `.toBeCalled()` and `.toHaveBeenCalled()` signatures), and `verbatimModuleSyntax` forces `import type` for type-only imports, which prevents test-double modules with only re-exported types from leaking into the runtime bundle. Writing a new TDD project from `tsc --init` now produces a harness that catches cross-framework type contamination at compile time before the first test is run.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — TypeScript 5.9 minimal defaults from tsc --init (TDD-annotated)
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",          // explicit ESM/CJS interop — no import ambiguity
    "target": "esnext",            // full ES2025+ support for using, Temporal, import defer
    "moduleDetection": "force",    // all .ts files treated as modules (no accidental global scope)
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,  // 'import type' required for type-only imports
    "isolatedModules": true,       // each file transpilable independently — fast ts-jest/esbuild
    "types": [],                   // zero ambient type injection — prevent @types/jest leaking
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,     // array[n] returns T | undefined — forces null-safe fixtures
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true    // {} != { prop: undefined } — stricter test data shapes
  }
}

// vitest.config.ts — pair with the tsc --init tsconfig
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    environment: "node",
    // No globals: true — forces explicit import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest"
    // Prevents the @types/jest global pollution that types: [] blocks at tsconfig level
  },
});

// verbatimModuleSyntax catches leaking test-double types into production builds:
// Before: import { FakeMailer } from "../test-doubles/FakeMailer.js"; // type AND value
// After (correct): import type { FakeMailer } from "../test-doubles/FakeMailer.js";
// If FakeMailer is used as a value (new FakeMailer()), TS errors at the import site immediately
const _example: import("vitest").ExpectStatic = {} as never; // illustrative only
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the TypeScript 5.9 `tsc --init` defaults for all new TDD projects — they encode accumulated community wisdom about isolation and are the right baseline. Do NOT apply `types: []` to existing projects without auditing every `@types/` package; removing an ambient type declaration the codebase depends on produces compile errors that are difficult to trace. Alternative: `typeRoots: ["node_modules/@types/vitest"]` is a more surgical approach than `types: []` when you need some ambient types but want to exclude others.

[official]

### 3. TDD for Jest 30 `jest.onGenerateMock` — Realistic Auto-Mock Baseline [official]

Jest 30 introduced `jest.onGenerateMock(moduleName, generator)` which registers a global callback that runs whenever Jest's automatic mock generator creates a mock for a specific module. In TDD, this eliminates per-test `mockReturnValue` boilerplate for commonly mocked modules: each test file only specifies the _deviation_ from the realistic baseline. The pattern is a global "mock schema" that defines what sensible defaults look like for each module, analogous to a fixture factory — but integrated into Jest's auto-mock system rather than requiring explicit import. Writing the `onGenerateMock` callback is itself a TDD exercise: the callback's shape documents the contractual surface of the mocked module and must be updated whenever the real module's API changes.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts — register realistic mock baselines for all test files
import { jest } from "@jest/globals";

// Realistic baseline for the analytics module — every test file starts here
jest.onGenerateMock("../src/analytics/tracker.js", () => ({
  track: jest.fn().mockReturnValue(Promise.resolve({ queued: true, eventId: "evt_mock" })),
  flush: jest.fn().mockReturnValue(Promise.resolve({ flushed: 0 })),
  isEnabled: jest.fn().mockReturnValue(true),
  configure: jest.fn(),
}));

jest.onGenerateMock("../src/auth/tokenService.js", () => ({
  sign: jest.fn().mockReturnValue("mock.jwt.token"),
  verify: jest.fn().mockReturnValue({ sub: "user_mock", exp: 9999999999 }),
  refresh: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ token: "refreshed.jwt.token" }),
}));

// analytics-service.test.ts — only specify the deviation from the baseline
import { describe, it, expect, jest } from "@jest/globals";
import { AnalyticsService } from "../src/analytics/AnalyticsService.js";

jest.mock("../src/analytics/tracker.js");
import { tracker } from "../src/analytics/tracker.js";

describe("AnalyticsService.recordPurchase", () => {
  it("tracks a purchase event with the correct payload", async () => {
    // Baseline: tracker.track already returns { queued: true } — no override needed
    const svc = new AnalyticsService(tracker);
    await svc.recordPurchase({ orderId: "ord_1", amountCents: 9900 });
    expect(tracker.track).toHaveBeenCalledWith("purchase", {
      orderId: "ord_1",
      amountCents: 9900,
    });
  });

  it("throws when the tracker is disabled", async () => {
    // Deviation from baseline: override isEnabled for this test only
    jest.mocked(tracker.isEnabled).mockReturnValueOnce(false);
    const svc = new AnalyticsService(tracker);
    await expect(svc.recordPurchase({ orderId: "ord_2", amountCents: 100 }))
      .rejects.toThrow("Analytics is disabled");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `jest.onGenerateMock` for modules mocked in more than five test files where a realistic baseline reduces per-file boilerplate. The callback is documentation of the module's contractual API and must be updated when the real module changes. Do NOT use `onGenerateMock` for modules with frequently changing return shapes — the callback becomes a maintenance liability. Alternative: a shared `mockFactories.ts` file with named builder functions achieves similar documentation value without tying into Jest's auto-mock mechanism, making it easier to migrate away from Jest.

[official]
