### 4. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `mockThrow` / `mockThrowOnce` — Concise Error-Path Red Phase [official]

Vitest 4.1 added `.mockThrow(error)` and `.mockThrowOnce(error)` as direct alternatives to the verbose `.mockImplementation(() => { throw new Error(...) })` pattern. In TDD, the error-path Red test is often the last to be written but the most important for fault tolerance. Shorter mock error syntax reduces the friction of writing error-path tests and removes a common mistake: forgetting to wrap the `throw` inside a `() =>` closure. `mockThrow` also accepts pre-constructed `Error` instances, enabling TDD for error identity checks (`instanceof`), error cause chains, and custom `Error` subclass assertions.

```typescript
// payment-processor.test.ts — Vitest 4.1 mockThrow/mockThrowOnce
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { PaymentProcessor } from "./PaymentProcessor.js";
import type { StripeClient } from "./StripeClient.js";

const mockStripe = {
  createCharge: vi.fn(),
  refund: vi.fn(),
} satisfies Record<keyof StripeClient, ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>>;

beforeEach(() => { vi.clearAllMocks(); });

describe("PaymentProcessor.charge", () => {
  it("returns a ChargeResult on success", async () => {
    mockStripe.createCharge.mockResolvedValue({ id: "ch_123", status: "succeeded" });
    const processor = new PaymentProcessor(mockStripe);
    const result = await processor.charge({ amountCents: 5000, currency: "USD" });
    expect(result.chargeId).toBe("ch_123");
  });

  it("throws PaymentDeclinedError when Stripe returns a card_declined error", async () => {
    // Vitest 4.1: mockThrowOnce with a pre-built error — no () => wrapper needed
    const declineError = Object.assign(new Error("card_declined"), { code: "card_declined" });
    mockStripe.createCharge.mockThrowOnce(declineError);

    const processor = new PaymentProcessor(mockStripe);
    await expect(processor.charge({ amountCents: 1000, currency: "USD" }))
      .rejects.toMatchObject({ message: expect.stringContaining("declined") });
  });

  it("throws NetworkError for permanent connection failure", async () => {
    // mockThrow (permanent): every call throws until explicitly cleared
    mockStripe.createCharge.mockThrow(new Error("ECONNREFUSED"));

    const processor = new PaymentProcessor(mockStripe);
    await expect(processor.charge({ amountCents: 500, currency: "USD" }))
      .rejects.toThrow("ECONNREFUSED");
    // Verify no retry was attempted on connection errors
    expect(mockStripe.createCharge).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it("retries once on a transient timeout then succeeds", async () => {
    // mockThrowOnce for first call; mockResolvedValue for the retry
    mockStripe.createCharge
      .mockThrowOnce(Object.assign(new Error("timeout"), { code: "ETIMEDOUT" }))
      .mockResolvedValue({ id: "ch_456", status: "succeeded" });

    const processor = new PaymentProcessor(mockStripe);
    const result = await processor.charge({ amountCents: 2000, currency: "USD" });
    expect(result.chargeId).toBe("ch_456");
    expect(mockStripe.createCharge).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `mockThrow`/`mockThrowOnce` for all synchronous error-path tests — they are more readable and less error-prone than `.mockImplementation(() => { throw ... })`. For async errors (rejected promises), continue using `.mockRejectedValue()`. Do NOT confuse `mockThrow` (synchronous throw) with `mockRejectedValue` (async rejection) — a synchronous throw from an `async` mock function still produces a rejected promise, but a synchronous caller testing `.mockThrow` will get the error thrown synchronously. Alternative: `.mockImplementation(() => { throw customError; })` remains valid but is more verbose; prefer `mockThrow` in new code.

[official]

---

### 5. TDD with Vitest 4.1 `viteModuleRunner: false` — Production-Closer Execution Mode [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced the experimental `viteModuleRunner: false` option which runs test files directly through Node.js without the Vite module runner sandbox. The benefit for TDD: faster startup and test execution that more closely matches the production `node` runtime. This matters for TDD cycles in projects that discovered test-production divergence caused by Vite's module transform pipeline (e.g., `import.meta.env` substitution, path aliases resolved differently in test vs production). With `viteModuleRunner: false`, the Red-phase failure represents a true production-mode failure — the implementation must work without Vite's runtime transformations.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — experimental native Node.js execution for production-fidelity TDD
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    environment: "node",
    // Vitest 4.1 experimental: disable Vite module runner, use native Node.js execution
    // Requires migrating @/ aliases to Node.js #/ subpath imports (package.json "imports")
    // Use when test-production module resolution divergence is confirmed
  },
  // NOTE: experimentalVmModules and viteModuleRunner settings are separate concerns;
  // consult Vitest 4.1 docs for the exact config key — experimental APIs may shift names
});

// package.json — subpath imports required when viteModuleRunner: false is in use
// {
//   "imports": {
//     "#utils/*": "./src/utils/*.js",
//     "#domain/*": "./src/domain/*.js"
//   }
// }

// formatter.test.ts — works identically in test and production with # imports
import { formatCurrency } from "#utils/formatter.js";
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";

describe("formatCurrency", () => {
  it("formats USD cents as dollar string", () => {
    expect(formatCurrency(9900, "USD")).toBe("$99.00");
  });

  it("formats EUR cents as euro string", () => {
    expect(formatCurrency(15050, "EUR")).toBe("€150.50");
  });

  it("returns zero-value formatted correctly", () => {
    expect(formatCurrency(0, "USD")).toBe("$0.00");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `viteModuleRunner: false` after identifying confirmed test-production module resolution divergence from Vite's transform pipeline. It requires migrating all `@/` aliases to Node.js `#/` subpath imports, a non-trivial refactor for large projects. Do NOT enable this option without first running the full test suite in both modes — some tests rely on Vite-specific transformations (e.g., `import.meta.glob`) incompatible with native Node.js. Alternative: TypeScript 6.0 `#/` subpath import syntax achieves the same production-fidelity benefit without disabling Vite's module runner, while enabling better tree-shaking.

[official]

---

### 6. TDD for Vitest 4.1 GitHub Actions Job Summary Reporter [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced a built-in GitHub Actions reporter that automatically appends a test summary table and flaky test permalinks to the Actions Job Summary page. For TDD workflows, this transforms the CI feedback loop: the Red-phase failure message appears directly in the pull request checks page without navigating into raw CI logs. The reporter activates automatically when `GITHUB_ACTIONS=true` is detected in the environment, requiring zero configuration. Combine it with `coverage.changed: true` to show per-PR coverage delta in the summary alongside test results. The "flaky test permalink" feature is TDD-relevant: any test that passes on retry is surfaced with a direct link to the failing run, tracking intermittent Red-phase regressions that indicate non-deterministic test design.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — GitHub Actions reporter + coverage.changed TDD integration
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // github-actions reporter activates automatically via GITHUB_ACTIONS env var.
    // Explicitly listing it ensures it also runs in other CI environments with the env var set.
    reporter: process.env["CI"] ? ["github-actions", "dot"] : ["verbose"],
    coverage: {
      enabled: process.env["CI"] === "true",
      provider: "v8",
      reporter: ["lcov", "text-summary"],
      // coverage.changed (Vitest 4.1): enforce thresholds only on PR-modified files
      // prevents failing the PR because of untouched legacy code below threshold
      thresholds: {
        branches: 80,
        functions: 85,
        lines: 85,
        statements: 85,
      },
    },
  },
});

// Expected Job Summary output in GitHub Actions PR check page:
// ┌─────────────────────────────────┬────────┬──────────┐
// │ Test Suite                      │ Status │ Duration │
// ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤
// │ PaymentProcessor › charge       │ ✓ Pass │   42ms   │
// │ OrderService › place            │ ✓ Pass │   87ms   │
// └─────────────────────────────────┴────────┴──────────┘
// Flaky tests detected: 1
//  ⚠ NotificationDispatcher › dispatch — passed on retry
//    Link: https://github.com/org/repo/actions/runs/1234567890
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Enable the GitHub Actions reporter for any TDD project hosted on GitHub — it costs nothing (auto-detected) and adds PR-level Red-phase visibility without changing the local development experience. Do NOT suppress the `github-actions` reporter with `reporter: ['dot']` in CI — you lose the Job Summary visibility. Alternative: `junit` reporter exports XML that can be parsed by third-party GitHub Actions (e.g., `dorny/test-reporter`) for a more customizable summary; the built-in reporter is simpler but less configurable.

[official]

---

### 7. TDD for Vitest 4.1 Test Tags as CI-Stage Filter [official]

Vitest 4.1 test tags allow attaching named labels to individual test cases via the `{ tags: ['smoke', 'integration'] }` option in the test body's options object. In a TDD pipeline, tags map to CI stages: `smoke` tests run on every commit, `integration` tests on PR merge, `e2e` tests nightly. Writing the tag in the Red phase communicates the intended test tier before implementation begins — it is a first-class TDD design decision, not an afterthought. The `--tags-filter` flag supports boolean algebra (`smoke AND NOT flaky`, `integration OR e2e`), making it possible to route tagged subsets to specific CI agents without modifying test files.

```typescript
// order-service.test.ts — tags as TDD pipeline-tier annotations
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import { OrderService } from "./OrderService.js";
import type { OrderRepository, PaymentGateway } from "./ports.js";

describe("OrderService", () => {
  it(
    "returns an order ID when placement succeeds",
    { tags: ["smoke", "unit"] },
    async () => {
      const repo = { save: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue("ord_1") } as unknown as OrderRepository;
      const pay = { charge: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ chargeId: "ch_1" }) } as unknown as PaymentGateway;
      const svc = new OrderService(repo, pay);
      const id = await svc.place({ userId: "u1", items: [{ sku: "A", qty: 1 }] });
      expect(id).toBe("ord_1");
    }
  );

  it(
    "rolls back the order if payment fails",
    { tags: ["smoke", "unit"] },
    async () => {
      const repo = {
        save: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue("ord_2"),
        delete: vi.fn(),
      } as unknown as OrderRepository;
      const pay = { charge: vi.fn().mockRejectedValue(new Error("card_declined")) } as unknown as PaymentGateway;
      const svc = new OrderService(repo, pay);
      await expect(svc.place({ userId: "u2", items: [{ sku: "B", qty: 1 }] }))
        .rejects.toThrow("card_declined");
      expect((repo as any).delete).toHaveBeenCalledWith("ord_2");
    }
  );

  // Integration tier — planned via it.todo with future tag assignment
  it.todo("persists the order to PostgreSQL"); // tags: ['integration']
  it.todo("charges Stripe with correct amount"); // tags: ['integration', 'payments']
});

// CI stage commands:
// Commit (< 30s): npx vitest run --reporter=dot --tags-filter="smoke AND unit"
// PR merge:       npx vitest run --tags-filter="smoke OR integration"
// Nightly:        npx vitest run  (no filter — runs all tags including e2e)
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use tags when a suite has grown to the point where running all tests on every commit causes feedback latency above two minutes. Tags are the TDD-preferred solution over file-path-based filtering because they keep all tests for a feature co-located. Do NOT assign tags inconsistently — a `smoke` test that takes 10 seconds destroys the fast-commit tier benefit. Alternative: Vitest project configuration (`projects` array) separates test types by config file rather than tag; use that approach when test types also have different environment or coverage requirements.

[official]

---

### 8. TDD for Jest 30 `test.each` `%$` Placeholder — Self-Documenting Parameterized Red Phase [official]

Jest 30 introduced the `%$` placeholder in `test.each` test title templates, which inserts the 1-based index of each test case. Combined with descriptive column names (`$input`, `$scenario`), this produces Red-phase failure messages that identify both the case number and the scenario without verbose manual labelling. The pattern is TDD-specific: the test title generated by `%$` appears in the failure output during the Red phase, and the numbered cases provide a direct reference to the test data table row that failed — useful for precise references in PR review comments ("case 6 is failing").

```typescript
// validators.test.ts — Jest 30 %$ placeholder for self-documenting parameterized tests
import { describe, it, expect } from "@jest/globals";
import { validateEmailAddress, type ValidationResult } from "./validators.js";

// %$ inserts 1-based case number; $input and $expected.valid inline values
describe("validateEmailAddress", () => {
  it.each<{ input: string; expected: ValidationResult }>([
    { input: "user@example.com",       expected: { valid: true,  error: null } },         // case 1
    { input: "user+tag@sub.domain.co", expected: { valid: true,  error: null } },         // case 2
    { input: "missing-at-sign",        expected: { valid: false, error: "invalid_format" } }, // case 3
    { input: "double@@at.com",         expected: { valid: false, error: "invalid_format" } }, // case 4
    { input: "",                       expected: { valid: false, error: "required" } },   // case 5
    { input: "a@b",                    expected: { valid: false, error: "invalid_format" } }, // case 6 - no TLD
  ])(
    "case %$ — '$input' is valid=$expected.valid (error: $expected.error)",
    ({ input, expected }) => {
      const result = validateEmailAddress(input);
      expect(result.valid).toBe(expected.valid);
      expect(result.error).toBe(expected.error);
    }
  );
});

// Red-phase failure output with %$:
//   ✗ validateEmailAddress › case 6 — 'a@b' is valid=false (error: invalid_format)
//     Expected: false  Received: true
// vs without %$:
//   ✗ validateEmailAddress › 'a@b' is valid=false (error: invalid_format)
// The case number makes PR comments precise: "case 6 fails — no-TLD check missing"
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `%$` in `test.each` tables with more than five cases where referring to a specific failing case in code reviews or issue comments is common. The case number is stable as long as cases are not reordered — reordering changes all subsequent numbers. Do NOT use `%$` as the sole identifier in commit messages — pair it with a descriptive title segment so the case is identifiable without looking at the test data table. Alternative: explicitly name each case with a `name` column in the test data table (`it.each([{ name: 'valid RFC email', ... }])('%s', ...)`) for maximum clarity at the cost of more verbose data tables.

[official]

---

### 9. TDD for Jest 30 `globalsCleanup: 'on'` — Cross-File Global Isolation [official]

Jest 30's `globalsCleanup: 'on'` option resets JavaScript globals (DOM properties, `window.*`, `navigator.*`) between test files. For TDD, this eliminates the class of cross-file contamination where one test file's setup bleeds into a later file via shared global state. The Red phase in isolation (single test file) passes, but the Red phase under full suite execution fails — a maddening non-deterministic pattern that `globalsCleanup: 'on'` prevents by construction. TDD projects should enable this option on initial setup so the clean-isolation invariant is baked in from the first test.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — Jest 30 globalsCleanup for strict TDD isolation
import type { Config } from "jest";

const config: Config = {
  testEnvironment: "jsdom",
  testEnvironmentOptions: {
    globalsCleanup: "on", // resets window/navigator/document globals between test files
  },
  setupFilesAfterFramework: ["<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts"],
};
export default config;

// jest.setup.ts — protecting specific globals from the cleanup sweep
import { protectProperties } from "jest-util";

// window.location.origin set here survives the globalsCleanup sweep via protectProperties
protectProperties(window, ["location"]);
Object.defineProperty(window, "location", {
  value: { origin: "https://app.test", href: "https://app.test/" },
  writable: true,
  configurable: true,
});

// order-form.test.ts — benefits from globalsCleanup: 'on'
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import { OrderForm } from "../src/OrderForm.js";

test("submits the form to the correct origin", () => {
  // With globalsCleanup: 'on', window.location.origin is reliably 'https://app.test'
  // regardless of what a preceding test file may have mutated on window.location
  render(<OrderForm />);
  expect(screen.getByTestId("form-action")).toHaveAttribute(
    "action",
    "https://app.test/api/orders"
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Enable `globalsCleanup: 'on'` for any Jest project using `jsdom` — it is the safest default for DOM-testing TDD. Use `protectProperties` from `jest-util` to exempt intentionally persistent globals. Do NOT enable `globalsCleanup: 'on'` without verifying every `window.*` assignment in `setupFilesAfterFramework` — the sweep is aggressive and will reset properties meant to be persistent baseline mocks. Alternative: `globalsCleanup: 'soft'` resets only undeclared (leaked) global assignments, making it safer as a migration step from no cleanup.

[official]

---

### 10. TDD with TypeScript 5.9 `--module node20` for Stable LTS Node.js Project Configuration [official]

TypeScript 5.9 stabilised `--module node20` as a separate option from `--module nodenext`. The distinction matters for TDD: `nodenext` reflects the latest Node.js module semantics (which may evolve), while `node20` is a frozen snapshot targeting Node.js v20 LTS. For TDD projects pinned to Node 20 LTS, `--module node20` eliminates future surprises where a TypeScript upgrade changes `nodenext` semantics for Node 21/22 features that are not present in Node 20. The TDD discipline: write tests against a known-stable module interface; avoid "works today but breaks after a TypeScript upgrade."

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — TypeScript 5.9 node20 for LTS-pinned TDD projects
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "node20",           // frozen Node.js v20 semantics — not affected by Node 22+ changes
    "moduleResolution": "node20",
    "target": "es2023",           // node20 implies es2023 as the default target
    "strict": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src"
  }
}

// Example: node20 correctly handles require() of ESM modules (Node.js 20.x+ feature)
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { loadPluginModule } from "./plugin-loader.js";

describe("loadPluginModule", () => {
  it("loads an ESM plugin correctly under node20 module semantics", async () => {
    // node20: require() of ES modules is valid in Node 20+ — TypeScript models this correctly
    const plugin = await loadPluginModule("./test-fixtures/esm-plugin.mjs");
    expect(plugin.name).toBe("test-esm-plugin");
    expect(typeof plugin.execute).toBe("function");
  });

  it("uses import attributes (with:) not deprecated import assertions (assert:)", async () => {
    // node20: import assertions are rejected; import attributes (with) are the correct syntax
    // This test ensures the plugin-loader uses the correct syntax
    await expect(loadPluginModule("./test-fixtures/json-plugin.json"))
      .resolves.toMatchObject({ type: "json-plugin" });
  });

  it("rejects modules using deprecated assert: import syntax at compile time", () => {
    // TypeScript with node20 will flag: import data from './data.json' assert { type: 'json' }
    // as deprecated; the correct form is: import data from './data.json' with { type: 'json' }
    // This test documents that the loader wrapper validates import syntax
    expect(() => loadPluginModule("./test-fixtures/legacy-assert.json"))
      .toThrow(/deprecated import assertion/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `--module node20` when the project is explicitly pinned to Node.js v20 LTS and you want TypeScript module semantics stable across TypeScript upgrades. When tracking the latest Node.js release (v22+), use `--module nodenext` to benefit from new module features as they stabilise. Do NOT use `--module node20` for browser or Deno projects — `node20` targets Node.js runtime semantics specifically. Alternative: `--module esnext` with a bundler (Vite, esbuild) for browser-targeting projects where `node20` semantics are irrelevant.

[official]

---

### 11. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `coverage.changed` — PR-Scoped Coverage Enforcement [official]

Vitest 4.1 added `coverage.changed` which, when enabled, restricts coverage threshold enforcement to files modified in the current PR or commit. This resolves a chronic TDD anti-pattern: a new PR adding two well-tested files fails CI because it trips a global 80% coverage threshold on unrelated legacy files. With `coverage.changed`, the TDD contract becomes "every file you touch must meet the threshold" — not "the entire codebase must meet the threshold right now." New development can proceed at the correct TDD cadence without being blocked by pre-existing coverage debt.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage.changed for PR-scoped TDD coverage enforcement
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      enabled: true,
      provider: "v8",
      reporter: ["lcov", "html", "text"],
      // coverage.changed: thresholds only applied to files differing from the base branch
      // Requires git — compares HEAD against origin/main (or VITEST_COVERAGE_BASE env var)
      thresholds: {
        lines: 85,
        functions: 90,
        branches: 80,
        statements: 85,
      },
    },
  },
});

// Without coverage.changed (existing behaviour):
//   PR adds PaymentRetry.ts (100% coverage) + touches StripeAdapter.ts (62% existing)
//   FAIL — StripeAdapter.ts has 62% coverage, below 85% threshold
//   Developer is blocked by legacy debt they didn't create

// With coverage.changed:
//   PaymentRetry.ts (new file, 100% coverage) — PASS
//   StripeAdapter.ts CHANGED LINES only — enforces 85% on the lines YOU changed
//   Legacy uncovered lines in StripeAdapter.ts — not counted against your PR

// CI command: npx vitest run --coverage --coverage.changed
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `coverage.changed` on any mature codebase with accumulated coverage debt — it unblocks feature TDD by scoping enforcement to files the developer is responsible for. Do NOT use `coverage.changed` as a replacement for tracking overall coverage trends; pair it with `lcov` reporter and Codecov or Coveralls to monitor global coverage drift over time. Alternative: per-directory `vitest.config.ts` with higher thresholds for actively developed modules achieves similar scoping without `coverage.changed`, but requires more configuration maintenance.

[official]

---

### 12. TDD for TypeScript 5.9 Cache Instantiation Fix — Complex Generic Type Tests [official]

TypeScript 5.9 introduced cache instantiation on type parameter mappers, fixing "excessive type instantiation depth" errors in complex libraries (Zod, tRPC, effect-ts). For TDD teams working on schema-heavy TypeScript code, this means tests involving deeply nested Zod schemas or chained generic utilities no longer time out or produce `TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep` during the Red phase. The fix makes the Red phase deterministic for previously un-testable complex generic signatures. TDD teams should use the TypeScript 5.9 upgrade as an opportunity to write type-level tests (`.test-d.ts` files with `expectTypeOf`) for previously "too complex to type-check" generic utilities.

```typescript
// schema-builder.test-d.ts — TypeScript 5.9 deep generic type testing (no longer times out)
import { describe, it } from "vitest";
import { expectTypeOf } from "vitest";
import { z } from "zod/v4";
import { buildApiSchema, type InferApiOutput } from "./schema-builder.js";

// TypeScript 5.8 and earlier: TS2589 (excessively deep) on nested schemas like this
// TypeScript 5.9 cache fix: these type assertions complete without hitting the depth limit

const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  customer: z.object({
    id: z.string(),
    address: z.object({
      street: z.string(),
      city: z.string(),
      country: z.enum(["US", "UK", "DE", "FR"]),
    }),
  }),
  items: z.array(z.object({
    sku: z.string(),
    qty: z.number(),
    price: z.object({ amount: z.number(), currency: z.string() }),
  })),
});

describe("InferApiOutput — deep generic type inference (TS 5.9 cache fix)", () => {
  it("infers the correct output type for a deeply nested Zod schema", () => {
    type OrderOutput = InferApiOutput<typeof OrderSchema>;
    // TypeScript 5.9: chained expectTypeOf calls work without TS2589
    expectTypeOf<OrderOutput["customer"]["address"]["country"]>()
      .toEqualTypeOf<"US" | "UK" | "DE" | "FR">();
    expectTypeOf<OrderOutput["items"][number]["price"]["amount"]>()
      .toEqualTypeOf<number>();
  });

  it("correctly infers discriminated union output type without type variable leaks", () => {
    const EventSchema = z.discriminatedUnion("type", [
      z.object({ type: z.literal("created"), createdAt: z.string() }),
      z.object({ type: z.literal("deleted"), deletedAt: z.string() }),
    ]);
    type Event = InferApiOutput<typeof EventSchema>;
    // TypeScript 5.9: union inference in complex generics no longer leaks type variables
    expectTypeOf<Event>().toMatchTypeOf<{ type: "created" | "deleted" }>();
  });

  it("preserves readonly modifier through double-wrapping in schema builder", () => {
    const readonlySchema = buildApiSchema(OrderSchema, { readonly: true });
    type ReadonlyOrder = InferApiOutput<typeof readonlySchema>;
    // Verify wrapping preserves field types
    expectTypeOf<ReadonlyOrder["id"]>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Write `.test-d.ts` type-level tests for any public generic API after upgrading to TypeScript 5.9 — the cache fix makes previously impossible type assertions practical. Do NOT write type-level tests for internal implementation details; focus on the public API surface that consumers depend on. The `expectTypeOf` approach is preferred over `// @ts-expect-error` comments because it is descriptive (documents expected types) rather than suppressive (silently hides errors). Alternative: `tsd` (npm) is a standalone type-testing tool; Vitest's built-in `expectTypeOf` is preferred for projects already on Vitest.

[official]

---

### 13. TDD for Vitest 4.1 Chai-Style Mock Assertions — Sinon Migration Path [official]

Vitest 4.1 added Chai-style mock assertions as an alternative to Jest-style matchers. The Chai syntax (`expect(fn).to.have.been.called`) is compatible with teams migrating from Sinon.js and Chai test suites to Vitest, reducing cognitive overhead during migration by preserving familiar assertion syntax. The TDD migration path: during the Red-phase rewrite of Sinon-based tests, Chai-style assertions pass the lint stage allowing incremental Green-phase migration. However, Chai-style assertions lack TypeScript type checking (the `.to.have.been` chain is a `Proxy` returning `any`), which is a meaningful tradeoff in a TDD workflow where type safety at the assertion site catches mistakes before the test runs.

```typescript
// email-service.test.ts — Chai-style vs Jest-style mock assertions (Vitest 4.1)
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { EmailService } from "./EmailService.js";
import type { MailTransport } from "./MailTransport.js";

const mockTransport = {
  send: vi.fn(),
  connect: vi.fn(),
  disconnect: vi.fn(),
} satisfies Record<keyof MailTransport, ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>>;

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.clearAllMocks();
  mockTransport.send.mockResolvedValue({ messageId: "msg_123", status: "sent" });
});

describe("EmailService.send", () => {
  it("connects, sends, and disconnects — Chai-style (Sinon migration path)", async () => {
    const svc = new EmailService(mockTransport);
    await svc.send({ to: "user@example.com", subject: "Hi", body: "Hello!" });

    // Chai-style — familiar for Sinon migrants; NOTE: NOT type-checked (Proxy → any)
    expect(mockTransport.connect).to.have.been.called;
    expect(mockTransport.send).to.have.been.calledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: "user@example.com" })
    );
    expect(mockTransport.disconnect).to.have.been.called;
  });

  it("connects, sends, and disconnects — Jest-style (preferred for new TDD code)", async () => {
    const svc = new EmailService(mockTransport);
    await svc.send({ to: "user@example.com", subject: "Hi", body: "Hello!" });

    // Jest-style — type-checked via @types/vitest; typos in matcher names caught at compile time
    expect(mockTransport.connect).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(mockTransport.send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: "user@example.com" })
    );
    expect(mockTransport.disconnect).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use Chai-style assertions ONLY during the migration window from a Sinon-based test suite. Once a test file is fully migrated, convert all Chai-style assertions to Jest-style (`toHaveBeenCalledWith`, `toHaveBeenCalledOnce`) to regain type safety. Do NOT use Chai-style assertions in new test files — they are untyped and typos like `calledWitch` instead of `calledWith` compile without error and silently pass (a false-Green with no safety net). Alternative: `vi.spyOn(obj, 'method')` with Jest-style matchers for all new spy-based tests.

[official]

---

### 14. TDD for Jest 30 Native `.mts` / `.cts` TypeScript File Support [official]

Jest 30 adds native support for `.mts` (ESM TypeScript) and `.cts` (CommonJS TypeScript) file extensions. TDD projects that enforce explicit module format via file extension — a TypeScript 5.x best practice — can now write test files as `*.test.mts` or `*.test.cts` without configuring custom `moduleNameMapper` entries. The `.mts` extension signals to both TypeScript and Jest that the file uses ESM semantics, preventing the accidental `require()` pattern in test utilities. Writing the first test for a new ESM-native module as `module.test.mts` is a TDD signal: the production module must also be `.mts` (or have `"type": "module"` in `package.json`), enforcing consistency between test and production module format at the file level.

```typescript
// payment-gateway.test.mts — Jest 30 native .mts ESM test file (no moduleNameMapper needed)
import { describe, it, expect, jest, beforeEach } from "@jest/globals";
import { PaymentGateway } from "../src/payment-gateway.mjs";
import type { ChargeRequest, ChargeResult } from "../src/payment-gateway.mjs";

jest.mock("../src/stripe-client.mjs");
import { StripeClient } from "../src/stripe-client.mjs";

const mockStripeClient = jest.mocked(StripeClient);

describe("PaymentGateway — ESM native (.mts)", () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    mockStripeClient.prototype.charge.mockClear();
  });

  it("creates a Stripe charge and returns a ChargeResult", async () => {
    mockStripeClient.prototype.charge.mockResolvedValue({
      id: "ch_mts_123",
      status: "succeeded",
      amount: 5000,
    });

    const gateway = new PaymentGateway(new StripeClient({ apiKey: "sk_test" }));
    const request: ChargeRequest = { amountCents: 5000, currency: "USD", userId: "u1" };
    const result: ChargeResult = await gateway.charge(request);

    expect(result.chargeId).toBe("ch_mts_123");
    expect(result.status).toBe("succeeded");
  });

  it("throws GatewayError on Stripe API failure", async () => {
    mockStripeClient.prototype.charge.mockRejectedValue(
      new Error("Your card has insufficient funds.")
    );
    const gateway = new PaymentGateway(new StripeClient({ apiKey: "sk_test" }));
    await expect(gateway.charge({ amountCents: 9999, currency: "USD", userId: "u2" }))
      .rejects.toMatchObject({ name: "GatewayError" });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `.mts` test files when migrating to full ESM and you want the file extension to document the module format explicitly. For projects with a mix of CommonJS and ESM modules in different subdirectories, `.mts`/`.cts` extensions eliminate the need for `"type": "module"` at the package level. Do NOT use `.mts` if the team is not yet on Jest 30 or Vitest 3.0+ — older test runners require `moduleNameMapper` configuration. Alternative: `"type": "module"` in `package.json` at the project level with `.ts` extensions is simpler for purely ESM projects — use `.mts` only when the project has a genuine mixed-format requirement.

[official]

---

### 15. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `test.extend` `onCleanup` Builder Pattern — Type-Safe Fixture Teardown [official]

Vitest 4.1 enhanced `test.extend()` with a builder pattern using `onCleanup()` for teardown instead of the older `[setup, { scope }]` tuple syntax. The builder pattern provides complete type inference from the fixture's return value without manual type declarations. In TDD, this means fixture authors get type-safe access to fixture values in test bodies automatically — no `as DatabaseConnection` casts needed. The `onCleanup` callback registers LIFO (last-in-first-out) teardown actions, which is critical for fixtures that must close connections, stop processes, or revert state in the correct dependency order.

```typescript
// fixtures/app.fixture.ts — Vitest 4.1 test.extend builder with onCleanup
import { test as base } from "vitest";
import { createApp, type AppInstance } from "../src/app.js";
import { createTestDatabase, type TestDatabase } from "../test-utils/db.js";

// Builder pattern: return value drives type inference — no manual interface needed
export const test = base
  .extend({
    // Database fixture: onCleanup registers teardown in LIFO order
    database: async ({}, use, { onCleanup }) => {
      const db = await createTestDatabase();
      onCleanup(async () => {
        await db.close(); // LIFO: this runs AFTER app.stop() below
      });
      await use(db);
    },
  })
  .extend({
    // App fixture depends on database — type-safe: 'database' is fully typed from above
    app: async ({ database }, use, { onCleanup }) => {
      const app = await createApp({ db: database.client });
      await app.start();
      onCleanup(async () => {
        await app.stop(); // LIFO order: app stops first, then database closes
      });
      await use(app);
    },
  });

// user-api.test.ts — type inference from builder: no fixture types needed
import { expect } from "vitest";
import { test } from "../fixtures/app.fixture.js";

test("POST /users creates a new user", async ({ app, database }) => {
  // app: AppInstance — inferred, no cast needed
  // database: TestDatabase — inferred, no cast needed
  const response = await app.inject({
    method: "POST",
    url: "/users",
    payload: { email: "new@example.com", role: "member" },
  });
  expect(response.statusCode).toBe(201);

  const created = await database.client.query(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1",
    ["new@example.com"]
  );
  expect(created.rows).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(created.rows[0].role).toBe("member");
});

test("GET /users/:id returns 404 for unknown IDs", async ({ app }) => {
  const response = await app.inject({ method: "GET", url: "/users/nonexistent-id" });
  expect(response.statusCode).toBe(404);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the `test.extend` builder pattern with `onCleanup` for all new Vitest fixture definitions — it is the Vitest 4.1 idiomatic API and provides better type inference than the older tuple syntax. LIFO cleanup order is critical when fixtures have dependencies: register cleanup in reverse dependency order (app before database, database before infrastructure). Do NOT use `onCleanup` outside `test.extend` fixtures — for ordinary test teardown, `afterEach` and `afterAll` are clearer. Alternative: the older `async ({}, use) => { const r = setup(); await use(r); await r.close(); }` inline pattern still works but does not support `onCleanup` for mid-fixture conditional teardown paths.

[official]

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 35 Additions

138. **[community] TypeScript 5.9's `ArrayBuffer` hierarchy break causes `Buffer.from(...)` to be unassignable to `ArrayBuffer` — code that previously passed `Buffer` directly to Web Crypto API functions (`crypto.subtle.digest(algorithm, data: ArrayBuffer)`) now fails to compile.** Tests that stub `crypto.subtle.digest` with a `Buffer` argument in `mockImplementation` compile under TypeScript 5.8 but produce `Argument of type 'Buffer' is not assignable to parameter of type 'ArrayBuffer'` under 5.9. WHY this matters: the failure appears in test mock setup code, not in production code, so developers first suspect the `vi.mock` pattern is wrong — they spend time debugging the mocking strategy before discovering it is a type hierarchy change. Fix: convert all `Buffer` arguments in crypto/binary test mocks to `Uint8Array` using `new Uint8Array(buffer.buffer, buffer.byteOffset, buffer.length)`; or add an explicit `buffer as unknown as ArrayBuffer` cast with a comment explaining the Node.js-to-Web-platform type mismatch.

139. **[community] Vitest 4.1 `test.extend` builder pattern type inference breaks down when two fixtures have the same property name at different extension levels — the later `.extend()` silently shadows the earlier fixture without a TypeScript error.** If `base.extend({ app: appFixture })` and then `.extend({ app: differentAppFixture })` is called on the result, the second `app` fixture completely replaces the first without any compiler warning — tests using `{ app }` receive the second implementation silently. WHY this matters: this silent shadowing is impossible to detect without inspecting the fixture chain; failures look like environment configuration issues rather than fixture composition errors. Fix: always use distinct descriptive names for each fixture at each extension level; treat fixture names as a globally unique namespace within a builder chain; document the full chain at the top of each fixture file.

140. **[community] Jest 30's `expect.arrayOf()` matcher is not recursive — `expect.arrayOf(expect.arrayOf(expect.any(Number)))` does NOT validate a 2D number array.** Only the outermost `arrayOf` constraint is evaluated; the inner `arrayOf` is treated as an opaque object and always passes. A developer writing a TDD contract test for a matrix-returning function uses nested `arrayOf` and gets a Green test even when inner arrays contain strings. WHY this matters: the false Green is particularly dangerous because the test intent is visually clear from reading the code — the developer believes nested structure is validated when it is not. Fix: assert each row explicitly with `result.forEach((row, i) => expect(row, \`row \${i}\`).toEqual(expect.arrayOf(expect.any(Number))))` until Jest adds recursive `arrayOf` support.

141. **[community] Vitest 4.1 `mockThrow` and `mockThrowOnce` do not trigger `catch` blocks in production code that uses `.then()` promise chains without `async/await`.** If production code is `service.fetch().then(processResult)` (no `await`), `mockThrow` on `fetch` causes `.then()` to be skipped, but the test's `.rejects.toThrow()` still works — masking a real production difference where the error propagation path diverges between promise-chain and `async/await` callers. WHY this matters: the TDD test confirms the error throws and rejects, but in production the `.then()` chain may swallow or re-wrap the error differently than the test asserts. Fix: write TDD tests that mirror the production consumption pattern — if production uses `.then()`, the test should too; never assume error propagation is identical between promise chains and `async/await` consumers.

142. **[community] TypeScript 5.9's `tsc --init` generates `"types": []` by default, breaking Vitest test files that rely on ambient global type injection from `@types/vitest`.** Projects initialized with `tsc --init` in TypeScript 5.9 get `"types": []` in the generated `tsconfig.json`. When test files use `describe`, `it`, `expect` as globals (via `globals: true` in `vitest.config.ts`), TypeScript no longer sees the global type declarations from `@types/vitest` because `types: []` suppresses all ambient types. The compiler reports `Cannot find name 'describe'` in every test file, not a configuration error. WHY this matters: the error message gives no hint that `types: []` is the root cause — developers add `/// <reference types="vitest/globals" />` to every test file instead of fixing the config. Fix: either add `"vitest/globals"` to the `types` array in `tsconfig.json` for the test scope, or (preferred) drop `globals: true` from Vitest config and use explicit `import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'` — which the Vitest team now recommends.

143. **[community] Jest 30's `globalsCleanup: 'on'` resets `performance.mark()` and `performance.measure()` entries between test files, breaking performance-budget tests that create marks in `beforeAll` and measure in individual tests.** Tests using the User Timing API (`performance.mark('start'); performance.measure('total', 'start')`) discover that `performance.getEntriesByName('start')` returns `[]` in test cases after the first file due to the cleanup sweep. WHY this matters: `performance.measure()` throws `'start' mark not found` — a runtime error, not a test assertion failure — making the root cause appear to be a broken test runner environment rather than a cleanup configuration issue. Fix: create `performance.mark()` entries inside `beforeEach` (not `beforeAll`) so they are recreated after each `globalsCleanup` sweep; or use `protectProperties(window.performance, ['mark', 'measure'])` to exclude the performance API from the sweep.

### 1. TDD for Vitest 4.0 `toMatchScreenshot` — Visual-Regression Red Phase as Design Contract [official]

Vitest 4.0 stabilised Browser Mode and introduced `toMatchScreenshot()` as a first-class assertion. In a TDD workflow, screenshots serve as **visual design contracts**: write the Red test first by asserting `toMatchScreenshot` against a component that does not yet exist; the initial run captures the baseline automatically (or fails with a missing-baseline error), prompting you to implement the design before committing. The Red phase is: component renders, but the snapshot does not match the agreed design mock. The Green phase is: implement the design until the snapshot matches. Refactor phase: extract shared styles/tokens without breaking the visual contract. Pair with `toBeInViewport` for ensuring critical UI elements are visible within the viewport before screenshot.

```typescript
// product-card.test.ts — Vitest 4.0 browser-mode screenshot TDD
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { render } from "@testing-library/vue";
import ProductCard from "./ProductCard.vue";

// Step 1 — Red: component exists but design not yet implemented
// First run captures baseline; subsequent runs diff against it
describe("ProductCard", () => {
  it("matches approved visual design at 375px", async () => {
    const { container } = render(ProductCard, {
      props: { title: "Widget Pro", price: 4999, currency: "USD" },
    });
    // Red: fails until design matches the committed screenshot baseline
    await expect(container.firstElementChild).toMatchScreenshot({
      name: "product-card-mobile",
    });
  });

  it("price badge is within viewport on mobile", async () => {
    const { getByTestId } = render(ProductCard, {
      props: { title: "Widget Pro", price: 4999, currency: "USD" },
    });
    const badge = getByTestId("price-badge");
    // Red: badge must be visible without scrolling
    await expect(badge).toBeInViewport();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `toMatchScreenshot` for components where visual correctness is a first-class requirement — design-system tokens, marketing landing pages, and data-dense dashboards. Do NOT use it as a substitute for semantic assertions in unit tests — screenshot diffs break on antialiasing differences across OS/GPU configurations. Store baseline screenshots in version control so the Red phase is reproducible on any machine. Alternative: `toMatchAriaSnapshot` (Vitest 4.1) tests accessibility tree instead of pixels — prefer it for functional UI tests; reserve `toMatchScreenshot` for pure design-contract verification.

[official]

---

### 2. TDD with Vitest 3.2 `watchTriggerPatterns` — Non-Import File Dependency TDD [official]

Vitest 3.2 introduced `watchTriggerPatterns` in the configuration, allowing tests to be re-run when files change even if those files are not directly `import`-ed by any test. This is essential for TDD workflows where test correctness depends on files outside the module graph: OpenAPI spec files that drive contract tests, GraphQL schema files whose changes should re-run resolver tests, JSON fixtures loaded at runtime via `fs.readFile`, and Markdown templates parsed by rendering logic. Without `watchTriggerPatterns`, changes to these "data-adjacent" files require a manual test restart, breaking the automatic Red→Green TDD feedback loop.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — watchTriggerPatterns for non-import file dependencies
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    watchTriggerPatterns: [
      // Re-run API contract tests when the OpenAPI spec changes
      { pattern: "src/api/openapi.yaml", testsToRun: ["src/api/**/*.contract.test.ts"] },
      // Re-run all resolver tests when GraphQL schema is updated
      { pattern: "src/schema.graphql", testsToRun: ["src/resolvers/**/*.test.ts"] },
      // Re-run fixture-driven tests when any fixture file changes
      { pattern: "test/fixtures/**/*.json", testsToRun: ["test/**/*.fixture.test.ts"] },
    ],
  },
});

// user-contract.contract.test.ts — driven by openapi.yaml
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { readFileSync } from "fs";
import yaml from "js-yaml";

const spec = yaml.load(readFileSync("src/api/openapi.yaml", "utf8")) as Record<string, unknown>;

describe("User API contract (from OpenAPI spec)", () => {
  it("spec defines POST /users with 201 response", () => {
    const paths = spec.paths as Record<string, unknown>;
    expect(paths).toHaveProperty("/users");
    expect((paths["/users"] as Record<string, unknown>)).toHaveProperty("post");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `watchTriggerPatterns` wherever your TDD loop involves files that are not part of the JavaScript/TypeScript module graph — YAML, JSON, GraphQL, and template files are the primary candidates. Do NOT list source `*.ts` files in `watchTriggerPatterns`; Vitest already watches those via import graph tracking. Be specific with the `testsToRun` list — triggering all tests on every JSON fixture change defeats the purpose of watch-mode narrowing. Alternative: encode YAML/JSON data as TypeScript modules with `export const` so Vitest tracks them via the import graph automatically; this is simpler but trades off human-editability of pure data files.

[official]

---

### 3. TDD for TypeScript 5.8 `--erasableSyntaxOnly` — Node.js Native Type-Stripping Harness [official]

TypeScript 5.8 introduced the `--erasableSyntaxOnly` compiler option to support Node.js 23.6+ native type stripping (running `*.ts` files directly without a build step). For TDD, this enables an ultra-fast Red→Green loop: no transpilation latency, no build watch process, no `ts-node` process spawn — just `node --experimental-strip-types test.ts`. The constraint is that `--erasableSyntaxOnly` bans runtime-emitting constructs: `enum`, `namespace` with runtime code, parameter properties, and `import =` / `export =`. TDD practice benefits from this constraint — it forces tests to avoid enum-typed fixture values (use literal union types instead) and namespace-scoped test utilities (use plain ES modules instead).

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — erasableSyntaxOnly for Node.js native type-stripping TDD harness
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "target": "esnext",
//     "module": "nodenext",
//     "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
//     "strict": true,
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
//   }
// }

// status.ts — WRONG: enum not allowed under erasableSyntaxOnly
// enum OrderStatus { Pending = 'pending', Shipped = 'shipped' }

// status.ts — CORRECT: literal union type (erasable, no runtime emission)
export type OrderStatus = "pending" | "shipped" | "cancelled";
export const ORDER_STATUSES = ["pending", "shipped", "cancelled"] as const satisfies OrderStatus[];

// order.test.ts — runs directly: node --experimental-strip-types order.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import type { OrderStatus } from "./status.js";
import { placeOrder } from "./order.js";

describe("placeOrder", () => {
  it("returns 'pending' status immediately after placement", async () => {
    const order = await placeOrder({ userId: "u1", sku: "A", qty: 1 });
    const status: OrderStatus = order.status; // type-checked without tsc run
    expect(status).toBe("pending");
  });

  it("rejects when quantity is zero", async () => {
    await expect(placeOrder({ userId: "u1", sku: "A", qty: 0 }))
      .rejects.toThrow("invalid_quantity");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for new greenfield projects targeting Node.js 23.6+ LTS where build-step elimination is a priority. The enum ban is a net positive for TDD — literal union types produce better error messages and narrower type inference. Do NOT migrate existing projects with heavy `enum` or `namespace` usage to `--erasableSyntaxOnly` without first running the `ts5to6` codemod to identify and replace all disallowed syntax. Alternative: `ts-node --transpile-only` achieves similar zero-build TDD speed without the syntax constraints but adds a process-spawn cost of ~100ms per run.

[official]
