## Cycle 39 — 2026-05-14

### 1. TDD for Jest 30 `jest.onGenerateMock` — Intercept Auto-Mock Generation Before Tests Run [official]

Jest 30 introduced `jest.onGenerateMock(moduleName, callback)`, which fires a callback every time Jest generates an automatic mock for a module via `jest.mock()` without a factory. The callback receives the auto-generated mock object and can mutate or replace properties before the mock is returned to the test. In a TDD workflow, this is used in the Red phase to attach return-value defaults so that stub calls do not silently return `undefined` and cause misleading assertion failures. Instead of repeating `mockReturnValue(...)` in every test's `beforeEach`, the hook centralises default stub behaviour in a single `jest.setup.ts` entry point.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts — global mock defaults via onGenerateMock
import type { MockedObject } from "jest-mock";

jest.onGenerateMock("./src/services/pricing.service", (mock: MockedObject<typeof import("./src/services/pricing.service")>) => {
  // Default all price calculations to return a safe zero during Red phase
  mock.calculateDiscount.mockReturnValue(0);
  mock.applyTax.mockReturnValue(0);
  mock.formatCurrency.mockReturnValue("$0.00");
});

// In your test file — auto-mock already has defaults injected
import { calculateDiscount } from "./src/services/pricing.service";
jest.mock("./src/services/pricing.service");

describe("CheckoutService (TDD Red phase)", () => {
  it("returns zero total when pricing service returns zero discount", () => {
    const result = applyCheckout({ subtotal: 100 });
    expect(result.discount).toBe(0); // driven by onGenerateMock default
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `jest.onGenerateMock` is powerful for large codebases where auto-mock defaults drift — every test suite that auto-mocks a module gets the same safe defaults without copy-paste. The risk is that centralised defaults can mask real contract violations: a collaborator that should return a specific shape starts returning the default zero and tests pass incorrectly. Pair with explicit `mockReturnValue` overrides inside tests where the actual return value is load-bearing to the assertion. Do NOT use `onGenerateMock` for modules where the test suite is specifically testing the real implementation — the callback fires even when the mock factory is subsequently overridden, which can produce unexpected prototype mutations.

[official]

---

### 2. TDD for Jest 30 `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame` — Animation and RAF-Driven Logic in Red Phase [official]

Jest 30 added `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()`, which advances fake timers to the next `requestAnimationFrame` boundary (approximately 16ms at 60fps) without requiring the developer to guess the exact millisecond offset. In a TDD workflow for animation state machines, scroll-triggered logic, or any RAF-driven behaviour, this call replaces fragile `jest.advanceTimersByTime(16)` calls that break when RAF polyfill timing changes. The Red phase test writes the assertion against observable state after one frame, calls `advanceTimersToNextFrame()`, and then re-asserts — the test fails because the production code does not yet implement the frame-step logic.

```typescript
// Carousel.test.ts — TDD Red phase for RAF-driven animation state
import { jest, describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from "@jest/globals";
import { Carousel } from "./Carousel";

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

describe("Carousel — RAF animation (TDD Red phase)", () => {
  it("advances slide index after one animation frame", () => {
    const carousel = new Carousel({ slides: ["A", "B", "C"] });

    carousel.startAutoPlay();
    expect(carousel.currentSlide).toBe(0); // before any frame

    jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame();
    // Red: Carousel.startAutoPlay() is not yet implemented → fails here
    expect(carousel.currentSlide).toBe(1);
  });

  it("stops advancing after pause() is called mid-frame", () => {
    const carousel = new Carousel({ slides: ["A", "B", "C"] });
    carousel.startAutoPlay();
    jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame();
    carousel.pause();
    jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame();
    expect(carousel.currentSlide).toBe(1); // stays at 1, not 2
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` only works when `jest.useFakeTimers()` is active and the implementation actually calls `requestAnimationFrame` (not `setInterval`). If production code uses `setInterval(fn, 16)` as a RAF approximation, `advanceTimersToNextFrame` will not trigger it — the tests will hang silently in the Green phase. Enforce that production RAF-driven code uses the real `requestAnimationFrame` API (not polyfill intervals) via an ESLint rule or code review checklist. The method advances exactly one frame — for multi-frame sequences, call it in a loop or use `jest.runAllTimers()` with care.

[official]

---

### 3. TDD for Jest 30 `expect.arrayOf` — Declarative Collection Shape Assertions [official]

Jest 30 introduced `expect.arrayOf(matcher)`, an asymmetric matcher that asserts every element of an array matches the inner matcher — equivalent to `every(element => element matches matcher)`. In a TDD Red phase, this drives API contract tests where the production code must return a typed collection: `expect(result.items).toEqual(expect.arrayOf(expect.any(Number)))` fails before `items` is implemented and passes once the implementation correctly populates all elements. It composes with other asymmetric matchers (`expect.objectContaining`, `expect.stringMatching`) to express structural invariants that `toMatchObject` on a single item cannot capture across a whole collection.

```typescript
// ProductRepository.test.ts — TDD with expect.arrayOf for collection contracts
import { describe, it, expect } from "@jest/globals";
import { ProductRepository } from "./ProductRepository";
import type { Product } from "./types";

const repo = new ProductRepository();

describe("ProductRepository.findByCategory (TDD Red phase)", () => {
  it("returns an array where every element has required Product fields", async () => {
    const results = await repo.findByCategory("electronics");

    // Red: ProductRepository is a stub returning [] — fails shape assertion
    expect(results).toEqual(
      expect.arrayOf(
        expect.objectContaining<Partial<Product>>({
          id: expect.any(String),
          name: expect.any(String),
          price: expect.any(Number),
          inStock: expect.any(Boolean),
        })
      )
    );
  });

  it("returns an array where every price is a non-negative number", async () => {
    const results = await repo.findByCategory("books");
    const prices = results.map((p) => p.price);
    // Validates the invariant: no product can have a negative price
    expect(prices).toEqual(expect.arrayOf(expect.not(expect.toBeLessThan(0))));
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `expect.arrayOf` is most valuable for collection-producing endpoints where a single bad element should fail the test — it produces a meaningful diff that identifies exactly which element violated the matcher, unlike `results.forEach(r => expect(r).toMatchObject(...))` which reports the same failure with less context. The limitation is that `expect.arrayOf` does not assert anything about the array's length or ordering — pair it with a `toHaveLength` assertion and, for ordered collections, a separate `toMatchObject` on specific indices. Do NOT use `expect.arrayOf` when the collection is empty by design (e.g., no results found) — an empty array passes `expect.arrayOf(anything)`, which can mask a bug where the query returns no results instead of the expected results.

[official]

---

### 4. TDD for Jest 30 `using` Keyword Spy Cleanup — Explicit Resource Management for Test Spies [official]

Jest 30 integrates with JavaScript's TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal (`using` keyword), allowing spies to be declared as `using spy = jest.spyOn(...)` inside a test body. When the test block exits — whether by normal completion or by thrown error — the spy is automatically restored to the original implementation, without needing `afterEach(() => jest.restoreAllMocks())`. In a TDD Red phase, this pattern makes spy cleanup deterministic per test rather than relying on shared teardown hooks, which is critical in multi-spy test suites where a forgotten cleanup contaminates subsequent tests.

```typescript
// EmailService.test.ts — TDD with using keyword spy cleanup
import { jest, describe, it, expect } from "@jest/globals";
import * as mailerModule from "./mailer";
import { EmailService } from "./EmailService";

describe("EmailService.sendWelcomeEmail (TDD Red phase)", () => {
  it("calls mailer.send with correct recipient and template", () => {
    // 'using' automatically restores spy when block exits — no afterEach needed
    using sendSpy = jest.spyOn(mailerModule, "send").mockResolvedValue({ messageId: "test-123" });

    const svc = new EmailService();
    // Red: EmailService.sendWelcomeEmail not yet implemented → spy never called
    svc.sendWelcomeEmail("alice@example.com");

    expect(sendSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({
        to: "alice@example.com",
        template: "welcome",
      })
    );
  }); // <- sendSpy.mockRestore() called automatically here

  it("does not call mailer.send on invalid email", () => {
    using sendSpy = jest.spyOn(mailerModule, "send");
    const svc = new EmailService();
    expect(() => svc.sendWelcomeEmail("not-an-email")).toThrow("InvalidEmail");
    expect(sendSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The `using` keyword requires TypeScript 5.4+ with `"lib": ["es2022", "esnext"]` and a target runtime that supports `Symbol.dispose`. Vitest and Jest 30 both support it — but older test environments, Babel transforms without the dispose plugin, and Node.js versions below 20.4 will throw `ReferenceError: Symbol.dispose is not defined`. The ergonomics are excellent for focused, per-test spy scoping, but the `using` block only covers the test body — `using` in a `describe` block or `beforeEach` does not work as expected because the scope exits after the describe/setup call, not after the test. Use `using` exclusively inside `it`/`test` bodies where the lexical scope matches the test lifetime.

[official]

---

### 5. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `detectAsyncLeaks` — Catch Leaked Timers and Handles in Red Phase [official]

Vitest 4.1 added `detectAsyncLeaks: true` (config option and `--detect-async-leaks` CLI flag), which tracks open timer handles, unresolved promises, and leaked async resources after each test completes. When enabled, a test that opens a `setInterval` or holds an open database connection without cleanup causes Vitest to fail that test with a `Leaked async resource` error rather than allowing the resource to silently pollute subsequent tests. In a TDD workflow, this turns resource-leak bugs into immediate Red failures rather than flaky test failures that appear two tests later.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable async leak detection for TDD discipline
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectAsyncLeaks: true, // Vitest 4.1+
    // Leak detection adds ~5-10% overhead; disable for pure unit test suites
    // and enable only for integration/e2e suites where handles are likely
  },
});

// EventBus.test.ts — TDD Red phase with async leak detection
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { EventBus } from "./EventBus";

describe("EventBus subscription lifecycle", () => {
  it("unsubscribes all listeners when dispose() is called", () => {
    const bus = new EventBus();
    const handler = vi.fn();

    bus.subscribe("order:created", handler);
    bus.emit("order:created", { id: "ORD-1" });
    expect(handler).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();

    // Red: EventBus.dispose() not yet implemented
    // Without dispose(), the internal setInterval for heartbeat is leaked
    // detectAsyncLeaks will fail the test with: "Leaked async resource: Timeout"
    bus.dispose();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `detectAsyncLeaks` adds approximately 5–10% overhead per test due to the async resource tracking mechanism. For large pure-unit test suites (hundreds of tests with no async resources), enable it only in integration test configurations where real I/O resources (timers, sockets, streams) are involved. Be aware that some third-party libraries intentionally keep background resources open (e.g., connection pool heartbeats) and will trigger false positives — add those libraries to a `detectAsyncLeaks.ignore` pattern if available, or disable leak detection selectively per describe block using `test.extend` context. The feature does not detect memory leaks in long-lived objects, only unclosed async handles tracked by Node's `AsyncLocalStorage` API.

[official]

---

### 6. TDD for Vitest 4.1 `tags` Configuration — Structured Test Taxonomy for Selective Red Phase Runs [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced a first-class `tags` configuration that allows test files and individual tests to be tagged (`@unit`, `@integration`, `@slow`, `@flaky`) and filtered via CLI (`--tags-filter "unit and !flaky"`). Tags also support shared options — a tag group can define a common `timeout` and `retry` count applied to all tagged tests. In a TDD workflow, tagging tests during the Red phase allows teams to run only the `@unit` fast loop locally while CI runs the full `@integration` suite, without maintaining separate config files for each.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — tag definitions with shared options
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    tags: {
      unit: { timeout: 500 },
      integration: { timeout: 10_000, retry: 2 },
      slow: { timeout: 30_000 },
      flaky: { retry: 3 },
    },
  },
});

// PaymentGateway.test.ts — tagged TDD tests
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";

describe("PaymentGateway @unit", () => {
  // Tag annotation in test name — matched by --tags-filter
  it("validates card number format @unit", () => {
    const result = validateCardNumber("4111111111111111");
    expect(result.valid).toBe(true);
  });

  it("rejects expired cards @unit", () => {
    const result = validateCardNumber("4111111111111111", { expiry: "01/20" });
    expect(result.valid).toBe(false);
    expect(result.error).toBe("CARD_EXPIRED");
  });
});

describe("PaymentGateway @integration", () => {
  it("processes payment through Stripe sandbox @integration", async () => {
    const result = await gateway.charge({ amount: 100, currency: "USD", cardToken: "tok_visa" });
    expect(result.status).toBe("succeeded");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Tags are matched as substring patterns in test names (e.g., `@unit` in the test title), so they require a naming convention enforced by code review or a custom ESLint rule — Vitest does not currently enforce tag presence at the type level. The `--tags-filter` boolean expression syntax (`"unit and !slow"`, `"api/*"`) is powerful but underdocumented, and complex expressions can produce unexpected empty test runs without error messages when no tests match. Always validate new tag filters with `--reporter verbose` first to confirm the expected subset is selected. Do NOT use tags as a substitute for proper test organisation into separate `describe` blocks — tags are for cross-cutting execution concerns (speed, environment), not for structural grouping.

[official]

---

### 7. TDD for TypeScript 5.8 `--erasableSyntaxOnly` — Runtime-Compatible Test Code [official]

TypeScript 5.8 introduced the `--erasableSyntaxOnly` compiler flag, which errors on any TypeScript syntax that cannot be removed by a type-stripper without changing runtime behaviour: `enum` declarations, runtime `namespace` code, parameter properties in class constructors (`constructor(public x: number)`), and `import =` / `export =` assignments. Enabling this flag in test files (`tsconfig.test.json`) ensures all test code is compatible with Node.js 23.6+ `--experimental-strip-types` and direct Vitest execution without a transpiler step. In a TDD Red phase, this means type errors in test files are caught immediately by the type-checker rather than surfacing as opaque runtime errors when `tsx` or `ts-node` is not available.

```jsonc
// tsconfig.test.json — strict runtime-compatible test code
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    // No enums, parameter properties, or runtime namespaces in test files
    // All TypeScript syntax must be type-only (erased at runtime)
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.test.ts", "src/**/*.spec.ts", "test/**/*.ts"]
}
```

```typescript
// Before: parameter property — BLOCKED by erasableSyntaxOnly in tests
class TestDouble {
  constructor(public readonly id: string) {} // ❌ erasableSyntaxOnly error
}

// After: explicit property assignment — passes erasableSyntaxOnly
class TestDouble {
  readonly id: string;
  constructor(id: string) {
    this.id = id; // ✅ pure type erasure — no runtime overhead
  }
}

// Enum in test — BLOCKED
enum Status { Active = "active", Inactive = "inactive" } // ❌

// Const assertion instead — passes
const Status = { Active: "active", Inactive: "inactive" } as const; // ✅
type Status = typeof Status[keyof typeof Status];
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `--erasableSyntaxOnly` produces breaking changes in test files that use `enum` for test data categories or use parameter properties in test double classes — both common patterns. The migration effort is real but finite: `enum` → `const` object + type alias; parameter properties → explicit assignments. The payoff is that test files run without a compilation step in Node.js 23.6+ and Deno 2.x, dramatically speeding up watch-mode TDD loops. Do NOT apply `erasableSyntaxOnly` to production source files unless the entire codebase has been audited — production code often uses `enum` for API contracts or parameter properties for DTO classes, and forcing migration there is a separate larger effort.

[official]

---

### 8. TDD for TypeScript 5.9 `import defer` — Lazy Fixture Initialisation in Test Suites [official]

TypeScript 5.9 introduced `import defer * as module from "./path"` (TC39 stage 3), which defers the execution of a module's side effects and top-level initialisation until a property of the module is first accessed. In a TDD workflow, this is useful for test suites that import large fixture generators, database seeders, or expensive schema validators — with `import defer`, the module is loaded into the module graph at parse time (providing full type information) but its initialisation cost is paid only in the tests that actually access its properties. This turns expensive fixture modules from suite-level overhead into test-local on-demand costs.

```typescript
// IntegrationTest.test.ts — TDD with deferred fixture initialisation
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import defer * as dbFixtures from "./fixtures/database-seed"; // deferred: no DB connection yet
import defer * as schemaFixtures from "./fixtures/json-schemas"; // deferred: no Ajv compile yet

// The imports above are parsed for types but NOT executed yet.
// Top-level fixture initialisation (DB connection, schema compilation) runs
// only when a test accesses a property.

describe("UserRepository — integration tests", () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    // dbFixtures.seed() runs HERE, not at module load time
    // Suites that don't reach this beforeEach avoid the cost entirely
    await dbFixtures.seed({ users: 10, orders: 50 });
  });

  it("finds user by email with correct shape", async () => {
    const user = await userRepo.findByEmail("alice@example.com");
    // schemaFixtures.UserSchema compiled here, not at module load
    const valid = schemaFixtures.UserSchema.validate(user);
    expect(valid.errors).toBeNull();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `import defer` is a TC39 stage-3 proposal with TypeScript 5.9 support — it requires `"module": "esnext"` or `"nodenext"` in the tsconfig and a runtime that supports the deferred evaluation semantics (Node.js 22.12+ with the `--experimental-import-defer` flag, or Vitest 5.x which bundles the transform). Vitest 4.x does not yet support `import defer` natively — the call will be executed eagerly in Vitest 4.x test runs. Verify runtime support before adopting in CI. The pattern is most valuable for integration test suites where fixture setup is the dominant cost; for unit tests with lightweight fixtures, the ergonomic overhead of remembering that the module is deferred outweighs the performance benefit.

[official]

---

### 9. TDD for TypeScript 6.0 `Map.prototype.getOrInsert` — Idiomatic Cache-Pattern Test Fixtures [official]

TypeScript 6.0 added type definitions for the ES2025 `Map.prototype.getOrInsert(key, defaultValue)` and `Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed(key, () => computedDefault)` methods. In TDD, these methods streamline the arrangement phase of test fixtures that build lookup tables or memoisation caches: instead of writing three lines (check, compute, set), the fixture setup collapses to a single expression. The Red phase test asserts that the production code correctly uses `getOrInsert` semantics (idempotent insertion — existing values are not overwritten), which is a common bug in hand-rolled cache code.

```typescript
// CacheService.test.ts — TDD for getOrInsert cache semantics
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { CacheService } from "./CacheService";

// Fixture builder using ES2025 Map.getOrInsert (TypeScript 6.0 types)
function buildTestRegistry(entries: Array<[string, number]>): Map<string, number> {
  const registry = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const [key, value] of entries) {
    registry.getOrInsert(key, value); // idempotent — first write wins
  }
  return registry;
}

describe("CacheService.getOrCompute (TDD Red phase)", () => {
  it("returns existing value without invoking factory", () => {
    const initial = buildTestRegistry([["priceOf:SKU-001", 99]]);
    const svc = new CacheService({ initialData: initial });
    const factorySpy = vi.fn(() => 150);

    // Red: CacheService.getOrCompute not yet implemented
    const result = svc.getOrCompute("priceOf:SKU-001", factorySpy);
    expect(result).toBe(99);          // existing value returned
    expect(factorySpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); // factory never invoked
  });

  it("calls factory and stores result for missing key", () => {
    const svc = new CacheService({ initialData: new Map() });
    const factorySpy = vi.fn(() => 200);

    const result = svc.getOrCompute("priceOf:SKU-002", factorySpy);
    expect(result).toBe(200);
    expect(factorySpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    // Second call must NOT invoke factory again
    const secondResult = svc.getOrCompute("priceOf:SKU-002", factorySpy);
    expect(secondResult).toBe(200);
    expect(factorySpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce(); // still once
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `Map.prototype.getOrInsert` requires `"lib": ["ES2025"]` in `tsconfig.json` and Node.js 24+ or a polyfill (the `core-js` v4 polyfill is available). Vitest's default test environment (`jsdom` or `node`) running on Node.js 22 will throw `TypeError: registry.getOrInsert is not a function` unless a polyfill is loaded in `setupFiles`. For teams on Node.js 22, add `import "core-js/actual/map/get-or-insert"` to `vitest.config.ts` `setupFiles` before adopting the pattern. On Node.js 24+ the method is native. Do NOT use `getOrInsert` in test fixtures for tests that specifically verify that the production code does NOT use idempotent insertion — the fixture will mask the bug by pre-inserting the value before the production code can overwrite it.

[official]

---

### 10. TDD for Vitest 5.0 Beta `configDefaults.reporters` — Extending Built-in Reporters Without Replacement [official]

Vitest 5.0 beta exposes `configDefaults.reporters` (the default reporter list) through its public API, allowing project configs to extend the built-in reporter set rather than replacing it entirely. Previously, any `reporters: [...]` override silently dropped all default reporters (including the interactive terminal UI), requiring teams to manually reconstruct the default list when adding a custom reporter. In a TDD workflow, this allows a project to add a custom Red-phase failure notifier (desktop notification, Slack webhook) as an additional reporter while preserving the full Vitest terminal output that developers rely on during watch mode.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — extending default reporters via configDefaults (Vitest 5.0 beta)
import { defineConfig, configDefaults } from "vitest/config";
import { SlackReporter } from "./tooling/SlackReporter";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    reporters: [
      ...configDefaults.reporters,   // preserve default terminal + dot reporters
      new SlackReporter({            // add custom reporter without replacing defaults
        webhookUrl: process.env["SLACK_WEBHOOK"],
        notifyOn: "failure",         // only post to Slack on Red phase
        includeFailureDetails: true,
      }),
    ],
  },
});

// tooling/SlackReporter.ts — minimal custom reporter shape (Vitest 5.0 Reporter interface)
import type { Reporter, TestCase } from "vitest/node";

export class SlackReporter implements Reporter {
  constructor(private config: { webhookUrl?: string; notifyOn: string; includeFailureDetails: boolean }) {}

  async onTestCaseFailed(test: TestCase): Promise<void> {
    if (!this.config.webhookUrl || this.config.notifyOn !== "failure") return;
    await fetch(this.config.webhookUrl, {
      method: "POST",
      body: JSON.stringify({ text: `FAILED: ${test.fullName}` }),
    });
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `configDefaults.reporters` is a Vitest 5.0 beta API — it may change before the stable release. Pin the exact `vitest@5.0.0-beta.x` version in `package.json` to prevent unexpected reporter signature changes from breaking CI. The spreading pattern (`...configDefaults.reporters`) is only correct when you want ALL defaults; if the project already customises the reporter list (e.g., using `verbose` instead of `default`), spreading `configDefaults.reporters` will add the default `dot` reporter back unexpectedly — check what `configDefaults.reporters` contains in your version before spreading. Custom reporters that perform async I/O (Slack, PagerDuty) should implement timeouts to avoid blocking test run completion when the webhook is unavailable.

[official]

---

### 11. TDD for `@fast-check/vitest` `beforeEach` / `afterEach` Lifecycle Hooks — Property State Reset Between Runs [official]

The `@fast-check/vitest` integration package (v0.3.0+) supports `beforeEach` and `afterEach` lifecycle hooks that run before and after each generated input during a property-based test run. This is distinct from Vitest's `beforeEach` (which runs before each `it` block) — the fast-check hooks run before and after each individual example that fast-check generates. In a TDD workflow for stateful systems (in-memory stores, event buses, reducers), these hooks reset shared state between generated inputs, preventing one failing input from contaminating the next generated input's starting conditions.

```typescript
// ShoppingCartReducer.prop.test.ts — property test with per-input state reset
import { describe, it } from "vitest";
import { fc, test } from "@fast-check/vitest";
import { createCart, CartState } from "./ShoppingCartReducer";

let cart: CartState;

describe("ShoppingCartReducer — invariants", () => {
  // @fast-check/vitest beforeEach: runs before EACH generated input, not each it()
  test.prop(
    [
      fc.array(
        fc.record({
          type: fc.constantFrom("ADD", "REMOVE", "UPDATE_QTY"),
          productId: fc.uuid(),
          quantity: fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 99 }),
        }),
        { minLength: 1, maxLength: 20 }
      ),
    ],
    {
      beforeEach: () => {
        // Reset cart state before every generated sequence of actions
        cart = createCart();
      },
      afterEach: () => {
        // Verify no negative quantities leaked from any action sequence
        for (const item of cart.items) {
          if (item.quantity < 0) throw new Error(`Quantity invariant violated: ${item.productId}`);
        }
      },
    }
  )("total is non-negative after any sequence of valid actions", (actions) => {
    for (const action of actions) {
      cart = cartReducer(cart, action);
    }
    fc.pre(cart.items.length > 0); // skip empty-cart edge case
    expect(cart.total).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The `@fast-check/vitest` `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks run inside each property iteration, meaning for `numRuns: 100` they execute 100 times — expensive setup (database seeding, schema compilation) inside these hooks multiplies the cost by the run count and can make property tests 100x slower than their deterministic equivalents. Reserve these hooks for in-memory state resets (O(1) operations) rather than I/O-bound setup. If the setup is expensive, pre-generate the initial state outside the property and clone it with `structuredClone()` inside `beforeEach`. Also note: if `beforeEach` throws, the property run is aborted with a misleading `PreconditionFailure` error rather than a `BeforeEachError` — wrap setup in try/catch and rethrow with context if debugging hook failures.

[official]

---

### 12. TDD with TypeScript 6.0 `stableTypeOrdering` — Deterministic Snapshot Tests for Generated Types [official]

TypeScript 6.0 introduced `--stableTypeOrdering`, which ensures that type union members and intersection members appear in a consistent, deterministic order in declaration files, hover text, and error messages. Without this flag, union member ordering can vary between TypeScript versions or even between clean builds and incremental builds, causing snapshot tests that capture type error messages or `tsc --declaration` output to fail non-deterministically. In a TDD workflow that uses snapshot tests to pin API surface or error message contracts, enabling `--stableTypeOrdering` is a prerequisite for reliable snapshot tests against TypeScript-generated output.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — enable stable type ordering for deterministic snapshot tests
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "stableTypeOrdering": true,
//     "declaration": true,
//     "emitDeclarationOnly": true
//   }
// }

// ApiContract.snapshot.test.ts — snapshot TDD for TypeScript declaration output
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { execSync } from "child_process";
import * as path from "path";

describe("API surface contract (snapshot TDD)", () => {
  it("exported types match pinned declaration snapshot", () => {
    // Run tsc --declaration --emitDeclarationOnly on the API module
    execSync("tsc --project tsconfig.declarations.json --noEmit false", {
      cwd: path.resolve(__dirname, ".."),
    });

    const declarationContent = require("fs").readFileSync(
      path.resolve(__dirname, "../dist/api.d.ts"),
      "utf8"
    );

    // stableTypeOrdering ensures union members always appear in the same order
    // Without it, `type Status = "active" | "inactive"` might become
    // `"inactive" | "active"` on a clean build — snapshot would fail
    expect(declarationContent).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `--stableTypeOrdering` adds approximately 25% overhead to TypeScript's type-checking pass because it sorts union and intersection members at each type-creation point rather than preserving insertion order. For large codebases (>500k LOC), this can add 30+ seconds to CI type-check runs. Enable it only in the `tsconfig` used for declaration emit and snapshot tests, not in the primary development tsconfig. If the team does not write snapshot tests against TypeScript output, the flag provides no benefit and should not be enabled. The determinism benefit is most valuable for library authors publishing `.d.ts` files where consumers' IDEs will display union members — consistent ordering prevents confusing documentation churn.

[official]

---

### 13. TDD for Jest 30 `jest.retryTimes` with `retryImmediately` — Targeted Flaky Test Quarantine [official]

Jest 30 extended `jest.retryTimes(n, options)` with two new options: `waitBeforeRetry: number` (milliseconds to wait between retries) and `retryImmediately: boolean` (retry the failing test before running subsequent tests in the suite, rather than queuing the retry at the end of the run). In a TDD workflow for known-flaky integration tests (network-dependent, timer-sensitive, or resource-contention-prone), `retryImmediately: true` keeps the retry co-located with the original failure in output logs, making it easier to distinguish "genuinely failing" from "transiently failing" during the Red phase without grep-searching across a long test log.

```typescript
// IntegrationSuite.test.ts — TDD with targeted retry for network-dependent tests
import { jest, describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from "@jest/globals";
import { DatabaseClient } from "./DatabaseClient";
import { PaymentProcessor } from "./PaymentProcessor";

// Configure retries only for this integration suite
// retryImmediately: retry right after failure, not at end of suite
jest.retryTimes(2, { retryImmediately: true, waitBeforeRetry: 500 });

let db: DatabaseClient;
beforeAll(async () => { db = await DatabaseClient.connect(process.env["TEST_DB_URL"]!); });
afterAll(async () => { await db.disconnect(); });

describe("PaymentProcessor — integration", () => {
  it("processes idempotent payment with same key twice without double-charging", async () => {
    const idempotencyKey = `test-${Date.now()}`;
    const first = await PaymentProcessor.charge({ amount: 50_00, idempotencyKey });
    const second = await PaymentProcessor.charge({ amount: 50_00, idempotencyKey });

    // Red: PaymentProcessor.charge not yet idempotency-aware — second charge succeeds
    expect(first.chargeId).toBe(second.chargeId); // same charge, not duplicate
    expect(await db.countCharges({ idempotencyKey })).toBe(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `retryImmediately: true` keeps retry noise visible in output alongside the original test — easier to triage than end-of-suite retry output — but it also means a flaky test blocks the test runner from advancing to the next test during each retry, increasing total wall-clock time for the suite when retries trigger frequently. Use `retryImmediately` only for tests that are network- or timing-sensitive and that need sequential retry semantics (e.g., a payment idempotency test that must not run concurrently with its retry). `waitBeforeRetry` is essential for tests that fail due to eventual consistency — add it whenever the failure is "data not yet visible in read replica" rather than a deterministic bug. NEVER add `retryTimes` to pure unit tests — a flaky unit test is always a test code bug, and retries hide it.

[official]

---

### 14. TDD for Vitest 5.0 Beta `aria` Snapshot Assertions — Accessibility Contracts as Red-Phase Specifications [official]

Vitest 5.0 beta (browser mode) introduces `toMatchAriaSnapshot()`, which serialises a DOM element's accessibility tree (ARIA roles, labels, descriptions, states) into a snapshot string and asserts it matches a pinned version. In a TDD workflow for accessible UI components, the Red phase writes the ARIA snapshot assertion before the component is built — `expect(screen.getByRole("dialog")).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` fails because the dialog does not yet exist. Once the component is implemented, the snapshot is captured and pinned. Subsequent regressions (missing `aria-label`, changed role from `"dialog"` to `"alertdialog"`) fail the snapshot test immediately rather than requiring manual accessibility audit.

```typescript
// Modal.accessibility.test.ts — TDD ARIA snapshot for accessible modal component
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { ConfirmModal } from "./ConfirmModal";

describe("ConfirmModal — accessibility contracts (TDD Red phase)", () => {
  it("renders accessible dialog with correct ARIA structure", async () => {
    render(
      <ConfirmModal
        title="Delete account"
        message="This action cannot be undone."
        onConfirm={vi.fn()}
        onCancel={vi.fn()}
        isOpen
      />
    );

    const dialog = screen.getByRole("dialog");

    // Red: ConfirmModal not yet implemented — toMatchAriaSnapshot fails
    // Once implemented, this snapshot is captured and pinned:
    // - role=dialog with aria-modal=true
    // - accessible name from aria-labelledby → "Delete account"
    // - two buttons: "Confirm" (destructive) and "Cancel"
    await expect(dialog).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - dialog "Delete account" [modal]:
        - heading "Delete account" [level=2]
        - text "This action cannot be undone."
        - button "Confirm"
        - button "Cancel"
    `);
  });

  it("moves focus to first interactive element on open", async () => {
    render(<ConfirmModal title="Delete account" message="..." onConfirm={vi.fn()} onCancel={vi.fn()} isOpen />);
    // Focus management contract — Confirm button is first focusable element
    expect(document.activeElement).toBe(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Confirm" }));
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` is a Vitest 5.0 beta API available only in browser mode (not jsdom/happy-dom environments) — it requires the `@vitest/browser` package and a real browser provider (Playwright or WebdriverIO). Running browser-mode tests in CI adds significant setup overhead (Playwright install, Chromium download) and is 10-50x slower than jsdom unit tests. Reserve ARIA snapshot tests for public-facing UI components that must meet accessibility standards and that will be reviewed by QA for accessibility compliance; do not write ARIA snapshots for internal utility components where the accessibility tree is trivially simple. Update snapshots intentionally with `vitest --update-snapshots` and code-review the diff to catch regressions in the accessibility tree.

[official]

---

### 15. TDD for Vitest 4.x `test.extend` Fixture Scope Hierarchy — Type-Safe Scope Violations at Compile Time [official]

Vitest 4.x's `test.extend()` fixture system enforces a scope hierarchy — `$test` (default, per-test), `$file` (per-file), and `$worker` (per-worker process) — and fixtures can only depend on other fixtures at the same or higher (longer-lived) scope. The `test.extend()` object syntax (introduced to complement the function syntax) expresses scope declarations as TypeScript literal keys (`$worker`, `$file`, `$test`), enabling the type-checker to catch scope hierarchy violations at compile time rather than at test runtime. In a TDD workflow, this means a test that tries to inject a `$test`-scoped database transaction into a `$file`-scoped connection pool fails with a TypeScript error during authoring, not with a confusing Vitest runtime error.

```typescript
// fixtures/database.ts — type-safe fixture scope hierarchy (Vitest 4.x)
import { test as base } from "vitest";

interface DbFixtures {
  connectionPool: DatabasePool;   // $file scope: one pool per test file
  transaction: DatabaseTransaction; // $test scope: one transaction per test
}

export const test = base.extend<DbFixtures>({
  // File-scoped: connection pool created once per file, shared across tests
  connectionPool: [
    async ({ task: _task }, use) => {
      const pool = await DatabasePool.create({ maxConnections: 5 });
      await use(pool);
      await pool.drain();
    },
    { scope: "file" }, // <- $file scope declaration
  ],

  // Test-scoped: transaction created fresh for each test, always rolled back
  transaction: async ({ connectionPool }, use) => {
    // Valid: $test fixture accessing $file fixture (file outlives test)
    const tx = await connectionPool.beginTransaction();
    await use(tx);
    await tx.rollback(); // clean slate for next test
  },
  // If transaction were declared as { scope: "file" } accessing a $test fixture,
  // TypeScript would emit: "Cannot use test-scoped fixture in file-scoped fixture"
});

// UserRepository.integration.test.ts — consuming scoped fixtures
import { test } from "./fixtures/database";
import { expect } from "vitest";

test("creates user and finds it within the same transaction", async ({ transaction }) => {
  await transaction.execute("INSERT INTO users(id, name) VALUES('u1', 'Alice')");
  const row = await transaction.queryOne("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 'u1'");
  expect(row?.name).toBe("Alice"); // visible inside transaction, not committed to DB
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The object syntax with explicit `$worker`/`$file`/`$test` scope keys provides compile-time safety but requires TypeScript's generic inference to resolve the fixture type from the `use()` callback return — when the generic inference fails (e.g., the fixture factory has multiple overloads), manual type annotations are required: `test.extend<DbFixtures, WorkerFixtures>({...})`. The function syntax (original Vitest fixture syntax) does not have the scope type-checking — teams migrating from function to object syntax will encounter compile errors for existing scope violations that were previously silent runtime failures. Fix scope violations in order from outermost (worker) to innermost (test) to avoid cascading type errors during migration.

[official]

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 39 Additions

163. **[community] Jest 30's removal of `toBeCalled()` and `toBeCalledWith()` aliases causes Jest 29 test suites to fail at import time in Jest 30 with `TypeError: expect(...).toBeCalled is not a function` — not a lint warning, but a hard runtime crash on the first assertion.** Teams upgrading from Jest 29 to Jest 30 run `npm install jest@30` and their CI immediately turns red. The failure message `TypeError: expect(...).toBeCalled is not a function` looks like a Jest configuration problem (wrong globals injection, missing `@types/jest`) rather than an API removal. Developers spend hours debugging `jest.config.ts` before consulting the migration guide. WHY this matters: the aliases were common in tutorials, blog posts, and StackOverflow answers written before Jest 29 — most codebases have hundreds of `toBeCalled()` calls. Fix: run the official Jest 30 codemod (`npx jest-codemods`) which rewrites `toBeCalled` → `toHaveBeenCalled`, `toBeCalledWith` → `toHaveBeenCalledWith`, and `toBeCalledTimes` → `toHaveBeenCalledTimes` across the entire codebase before bumping the Jest version in `package.json`.

164. **[community] Vitest 4.1's `detectAsyncLeaks` flags Node.js `net.createServer()` test doubles as leaked handles even when the server is correctly `close()`-d — the flag fires because `close()` is async and the `afterEach` hook completes before the `close` callback fires, leaving the handle open at the moment Vitest checks.** A developer adds `detectAsyncLeaks: true` to a Vitest config for a server component integration suite. Every test that creates and closes a test HTTP server fails with `Leaked async resource: TCPServerWrap`. The servers are correctly closed — the developer added `server.close()` in `afterEach` — but `server.close()` is fire-and-forget: it initiates graceful shutdown but the handle is not released until the `close` event fires. WHY this matters: the fix is not obvious — `detectAsyncLeaks` does not tell you that the close is in-progress vs. forgotten. Fix: always `await` server close with a promisified wrapper (`await promisify(server.close.bind(server))()`) in `afterEach`, or use `server.closeAllConnections()` (Node 18.2+) followed by `await promisify(server.close.bind(server))()` to force-close existing connections before graceful shutdown.

165. **[community] TypeScript 6.0's new default `"module": "esnext"` breaks Jest configurations that rely on `ts-jest` with `"module": "commonjs"` — `ts-jest` transforms are no longer applied to `.ts` test files when the module format mismatches, producing `SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement in a module` on the first `import` in a test file.** Teams upgrading their `tsconfig.json` to TypeScript 6.0 defaults without reviewing `ts-jest` configuration experience a complete test suite outage. The error appears to be a Node.js `--experimental-vm-modules` configuration issue, not a TypeScript change. WHY this matters: `ts-jest` reads the project `tsconfig.json` by default — switching to `"esnext"` forces `ts-jest` to emit ES modules, but Jest's default module system is CommonJS, creating an incompatibility. Fix: add an explicit `tsconfig` override in `jest.config.ts` pointing `ts-jest` to a `tsconfig.cjs.json` with `"module": "commonjs"`, or migrate to Vitest (which natively handles ESM via Vite's transform pipeline) rather than fighting `ts-jest` + Jest CJS compatibility indefinitely.

166. **[community] `@fast-check/vitest`'s `test.prop` with `numRuns: 1000` in a Vitest workspace multi-project config runs 1000 iterations per project shard — in a 4-project workspace, a single `test.prop` block runs 4000 total iterations, making property tests 4x slower than expected and burning through CI credits.** A developer sets `numRuns: 1000` globally in `vitest.config.ts` expecting 1000 property iterations per test. The Vitest workspace spawns 4 projects (unit, integration, browser, e2e), and each project independently respects `numRuns: 1000` — the property test runs 1000 times per project. WHY this matters: the slowdown is not obvious because each individual project's test run looks correct in isolation — only a wall-clock comparison between single-project and multi-project runs reveals the multiplication. Fix: set `numRuns` per-environment in the workspace projects config (`{ project: "unit", test: { numRuns: 1000 } }` and `{ project: "integration", test: { numRuns: 100 } }`) so fast unit property tests run 1000 iterations and slow integration property tests run fewer; or scope `@fast-check/vitest` globals to specific projects using `projects` includes/excludes.

167. **[community] Jest 30's `jest.onGenerateMock` callback mutates the auto-mock object in place — developers who `return` a replacement object from the callback instead of mutating the received object find that their replacement is silently ignored and the original auto-mock is used instead.** A developer writes `jest.onGenerateMock("./api/client", (mock) => ({ ...mock, fetch: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({}) }))` expecting the spread object to replace the auto-mock. The callback return value is discarded — Jest only observes mutations to the `mock` parameter. The test runs with the original auto-mock (all methods return `undefined`) and the custom `fetch` mock is never installed. WHY this matters: the `jest.onGenerateMock` callback signature looks like a mapping function (take old, return new) but behaves like a mutation hook (mutate the argument in place) — a common FP-vs-mutation API confusion. Fix: mutate the mock parameter directly: `mock.fetch = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({})` rather than returning a new object; add a code review checklist item that `jest.onGenerateMock` callbacks must not use `return`.

168. **[community] Vitest `test.extend` fixtures that call `onCleanup` multiple times within the same fixture factory throw `Error: onCleanup can only be called once per fixture` — this error is deferred and surfaces at teardown time (after the test completes), not at setup time, making the stack trace point to the cleanup phase rather than the fixture line that called `onCleanup` twice.** A developer refactors a fixture factory to conditionally register cleanup for two different resources and accidentally calls `onCleanup(fn1)` and `onCleanup(fn2)` in the same factory. The test setup succeeds, the test body runs, and the error appears in the teardown phase with a stack trace pointing to Vitest internals rather than the fixture file. WHY this matters: the delayed error makes it appear that the problem is in another test's cleanup rather than the current fixture — developers look at the wrong fixture or blame a `afterEach` hook. Fix: combine multiple cleanup operations into a single `onCleanup(() => { fn1(); fn2(); })` call, or split into separate fixtures with separate `onCleanup` registrations; add an ESLint rule to detect multiple `onCleanup` calls within the same function scope.
