### 23. TDD for Vitest Fixture Override — Per-Suite Fixture Customisation Without Duplication [official]

Vitest 4.1+ introduced `test.override()` (also exposed as `describe.extend` override capability), which allows a nested `describe` block to customise the value of an inherited fixture without duplicating the full fixture definition. In TDD, this is the correct pattern when most tests need a "default" fixture state but a handful of tests need a specific variant — instead of creating two separate `test.extend` calls with near-identical fixture definitions, a single base fixture is defined at the top level and overridden locally.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/db-fixture.ts
import { test as baseTest } from "vitest";

interface DbFixtures {
  db: {
    host: string;
    port: number;
    name: string;
    connect(): Promise<{ query(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> }>;
  };
}

export const test = baseTest.extend<DbFixtures>({
  db: async ({ task }, use) => {
    const config = { host: "localhost", port: 5432, name: `test_${task.id}` };
    const connection = await createTestConnection(config);
    await use({ ...config, connect: () => createTestConnection(config) });
    await connection.close();
  },
});

// test/reporting/report-generator.test.ts
import { describe, expect } from "vitest";
import { test } from "../fixtures/db-fixture";
import { ReportGenerator } from "../../src/reporting/report-generator";

// Most tests use the default db fixture
test("ReportGenerator.generateSummary returns empty for empty DB", async ({ db }) => {
  const conn = await db.connect();
  const gen = new ReportGenerator(conn);
  expect(await gen.generateSummary()).toEqual({ total: 0, items: [] });
});

// Override: this describe block needs a seeded read-replica database
describe("with seeded read-replica", () => {
  // Vitest 4.1+ fixture override: replace db.name for this scope only
  test.override({
    db: async ({ task }, use) => {
      const replica = { host: "replica.local", port: 5433, name: "test_readonly" };
      const conn = await createTestConnection(replica);
      await seedReplicaData(conn);
      await use({ ...replica, connect: () => createTestConnection(replica) });
      await conn.close();
    },
  });

  test("ReportGenerator uses replica when primary is overloaded", async ({ db }) => {
    const conn = await db.connect();
    expect(conn).toBeDefined(); // db.host === "replica.local"
    const gen = new ReportGenerator(conn);
    const summary = await gen.generateSummary();
    expect(summary.total).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Fixture override is the right abstraction when a small subset of tests needs a variant of a shared fixture. It avoids fixture duplication and keeps the base fixture definition as the single source of truth. The tradeoff is that `test.override` is Vitest 4.1+ specific; on older Vitest versions, you must create a separate `test.extend` call or use `beforeEach` to mutate fixture state. When the overridden fixture represents a meaningfully different subsystem (a replica database vs a primary), consider whether it deserves its own named fixture (`testWithReplica`) rather than an anonymous override — named fixtures are more self-documenting in test output.

[official]

---

### 24. TDD for Test Double Taxonomy — Choosing the Right Double for the Right Phase [community]

The classic Martin Fowler test double taxonomy (dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake) maps directly onto TDD phases in ways that are often ignored in practice. Selecting the wrong double type produces tests that either under-specify (stubs used when interaction verification is needed) or over-specify (mocks used when only a return value is needed), making the test suite fragile. In TypeScript TDD, a crisp decision rule: use a **fake** (real implementation, simplified) when correctness of collaboration matters; use a **stub** when only a return value is needed; use a **spy** when you need to verify a side effect was triggered; use a **mock** (pre-programmed expectations) only for command-style calls where the interaction IS the behaviour.

```typescript
// The four double types in TypeScript TDD — each with explicit use case

// 1. STUB — control return value only; no interaction verification
const stubEmailSender: EmailSender = {
  send: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: "stub-id-123" }),
};

// 2. SPY — record calls but delegate to real implementation
import { emailClient } from "../src/email-client";
const spyOnSend = vi.spyOn(emailClient, "send");
// After test: expect(spyOnSend).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ to: "alice@example.com" }));

// 3. FAKE — simplified working implementation for in-memory substitution
class FakeEmailSender implements EmailSender {
  public readonly sent: Array<{ to: string; subject: string; body: string }> = [];

  async send(msg: { to: string; subject: string; body: string }): Promise<{ messageId: string }> {
    this.sent.push(msg);
    return { messageId: `fake-${this.sent.length}` };
  }
}

// 4. MOCK — pre-programmed expected interactions (Arrange phase)
// Use only when the interaction contract IS the specification
const mockAuditLog: AuditLog = {
  record: vi.fn(), // Will assert: expect(mockAuditLog.record).toHaveBeenCalledOnce()
};

// test/notification-service.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { NotificationService } from "../src/notification-service";

test("NotificationService.notify — use FAKE for correctness of side-effect state", async () => {
  const fakeEmail = new FakeEmailSender();
  const svc = new NotificationService(fakeEmail);

  await svc.notify("alice@example.com", "Welcome!", "Hello Alice");

  // Assert on the fake's state — no fragile spy call matching
  expect(fakeEmail.sent).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(fakeEmail.sent[0].to).toBe("alice@example.com");
  expect(fakeEmail.sent[0].subject).toBe("Welcome!");
});

test("NotificationService.notify — use MOCK for audit log interaction contract", async () => {
  const fakeEmail = new FakeEmailSender();
  const mockAudit: AuditLog = { record: vi.fn() };
  const svc = new NotificationService(fakeEmail, mockAudit);

  await svc.notify("alice@example.com", "Welcome!", "Hello Alice");

  // Interaction IS the spec: audit log must be called exactly once
  expect(mockAudit.record).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(mockAudit.record).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({ action: "notification_sent", recipient: "alice@example.com" })
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The single most common TDD double mistake is using a mock (pre-programmed expectations) when a fake or stub would be sufficient. Over-use of mocks produces tests that verify implementation structure rather than behavioural contracts — they break whenever the internal call sequence changes even when the observable behaviour is identical. Reserve mocks for command-style operations (write, delete, enqueue, audit) where the call itself IS the side effect the test is specifying. For query-style operations (returning data), prefer stubs or fakes. For state-verifying integration checks, prefer fakes with inspectable state.

[community]

---

### 25. TDD for Vitest `vi.mock` with `{ spy: true }` — Browser Mode Module Mocking [official]

In Vitest Browser Mode, `vi.spyOn` on module exports does not work because browser-native ESM does not allow property reassignment on a module namespace object. Vitest 4.x introduced `vi.mock('./module', { spy: true })` as the Browser Mode equivalent: it wraps every export of the target module in a `vi.fn()` spy that delegates to the real implementation, without replacing the module binding. In TDD, `{ spy: true }` is the correct double type for browser component tests where you need to verify that a service function was called (interaction verification) while still exercising the real implementation for correctness.

```typescript
// src/services/analytics.ts — module to spy on in browser mode
export function trackEvent(name: string, props: Record<string, unknown>): void {
  if (typeof navigator !== "undefined") {
    navigator.sendBeacon("/analytics", JSON.stringify({ name, props }));
  }
}

export function trackPageView(path: string): void {
  trackEvent("page_view", { path });
}

// test/components/CheckoutButton.browser.test.tsx
// vitest.config.ts: browser: { enabled: true, provider: 'playwright', name: 'chromium' }
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { render } from "vitest-browser-react";
import { page, userEvent } from "@vitest/browser/context";
import { CheckoutButton } from "../../src/components/CheckoutButton";

// { spy: true } wraps all exports in vi.fn() but keeps real implementation
vi.mock(import("../../src/services/analytics"), { spy: true });

import * as analytics from "../../src/services/analytics";

beforeEach(() => { vi.clearAllMocks(); });

test("CheckoutButton tracks analytics event on click", async () => {
  render(<CheckoutButton cartId="cart-123" />);

  await userEvent.click(page.getByRole("button", { name: "Checkout" }));

  // Interaction contract: trackEvent was called with correct payload
  expect(analytics.trackEvent).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(analytics.trackEvent).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    "checkout_initiated",
    expect.objectContaining({ cartId: "cart-123" })
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `{ spy: true }` is the Browser Mode answer to `vi.spyOn` limitations and is appropriate whenever you need interaction verification without blocking the real implementation. It is not appropriate when the real implementation has browser-side effects you need to suppress (e.g., `navigator.sendBeacon` firing real network requests in tests) — in that case, use a full `vi.mock` factory to replace the export with a no-op stub. The constraint is that `{ spy: true }` requires Vitest 4.x+ and only works in Browser Mode; in Node runner mode, prefer `vi.spyOn` for the same pattern.

[official]

---

### 26. TDD for Custom Domain Snapshot Adapters — Semantic Comparison Beyond String Equality [official]

Vitest 4.1.4+ introduced custom domain adapters for the snapshot system, enabling semantic comparison pipelines beyond the default string-equality check. A domain adapter receives the serialised snapshot string and the current serialised value and returns whether they match — allowing pattern-based matching, subset assertions, and version-tolerant comparisons. In TDD, a domain adapter for API response snapshots can ignore irrelevant fields (timestamps, generated IDs) while asserting on stable structural fields, eliminating the snapshot churn that makes API response snapshots unusable in practice.

```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts — register a domain snapshot adapter for API responses
import { expect } from "vitest";

// Domain adapter: ignore volatile fields (id, createdAt, updatedAt) during comparison
expect.addSnapshotAdapter({
  name: "api-response",
  test(serialised: string): boolean {
    return serialised.startsWith("// @api-response-snapshot");
  },
  serialize(value: unknown): string {
    return `// @api-response-snapshot\n${JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)}`;
  },
  compare(received: string, stored: string): boolean {
    // Parse both; compare only non-ignored fields
    const receivedObj = JSON.parse(received.replace(/^\/\/ @api-response-snapshot\n/, ""));
    const storedObj   = JSON.parse(stored.replace(/^\/\/ @api-response-snapshot\n/, ""));
    return deepMatchIgnoringVolatile(receivedObj, storedObj, ["id", "createdAt", "updatedAt"]);
  },
});

function deepMatchIgnoringVolatile(a: unknown, b: unknown, ignoreKeys: string[]): boolean {
  if (typeof a !== "object" || typeof b !== "object" || a === null || b === null) return a === b;
  const aObj = a as Record<string, unknown>;
  const bObj = b as Record<string, unknown>;
  return Object.keys(bObj).every((key) =>
    ignoreKeys.includes(key) ? true : deepMatchIgnoringVolatile(aObj[key], bObj[key], ignoreKeys)
  );
}

// test/api/user-profile.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { fetchUserProfile } from "../../src/api/user-profile";

test("fetchUserProfile response matches structural snapshot (volatile fields ignored)", async () => {
  const profile = await fetchUserProfile("alice");

  // Snapshot: id, createdAt, updatedAt are ignored by domain adapter
  expect(profile).toMatchSnapshot("user-profile-alice");
  // On first run: creates snapshot. On subsequent runs: compares, ignoring volatile fields.
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Custom domain adapters are powerful but add significant maintenance burden: the adapter's comparison logic becomes part of the test infrastructure and must be maintained, documented, and tested itself (meta-TDD: write tests for your test infrastructure). Use them when a class of snapshots consistently produces false-positive snapshot failures due to volatile fields, and when the volatile fields cannot be excluded via explicit `expect.objectContaining` matchers at the test level. For most cases, `expect.objectContaining` and `expect.stringMatching` at the assertion level are simpler and more discoverable than a global domain adapter.

[official]

---

### 27. TDD for Jest 30 `randomize` + `showSeed` — Exposing Order Dependencies in the Red Phase [official]

Jest 30's `randomize: true` configuration option randomises the execution order of tests within each file on every run, using a seed printed to the console when `showSeed: true` is also enabled. In TDD, random test ordering is a second-order Red phase tool: it converts a hidden order dependency (test B passes only when test A runs first) into an explicit, reproducible failure. When `randomize` is enabled, a test that secretly relied on shared mutable state from a prior test fails on some seeds and passes on others — making the dependency visible as flakiness. The seed can then be used to reproduce the exact failure order for debugging.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — minimal TDD configuration for order-dependency detection
import { defineConfig } from "jest";

export default defineConfig({
  randomize: true,      // Random order per run
  showSeed: true,       // Print seed in output: "Randomized with seed: 123456789"
  resetMocks: true,     // Clear mock state between tests (prevents mock leakage)
  restoreMocks: true,   // Restore vi.spyOn originals between tests

  // To reproduce: jest --seed=<printed seed value>
});

// test/shopping-cart.test.ts — BEFORE: hidden order dependency
let cart: ShoppingCart;

beforeAll(() => { cart = new ShoppingCart(); }); // shared state — WRONG

test("addItem increases item count", () => {
  cart.addItem({ sku: "A", qty: 1 });
  expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(1);       // passes only if tests run in order
});

test("removeItem decreases item count", () => {
  cart.addItem({ sku: "B", qty: 1 });
  cart.removeItem("B");
  expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(1);       // depends on first test having run first
});

// AFTER: each test owns its state (randomize-safe)
function makeCart(): ShoppingCart { return new ShoppingCart(); }

test("addItem increases item count", () => {
  const cart = makeCart();
  cart.addItem({ sku: "A", qty: 1 });
  expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(1);       // independent of any other test
});

test("removeItem decreases item count", () => {
  const cart = makeCart();
  cart.addItem({ sku: "B", qty: 1 });
  cart.removeItem("B");
  expect(cart.items).toHaveLength(0);       // independent; also fixed the assertion
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `randomize: true` is most valuable during the initial TDD loop when a test suite is being built out: it catches order dependencies before they accumulate into a legacy shared-state problem. For mature suites, enable it in CI and treat any seed-dependent failure as a bug. The tradeoff is that tests relying on `beforeAll` shared state (intentionally, for performance reasons like a single database seed) will produce false failures under randomisation — guard these with `describe` blocks that scope the `beforeAll` to the group of tests that legitimately share the setup.

[official]

---

### 28. TDD for Inline Type-Level Tests — `expectTypeOf` as a First-Class Red Signal [official]

Vitest's `expectTypeOf` API, running in `*.test-d.ts` files (or inline in regular test files), provides compile-time type assertions that fail the test run if a type assertion does not hold. In TDD, type-level tests are a Red phase tool for library and utility type development: the failing type test specifies the type contract before the implementation is written. This creates a strictly-typed TDD loop where both behavioural tests (what the function does) and type tests (what the function returns) must be Green before the Refactor phase begins.

```typescript
// src/utils/pick.ts — under development; only the type signature exists
export declare function pick<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(
  obj: T,
  keys: K[]
): Pick<T, K>;

// test/utils/pick.test-d.ts — type-level TDD (runs as part of vitest --typecheck)
import { expectTypeOf, test } from "vitest";
import { pick } from "../../src/utils/pick";

// Red phase: these assertions specify the type contract before implementation is written

test("pick returns an object with only the specified keys", () => {
  const obj = { a: 1, b: "hello", c: true };

  // Assert: picked type is { a: number; b: string } — c is excluded
  expectTypeOf(pick(obj, ["a", "b"])).toEqualTypeOf<{ a: number; b: string }>();
});

test("pick key array must contain keyof T", () => {
  const obj = { x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 };

  // Assert: 'w' is not a key of obj — should produce a type error
  // @ts-expect-error — 'w' is not assignable to keyof { x: number, y: number, z: number }
  pick(obj, ["w"]);
});

test("pick preserves optional properties", () => {
  const obj: { required: string; optional?: number } = { required: "yes" };

  expectTypeOf(pick(obj, ["required", "optional"])).toEqualTypeOf<{
    required: string;
    optional?: number;
  }>();
});

test("pick result is a subtype of the original object", () => {
  type User = { id: string; name: string; email: string; createdAt: Date };
  const user: User = { id: "1", name: "Alice", email: "a@b.com", createdAt: new Date() };

  const partial = pick(user, ["id", "name"]);
  expectTypeOf(partial).toMatchTypeOf<{ id: string; name: string }>();
  // The following must NOT compile — email was not picked
  expectTypeOf(partial).not.toHaveProperty("email");
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Type-level TDD with `expectTypeOf` is appropriate for utility types, generic library functions, and any code where the type signature is itself a deliverable (used by downstream consumers). It should not be applied to application code where the type is a private implementation detail — over-specifying private types through type tests creates refactoring friction without consumer benefit. Enable `typecheck: true` in `vitest.config.ts` to run `.test-d.ts` files as part of the standard test suite; they report as test failures alongside behavioural tests and are updated with the same `--update` flag as snapshots.

[official]

---

### 29. TDD for MSW `onUnhandledRequest` Strategy — Hardening Test Network Boundaries [community]

Mock Service Worker's `onUnhandledRequest` option controls what happens when a test makes a network request that has no matching handler: `"error"` (fail the test), `"warn"` (log a warning), or `"bypass"` (send to real network). In TDD, `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` is the correct default for the Red phase: any unmatched network call is an undeclared dependency that must be explicitly mocked or `passthrough`-ed. Setting it to `"error"` converts undeclared network calls into immediate, reproducible test failures rather than the subtle flakiness that `"bypass"` produces.

```typescript
// test/setup/msw-server.ts — production-grade MSW server setup for TDD
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
import { http, HttpResponse, passthrough } from "msw";

// Default handlers: block all unknown requests
export const server = setupServer();

// test/setup.ts — global test lifecycle
import { beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach } from "vitest";
import { server } from "./setup/msw-server";

beforeAll(() =>
  server.listen({
    // Red-phase discipline: any unmatched request = test failure
    onUnhandledRequest: "error",
  })
);

afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());  // Reset per-test overrides
afterAll(() => server.close());

// test/checkout/checkout-service.test.ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";
import { server } from "../setup/msw-server";
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { CheckoutService } from "../../src/checkout/checkout-service";

test("CheckoutService.complete charges card and creates order", async () => {
  // Explicit handler declarations — TDD requires knowing every outbound call
  server.use(
    http.post("https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges", () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ id: "ch_test_123", status: "succeeded" }, { status: 201 })
    ),
    http.post("https://api.internal/orders", () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ id: "order-789", status: "created" }, { status: 201 })
    ),
  );

  const svc = new CheckoutService();
  const result = await svc.complete({ cartId: "cart-1", paymentToken: "tok_visa" });

  expect(result.orderId).toBe("order-789");
  expect(result.chargeId).toBe("ch_test_123");
  // If CheckoutService makes any OTHER network call, the test fails immediately
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` is the right default for feature-level unit and integration tests. It is too strict for exploratory tests or test suites that intentionally call real endpoints (e.g., contract tests). For those cases, use `"bypass"` or `"warn"` per-server-instance. The main tradeoff: when introducing MSW into a legacy codebase, `"error"` will cause many existing tests to fail immediately as their undeclared network calls are exposed. This is the correct TDD response — treat each failure as a Red signal that demands an explicit mock declaration or a deliberate `passthrough()` to acknowledge that the call is intentional.

[community]

---

### 30. TDD for TypeScript `NoInfer<T>` — Preventing Over-Broad Fixture Inference [official]

TypeScript 5.4 introduced the `NoInfer<T>` utility type, which suppresses inference contributions from a specific type parameter position — any value placed in a `NoInfer<T>` slot is checked against the inferred type but does not contribute to the inference itself. In TDD, `NoInfer<T>` is the correct tool for fixture factory functions where one parameter should drive the type and a second parameter should be validated against the inferred type but not influence it. Without `NoInfer<T>`, factory functions can infer a broader type from the default/fallback value, silently accepting values that should be type errors.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/typed-event-fixture.ts
// Without NoInfer<T>: defaultValue widens the inferred T to string | number
function createEventFixture<T>(
  events: T[],
  defaultValue: T,                    // T is inferred from BOTH events AND defaultValue
): { events: T[]; default: T } {
  return { events, default: defaultValue };
}

// BUG: T is inferred as string | number (union of both arrays)
// The 42 default is accepted even though events[] only contains strings
const BAD = createEventFixture(["click", "hover"], 42);
//                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^   ^^
//                              T inferred as string  also contributes: number => T = string|number

// With NoInfer<T>: defaultValue is checked against T but does not widen it
function createEventFixtureStrict<T>(
  events: T[],
  defaultValue: NoInfer<T>,           // checked against T but does not contribute to inference
): { events: T[]; default: T } {
  return { events, default: defaultValue };
}

// CORRECT: T is inferred as string from events[]; 42 is a type error
// Type error: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type 'NoInfer<string>'
// const BAD2 = createEventFixtureStrict(["click", "hover"], 42);

// test/event-dispatcher.test.ts
import { test, expect, expectTypeOf } from "vitest";
import { EventDispatcher } from "../src/event-dispatcher";

const fixture = createEventFixtureStrict(
  ["click", "hover", "focus"] as const,
  "click",    // must be one of the event strings — type-checked
);

test("EventDispatcher dispatches only registered event types", () => {
  const dispatcher = new EventDispatcher(fixture.events);

  dispatcher.dispatch(fixture.default);                    // "click" is valid
  expect(dispatcher.lastDispatched()).toBe("click");
});

test("EventDispatcher fixture has correctly inferred type", () => {
  expectTypeOf(fixture.default).toEqualTypeOf<"click" | "hover" | "focus">();
  expectTypeOf(fixture.events).toEqualTypeOf<readonly ["click", "hover", "focus"]>();
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `NoInfer<T>` is a precision tool for generic fixture factories and test-data builders where one argument drives the type and others must be validated against it. Overuse of `NoInfer<T>` produces confusing type errors for test authors who do not understand why their perfectly valid value is being rejected — always document the intent in JSDoc. The tradeoff is cognitive overhead for test authors unfamiliar with the pattern. Reserve `NoInfer<T>` for shared fixture utilities that are used in many test files and where the inference-widening bug has already caused a real test defect.

[official]

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 43 Additions

186. **[community] Vitest Browser Mode `vi.spyOn` on module exports silently fails — spied-on functions are not replaced in the browser ESM namespace, so assertions like `expect(analytics.trackEvent).toHaveBeenCalled()` always report zero calls even though the function was actually invoked.** A developer migrates a Node-runner component test to Browser Mode and adds `vi.spyOn(analytics, "trackEvent")`. The test passes in Node runner but in Browser Mode the spy assertion always shows `0` calls because browser-native ESM modules are sealed objects. WHY this matters: the test gives a false green — the component IS calling `trackEvent`, but the spy is not intercepting it, producing a test that verifies nothing about the analytics contract. Fix: replace `vi.spyOn` with `vi.mock(import("../analytics"), { spy: true })` for Browser Mode; the `{ spy: true }` variant wraps exports at the module resolution level rather than at the object property level.

187. **[community] TypeScript `NoInfer<T>` causes unexpected type errors when used in fixture factories that are called with `as const` literals — the `as const` suffix narrows T to a readonly tuple, but `NoInfer<T>` then rejects non-`as const` string literals as the default value because they are inferred as `string` rather than a member of the tuple.** A developer writes `createEventFixtureStrict(["click", "hover"] as const, "click")` and gets a type error claiming `"click"` is not assignable to `NoInfer<readonly ["click", "hover"]>`. The error is misleading because `"click"` IS a valid string literal — the issue is that `events` was inferred as the tuple type `readonly ["click", "hover"]` (an array), not the element type `"click" | "hover"`. WHY this matters: the fixture factory's generic parameter `T` was intended to capture the event name union, not the tuple itself. Fix: write `createEventFixtureStrict<"click"|"hover">(["click","hover"] as const, "click")` with an explicit type argument, or change the factory's `events` parameter to `readonly T[]` and let T be the element type, not the array type.

188. **[community] Jest 30 `randomize: true` interacts badly with `beforeAll` hooks that seed a shared in-memory store — when tests run in randomised order, the first test to execute may see an empty store if a lazy-init or nested-describe `beforeAll` has not yet fired, causing the first N tests to fail with "entity not found" while later tests pass because they happen to run after the seed.** A legacy test file uses `beforeAll(() => seedStore(sharedStore))` with multiple `test` blocks that all read from `sharedStore`. With `randomize: true`, Jest randomises the order of `test` declarations but still runs `beforeAll` first — however, if the seed is lazy (only populates on first access) or if nested `describe` blocks have their own `beforeAll` hooks, the execution order becomes non-deterministic. WHY this matters: the failure appears as a data race even though there is no real concurrency. Fix: audit all `beforeAll` hooks for implicit ordering assumptions; either move shared state to `beforeEach` with fresh data per test, or wrap related tests in a `describe` block so `beforeAll` scoping is explicit and unambiguous.

189. **[community] MSW `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` throws synchronously during `beforeAll` teardown when the test suite is shut down — if a network request fires during `server.close()` cleanup (from a lingering `setTimeout` or unresolved promise), the synchronous error throw corrupts the test runner's cleanup phase, producing `Cannot log after tests are done` or similar errors that obscure the real test failures.** A team enables `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` and immediately sees cryptic cleanup errors in CI. Investigation reveals a `setInterval` in a background service that continues polling after tests end, hitting an unregistered endpoint during `server.close()`. WHY this matters: the corrupted cleanup output makes it hard to identify which actual test produced the lingering timer. Fix: add an `afterAll` that explicitly clears all known intervals and awaits all pending promises before `server.close()` is called; use `vi.useFakeTimers()` in tests that start background timers to prevent them from leaking into cleanup.

190. **[community] Pact `MatchersV3.eachLike` always generates an array with exactly one element during consumer tests — developers write `eachLike({ sku: "A" })` expecting the generated request body to include multiple items for a realistic test, but `eachLike` generates a single-item array at the consumer test level; the "each like" constraint is only enforced during provider verification, not during consumer mock generation.** A developer writes a Pact contract test for a bulk-order endpoint using `eachLike({ sku: "A", qty: 1 })` and the consumer test passes with a single-item request body. In production, the provider rejects a 0-item or 3-item request because the consumer's pact never tested those cardinalities. WHY this matters: `eachLike` is a structural matcher for provider verification, not a generator for consumer test data variety. Fix: explicitly build multi-item request bodies in consumer tests using `[{ sku: "A" }, { sku: "B" }, { sku: "C" }]` and wrap the whole array in `eachLike` only to specify the element schema — the min-count constraint in the Pact file tells the verifier the provider must handle at least one item, not that the consumer tested multiple items.

191. **[community] TypeScript 5.8's granular branch-type checking in return statements breaks existing code that returned `any` from a cache `Map.get()` call — `Map<string, any>.get(key)` returns `any | undefined` in 5.8's branch checker, which is no longer silently assignable to a non-any return type, producing new compile errors in codebases that previously relied on `any` propagation to suppress type mismatches.** A team upgrades to TypeScript 5.8 and CI immediately reports new type errors in cache-access patterns like `return cache.has(key) ? cache.get(key) : computeValue(key)` where the cache was typed as `Map<string, any>`. In 5.7, `any` suppressed the mismatch; in 5.8, each branch is checked independently and `any | undefined` is not assignable to the function's non-nullable return type. WHY this matters: the errors are real — every such `any`-typed cache was a latent type safety hole. Fix: treat each 5.8 branch error as a TDD Red signal: write a test asserting the correct return type, then fix the cache type to `Map<string, ConcreteType>` and add the appropriate null check before calling the fix "Green".

### 31. TDD for Vitest `test.extend` File-Scoped Fixtures — Sharing Expensive Resources Across a Test Suite [official]

Vitest's `test.extend` fixture system supports three scope levels: test (default), file, and worker. File-scoped fixtures initialise once per test file and are shared across all tests within that file, making them ideal for expensive setup operations like spinning up a local HTTP server, opening a database connection, or building a webpack bundle — operations that are too slow to repeat per test but whose shared state risk is acceptable when properly managed. In TDD, file-scoped fixtures allow the Red phase to describe tests against a real running service without each test paying the full cold-start cost. The Green phase makes tests pass without fixture changes; the Refactor phase may promote a file-scope fixture to worker scope if the same resource can safely be shared across files.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/file-server.fixture.ts
import { test as baseTest } from "vitest";
import { createServer, type Server } from "http";
import { AddressInfo } from "net";

interface FileServerFixtures {
  serverUrl: string;
}

// File-scoped fixture: server starts once per file, not once per test
export const test = baseTest.extend<FileServerFixtures, { httpServer: Server }>({
  // Worker-scope declaration (in second generic) for the underlying server
  httpServer: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const server = createServer((req, res) => {
        if (req.url === "/health") {
          res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
          res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: "ok" }));
        } else {
          res.writeHead(404);
          res.end();
        }
      });

      await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve));
      await use(server);
      await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) =>
        server.close((err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve()))
      );
    },
    { scope: "file" }, // shared across all tests in the file
  ],

  serverUrl: async ({ httpServer }, use) => {
    const { port } = httpServer.address() as AddressInfo;
    await use(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}`);
  },
});

// test/api-client/api-client.test.ts
import { test } from "../fixtures/file-server.fixture";
import { expect } from "vitest";
import { ApiClient } from "../../src/api-client";

test("ApiClient.health returns ok for a live server", async ({ serverUrl }) => {
  const client = new ApiClient(serverUrl);
  const result = await client.health();
  expect(result.status).toBe("ok");
});

test("ApiClient.get404 throws NotFoundError for missing resource", async ({ serverUrl }) => {
  const client = new ApiClient(serverUrl);
  await expect(client.get("/missing")).rejects.toThrow("NotFoundError");
  // Both tests share the same server instance — cold-start paid once
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** File-scoped fixtures are appropriate when the resource setup cost dominates test execution time and the resource is stateless between tests (or state is reset in a lightweight teardown inside the fixture). They are inappropriate when the resource carries mutable state that tests modify — each test would see side effects from previous tests, reintroducing the shared-state problems that test isolation is designed to eliminate. Always pair file-scoped resources with an `afterEach` reset step inside the fixture body, or restrict to truly read-only resources.

[official]

---

### 32. TDD for TypeScript `satisfies` Operator in Test Fixture Declarations — Type-Validated but Inference-Preserving Fixtures [official]

The TypeScript `satisfies` operator (introduced in 4.9) checks a value against a type without widening the inferred type — unlike an explicit annotation (`: RouteConfig`) which widens to the annotated type, `satisfies RouteConfig` keeps the literal types while still catching shape mismatches. In TDD, `satisfies` is the correct tool for fixture declarations where downstream type assertions depend on literal inference. A fixture declared as `const config = { method: "POST" } satisfies RouteConfig` keeps `method` inferred as `"POST"` (not `string`), so `expectTypeOf(config.method).toEqualTypeOf<"POST">()` remains valid in the Green phase. An explicit `: RouteConfig` annotation would widen `method` to `string`, silently breaking the downstream type assertion.

```typescript
// src/types/route-config.ts
interface RouteConfig {
  method: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH";
  path: string;
  authenticated: boolean;
  rateLimit?: number;
}

// test/fixtures/route-fixtures.ts
import type { RouteConfig } from "../../src/types/route-config";
import { expectTypeOf, test, expect } from "vitest";

// BAD: annotation widens `method` to "GET" | "POST" | ... losing the literal "POST"
// const badFixture: RouteConfig = { method: "POST", path: "/orders", authenticated: true };

// GOOD: satisfies validates the shape but preserves literal inference
const createOrderRoute = {
  method: "POST",
  path: "/orders",
  authenticated: true,
  rateLimit: 100,
} satisfies RouteConfig;

// Literal inference is preserved — method is "POST", not the union
type MethodType = typeof createOrderRoute.method; // "POST"

// test/router/router.test.ts
import { Router } from "../../src/router";

test("Router registers POST route with correct literal method type", () => {
  const router = new Router();
  router.register(createOrderRoute);

  const registered = router.find("/orders");
  expect(registered?.method).toBe("POST");

  // Type-level assertion — only valid because satisfies preserved the literal
  expectTypeOf(createOrderRoute.method).toEqualTypeOf<"POST">();
});

test("Router rejects invalid route method at type level", () => {
  // @ts-expect-error — "TRACE" is not a valid method in RouteConfig
  const invalidRoute = { method: "TRACE", path: "/debug", authenticated: false } satisfies RouteConfig;
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `satisfies` is the right choice when a fixture or constant must simultaneously (a) be validated against an interface and (b) have its literal type available for downstream assertions or overload resolution. The main cost is unfamiliarity — developers who encounter `satisfies` for the first time in a test file sometimes replace it with an explicit annotation "to fix the type error" and unintentionally break the literal inference. Document the intent with a comment explaining why `satisfies` is used instead of an annotation.

[official]

---

### 33. TDD for Vitest `expect.poll` — Retry-Based Async Assertions Without Manual `waitFor` Loops [official]

Vitest 2.0+ introduced `expect.poll()`, a polling-based assertion wrapper that retries a failing assertion on a configurable interval until it passes or a timeout expires. In TDD, `expect.poll` replaces fragile `while`-loop polling and arbitrary `setTimeout` waits in the Red phase: the failing assertion describes the eventual state, and the Green phase implements the mechanism that drives the system to that state. Unlike `vi.waitFor`, `expect.poll` accepts a standard `expect` chain directly, making the Red-phase intent readable without a callback wrapper. The polling interval and timeout are configurable, and `expect.poll` fails immediately on non-retriable errors (thrown exceptions), distinguishing between "not yet" (retry) and "broken" (fail immediately).

```typescript
// src/job-queue/job-processor.ts (interface under test)
export interface JobProcessor {
  enqueue(jobId: string, payload: unknown): void;
  getStatus(jobId: string): "pending" | "processing" | "done" | "failed";
  getResult(jobId: string): unknown;
}

// test/job-queue/job-processor.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { InMemoryJobProcessor } from "../../src/job-queue/in-memory-job-processor";

let processor: InMemoryJobProcessor;

beforeEach(() => {
  processor = new InMemoryJobProcessor({ workers: 2, processingDelayMs: 50 });
});

test("job transitions to done status after processing completes", async () => {
  processor.enqueue("job-1", { task: "compress-image", url: "https://example.com/img.png" });

  // Red phase: expect.poll retries every 25ms for up to 2s
  // No manual setTimeout or while loop — intent is self-documenting
  await expect.poll(
    () => processor.getStatus("job-1"),
    { interval: 25, timeout: 2000 }
  ).toBe("done");

  expect(processor.getResult("job-1")).toMatchObject({ success: true });
});

test("processor runs two jobs concurrently and both complete", async () => {
  processor.enqueue("job-a", { task: "send-email", to: "a@example.com" });
  processor.enqueue("job-b", { task: "send-email", to: "b@example.com" });

  // Poll for both jobs — they should complete near-simultaneously under 2 workers
  await expect.poll(() => processor.getStatus("job-a"), { timeout: 2000 }).toBe("done");
  await expect.poll(() => processor.getStatus("job-b"), { timeout: 2000 }).toBe("done");
});

test("expect.poll fails immediately on processor exception, not after timeout", async () => {
  processor.enqueue("bad-job", { task: "invalid-task" });

  // When getStatus throws (not returns a non-matching value), poll re-throws immediately
  // This distinguishes "eventual convergence" failures from "broken" failures
  await expect(
    expect.poll(() => {
      const status = processor.getStatus("bad-job");
      if (status === "failed") throw new Error("Job failed: invalid task type");
      return status;
    }, { timeout: 2000 }).toBe("done")
  ).rejects.toThrow("Job failed: invalid task type");
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `expect.poll` is appropriate for testing asynchronous state transitions that are driven by background processes (job queues, event buses, timers, WebSocket messages). It should not be used as a substitute for properly awaiting asynchronous operations — if the system under test exposes a promise-based API, `await` it directly rather than polling. The timeout introduces wall-clock dependency into tests, which can cause CI flakiness on slow runners; use generous timeouts (2-5x the expected completion time on developer hardware) and consider `vi.useFakeTimers()` for processors whose timing can be controlled.

[official]

---

### 34. TDD for TypeScript Mapped Types as Test Schema Validators — Compile-Time Completeness Enforcement [official]

TypeScript mapped types can enforce that a test suite covers all members of a union or all keys of an interface — this is "compile-time test completeness." A mapped type like `type CoverageMap<T extends Record<string, unknown>> = { [K in keyof T]-?: () => void }` demands a test function entry for every key in `T`. When a new property is added to the interface, TypeScript reports a compile error in the test file's coverage map, forcing the developer to acknowledge the new property before the build passes. This is a Red signal without writing a failing test: the compiler enforces coverage before execution.

```typescript
// src/types/checkout-state.ts
interface CheckoutState {
  cartId: string;
  customerId: string;
  shippingAddress: ShippingAddress;
  paymentMethod: "card" | "paypal" | "bank_transfer";
  couponCode?: string;
  giftWrap: boolean;
}

// test/checkout/checkout-reducer.coverage-map.test-d.ts
// Compile-time coverage map: every key of CheckoutState must have an entry
import { expectTypeOf, test } from "vitest";
import type { CheckoutState } from "../../src/types/checkout-state";

// Mapped type: all keys of CheckoutState must be exercised
type CheckoutStateCoverageMap = {
  [K in keyof Required<CheckoutState>]: boolean;
};

// Declare which fields are covered — compile error if a new field is added to CheckoutState
// and not added here (the property would be missing from the mapped type)
const coverageDeclaration = {
  cartId: true,
  customerId: true,
  shippingAddress: true,
  paymentMethod: true,
  couponCode: true,   // optional fields must still be declared as Required<T> forces -?
  giftWrap: true,
} satisfies CheckoutStateCoverageMap;

// If CheckoutState grows a new field (e.g., `loyaltyPoints: number`), TypeScript
// reports: "Property 'loyaltyPoints' is missing in type..."
// — this is the Red signal that triggers writing a new test

test("coverage declaration is complete for all CheckoutState fields", () => {
  // Runtime assertion: every declared coverage entry is true (not just declared)
  const allCovered = Object.values(coverageDeclaration).every(Boolean);
  expect(allCovered).toBe(true);
  expectTypeOf(coverageDeclaration).toMatchTypeOf<CheckoutStateCoverageMap>();
});

// The actual test coverage lives in checkout-reducer.test.ts
// This file just enforces that each field has at least one dedicated test description
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Compile-time coverage maps are valuable for domain objects with many fields that are likely to grow over time — `CheckoutState`, `UserProfile`, `ConfigOptions`. They are overkill for small, stable interfaces where the compile-time overhead and maintenance cost (updating the coverage map for every interface change) outweighs the benefit. The tradeoff is that this pattern creates two places that must be updated when an interface changes: the interface itself and the coverage map. Consider this an investment for high-churn, high-stakes domain objects.

[official]

---

### 35. TDD for Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers` with `shouldAdvanceTime` — Real-Time Simulation in Deterministic Tests [official]

Vitest's fake timer system supports a `shouldAdvanceTime: true` option that automatically advances fake timers in real-time as the test runs — the fake timer wall clock ticks at 1:1 with real time, but all `setTimeout`/`setInterval` callbacks are executed synchronously via the fake timer machinery. This allows tests that consume real-time APIs (e.g., `Date.now()`, `performance.now()`) to work correctly without explicit `vi.advanceTimersByTime()` calls, while still maintaining determinism. In TDD, this option is useful for integration-level tests where the Red phase requires real-looking time progression (e.g., cache TTL expiration, token refresh scheduling) but complete manual advancement would require brittle step-by-step `advanceTimersByTime` choreography.

```typescript
// src/cache/ttl-cache.ts (interface under test)
export class TtlCache<K, V> {
  private store = new Map<K, { value: V; expiresAt: number }>();

  set(key: K, value: V, ttlMs: number): void {
    this.store.set(key, { value, expiresAt: Date.now() + ttlMs });
  }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    const entry = this.store.get(key);
    if (!entry) return undefined;
    if (Date.now() > entry.expiresAt) {
      this.store.delete(key);
      return undefined;
    }
    return entry.value;
  }
}

// test/cache/ttl-cache.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from "vitest";
import { TtlCache } from "../../src/cache/ttl-cache";

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

test("TtlCache entry expires after TTL elapses", async () => {
  const cache = new TtlCache<string, number>();
  cache.set("price", 99, 100 /* ms */);

  expect(cache.get("price")).toBe(99);

  // Advance fake timers by 150ms — entry should now be expired
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(150);

  expect(cache.get("price")).toBeUndefined();
});

test("TtlCache entry survives if accessed before TTL", async () => {
  const cache = new TtlCache<string, string>();
  cache.set("session", "abc123", 1000 /* ms */);

  // Advance to 500ms — entry still live
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(500);
  expect(cache.get("session")).toBe("abc123");

  // Advance to 1100ms — now expired
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(600);
  expect(cache.get("session")).toBeUndefined();
});

test("TtlCache allows re-setting an expired key", () => {
  const cache = new TtlCache<string, boolean>();
  cache.set("flag", true, 50);

  vi.advanceTimersByTime(100);
  expect(cache.get("flag")).toBeUndefined();

  cache.set("flag", false, 200);
  expect(cache.get("flag")).toBe(false);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `shouldAdvanceTime: true` is appropriate when the code under test uses `Date.now()` or `performance.now()` for business logic (TTL, rate limiting, token expiry) and explicit step-by-step time advancement would obscure the test's intent. The tradeoff is that `shouldAdvanceTime` ticks the real system clock in the background, which can cause flakiness if test execution itself is slow (e.g., on heavily loaded CI runners where 100ms of real time passes before a `vi.advanceTimersByTime(50)` call). For pure unit tests that control every timer themselves, prefer `shouldAdvanceTime: false` (the default) and advance time manually for full determinism.

[official]

---

### 36. TDD for TypeScript Discriminated Union Exhaustiveness — `assertNever` as a Compile-Time Red Signal [official]

The `assertNever` pattern uses TypeScript's `never` type to enforce exhaustive handling of discriminated unions at compile time. In TDD, `assertNever` is placed in the `default` branch of a `switch` statement or the final `else` of an `if`-`else if` chain over a discriminated union. When a new variant is added to the union, the compiler reports a type error in the `assertNever` call because the unhandled variant's type is not assignable to `never`. This is a compile-time Red signal that fires before any test runs, directing the developer to the exact handler location that needs updating.

```typescript
// src/types/payment-event.ts
type PaymentEvent =
  | { type: "authorised"; authCode: string; amount: number }
  | { type: "captured"; captureId: string; amount: number }
  | { type: "refunded"; refundId: string; amount: number }
  | { type: "declined"; reason: string };

// src/payment/payment-handler.ts
function assertNever(value: never, message: string): never {
  throw new Error(`${message}: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

export function handlePaymentEvent(event: PaymentEvent): string {
  switch (event.type) {
    case "authorised":
      return `Authorised ${event.amount} with code ${event.authCode}`;
    case "captured":
      return `Captured ${event.amount} as ${event.captureId}`;
    case "refunded":
      return `Refunded ${event.amount} as ${event.refundId}`;
    case "declined":
      return `Declined: ${event.reason}`;
    default:
      // If PaymentEvent grows a new variant (e.g., "disputed"), TypeScript errors here:
      // Argument of type '{ type: "disputed"; ... }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'
      return assertNever(event, "Unhandled PaymentEvent type");
  }
}

// test/payment/payment-handler.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { handlePaymentEvent } from "../../src/payment/payment-handler";

test.each<[PaymentEvent, string]>([
  [{ type: "authorised", authCode: "AUTH-1", amount: 100 }, "Authorised 100 with code AUTH-1"],
  [{ type: "captured", captureId: "CAP-1", amount: 100 }, "Captured 100 as CAP-1"],
  [{ type: "refunded", refundId: "REF-1", amount: 50 }, "Refunded 50 as REF-1"],
  [{ type: "declined", reason: "Insufficient funds" }, "Declined: Insufficient funds"],
])("handlePaymentEvent handles %s correctly", (event, expectedMessage) => {
  expect(handlePaymentEvent(event)).toBe(expectedMessage);
});

test("handlePaymentEvent throws on unhandled runtime event type", () => {
  // Cast to bypass compile-time check — simulates a future variant reaching old code
  const unknownEvent = { type: "disputed", disputeId: "D-1" } as unknown as PaymentEvent;
  expect(() => handlePaymentEvent(unknownEvent)).toThrow("Unhandled PaymentEvent type");
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `assertNever` exhaustiveness checking is ideal for discriminated unions that model domain state machines (payment events, order statuses, user roles) where adding a new variant without handling it would be a silent bug. The tradeoff is verbosity in the `switch` default branch and the requirement that all variant types flow to a single handler function (rather than being spread across the codebase). Avoid `assertNever` in union-processing functions that deliberately ignore some variants — use `default: break` there to signal intentional non-exhaustiveness, and rely on runtime tests for those paths.

[official]

---

### 37. TDD for `fast-check` Stateful Property Testing — Model-Based Testing with `fc.commands` [community]

Fast-check's `fc.commands` API enables stateful (model-based) property testing: a sequence of commands is generated, each command has a precondition (can I apply this in the current state?), a run function (apply to the real system), and a postcondition (does the real system match the model after applying?). In TDD, stateful property tests are written in the Red phase as a model of the intended behavior — the model is typically a simple in-memory representation of the system. The Green phase implements the real system until all generated command sequences satisfy the model. This catches state-transition bugs that are invisible to example-based tests because no human would think to generate the exact sequence that triggers the bug.

```typescript
// test/cart/shopping-cart-model.test.ts
import fc from "fast-check";
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { ShoppingCart } from "../../src/cart/shopping-cart";

// Model: simple in-memory representation of cart state
interface CartModel {
  items: Map<string, number>; // skuId -> quantity
}

// Command: Add item to cart
class AddItemCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, ShoppingCart> {
  constructor(readonly skuId: string, readonly quantity: number) {}

  check(model: CartModel): boolean {
    return this.quantity > 0 && this.quantity <= 10;
  }

  run(model: CartModel, real: ShoppingCart): void {
    model.items.set(this.skuId, (model.items.get(this.skuId) ?? 0) + this.quantity);
    real.addItem(this.skuId, this.quantity);

    // Postcondition: real cart quantity must match model
    expect(real.getQuantity(this.skuId)).toBe(model.items.get(this.skuId));
  }

  toString(): string {
    return `AddItem(${this.skuId}, ${this.quantity})`;
  }
}

// Command: Remove item from cart
class RemoveItemCommand implements fc.Command<CartModel, ShoppingCart> {
  constructor(readonly skuId: string) {}

  check(model: CartModel): boolean {
    return (model.items.get(this.skuId) ?? 0) > 0;
  }

  run(model: CartModel, real: ShoppingCart): void {
    model.items.delete(this.skuId);
    real.removeItem(this.skuId);

    expect(real.getQuantity(this.skuId)).toBe(0);
  }

  toString(): string {
    return `RemoveItem(${this.skuId})`;
  }
}

test("ShoppingCart satisfies cart model for all command sequences", () => {
  const skuArbitrary = fc.constantFrom("SKU-A", "SKU-B", "SKU-C");

  const commands = fc.commands([
    skuArbitrary.chain((sku) =>
      fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 10 }).map((qty) => new AddItemCommand(sku, qty))
    ),
    skuArbitrary.map((sku) => new RemoveItemCommand(sku)),
  ]);

  fc.assert(
    fc.property(commands, (cmds) => {
      const model: CartModel = { items: new Map() };
      const real = new ShoppingCart();
      fc.modelRun(() => ({ model, real }), cmds);
    }),
    { numRuns: 200, seed: 42 }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Model-based testing with `fc.commands` is appropriate for systems with meaningful state transitions — shopping carts, user account balances, reservation systems, concurrent queues. It is overkill for stateless pure functions where regular property tests suffice. The main cost is the effort to write the model and each command class; this investment pays off when the system has more than 3-4 interacting state transitions, because the combinatorial coverage that generated sequences provide quickly exceeds what example-based tests can reasonably cover.

[community]

---

### 38. TDD for Vitest `--coverage.include` Glob Patterns — Accurate Uncovered-Code Detection in the Red Phase [official]

Vitest's coverage configuration supports `include` and `exclude` glob patterns that determine which source files appear in the coverage report. In TDD, the `include` pattern is a Red-phase artifact: it defines the set of files that must have coverage, and any file matching `include` that has zero coverage is a failing signal — it represents untested production code. A common mistake is omitting `include` and relying on Vitest's default (report only files imported by tests), which hides files that no test imports yet. Adding `include: ["src/**/*.ts"]` forces all source files — including brand-new ones with no test yet — to appear in the report with 0% coverage.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — configuration enforcing coverage completeness
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",

      // Include ALL source files — not just those imported by tests
      // Files with no tests appear as 0% covered = Red signal
      include: ["src/**/*.ts"],
      exclude: [
        "src/**/*.d.ts",
        "src/**/*.test.ts",
        "src/**/index.ts",          // barrel files — no logic to test
        "src/**/__mocks__/**",
      ],

      // Thresholds enforced globally — CI fails if any metric drops below
      thresholds: {
        branches: 80,
        functions: 90,
        lines: 85,
        statements: 85,

        // Per-file overrides for critical paths
        "src/payment/**/*.ts": {
          branches: 100,
          functions: 100,
        },
      },

      reporter: ["text", "lcov", "json-summary"],
      reportsDirectory: "./coverage",
    },
  },
});

// test/coverage-completeness.test.ts
// Meta-test: verifies that every public module in src/ is imported somewhere
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { glob } from "glob";
import * as path from "path";

test("all src modules are imported by at least one test", async () => {
  const srcFiles = await glob("src/**/*.ts", {
    ignore: ["src/**/*.d.ts", "src/**/__mocks__/**", "src/**/index.ts"],
  });

  const testFiles = await glob("test/**/*.test.ts");
  const testContents = await Promise.all(
    testFiles.map((f) => import("fs").then((fs) => fs.promises.readFile(f, "utf8")))
  );
  const allImports = testContents.join("\n");

  const uncoveredModules = srcFiles.filter((srcFile) => {
    const moduleName = path.basename(srcFile, ".ts");
    return !allImports.includes(moduleName);
  });

  // Red: this list should be empty — any entry is an untested module
  expect(uncoveredModules).toEqual([]);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Forcing all source files into the coverage report via `include` is the correct default for production codebases where complete coverage is a stated requirement. The tradeoff is noise during early development: stub files, placeholder modules, and generated code all appear as 0% covered. Manage this by keeping the `exclude` list up to date and using per-directory thresholds to gradually ratchet coverage requirements upward. Avoid setting `thresholds` to 100% globally early in a project — it makes the Red-phase write cycle painfully slow; prefer 80% globally and 100% for critical payment/auth paths.

[official]

---

### 39. TDD for TypeScript `infer` in Conditional Types — Test-Driven Generic Utility Validation [official]

TypeScript conditional types with `infer` extract sub-types from complex types, enabling utilities like `UnpackPromise<T>`, `ReturnType<T>`, and `ParameterTuple<T>`. In TDD, these utility types are validated with `.test-d.ts` type-level tests before the utility implementation exists: the Red phase writes `expectTypeOf` assertions against the expected inferred type; the Green phase writes the `infer`-based conditional type until all assertions pass; the Refactor phase extracts edge cases. Writing type-level tests first forces precise thinking about the inference semantics — what should happen with `never`, `unknown`, nested generics, and union distribution.

```typescript
// test/utils/unpack-promise.test-d.ts
import { expectTypeOf, test } from "vitest";
// Note: UnpackPromise does not exist yet — Red phase
import type { UnpackPromise } from "../../src/utils/unpack-promise";

test("UnpackPromise extracts the resolved type from a Promise", () => {
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<Promise<string>>>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<Promise<number>>>().toEqualTypeOf<number>();
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<Promise<{ id: string }>>>().toEqualTypeOf<{ id: string }>();
});

test("UnpackPromise is identity for non-Promise types", () => {
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<string>>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<number>>().toEqualTypeOf<number>();
});

test("UnpackPromise handles nested Promise by unpacking one level", () => {
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<Promise<Promise<boolean>>>>().toEqualTypeOf<Promise<boolean>>();
});

test("UnpackPromise distributes over unions", () => {
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<Promise<string> | Promise<number>>>().toEqualTypeOf<string | number>();
});

test("UnpackPromise handles never correctly", () => {
  expectTypeOf<UnpackPromise<never>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
});

// Green phase: implement the utility type to make all assertions pass
// src/utils/unpack-promise.ts
export type UnpackPromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;

// Additional higher-order variant for async function return types
export type AsyncReturnType<F extends (...args: unknown[]) => Promise<unknown>> =
  F extends (...args: unknown[]) => Promise<infer R> ? R : never;

// test/utils/async-return-type.test-d.ts
test("AsyncReturnType extracts the resolved return type of async functions", () => {
  async function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<{ id: string; name: string }> {
    return { id, name: "Alice" };
  }

  expectTypeOf<AsyncReturnType<typeof fetchUser>>().toEqualTypeOf<{ id: string; name: string }>();
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Type-level TDD with `infer`-based conditional types is appropriate for shared utility type libraries used across many modules — the investment in type tests ensures that refactoring the utility does not silently break downstream consumers. It is not worth the overhead for one-off inline conditional types used in a single file. Enable `typecheck: true` in `vitest.config.ts` to make `.test-d.ts` files participate in the test run; without this, type errors in these files are invisible until a consuming file tries to use the utility.

[official]

---

### 40. TDD for Jest `--testNamePattern` and Vitest `--reporter=verbose` — Focused Red-Phase Debugging [official]

Both Jest and Vitest support test name filtering at the CLI level: Jest's `--testNamePattern=<regex>` and Vitest's `--reporter=verbose` combined with `test.only` and `describe.only` enable the TDD Red phase to be executed in isolation, confirming the failure is exactly what is expected before any implementation is written. A frequent mistake is running the entire suite during the Red phase and attributing other test failures to the new feature; focused execution confirms which failures belong to the current Red step. Vitest also supports `--reporter=dot` for fast CI output and `--reporter=verbose` for step-by-step Red-Green observation in development.

```typescript
// Demonstrating focused TDD execution patterns

// test/auth/token-validator.test.ts
import { test, describe, expect } from "vitest";
import { TokenValidator } from "../../src/auth/token-validator";

// Red phase: test.only focuses the run to just this test block
// vitest --reporter=verbose confirms exactly one failing test
describe.only("TokenValidator — Red phase: expiry validation", () => {
  test("rejects token with expiry in the past", () => {
    const validator = new TokenValidator({ clockSkewMs: 0 });
    const expiredToken = createMockToken({ exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 60 });

    expect(() => validator.validate(expiredToken)).toThrow("TokenExpiredError");
  });

  test("accepts token with expiry in the future", () => {
    const validator = new TokenValidator({ clockSkewMs: 0 });
    const validToken = createMockToken({ exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 300 });

    expect(() => validator.validate(validToken)).not.toThrow();
  });

  test("accepts token within clock skew tolerance", () => {
    const validator = new TokenValidator({ clockSkewMs: 5000 });
    // Token expired 3 seconds ago, but within 5s skew window
    const borderlineToken = createMockToken({ exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 3 });

    expect(() => validator.validate(borderlineToken)).not.toThrow();
  });
});

function createMockToken(claims: { exp: number }): string {
  const header = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ alg: "HS256", typ: "JWT" })).toString("base64url");
  const payload = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(claims)).toString("base64url");
  return `${header}.${payload}.mock-signature`;
}

// CLI usage during TDD cycle:
// Red:    vitest run --reporter=verbose test/auth/token-validator.test.ts
// Green:  [implement TokenValidator.validate] then rerun
// Refactor: vitest run (full suite) to confirm no regressions
//
// Jest equivalent:
// Red:    jest --testPathPattern=auth/token-validator --testNamePattern="expiry" --verbose
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Focused test execution via `test.only` and `describe.only` is a TDD discipline tool for the Red phase — it confirms the exact failure before implementation and prevents confusion from pre-existing failures in unrelated tests. The main risk is committing files with `.only` modifiers, which silently skips all other tests in CI. Enforce a lint rule (`no-focused-tests` in `eslint-plugin-vitest` or `jest/no-focused-tests`) to catch committed `.only` calls. Some teams also run `grep -r "\.only(" test/` in a pre-commit hook as a lightweight guard.

[official]

---

### 41. TDD for TypeScript `const` Assertions with `as const satisfies` — Immutable Configuration-Driven Test Data [official]

TypeScript 5.0 introduced the ability to combine `as const` and `satisfies` in a single expression: `value as const satisfies T`. This combination preserves maximal literal-type inference (from `as const`) while also validating the value against a type constraint (from `satisfies`). In TDD, `as const satisfies` is the correct tool for building immutable, type-validated test configuration tables — route tables, error code maps, feature flag definitions — where downstream assertions need the literal type and the structure must conform to a known schema.

```typescript
// src/types/feature-flags.ts
interface FeatureFlag {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly enabled: boolean;
  readonly rolloutPercentage: number;
  readonly environments: readonly ("development" | "staging" | "production")[];
}

type FeatureFlagMap = Record<string, FeatureFlag>;

// test/fixtures/feature-flag-fixtures.ts
import type { FeatureFlagMap } from "../../src/types/feature-flags";

// as const: preserves literal types (e.g., environments is readonly ["development"] not string[])
// satisfies: validates shape against FeatureFlagMap (catches missing/extra fields at compile time)
export const TEST_FLAGS = {
  newCheckout: {
    name: "new-checkout",
    enabled: true,
    rolloutPercentage: 100,
    environments: ["development", "staging"] as const,
  },
  betaDashboard: {
    name: "beta-dashboard",
    enabled: false,
    rolloutPercentage: 0,
    environments: ["development"] as const,
  },
} as const satisfies FeatureFlagMap;

// test/feature-flags/feature-flag-service.test.ts
import { test, expect, expectTypeOf } from "vitest";
import { FeatureFlagService } from "../../src/feature-flags/feature-flag-service";
import { TEST_FLAGS } from "../fixtures/feature-flag-fixtures";

test("FeatureFlagService enables flags for correct environment", () => {
  const service = new FeatureFlagService(TEST_FLAGS, { env: "staging" });

  // newCheckout: enabled: true, environments includes staging
  expect(service.isEnabled("newCheckout")).toBe(true);

  // betaDashboard: environments is ["development"] only, staging is excluded
  expect(service.isEnabled("betaDashboard")).toBe(false);
});

test("TEST_FLAGS preserves literal types through as const satisfies", () => {
  // Literal types preserved by as const
  expectTypeOf(TEST_FLAGS.newCheckout.enabled).toEqualTypeOf<true>();
  expectTypeOf(TEST_FLAGS.betaDashboard.enabled).toEqualTypeOf<false>();

  // environments is readonly tuple, not string[]
  expectTypeOf(TEST_FLAGS.newCheckout.environments).toEqualTypeOf<
    readonly ["development", "staging"]
  >();
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `as const satisfies` is the preferred pattern over plain `as const` when the fixture needs both literal inference and shape validation. It is preferred over an explicit type annotation when literal types must flow to type-level assertions. The syntax is slightly surprising for developers unfamiliar with it — adding a comment like `// as const: keeps literal types | satisfies: validates shape` reduces confusion. Avoid `as const satisfies` for large, frequently mutated fixtures where the literal-type overhead (very wide union types from deeply nested `as const` expressions) slows the TypeScript language server.

[official]

---

### 42. TDD for Vitest `vi.stubGlobal` — Replacing Browser/Node Globals Safely in the Red Phase [official]

Vitest's `vi.stubGlobal(name, value)` replaces a named global (e.g., `fetch`, `localStorage`, `crypto`, `navigator`) with a controlled stub for the duration of a test, and restores the original value when `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` is called (typically in `afterEach`). In TDD, `vi.stubGlobal` is the correct tool for the Red phase when code under test reads directly from globals — replacing `global.fetch` with a failing stub immediately causes the test to fail (Red), confirming that the production code does indeed call `fetch`. The Green phase provides a passing stub; the Refactor phase may extract the global dependency into an injected parameter.

```typescript
// src/geo/location-service.ts (interface under test — reads navigator.geolocation)
export class LocationService {
  async getCurrentPosition(): Promise<GeolocationCoordinates> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      if (!navigator.geolocation) {
        reject(new Error("Geolocation not supported"));
        return;
      }
      navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(
        (pos) => resolve(pos.coords),
        (err) => reject(new Error(err.message))
      );
    });
  }
}

// test/geo/location-service.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi, afterEach } from "vitest";
import { LocationService } from "../../src/geo/location-service";

afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllGlobals();
});

test("getCurrentPosition resolves with coordinates when geolocation succeeds", async () => {
  const mockCoords: GeolocationCoordinates = {
    latitude: 51.5074,
    longitude: -0.1278,
    accuracy: 10,
    altitude: null,
    altitudeAccuracy: null,
    heading: null,
    speed: null,
  };

  // Stub navigator.geolocation before the test exercises it
  vi.stubGlobal("navigator", {
    geolocation: {
      getCurrentPosition: (
        success: PositionCallback,
        _error: PositionErrorCallback
      ) => success({ coords: mockCoords } as GeolocationPosition),
    },
  });

  const service = new LocationService();
  const coords = await service.getCurrentPosition();

  expect(coords.latitude).toBe(51.5074);
  expect(coords.longitude).toBe(-0.1278);
});

test("getCurrentPosition rejects when geolocation is unavailable", async () => {
  vi.stubGlobal("navigator", { geolocation: undefined });

  const service = new LocationService();
  await expect(service.getCurrentPosition()).rejects.toThrow("Geolocation not supported");
});

test("getCurrentPosition rejects when geolocation returns an error", async () => {
  vi.stubGlobal("navigator", {
    geolocation: {
      getCurrentPosition: (
        _success: PositionCallback,
        error: PositionErrorCallback
      ) => error({ message: "PERMISSION_DENIED", code: 1 } as GeolocationPositionError),
    },
  });

  const service = new LocationService();
  await expect(service.getCurrentPosition()).rejects.toThrow("PERMISSION_DENIED");
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `vi.stubGlobal` is appropriate for testing code that reads browser or Node globals directly. It is not a substitute for proper dependency injection — code that accepts a `GeolocationAPI` interface parameter is easier to test, more portable, and more explicit about its dependencies. Use `vi.stubGlobal` as a retrofit tool for legacy code that reads globals directly, or as a temporary measure in the Red phase when refactoring to injection is deferred. Always call `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in `afterEach` to prevent stub state from leaking into subsequent tests.

[official]
