### 43. TDD for TypeScript Branded Types — Compile-Time Identity Validation in Fixture Factories [community]

Branded types (also called nominal types or opaque types) use an intersection with a phantom brand property to distinguish structurally identical types at compile time. In TDD, branded types enforce that fixture factories for domain identifiers (user IDs, order IDs, payment tokens) return the correct branded type — preventing test code from accidentally passing a `UserId` where an `OrderId` is expected. The Red phase writes a fixture that returns the wrong branded type and confirms the compiler rejects it; the Green phase produces the correctly branded fixture.

```typescript
// src/types/branded.ts
declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly [__brand]: B };

export type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
export type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;
export type PaymentToken = Brand<string, "PaymentToken">;

export const UserId = (id: string): UserId => id as UserId;
export const OrderId = (id: string): OrderId => id as OrderId;
export const PaymentToken = (token: string): PaymentToken => token as PaymentToken;

// test/fixtures/id-fixtures.ts
import type { UserId, OrderId, PaymentToken } from "../../src/types/branded";
import { UserId as makeUserId, OrderId as makeOrderId, PaymentToken as makeToken } from "../../src/types/branded";

export const testUserId = (suffix = "001"): UserId =>
  makeUserId(`user-test-${suffix}`);

export const testOrderId = (suffix = "001"): OrderId =>
  makeOrderId(`order-test-${suffix}`);

export const testPaymentToken = (suffix = "001"): PaymentToken =>
  makeToken(`tok_test_${suffix}`);

// test/checkout/checkout-service.test.ts
import { test, expect, expectTypeOf } from "vitest";
import { CheckoutService } from "../../src/checkout/checkout-service";
import { testUserId, testOrderId, testPaymentToken } from "../fixtures/id-fixtures";
import type { UserId, OrderId } from "../../src/types/branded";

test("CheckoutService.createOrder returns a branded OrderId", async () => {
  const service = new CheckoutService();
  const userId = testUserId();
  const token = testPaymentToken();

  const orderId = await service.createOrder(userId, token);

  // Runtime: orderId is a string
  expect(typeof orderId).toBe("string");
  expect(orderId).toMatch(/^order-/);

  // Type-level: orderId is OrderId, not UserId or plain string
  expectTypeOf(orderId).toEqualTypeOf<OrderId>();
});

test("CheckoutService.createOrder rejects UserId in place of PaymentToken at type level", () => {
  const service = new CheckoutService();
  const userId = testUserId();

  // @ts-expect-error — UserId is not assignable to PaymentToken
  service.createOrder(userId, userId);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Branded types add significant safety to domain-identifier-heavy codebases where mixing IDs is a real bug risk (passing a user ID to an endpoint expecting an order ID). The tradeoff is boilerplate: every identifier type needs a brand declaration and a constructor function, and every fixture factory must return the branded variant. In small codebases with few identifier types, the overhead exceeds the benefit. Reserve branded types for production code with multiple structurally identical identifier types used in security-sensitive operations (authentication, authorization, payment).

[community]

---

### 44. TDD for Vitest Worker Thread Parallelism — `poolOptions.threads` and Isolation Boundaries [official]

Vitest's default pool is `threads` (worker threads), and `poolOptions.threads` controls the number of concurrent worker threads and their isolation level. Understanding worker thread isolation is critical for TDD because tests that pass in isolation can fail under parallelism if they share mutable state through module-level singletons, global `Map`/`Set` instances, or file system state. The TDD discipline for concurrent execution is: write each test so it would pass if run alone in a fresh process, verify with `vitest run --pool=forks` (process isolation) for a stricter isolation check, and use `vitest run --reporter=verbose --sequence.shuffle=true` to surface order dependencies.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — parallelism and isolation configuration
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    pool: "threads",  // default — worker threads, shared V8 heap but isolated module registry
    poolOptions: {
      threads: {
        minThreads: 2,
        maxThreads: 8,
        isolate: true,  // fresh module registry per test file (default: true)
        // useAtomics: true,  // Faster synchronisation via SharedArrayBuffer (requires COOP headers)
      },
    },

    // Shuffle test file execution order to expose order dependencies
    sequence: {
      shuffle: true,
      seed: Date.now(), // Different order each run; --reporter=verbose shows the seed for replay
    },
  },
});

// test/singleton-isolation.test.ts
// Demonstrates the module-singleton problem and its TDD-compliant fix
import { test, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";

// BAD: module-level singleton — shared across all tests in this worker
// const sharedRegistry = new Map<string, string>();

// GOOD: factory function ensures per-test isolation
import { createRegistry } from "../../src/registry/registry";

let registry: ReturnType<typeof createRegistry>;

beforeEach(() => {
  // Fresh registry instance per test — not shared with other tests
  registry = createRegistry();
});

test("registry stores and retrieves a value", () => {
  registry.set("key1", "value1");
  expect(registry.get("key1")).toBe("value1");
});

test("registry is empty at start of each test", () => {
  // Would fail if registry were module-level singleton and previous test ran first
  expect(registry.size).toBe(0);
});

test("registry.delete removes entries correctly", () => {
  registry.set("key2", "value2");
  registry.delete("key2");
  expect(registry.has("key2")).toBe(false);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `pool: "threads"` with `isolate: true` is the correct default — it provides module-level isolation at worker-thread speed. `pool: "forks"` (separate processes) provides stronger isolation (no shared heap) at the cost of slower startup. Use `pool: "forks"` for test files that manipulate process-level globals (`process.env`, `process.cwd()`, `process.exit`) or that use native modules that are not thread-safe. Use `pool: "vmThreads"` for maximum isolation within a single process when fork overhead is unacceptable. The `sequence.shuffle: true` option should be a CI default to prevent order-dependent tests from passing consistently due to accidental execution order.

[official]

---

### 45. TDD for TypeScript `--exactOptionalPropertyTypes` — Strict Optional Fixture Validation [official]

TypeScript's `--exactOptionalPropertyTypes` flag (introduced in 4.4) changes how optional properties are checked: without the flag, `{ prop?: string }` accepts `{ prop: undefined }` as a valid assignment; with the flag, `prop: undefined` is only assignable if the type is explicitly `string | undefined`. In TDD, enabling `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` in `tsconfig.test.json` makes fixture factories stricter — test code that writes `prop: undefined` to satisfy an optional field is now a compile error, forcing the developer to either use a completely absent property or explicitly declare the type as `T | undefined`. This surfaces a class of latent bugs where tests were silently passing `undefined` values that production code would reject.

```typescript
// tsconfig.test.json — stricter optional property checking for tests
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "strict": true
  },
  "include": ["test/**/*.ts", "test/**/*.test-d.ts"]
}

// src/types/user-profile.ts
interface UserProfile {
  id: string;
  displayName: string;
  avatarUrl?: string;       // optional — absent or string, NOT string | undefined
  bio?: string;             // optional — absent or string
  linkedAccountId?: string; // optional — absent or string
}

// test/fixtures/user-profile-fixture.ts
import type { UserProfile } from "../../src/types/user-profile";

// BAD (fails with exactOptionalPropertyTypes): explicitly writing undefined
// export const minimalUser = (): UserProfile => ({
//   id: "user-001",
//   displayName: "Test User",
//   avatarUrl: undefined, // error: undefined is not assignable to string (with exactOptionalPropertyTypes)
// });

// GOOD: omit optional fields that are not set
export const minimalUser = (): UserProfile => ({
  id: "user-001",
  displayName: "Test User",
  // avatarUrl, bio, linkedAccountId are absent — not explicitly undefined
});

export const fullUser = (): UserProfile => ({
  id: "user-002",
  displayName: "Full User",
  avatarUrl: "https://cdn.example.com/avatars/002.png",
  bio: "Test user with all fields populated",
  linkedAccountId: "ext-acc-456",
});

// test/profile/profile-renderer.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { ProfileRenderer } from "../../src/profile/profile-renderer";
import { minimalUser, fullUser } from "../fixtures/user-profile-fixture";

test("ProfileRenderer renders minimal user without avatar", () => {
  const renderer = new ProfileRenderer();
  const html = renderer.render(minimalUser());

  expect(html).toContain("Test User");
  expect(html).not.toContain("<img"); // no avatar element when avatarUrl is absent
});

test("ProfileRenderer renders avatar when avatarUrl is present", () => {
  const renderer = new ProfileRenderer();
  const html = renderer.render(fullUser());

  expect(html).toContain('<img src="https://cdn.example.com/avatars/002.png"');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is a high-value flag for codebases where the difference between "absent" and "`undefined`" is semantically meaningful — REST APIs that use `PATCH` semantics (absent means "don't update", `undefined` means "clear the field"), GraphQL resolvers that distinguish `null` from missing fields, and database mappers that check `key in obj` rather than `obj[key] !== undefined`. The tradeoff is breaking changes: enabling this flag on an existing codebase typically surfaces dozens of compile errors in test fixtures that used `prop: undefined` as a convenience shorthand. Introduce it per-directory using path-specific `tsconfig.json` files rather than globally.

[official]

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 44 Additions

192. **[community] Vitest `expect.poll` silently succeeds when the polled function throws during an assertion inside a `test.concurrent` block — the thrown assertion error from inside the poll callback is caught by `expect.poll`'s retry mechanism and treated as a retriable failure rather than a fatal assertion error, so a concurrent test that should fail with "expected X to be Y" retries until timeout and then fails with "poll timed out" instead of the actual assertion message.** A developer writes `await expect.poll(() => { expect(result.status).toBe("done"); return result.status; })` and is confused when the timeout error gives no hint about what the actual status was at expiry. WHY this matters: the real failure message ("expected 'failed' to be 'done'") is swallowed, making debugging significantly harder in CI where the test output is the only diagnostic. Fix: return the value from `expect.poll`'s callback and chain the assertion outside — `await expect.poll(() => result.status).toBe("done")` — so any mismatch produces a clear diff-style failure message rather than a timeout.

193. **[community] TypeScript `satisfies` with a recursive interface incorrectly reports "excessively deep type instantiation" errors for fixture objects that are 3-4 levels deep — the error does not mean the fixture is invalid, it means the TypeScript checker hit its recursion limit while validating the `satisfies` constraint, producing a misleading error that looks like a type mismatch.** A developer creates a fixture for a recursive `TreeNode<T>` type using `satisfies TreeNode<string>` and gets "Type instantiation is excessively deep" at depth 4 nodes. The fixture is structurally valid — the error is a checker limitation. WHY this matters: developers often respond by removing `satisfies` entirely, losing compile-time validation. Fix: break the recursive structure into separately-declared subtree fixtures and compose them: `const leaf = { value: "x", children: [] } satisfies TreeNode<string>; const subtree = { value: "y", children: [leaf] } satisfies TreeNode<string>;` — each level stays within the recursion limit.

194. **[community] Jest `--testNamePattern` regex flag does not escape dots in test names — a test named "v1.0.0 returns expected schema" will be matched by `--testNamePattern="v1.0.0"` but also by `--testNamePattern="v1000"` because `.` in regex matches any character.** A developer runs `jest --testNamePattern="v1.0.0"` intending to run only the version-related test, but all tests whose names contain any six-character sequence matching `v1X0Y0` (where X and Y are any character) also execute. WHY this matters: in a large suite this can cause unexpected tests to run (and potentially fail) during a focused Red-phase session, confusing the developer about which test their current implementation is supposed to fix. Fix: escape dots in `testNamePattern` strings — `jest --testNamePattern="v1\\.0\\.0"` or use `--testNamePattern="v1[.]0[.]0"` to match only the literal version string.

195. **[community] Vitest `vi.stubGlobal("fetch", mockFetch)` does not affect calls to `fetch` made inside Web Workers or `SharedWorker` contexts spawned by the component under test — the stub replaces `globalThis.fetch` in the main thread's JavaScript environment, but the Worker thread has its own global scope where `fetch` remains the native implementation.** A developer stubs `fetch` to return a mock response and tests a component that delegates data fetching to a Web Worker. The mock is never called, and the Worker makes real network requests. WHY this matters: the test appears to be testing isolation but actually allows real network traffic through a side channel, producing non-deterministic results in CI environments without internet access. Fix: use MSW (Mock Service Worker) with a `ServiceWorker` handler that intercepts fetch at the network level rather than the JavaScript global level — MSW's service worker registers a real browser service worker that intercepts fetch for all execution contexts including Workers.

196. **[community] TypeScript `as const satisfies` expressions on arrays with mixed literal types can produce extremely slow type-checking when the array has more than ~20 elements — each element's literal type is preserved and `satisfies` validates the full tuple against the constraint type, creating an O(n²) or worse type-checking cost for large arrays.** A developer creates a test fixture with 50 route definitions using `as const satisfies RouteConfig[]` and notices that TypeScript language server response time in the fixture file degrades from under 100ms to over 5s. The issue is that `as const` on a 50-element array produces a 50-member tuple type, and `satisfies` validates each member against `RouteConfig`, triggering repeated type instantiation. WHY this matters: slow type-checking in fixture files creates friction in the TDD inner loop, where fast compiler feedback is essential. Fix: split large fixture arrays into smaller const arrays (10-15 elements each) and compose them: `const routes = [...routesA, ...routesB] satisfies RouteConfig[]` — the spread combines at the value level while each sub-array's `satisfies` check stays within the fast-path threshold.

197. **[community] Vitest `--coverage` with `provider: "v8"` reports incorrect branch coverage for TypeScript code that uses optional chaining (`?.`) and nullish coalescing (`??`) — the V8 engine inlines these to bytecode branches that do not map 1:1 to the TypeScript source positions, causing coverage reports to show uncovered branches for code that is clearly exercised by tests.** A developer has 100% test coverage by line and function but V8 reports 60% branch coverage for a module full of `?.` and `??` expressions. Attempting to write tests to cover the "missing" branches is frustrating because no test combination can change the coverage number — the uncovered branches exist only in the compiled bytecode. WHY this matters: the coverage gate in CI fails despite the code being genuinely well-tested. Fix: switch to `provider: "istanbul"` for TypeScript projects that use extensive optional chaining; istanbul instruments the TypeScript source via Babel transformation, producing source-accurate branch coverage that correctly handles `?.` and `??` as two branches (present/absent) rather than the bytecode's multiple internal branches.

## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### 46. TDD for Vitest `test.for` — Parametrized Tests with Full `TestContext` Access [official]

`test.for` is the context-aware successor to `test.each` in Vitest 4.x. While `test.each` spreads arrays and loses the fixture context, `test.for` injects the full `TestContext` as a second argument alongside the test-case data, enabling parametrized suites that still use fixture-scoped resources (databases, HTTP clients, temporary directories). This is particularly valuable in the Red phase when you need to run the same failing assertion across multiple data shapes while sharing a single expensive fixture setup. Unlike `test.each` with destructured tuples, `test.for` preserves type-safety for each test-case object without requiring manual type casts.

```typescript
// src/pricing/__tests__/discount-engine.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { DiscountEngine } from "../discount-engine";

interface DiscountCase {
  label: string;
  customerTier: "free" | "pro" | "enterprise";
  cartTotal: number;
  expectedDiscount: number;
}

const cases: DiscountCase[] = [
  { label: "free tier gets no discount",       customerTier: "free",       cartTotal: 100, expectedDiscount: 0    },
  { label: "pro tier gets 10% on $100+",       customerTier: "pro",        cartTotal: 100, expectedDiscount: 10   },
  { label: "enterprise gets 20% on any amount",customerTier: "enterprise", cartTotal: 50,  expectedDiscount: 10   },
  { label: "pro tier no discount below $50",   customerTier: "pro",        cartTotal: 40,  expectedDiscount: 0    },
];

// test.for does NOT spread arrays — each element is the full object, TestContext is second arg
test.for(cases)("DiscountEngine: $label", ({ customerTier, cartTotal, expectedDiscount }, { expect }) => {
  const engine = new DiscountEngine();
  const result = engine.calculate({ tier: customerTier, total: cartTotal });
  expect(result.discountAmount).toBe(expectedDiscount);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.for` is strictly more capable than `test.each` when fixture context is needed, but adds a function-argument signature that is unfamiliar to developers accustomed to `test.each`'s template-literal titles. For pure data-driven tests with no fixture access, `test.each` with its `%s`/`%p` template interpolation is still slightly more concise. Migrate to `test.for` when the test body starts reaching outside `TestContext` to share state (a strong signal that file-scoped fixtures are needed).

---

### 47. TDD for Vitest `test.override` — Fixture Value Injection for Suite-Specific Scenarios [official]

`test.override` (Vitest 4.1+) allows a `describe` block to replace specific fixture values inherited from `test.extend` without redefining the entire fixture chain. This enables the TDD pattern of a single base fixture setup shared across the file, with individual suites overriding only the values relevant to their scenario — for example, swapping the `userRole` fixture from `"viewer"` to `"admin"` for an authorisation-focused describe block. The override propagates to all nested tests and nested describes, matching the scope semantics of `beforeAll`. This eliminates the "fixture duplication" anti-pattern where developers copy-paste a `test.extend` call with one value changed.

```typescript
// auth/__tests__/permissions.test.ts
import { test as base, expect, describe } from "vitest";

// Base fixture: defaults to a read-only viewer context
const test = base.extend<{ userRole: string; authToken: string }>({
  userRole: "viewer",
  authToken: async ({ userRole }, use) => {
    const token = await issueTestToken({ role: userRole });
    await use(token);
    await revokeTestToken(token);
  },
});

// Override userRole for the admin suite — authToken fixture re-runs with "admin"
describe("Admin permissions", () => {
  test.override({ userRole: "admin" });

  test("can delete resources", async ({ authToken }) => {
    const response = await deleteResource("/api/resources/123", authToken);
    expect(response.status).toBe(204);
  });

  test("can promote other users", async ({ authToken }) => {
    const response = await promoteUser("/api/users/456", authToken);
    expect(response.status).toBe(200);
  });
});

describe("Viewer permissions", () => {
  // userRole remains "viewer" — no override needed
  test("cannot delete resources", async ({ authToken }) => {
    const response = await deleteResource("/api/resources/123", authToken);
    expect(response.status).toBe(403);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.override` only works with fixtures defined via `test.extend` — it has no effect on values passed directly as variables in the test body. This means converting from inline `beforeEach` setup to `test.extend`-based fixtures is a prerequisite. The benefit is substantial: removing duplicate `extend` chains reduces fixture maintenance cost significantly. If your project mixes `beforeEach` and `test.extend` patterns, introduce `test.override` incrementally starting with the fixtures that vary most across suites.

---

### 48. TDD for Vitest `test.aroundEach` / `test.aroundAll` — Unified Setup-Teardown Lifecycle Hooks [official]

`test.aroundEach` and `test.aroundAll` (Vitest 4.1+) are continuation-style hooks that replace paired `beforeEach`/`afterEach` and `beforeAll`/`afterAll` blocks with a single generator function. The generator `yield`s control to the test (or suite), and cleanup logic runs after the yield — eliminating the temporal coupling between setup and teardown code scattered across two separate callbacks. This pattern closely mirrors how Go test helpers and Rust fixtures work, and is well-suited to resources that require symmetric cleanup: database transactions, temporary files, network server processes, and test-mode feature flags.

```typescript
// integrations/__tests__/database-transaction.test.ts
import { test as base, expect } from "vitest";
import { getTestDb } from "../test-helpers/db";

// aroundEach wraps every test in a transaction that is always rolled back
const test = base.extend<{ db: ReturnType<typeof getTestDb> }>({
  db: [
    async function* ({ task }, use) {
      // aroundEach via generator fixture: yield = run the test
      const db = getTestDb();
      await db.begin();
      await use(db); // test body runs here
      await db.rollback(); // always rolls back — test data never persists
    },
    { scope: "test" },
  ],
});

test("inserting a user is visible within the transaction", async ({ db }) => {
  await db.query("INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES ('u1', 'Alice')");
  const row = await db.query("SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 'u1'");
  expect(row.rows[0].name).toBe("Alice");
});

test("previous test's insert is not visible (rolled back)", async ({ db }) => {
  const row = await db.query("SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 'u1'");
  expect(row.rowCount).toBe(0); // rollback cleaned up
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Generator-based fixtures require TypeScript to have `lib: ["ES2015.Generator"]` or `downlevelIteration` enabled, and editors sometimes struggle with type inference inside `async function*` fixture definitions. The primary alternative — separate `beforeEach`/`afterEach` — works with any test runner, but the paired structure requires developers to manually ensure symmetric cleanup. Generator fixtures enforce symmetry structurally: if a test throws, the `finally` block (or post-yield code) still executes. Use `aroundAll` (suite-level) for resources with expensive startup costs (e.g., a Docker container) and `aroundEach` (test-level) for per-test isolation (transactions, temp files).

---

### 49. TDD for Vitest `test.tags` — Filtering and Organizing Tests by Cross-Cutting Concerns [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduces a `test.tags` metadata system that decorates tests with arbitrary string labels (`@smoke`, `@regression`, `@slow`, `@wip`) without modifying test names or file paths. Tags enable CI pipeline segmentation: a pull-request pipeline runs `vitest --testTag @smoke` (fast, critical-path only), while a nightly pipeline runs `vitest --testTag @regression` for exhaustive coverage. In TDD, tagging new tests `@wip` during the Red phase makes it easy to re-run only the work-in-progress tests across an entire monorepo without using `test.only` (which carries the risk of accidentally committing focused tests).

```typescript
// checkout/__tests__/payment-flow.test.ts
import { test, expect, describe } from "vitest";
import { PaymentProcessor } from "../payment-processor";

// Smoke: must pass on every PR
test("payment succeeds for valid Visa card", { tags: ["@smoke"] }, async () => {
  const processor = new PaymentProcessor({ provider: "stripe-test" });
  const result = await processor.charge({ amount: 5000, currency: "usd", token: "tok_visa" });
  expect(result.status).toBe("succeeded");
});

// Regression: only in nightly runs (slow 3D-Secure simulation)
test("payment succeeds through 3D-Secure challenge", { tags: ["@regression", "@slow"] }, async () => {
  const processor = new PaymentProcessor({ provider: "stripe-test" });
  const result = await processor.charge({ amount: 5000, currency: "usd", token: "tok_threeDSecureRequired2" });
  expect(result.status).toBe("succeeded");
});

// WIP: active Red-phase test under development
test("payment fails gracefully on network timeout", { tags: ["@wip"] }, async () => {
  const processor = new PaymentProcessor({ provider: "stripe-test", timeout: 1 });
  await expect(processor.charge({ amount: 5000, currency: "usd", token: "tok_visa" })).rejects.toThrow("network timeout");
});

// Run with: vitest --testTag @smoke
// Run with: vitest --testTag @regression
// Run with: vitest --testTag @wip
```

**Tradeoff.** Tags are metadata — they do not affect test execution order or isolation. Over-tagging creates maintenance burden (tags drift out of sync as tests evolve), so establish a small canonical tag vocabulary (3-5 tags project-wide) and document them in the project's `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Tags also do not replace file-based organization — a test in a slow integration file tagged `@smoke` will still load all the slow file's dependencies. For maximum filter speed, combine tags with `--project` (workspace filtering) to limit the module graph, not just the test execution.

---

### 50. TDD for Vitest ARIA Snapshots — Accessibility-Driven Red Signals for UI Components [official]

Vitest 4.1.4+ introduces experimental ARIA snapshot matchers (`toMatchAriaSnapshot`, `toMatchAriaInlineSnapshot`) that capture the accessibility tree of a DOM element as a human-readable YAML-like text rather than an HTML string. In TDD, ARIA snapshots are a superior Red-phase signal for UI components: a failing ARIA snapshot pinpoints exactly which accessible role, name, or state changed (e.g., `button "Submit" disabled` becoming `button "Submit"` without `disabled`), while an HTML snapshot failure requires parsing raw markup to identify the semantic impact. ARIA snapshots are stable across cosmetic refactors (class renames, layout changes) but catch accessibility regressions immediately.

```typescript
// components/__tests__/login-form.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import { LoginForm } from "../LoginForm";

test("LoginForm has correct accessible structure in initial state", () => {
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={vi.fn()} />);
  const form = screen.getByRole("form", { name: /login/i });

  // ARIA inline snapshot — fails if roles, names, or states change
  expect(form).toMatchAriaInlineSnapshot(`
    - form "Login":
      - textbox "Email address"
      - textbox "Password"
      - button "Sign in"
  `);
});

test("LoginForm shows error state with accessible announcement", () => {
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={vi.fn()} error="Invalid credentials" />);
  const form = screen.getByRole("form", { name: /login/i });

  expect(form).toMatchAriaInlineSnapshot(`
    - form "Login":
      - alert "Invalid credentials"
      - textbox "Email address"
      - textbox "Password"
      - button "Sign in"
  `);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** ARIA snapshots test the accessibility API, not the visual rendering — they will not catch a missing CSS color or incorrect font size. They are an addition to, not a replacement for, visual regression tests. The experimental status means the snapshot format may change between minor versions; pin your Vitest version when ARIA snapshot tests are critical CI gates. ARIA snapshots are most valuable for component libraries and design systems where accessibility regressions have downstream impact across many consuming apps.

---

### 51. TDD for Vitest `toMatchFileSnapshot` — Readable Multi-Line Output Assertions with Syntax Highlighting [official]

`toMatchFileSnapshot(filePath)` stores a snapshot in a file you specify, rather than an auto-generated `.snap` file. This enables snapshot files with meaningful extensions (`.html`, `.json`, `.graphql`, `.sql`) that render with syntax highlighting in editors and code review tools. In TDD, `toMatchFileSnapshot` is the right tool for code generators, template renderers, schema serializers, and query builders — any production code whose output is a long structured string. The file path doubles as documentation: `__snapshots__/sql/select-with-pagination.sql` communicates exactly what the test verifies without reading the test body.

```typescript
// query-builder/__tests__/select-builder.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { SelectBuilder } from "../select-builder";
import path from "node:path";

const SNAP = (name: string) =>
  path.join(__dirname, "__snapshots__/sql", `${name}.sql`);

test("SelectBuilder generates correct paginated query", async () => {
  const builder = new SelectBuilder("products");
  const sql = builder
    .select(["id", "name", "price"])
    .where("category", "=", "electronics")
    .orderBy("price", "ASC")
    .limit(20)
    .offset(40)
    .build();

  // Stored in __snapshots__/sql/select-paginated.sql — readable with SQL highlighting
  await expect(sql).toMatchFileSnapshot(SNAP("select-paginated"));
});

test("SelectBuilder generates correct JOIN query", async () => {
  const builder = new SelectBuilder("orders");
  const sql = builder
    .select(["orders.id", "users.name", "orders.total"])
    .join("users", "orders.user_id = users.id")
    .where("orders.status", "=", "completed")
    .build();

  await expect(sql).toMatchFileSnapshot(SNAP("select-join-users"));
});
```

**Tradeoff.** File snapshots are committed to the repository, which makes diffs readable in pull requests — the `.sql` or `.html` file shows exactly what changed. The downside is that the snapshot directory grows with every new test case; use a consistent directory structure and naming convention to avoid confusion. `toMatchFileSnapshot` requires `async`/`await` (the matcher is always a Promise), which catches some developers off-guard when converting from `toMatchSnapshot()`. Unlike inline snapshots, file snapshots are not automatically deleted when tests are removed — add a CI check that orphaned snapshot files trigger a warning.

---

### 52. TDD for Vitest `expect.addSnapshotSerializer` — Semantic Snapshot Rendering for Domain Objects [official]

`expect.addSnapshotSerializer` registers a custom snapshot renderer that transforms specific value types before snapshotting. In TDD, custom serializers convert opaque domain objects (Date instances, BigInt currency values, UUID objects, binary buffers) into human-readable representations that survive serialisation without losing semantic meaning. Without a custom serializer, `toMatchSnapshot()` on a `Date` produces a full ISO string that breaks when tests run across timezones; with a serializer, you can normalise to a stable representation like `Date<2026-05-14>`.

```typescript
// test/setup/snapshot-serializers.ts  (imported in vitest.config.ts setupFiles)
import { expect } from "vitest";

// Serialiser 1: Dates — normalise to date-only, timezone-agnostic
expect.addSnapshotSerializer({
  test(val): val is Date {
    return val instanceof Date;
  },
  print(val: Date): string {
    return `Date<${val.toISOString().slice(0, 10)}>`;
  },
});

// Serialiser 2: Money values — show amount + currency symbol, hide floating point noise
expect.addSnapshotSerializer({
  test(val): val is { amount: number; currency: string } {
    return typeof val === "object" && val !== null && "amount" in val && "currency" in val;
  },
  print(val: { amount: number; currency: string }): string {
    return `Money<${val.currency} ${(val.amount / 100).toFixed(2)}>`;
  },
});

// test/orders/__tests__/order-summary.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { buildOrderSummary } from "../order-summary";

test("OrderSummary snapshot is stable across timezones and floating-point noise", () => {
  const summary = buildOrderSummary({
    orderId: "ord-001",
    createdAt: new Date("2026-05-14T13:00:00Z"),
    total: { amount: 4999, currency: "USD" },
  });

  expect(summary).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
    {
      "createdAt": Date<2026-05-14>,
      "orderId": "ord-001",
      "total": Money<USD 49.99>,
    }
  `);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom serializers are global — once registered in `setupFiles`, they apply to every snapshot in the test suite. This is almost always desirable (you want `Date` normalisation everywhere), but it means a poorly written serializer can silently corrupt snapshots for an entire project. Guard each serializer's `test()` function with precise type checks and test the serializer itself with a unit test. Register serializers in a dedicated `setupFiles` entry (not `globalSetup`) so they are available inside the worker process where tests run.

---

### 53. TDD for TypeScript `satisfies` with Union Discriminants — Compile-Time Fixture Shape Enforcement [official]

TypeScript's `satisfies` operator validates that a value conforms to a type without widening the value's inferred type. In TDD fixtures, `satisfies` with a discriminated union enforces that every fixture object uses a valid discriminant value, while preserving the narrow literal type for use in downstream assertions. This eliminates a class of bugs where a fixture silently uses an invalid discriminant (e.g., `type: "CLOSE"` instead of `type: "CLOSED"`) — the production code never receives it during tests, so the handler for the typo-variant is never exercised, and the test passes incorrectly.

```typescript
// domain/__tests__/fixtures/order-status-fixtures.ts
type OrderStatus =
  | { type: "PENDING";   createdAt: Date }
  | { type: "CONFIRMED"; confirmedAt: Date; confirmationCode: string }
  | { type: "SHIPPED";   trackingNumber: string; carrier: string }
  | { type: "DELIVERED"; deliveredAt: Date }
  | { type: "CANCELLED"; reason: string; cancelledAt: Date };

// satisfies enforces the discriminant — typos are compile errors, not silent mismatch
export const pendingOrder = {
  type: "PENDING",
  createdAt: new Date("2026-05-14T09:00:00Z"),
} satisfies OrderStatus;

export const shippedOrder = {
  type: "SHIPPED",
  trackingNumber: "1Z999AA10123456784",
  carrier: "UPS",
} satisfies OrderStatus;

export const cancelledOrder = {
  type: "CANCELLED",
  reason: "Customer request",
  cancelledAt: new Date("2026-05-14T11:00:00Z"),
} satisfies OrderStatus;

// Test: the narrow type is preserved — pendingOrder.type is "PENDING", not OrderStatus["type"]
import { test, expect, assertType } from "vitest";
import { getStatusLabel } from "../../order-utils";

test("getStatusLabel returns correct label for each status", () => {
  expect(getStatusLabel(pendingOrder)).toBe("Awaiting confirmation");
  expect(getStatusLabel(shippedOrder)).toBe("In transit");
  expect(getStatusLabel(cancelledOrder)).toBe("Cancelled");
});

// Compile-time check: narrowing still works after satisfies
assertType<"PENDING">(pendingOrder.type); // inferred as literal, not union
```

**Tradeoff.** `satisfies` validates shape but does not enforce exhaustiveness — you can have 5 union members and only 3 fixtures without a compile error. Combine `satisfies` with a mapped-type completeness check (Cycle 44 Pattern 34) if fixture exhaustiveness is required: `type _AssertAllStatusesCovered = { [K in OrderStatus["type"]]: Extract<OrderStatus, { type: K }> }`. This creates a compile-time failure if a new union member is added without a corresponding fixture.

---

### 54. TDD for TypeScript `NoInfer<T>` — Preventing Overly-Broad Fixture Inference in Generic Test Helpers [official]

TypeScript 5.4 introduced `NoInfer<T>`, which prevents a type parameter from being inferred from a specific argument position. In TDD, this is critical for generic fixture builder helpers: when a `buildEntity<T>(defaults: T, overrides: Partial<T>): T` function infers `T` from `overrides` instead of `defaults`, a partial override object can silently widen `T` to an incomplete type, allowing fixtures with missing required fields to type-check. Wrapping `overrides` in `NoInfer<Partial<T>>` forces TypeScript to infer `T` only from `defaults`, then validate `overrides` against that inferred type.

```typescript
// test/helpers/build-entity.ts
export function buildEntity<T extends object>(
  defaults: T,
  overrides: NoInfer<Partial<T>> = {}
): T {
  return { ...defaults, ...overrides };
}

// domain/user.ts
interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  role: "admin" | "member" | "viewer";
  createdAt: Date;
}

// test/fixtures/user-fixtures.ts
import { buildEntity } from "../helpers/build-entity";

// Without NoInfer: overrides could widen T to {role: string} if role had a typo
// With NoInfer: T is inferred from defaults (full User), overrides must satisfy Partial<User>
export const adminUser = buildEntity<User>(
  {
    id:        "u-001",
    name:      "Alice Admin",
    email:     "alice@example.com",
    role:      "admin",
    createdAt: new Date("2026-01-01"),
  },
  { name: "Custom Admin" } // Partial<User> — validated against the inferred T
);

// Compile error (correctly caught with NoInfer):
// buildEntity<User>({ ...validDefaults }, { role: "superuser" });
// ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
// Type '"superuser"' is not assignable to type '"admin" | "member" | "viewer"'

// test: narrowing preserved, overrides applied correctly
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
test("buildEntity applies overrides without widening the base type", () => {
  expect(adminUser.name).toBe("Custom Admin");
  expect(adminUser.role).toBe("admin"); // default preserved since not overridden
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `NoInfer<T>` requires TypeScript 5.4+ — verify your `typescript` version in `package.json` before adopting. For older TypeScript targets, the equivalent workaround is to accept `overrides` as `Partial<Omit<T, never>>` with an explicit generic constraint, though this is less ergonomic. `NoInfer` is specifically designed for this fixture-builder scenario and has essentially no downside when used in test helper code; use it without hesitation in any generic `build*` or `make*` helper that accepts both defaults and overrides.

---

### 55. TDD for Vitest Browser Mode `userEvent` — Authentic DOM Interaction Testing in the Red Phase [official]

Vitest Browser Mode's `userEvent` API dispatches interactions through the browser's native event system (Chrome DevTools Protocol or WebDriver) rather than synthetic JavaScript events. In TDD, this distinction matters for the Red phase: a failing test using `userEvent.click(button)` is guaranteed to fail because the button's actual click handler does not implement the expected behaviour — not because a simulated event bypassed an event listener that uses `addEventListener` with `useCapture` or relies on browser-native focus management. This eliminates an entire class of false-green tests where the implementation works in a real browser but passes synthetic event tests trivially.

```typescript
// components/__tests__/counter-button.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { render, screen } from "vitest-browser-react";
import { userEvent } from "@vitest/browser/context";
import { CounterButton } from "../CounterButton";

test("CounterButton increments on click — Red: fails before implementation", async () => {
  render(<CounterButton initialCount={0} />);

  const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /increment/i });
  const counter = screen.getByRole("status");

  // Initial state
  expect(counter).toHaveTextContent("0");

  // Authentic browser click — not a synthetic dispatchEvent
  await userEvent.click(button);
  expect(counter).toHaveTextContent("1");

  await userEvent.click(button);
  await userEvent.click(button);
  expect(counter).toHaveTextContent("3");
});

test("CounterButton accepts keyboard interaction", async () => {
  render(<CounterButton initialCount={5} />);
  const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /increment/i });

  // Tab to focus, then Space to activate — tests real keyboard accessibility
  await userEvent.tab();
  await userEvent.keyboard(" "); // Space key
  expect(screen.getByRole("status")).toHaveTextContent("6");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Browser Mode tests are slower than JSDOM-based tests (full browser launch overhead per worker) and require a configured browser provider (`playwright` or `webdriverio`). The authenticity benefit is highest for components with complex event handling: drag-and-drop, focus traps, custom keyboard shortcuts, and pointer events. For simple unit-level component tests (pure render output, no interaction), JSDOM with `@testing-library/user-event` is faster and sufficient. Use Browser Mode as the default for integration-level component tests and for any component that interacts with browser APIs that JSDOM does not implement faithfully (ResizeObserver, IntersectionObserver, Web Animations API).

---

### 56. TDD for TypeScript `ReturnType` / `Parameters` Utility Types — Test Helper Type Derivation Without Import Coupling [official]

`ReturnType<F>` and `Parameters<F>` derive types directly from a function's signature, allowing test helpers and fixture factories to stay in sync with the production API without importing the concrete types. In TDD, this pattern is invaluable when the return type of a production function is complex, private, or frequently changing: the test helper declares `type Result = ReturnType<typeof myFunction>` and automatically tracks every change to `myFunction`'s return type at compile time. If `myFunction` adds a required field, the fixture factory's `Partial<ReturnType<typeof myFunction>>` assertion immediately reports the gap.

```typescript
// services/inventory.ts
export async function fetchInventoryItem(sku: string) {
  // returns: { sku, name, quantity, price, warehouse, lastUpdated }
  return db.inventoryItems.findUnique({ where: { sku } });
}

// test/helpers/inventory-fixtures.ts
import { fetchInventoryItem } from "../../services/inventory";

// Derived types — stay in sync with the production signature automatically
type InventoryItem = NonNullable<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchInventoryItem>>>;
type FetchParams    = Parameters<typeof fetchInventoryItem>;

// Fixture factory: Partial override of the full return type
export function buildInventoryItem(
  overrides: Partial<InventoryItem> = {}
): InventoryItem {
  return {
    sku:         "SKU-001",
    name:        "Test Widget",
    quantity:    100,
    price:       999,
    warehouse:   "WH-A",
    lastUpdated: new Date("2026-05-14"),
    ...overrides,
  };
}

// If fetchInventoryItem adds a new required field, buildInventoryItem gets a
// compile error immediately — no manual type maintenance needed.

// test/inventory/__tests__/inventory-display.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { InventoryDisplay } from "../InventoryDisplay";
import { buildInventoryItem } from "../../helpers/inventory-fixtures";

test("InventoryDisplay shows out-of-stock badge when quantity is 0", () => {
  const item = buildInventoryItem({ quantity: 0 });
  const { getByRole } = render(<InventoryDisplay item={item} />);
  expect(getByRole("status")).toHaveTextContent("Out of stock");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `ReturnType` on async functions requires wrapping with `Awaited<>` (as shown above) — a frequently missed step that produces `Promise<Item>` instead of `Item`. For functions with overloads, `ReturnType` extracts the last overload's return type, which may not be the most general form; in that case, prefer explicit type imports. This pattern increases compile-time coupling between test helpers and production code, which is the intended behaviour — if you want test helpers that can drift from production types, use `Partial<Record<string, unknown>>` instead.

---

### 57. TDD for Vitest Retry Configuration — Flake Quarantine Without Masking Real Failures [official]

Vitest's per-test `retry` option (and the suite-level `retry` config) re-runs a failing test up to N times before marking it as failed. In TDD, retry configuration serves a specific quarantine purpose: isolating known-flaky integration tests (network timeouts, timing-sensitive animations, race conditions in test infrastructure) so they do not block the Red-Green-Refactor loop for unrelated work. The key discipline is that retry must never be applied to unit tests — retrying a unit test that fails deterministically hides a real bug. Vitest 4.x also supports `retry: { times, delay, retry }` with a conditional retry function, enabling smarter quarantine (only retry on `ECONNRESET`, not on assertion failures).

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Global retry: 0 (never retry by default — forces explicit opt-in)
    retry: 0,
    projects: [
      {
        // Unit tests: zero retries — a failing unit test is always a real failure
        test: { include: ["src/**/*.unit.test.ts"], retry: 0 },
      },
      {
        // Integration tests: 2 retries for infrastructure flakiness, 500ms delay
        test: {
          include: ["src/**/*.integration.test.ts"],
          retry: { times: 2, delay: 500 },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});

// test: per-test override — only retry this specific flaky external API call
import { test, expect } from "vitest";

test(
  "payment provider webhook delivery is eventually consistent",
  { retry: 3 },
  async () => {
    await triggerWebhook("payment.succeeded", { amount: 9900 });
    // Webhook delivery is async — may need up to 3 retries across 500ms delay
    await expect
      .poll(() => db.events.count({ where: { type: "payment.succeeded" } }), { timeout: 2000 })
      .toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Retry configuration in TDD is a liability if misused: it converts deterministic Red signals into intermittent flakes that only fail after timeout, making the Red phase ambiguous. Establish a team rule: retries are permitted only in the `integration.test.ts` tier with a Jira/GitHub issue tracking the underlying flakiness. Unit tests must have `retry: 0` explicitly (via project config or lint rule) so that adding `retry` to a unit test triggers a code review flag. Regularly review retry usage — if a test has been retrying for >2 sprints, the root cause must be fixed rather than retried indefinitely.

---

### 58. TDD for TypeScript Template Literal Types as Compile-Time API Route Validators [official]

TypeScript template literal types can construct and validate string shapes at the type level, enabling compile-time enforcement of API route conventions in test fixtures. In TDD, this prevents a class of bugs where fixture factories hard-code route strings that do not follow the project's conventions (`"/api/v2/users"` vs `"/api/users"` vs `"api/users"`), causing 404s that only manifest at runtime. A template literal type `type ApiRoute = /${string}` or more precise `type UserRoute = /api/users/${string | number}` rejects malformed route strings at fixture construction time.

```typescript
// test/helpers/route-types.ts
// Enforce all test routes start with /api/ and use lowercase segments
type ApiVersion = "v1" | "v2";
type HttpMethod  = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "PATCH" | "DELETE";

type ApiRoute = `/api/${ApiVersion}/${string}`;

interface RouteFixture {
  method:   HttpMethod;
  path:     ApiRoute;
  statusIn: number[];
}

function defineRoute(fixture: RouteFixture): RouteFixture {
  return fixture;
}

// Compile error: "/api/v3/users" — "v3" is not "v1" | "v2"
// defineRoute({ method: "GET", path: "/api/v3/users", statusIn: [200] });

// Compile error: "api/v1/users" — missing leading slash
// defineRoute({ method: "GET", path: "api/v1/users", statusIn: [200] });

// Valid fixtures
export const getUserRoute = defineRoute({
  method:   "GET",
  path:     "/api/v1/users/123",
  statusIn: [200, 404],
});

export const createUserRoute = defineRoute({
  method:   "POST",
  path:     "/api/v2/users",
  statusIn: [201, 422],
});

// test/routes/__tests__/user-routes.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { apiClient } from "../../helpers/api-client";
import { getUserRoute, createUserRoute } from "../../helpers/route-types";

test("GET /api/v1/users/:id returns 200 for existing user", async () => {
  const res = await apiClient.request(getUserRoute.method, getUserRoute.path);
  expect(getUserRoute.statusIn).toContain(res.status);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Template literal type validation is structural, not semantic — `/api/v1/anything-at-all` satisfies `ApiRoute` even if `/api/v1/anything-at-all` is not a real endpoint. For full API contract validation, combine template literal types with a generated route registry (from OpenAPI or tRPC router types) and validate fixture paths against `keyof RouterPaths` instead of a generic template. This provides both structural format checking and semantic endpoint existence checking, at the cost of requiring a generated type file in the test infrastructure.

---

### 59. TDD for Vitest `expect.poll` with `interval` and `timeout` — Deterministic Async Assertion Timing [official]

`expect.poll` re-evaluates a getter function repeatedly until an assertion passes or a timeout expires. Vitest 4.x extends `expect.poll` with explicit `interval` (milliseconds between retries) and `timeout` controls, enabling deterministic timing in async TDD scenarios: event-driven state machines, eventually-consistent caches, WebSocket message queues, and background job processors. The key TDD discipline is setting `timeout` to the maximum acceptable latency for the production code, making the poll assertion both a correctness check and a performance budget — a test that passes at 4900ms when `timeout` is 5000ms is a warning sign.

```typescript
// jobs/__tests__/background-processor.test.ts
import { test, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { BackgroundProcessor } from "../background-processor";
import { InMemoryQueue } from "../in-memory-queue";

let processor: BackgroundProcessor;
let queue: InMemoryQueue;

beforeEach(() => {
  queue = new InMemoryQueue();
  processor = new BackgroundProcessor(queue, { workers: 2 });
  processor.start();
});

afterEach(() => processor.stop());

test("BackgroundProcessor completes a submitted job within 500ms", async () => {
  const jobId = await queue.submit({ type: "send-email", recipient: "test@example.com" });

  // Poll every 50ms, fail if not completed within 500ms
  await expect
    .poll(() => queue.getJobStatus(jobId), { interval: 50, timeout: 500 })
    .toBe("completed");
});

test("BackgroundProcessor processes 10 concurrent jobs within 2s", async () => {
  const jobIds = await Promise.all(
    Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) =>
      queue.submit({ type: "resize-image", imageId: `img-${i}` })
    )
  );

  // Poll the count of completed jobs — assert all 10 complete within budget
  await expect
    .poll(
      () => jobIds.filter(id => queue.getJobStatus(id) === "completed").length,
      { interval: 100, timeout: 2000 }
    )
    .toBe(10);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.poll` with a short `interval` (10-20ms) in a suite with many async tests can create significant CPU overhead from rapid polling — prefer `interval: 50` or higher for production CI. The `timeout` value is also a test execution budget: setting it too high makes the suite slow when the production code is broken (the test runs to timeout before failing). Set `timeout` to 2-3x the expected completion time in a healthy system, not the maximum theoretically possible time. For deterministic fake-timer scenarios, use `vi.useFakeTimers()` with `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` instead of `expect.poll` — fake timers are instantaneous and eliminate the real-time wait entirely.

---

### 60. TDD for Vitest Workspace Projects — Per-Package Test Configuration in Monorepos [official]

Vitest's workspace mode (`vitest.workspace.ts`) enables a single `vitest` process to orchestrate multiple test projects with independent configurations — different environments (`node`, `jsdom`, `edge-runtime`), different transforms, different coverage boundaries, and different global setups. In TDD for monorepos, workspace projects enforce that a package's tests run only against that package's source (preventing implicit cross-package imports that would pass in development but fail in production isolation) and that each package's test environment matches its deployment target (a Node.js API package uses `environment: "node"`, a React component library uses `environment: "jsdom"`).

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts (monorepo root)
import { defineWorkspace } from "vitest/config";

export default defineWorkspace([
  // Package 1: Node.js API — no DOM, strict isolation
  {
    test: {
      name:        "api",
      root:        "./packages/api",
      environment: "node",
      include:     ["src/**/*.test.ts"],
      coverage: {
        include: ["src/**"],
        exclude: ["src/**/*.d.ts", "src/generated/**"],
      },
    },
  },

  // Package 2: React component library — JSDOM + browser-like globals
  {
    test: {
      name:        "ui",
      root:        "./packages/ui",
      environment: "jsdom",
      setupFiles:  ["./test/setup/dom-matchers.ts"],
      include:     ["src/**/*.test.tsx"],
    },
  },

  // Package 3: Edge runtime functions — edge-runtime environment
  {
    test: {
      name:        "edge",
      root:        "./packages/edge",
      environment: "edge-runtime",
      include:     ["src/**/*.test.ts"],
      deps: {
        // Prevent Node.js built-ins from leaking into edge tests
        interopDefault: false,
      },
    },
  },
]);

// Run all projects: vitest
// Run single project: vitest --project api
// Run with coverage: vitest --coverage --project ui
```

**Tradeoff.** Workspace mode adds configuration overhead — each project needs its own `root`, `include`, and environment settings. The payoff is complete test environment isolation: a component library test that accidentally imports a Node.js `fs` module will fail immediately in `jsdom` mode rather than silently passing because the monorepo's root `vitest.config.ts` happened to run in `node` mode. The `--project` flag enables incremental TDD: during a focused sprint on the `api` package, run `vitest --project api --watch` to avoid loading the `ui` and `edge` projects entirely, giving the fastest possible feedback loop.

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 45 Additions

198. **[community] Vitest `test.for` does NOT spread array elements like `test.each` — a developer who migrates from `test.each([["a", 1], ["b", 2]])((label, value) => ...)` to `test.for([["a", 1], ["b", 2]])((label, value) => ...)` gets a compile error because `test.for` passes the full array element as the first argument, not destructured positional parameters.** The test body receives `(["a", 1], ctx)` — an array — rather than `("a", 1)`. WHY this matters: the migration from `test.each` to `test.for` looks mechanical but silently changes the calling convention, causing TypeScript to report that the first argument is `(string | number)[]` rather than `string`, often producing confusing errors in the assertion lines rather than at the function signature. Fix: use object arrays with `test.for` (`[{ label: "a", value: 1 }, ...]`) and destructure in the test body — this is the idiomatic `test.for` pattern and produces self-documenting test titles via `$label` template interpolation.

199. **[community] Vitest `test.override` with a fixture that has side effects (e.g., a fixture that writes to a database on setup) re-runs the entire fixture chain for the overriding suite — this means the side-effect runs twice if both the base suite and the override suite share the same file, causing duplicate database rows, double-charged test accounts, or duplicate log entries that pollute other tests.** A developer adds `test.override({ userRole: "admin" })` to a describe block and notices that the `authToken` fixture (which calls an external auth service) fires twice per test — once for the base fixture and once for the override. WHY this matters: in integration test suites, fixture side effects are expected to run once per test; double execution can cause unique-constraint violations or exhausted rate limits in sandboxed environments. Fix: ensure fixtures used with `test.override` are idempotent or clean up after themselves using the generator fixture pattern (`async function*`), so the post-`use` cleanup handles any state created during setup.

200. **[community] TypeScript `satisfies` on a fixture object with an `as const` assertion produces the intersection of both constraints, which narrows the type to a literal tuple when the fixture contains an array field — the inferred type becomes `readonly ["admin", "member"]` instead of `("admin" | "member")[]`, causing downstream functions that accept mutable arrays to reject the fixture with "Argument of type 'readonly [...]' is not assignable to parameter of type '...'".** A developer writes `const roles = { allowed: ["admin", "member"] } as const satisfies RoleConfig` and passes `roles.allowed` to a function expecting `string[]`, getting a confusing error about `readonly` vs mutable arrays. WHY this matters: `as const satisfies` is a common pattern from Cycle 44 Pattern 41, but combining it with array fields in fixtures creates unexpected `readonly` inference that breaks function arguments expecting mutable arrays. Fix: either omit `as const` from fixtures with array fields that are passed to mutable-array parameters, or use `[...roles.allowed]` at the call site to create a mutable copy.

201. **[community] Vitest `toMatchAriaInlineSnapshot` (experimental) fails with a cryptic "snapshot content mismatch" error when the component under test renders any dynamic ARIA attributes — `aria-label` values interpolated from props, `aria-describedby` pointing to a generated ID, or `aria-controls` with a random UUID — because ARIA snapshots capture the full accessibility tree including these dynamic values, and any variation between runs causes a snapshot mismatch identical to a real regression.** A developer writes an ARIA snapshot for a dialog component that generates a unique `aria-labelledby` ID per render and finds that the snapshot fails on every second run with a different ID. WHY this matters: the developer may believe ARIA snapshots are unreliable and abandon them entirely, losing accessibility regression protection. Fix: stabilise dynamic ARIA IDs in tests by passing a fixed `id` prop in test renders, or mock the ID generator (`vi.stubGlobal('crypto', { randomUUID: () => 'test-uuid-001' })`), so the snapshot captures a deterministic accessibility tree.

202. **[community] Vitest workspace `--project` flag filtering does not apply to `globalSetup` files — a `globalSetup` file in `vitest.workspace.ts` that provisions shared infrastructure (e.g., starts a Docker Postgres container) runs for every `vitest` invocation regardless of which `--project` flag is specified, meaning running `vitest --project ui` for a quick component TDD session still incurs the full database container startup time.** A developer adds a database globalSetup for the `api` project but finds that `vitest --project ui` takes 30 extra seconds to start the database before running any tests. WHY this matters: the fast-feedback TDD loop for UI components is broken by infrastructure provisioning that is irrelevant to the component tests. Fix: move infrastructure globalSetup into a project-level `globalSetup` (specified inside the project's config block) rather than the workspace root — each project's `globalSetup` only runs when that project is included in the current test run.

203. **[community] TypeScript template literal types used as route validators in test fixtures are not validated against the actual router's registered routes — a route string like `/api/v1/users/${userId}` satisfies the template literal type but returns 404 at runtime because the actual router uses `/api/v1/user/${userId}` (singular).** A developer relies on compile-time template literal validation and does not write any test that actually calls the route, assuming type safety means the route exists. WHY this matters: template literal types validate string shape (prefix, format, version segment) but have no connection to the runtime routing table — they are a formatting guard, not an existence guard. Fix: generate route types from the production router (tRPC's `RouterInputs`/`RouterOutputs`, OpenAPI type generation, or a `satisfies Routes` assertion on the router definition) so that test fixtures validated against fixture types are also transitively validated against the registered route map.
