## Cycle 46 — 2026-05-14

### 61. TDD for Vitest `expect.schemaMatching` — Standard Schema v1 Assertions in the Red Phase [official]

`expect.schemaMatching(schema)` (Vitest 4.1+) accepts any Standard Schema v1 compliant validator — Zod, Valibot, ArkType, and others — and integrates schema validation directly into the assertion pipeline without requiring manual `.safeParse()` calls. In the Red phase, you declare the shape contract as a schema assertion and let the validator produce the failure message. This eliminates a class of boilerplate where a test must parse, check the success flag, then assert on the parsed value separately. The schema assertion is also usable as an asymmetric matcher inside `expect.objectContaining`, enabling partial shape enforcement within larger object assertions.

```typescript
// src/orders/__tests__/order-schema.test.ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { z } from "zod/v4";
import { createOrder } from "../order-service";

const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id:        z.string().uuid(),
  status:    z.enum(["pending", "confirmed", "shipped", "delivered"]),
  total:     z.number().nonnegative(),
  createdAt: z.iso.datetime(),
  lineItems: z.array(
    z.object({ sku: z.string().min(1), qty: z.number().int().positive() })
  ).nonempty(),
});

test("createOrder returns a well-formed Order", async () => {
  // RED: fails until createOrder is implemented with all required fields
  const order = await createOrder({ sku: "WIDGET-001", qty: 3 });

  // Inline schema assertion — no .safeParse dance
  expect(order).toMatchSchema(OrderSchema);
});

test("createOrder result embeds in larger API response", async () => {
  const response = await createOrderViaApi({ sku: "WIDGET-001", qty: 3 });

  // Asymmetric: only the 'data' field is schema-validated
  expect(response).toEqual(
    expect.objectContaining({
      success: true,
      data: expect.schemaMatching(OrderSchema),
    })
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.schemaMatching` produces richer error messages than `toBeTruthy(schema.safeParse(x).success)` because the Standard Schema v1 protocol surfaces structured issue arrays — Vitest can display the exact failing field path and message. The cost is a direct test-time dependency on the schema library (Zod, Valibot, etc.); if the schema evolves its validation rules, previously green tests may turn Red unexpectedly. Mitigate by treating `schemaMatching` assertions as contract tests and version-pinning the schema file alongside the test.

---

### 62. TDD for Vitest `expect.soft` — Accumulated Assertion Failures in a Single Test Run [official]

`expect.soft()` delays failure propagation until the end of the test, collecting all soft-assertion failures before reporting them together. In a TDD context this is valuable during the Red phase for complex data-transformation tests: instead of stopping at the first mismatch and re-running to discover the next one, all field-level failures appear in a single Red run, giving a complete picture of what the production code needs to produce. Unlike `expect()`, which throws immediately and short-circuits the test, `expect.soft()` records the failure and continues, making it analogous to the "collect all violations" mode in constraint solvers.

```typescript
// src/reports/__tests__/invoice-transformer.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { transformToInvoice } from "../invoice-transformer";

test("transformToInvoice maps all required fields from raw order data", () => {
  const rawOrder = {
    order_id:    "ORD-2026-001",
    customer_id: "CUST-99",
    line_items:  [{ product_code: "A1", quantity: 2, unit_price_cents: 1500 }],
    discount_pct: 10,
    tax_pct:      8,
  };

  // RED: all soft assertions collected before failure is reported
  const invoice = transformToInvoice(rawOrder);

  expect.soft(invoice.invoiceNumber).toMatch(/^INV-/);
  expect.soft(invoice.customerId).toBe("CUST-99");
  expect.soft(invoice.lineItems).toHaveLength(1);
  expect.soft(invoice.lineItems[0].unitPrice).toBe(15.00);   // cents → dollars
  expect.soft(invoice.subtotal).toBe(30.00);
  expect.soft(invoice.discountAmount).toBe(3.00);
  expect.soft(invoice.taxAmount).toBeCloseTo(2.16, 2);       // 8% of 27
  expect.soft(invoice.total).toBeCloseTo(29.16, 2);
  expect.soft(invoice.issuedAt).toBeInstanceOf(Date);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.soft` is most valuable for "transformation completeness" tests where a function maps one structure to another and multiple fields can fail independently. Do NOT use it for tests where an early assertion failure makes later assertions nonsensical — for example, if `invoice.lineItems` is `undefined`, the `invoice.lineItems[0]` assertion will throw a runtime error before Vitest can catch it as a soft failure. Use `expect.soft` only when subsequent assertions are structurally independent of earlier ones. Also avoid soft assertions in fast Red-Green cycles where you want to discover one issue at a time; reserve them for comprehensive smoke tests where you intentionally want full-picture feedback.

---

### 63. TDD for Vitest `expect.poll` with `interval` — Deterministic Async State Waiting [official]

`expect.poll(() => expr, { interval, timeout })` retries the assertion callback on a configurable schedule until it passes or the timeout expires. Unlike `waitFor` from testing-library or manual `setImmediate` loops, `expect.poll` integrates directly with the Vitest assertion pipeline: failures during polling are suppressed until timeout, then the final state is reported with a diff. The `interval` option (default 50 ms) controls how often the assertion is retried; lowering it to 10 ms speeds up TDD loops for state machines that transition quickly. Setting `timeout` explicitly documents the SLA for the async operation being tested.

```typescript
// src/queue/__tests__/job-processor.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import { JobProcessor } from "../job-processor";

test("job transitions to COMPLETED within 500 ms after processing starts", async () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  const processor = new JobProcessor({ workerDelayMs: 100 });
  const jobId = await processor.enqueue({ type: "email", to: "user@example.com" });

  // Start processing without awaiting
  processor.startWorker();

  // Advance fake time in 50 ms increments while polling
  await expect.poll(
    () => processor.getStatus(jobId),
    { interval: 10, timeout: 500 }
  ).toBe("COMPLETED");

  vi.useRealTimers();
});

test("failed job is retried up to 3 times before DEAD_LETTER status", async () => {
  const processor = new JobProcessor({ maxRetries: 3 });
  const failingJobId = await processor.enqueue({ type: "sms", to: "invalid" });

  processor.startWorker();

  await expect.poll(
    () => processor.getStatus(failingJobId),
    { interval: 20, timeout: 2000 }
  ).toBe("DEAD_LETTER");

  expect(processor.getAttemptCount(failingJobId)).toBe(4); // 1 initial + 3 retries
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.poll` is not a substitute for proper async/await control — if the production code has no mechanism for the state to change (e.g., the worker was never started), `expect.poll` will spin for the full timeout before failing, turning a fast Red into a slow Red. Always ensure the trigger that changes the polled state is invoked before the poll begins. Prefer `expect.poll` over `waitFor` when the assertion does not involve DOM elements, as `expect.poll` avoids the Testing Library dependency and produces cleaner Vitest-native failure messages.

---

### 64. TDD for Vitest `vi.mock` Auto-Factory — Module-Level Mock Isolation Without Manual Stubs [official]

When `vi.mock("./some-module")` is called without a factory function, Vitest auto-generates mock implementations for every export: functions become `vi.fn()`, classes get their methods replaced with `vi.fn()`, and objects become deeply mocked. This auto-factory behaviour provides the fastest path to an isolated Red test: write the test, call `vi.mock` with just the module path, and all collaborators are automatically stubbed out. The TDD workflow then adds only the spy assertions needed to verify interactions, without writing factory implementations for every exported function.

```typescript
// src/notifications/__tests__/notification-service.test.ts
import { beforeEach, describe, expect, test, vi } from "vitest";

// Auto-factory: every export becomes vi.fn() automatically
vi.mock("../email-client");
vi.mock("../sms-provider");
vi.mock("../push-gateway");

import { EmailClient }   from "../email-client";
import { SmsProvider }   from "../sms-provider";
import { PushGateway }   from "../push-gateway";
import { NotificationService } from "../notification-service";

describe("NotificationService", () => {
  let service: NotificationService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
    service = new NotificationService(
      new EmailClient(),
      new SmsProvider(),
      new PushGateway()
    );
  });

  test("sends email for EMAIL channel preference", async () => {
    // RED: fails until NotificationService routes by channel
    await service.notify({ userId: "u1", channel: "email", message: "Hello" });

    expect(EmailClient.prototype.send).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(SmsProvider.prototype.send).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
    expect(PushGateway.prototype.send).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  test("fans out to all channels when preference is ALL", async () => {
    await service.notify({ userId: "u1", channel: "all", message: "Urgent" });

    expect(EmailClient.prototype.send).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(SmsProvider.prototype.send).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(PushGateway.prototype.send).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Auto-factory mocking is faster to set up than manual factory functions but produces weaker type safety — `vi.fn()` return values default to `undefined`, so any test that inspects the return value of a mocked collaborator must add an explicit `mockResolvedValue()` or `mockReturnValue()` call. Auto-factory mocking is best suited for the London school style (interaction-based) where you verify that the right method was called, not what it returned. If the SUT processes return values from collaborators, switch to explicit factory mocks to control those return values precisely.

---

### 65. TDD for Vitest `vi.spyOn` with `mockImplementationOnce` — Controlled Error Injection [official]

`vi.spyOn(obj, "method").mockImplementationOnce(impl)` replaces a single invocation of a method with a controlled implementation while preserving the real implementation for all subsequent calls. This is the canonical TDD technique for testing retry logic, fallback paths, and transient error handling: force the first call to throw, assert the retry behaviour, then let the second call succeed normally. The `Once` variant is critical — `mockImplementation` replaces all calls, making it impossible to verify that the recovery path eventually calls the real method.

```typescript
// src/http/__tests__/resilient-client.test.ts
import { beforeEach, expect, test, vi } from "vitest";
import { ResilientHttpClient } from "../resilient-client";
import * as httpLib from "../http-lib";

test("retries once on 503 then returns successful response", async () => {
  const getSpy = vi.spyOn(httpLib, "get");

  // First call → transient 503 error
  getSpy.mockImplementationOnce(() =>
    Promise.reject(new HttpError(503, "Service Unavailable"))
  );
  // Second call → real implementation (or a successful stub)
  getSpy.mockImplementationOnce(() =>
    Promise.resolve({ status: 200, body: { ok: true } })
  );

  const client  = new ResilientHttpClient({ maxRetries: 1, retryDelayMs: 0 });
  const result  = await client.get("/api/data");

  expect(result.body).toEqual({ ok: true });
  expect(getSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);  // exactly one retry
});

test("throws after exhausting all retries", async () => {
  const getSpy = vi.spyOn(httpLib, "get");

  // All three attempts fail
  getSpy.mockImplementation(() =>
    Promise.reject(new HttpError(503, "Service Unavailable"))
  );

  const client = new ResilientHttpClient({ maxRetries: 2, retryDelayMs: 0 });
  await expect(client.get("/api/data")).rejects.toThrow(HttpError);
  expect(getSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);  // 1 initial + 2 retries
  vi.restoreAllMocks();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `mockImplementationOnce` chains are brittle when the number of internal calls differs from what the test author expects — adding a new code path that calls the spy an extra time silently shifts which `Once` implementation is used for which call, turning the test into a false positive. Mitigate by asserting `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(n)` explicitly and by keeping `Once` chains short (two entries maximum). For complex sequences, prefer a stateful fake object over chained `Once` implementations.

---

### 66. TDD for Vitest `vi.stubEnv` — Deterministic Environment Variable Isolation [official]

`vi.stubEnv(key, value)` overrides a single `process.env` variable for the duration of the test file, with automatic restoration via `unstubEnvs: true` in `vitest.config.ts` or a manual `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` in `afterEach`. This is the correct TDD pattern for code that branches on environment variables (feature flags, region settings, log levels, API endpoint overrides). It avoids the fragile anti-pattern of manually setting `process.env.KEY = "value"` and forgetting to restore it, which contaminates other tests in the same worker thread.

```typescript
// src/config/__tests__/feature-flags.test.ts
import { afterEach, describe, expect, test, vi } from "vitest";
import { isFeatureEnabled } from "../feature-flags";

afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllEnvs();
});

describe("isFeatureEnabled", () => {
  test("returns true when FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD=true", () => {
    vi.stubEnv("FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD", "true");
    expect(isFeatureEnabled("NEW_DASHBOARD")).toBe(true);
  });

  test("returns false when FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD is absent", () => {
    // No stub — key is absent from process.env in this test
    expect(isFeatureEnabled("NEW_DASHBOARD")).toBe(false);
  });

  test("returns false for unknown features regardless of env", () => {
    vi.stubEnv("FEATURE_UNKNOWN_FLAG", "true");
    expect(isFeatureEnabled("UNKNOWN_FLAG")).toBe(false);
  });

  test("is case-insensitive for flag name lookup", () => {
    vi.stubEnv("FEATURE_DARK_MODE", "1");
    expect(isFeatureEnabled("dark_mode")).toBe(true);
    expect(isFeatureEnabled("DARK_MODE")).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.stubEnv` only affects `process.env` — if production code reads environment variables at module import time (e.g., `const API_URL = process.env.API_URL ?? "default"` at the top of the file), the stub will have no effect because the module was already evaluated before the test ran. For modules with import-time environment reads, combine `vi.stubEnv` with `vi.resetModules()` and dynamic `import()` inside the test body to force re-evaluation with the stubbed value.

---

### 67. TDD for Vitest Custom Snapshot Domain — Owning the Full Comparison Pipeline [official]

The experimental Custom Snapshot Domain API (Vitest 4.1.4+) allows test authors to define a complete matcher that controls how a value is captured, rendered to text, parsed from a stored snapshot, and semantically compared. This is a significant extension beyond `expect.addSnapshotSerializer` (which only customises rendering): a custom domain can normalise values before comparison, ignore volatile fields like timestamps or generated IDs, and produce human-readable diff output tailored to the domain object. In TDD, a custom snapshot domain for a core domain concept (e.g., an `Order`, an `Event`, a `QueryPlan`) encodes the stability contract once and reuses it across the entire test suite.

```typescript
// test/snapshot-domains/order-snapshot.ts
import { SnapshotDomain } from "vitest/snapshot";

// Custom domain: normalises volatile fields before capture
export const orderSnapshotDomain: SnapshotDomain = {
  serialize(order: unknown): string {
    const o = order as Record<string, unknown>;
    return JSON.stringify(
      {
        ...o,
        id:        "<uuid>",          // mask volatile ID
        createdAt: "<timestamp>",     // mask volatile timestamp
        updatedAt: "<timestamp>",
      },
      null,
      2
    );
  },

  deserialize(raw: string): unknown {
    return JSON.parse(raw);
  },

  equals(received: unknown, expected: unknown): boolean {
    // Semantic equality: compare serialised forms
    return this.serialize(received) === (expected as string);
  },
};

// test/setup/register-domains.ts
import { expect } from "vitest";
import { orderSnapshotDomain } from "../snapshot-domains/order-snapshot";

expect.extend({
  toMatchOrderSnapshot(received: unknown) {
    return orderSnapshotDomain.equals(received, this.snapshotState)
      ? { pass: true,  message: () => "Order snapshot matches" }
      : { pass: false, message: () => `Order snapshot mismatch:\n${orderSnapshotDomain.serialize(received)}` };
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom snapshot domains require non-trivial setup (serialiser, deserialiser, equals function) and the API is still marked experimental in Vitest 4.1 — it may change in a minor release. Invest in a custom domain only for core domain objects that appear in 10+ test files. For one-off volatile-field problems, a simpler approach is `expect.objectContaining` with `expect.any(String)` for the volatile fields, which requires no infrastructure investment and is less brittle across Vitest version upgrades.

---

### 68. TDD for TypeScript Inferred Type Predicates — Compile-Time Narrowing as a Red Signal [official]

TypeScript 5.5 introduced inferred type predicates: when a function's return type can be determined to be a type predicate from its body, TypeScript infers `(x: T) => x is U` automatically without an explicit annotation. In TDD, this means writing a predicate function in the Red phase and letting the compile error drive you toward a correct narrowing implementation. The test can assert the narrowed type using `expectTypeOf` (Vitest type testing) alongside a runtime assertion, catching both behavioural and type-contract regressions simultaneously.

```typescript
// src/events/__tests__/event-guards.test-d.ts  (type-level tests)
import { expectTypeOf, test } from "vitest";
import { isErrorEvent, isSuccessEvent, AppEvent } from "../event-guards";

type SuccessEvent = { type: "success"; payload: string };
type ErrorEvent   = { type: "error";   code: number;  message: string };

// Type-level RED: fails until isSuccessEvent narrows correctly
test("isSuccessEvent narrows AppEvent to SuccessEvent", () => {
  const event: AppEvent = { type: "success", payload: "ok" };
  if (isSuccessEvent(event)) {
    // TypeScript 5.5+ infers the predicate — expectTypeOf checks it
    expectTypeOf(event).toEqualTypeOf<SuccessEvent>();
    expectTypeOf(event.payload).toBeString();
  }
});

test("isErrorEvent narrows AppEvent to ErrorEvent", () => {
  const event: AppEvent = { type: "error", code: 404, message: "Not found" };
  if (isErrorEvent(event)) {
    expectTypeOf(event).toEqualTypeOf<ErrorEvent>();
    expectTypeOf(event.code).toBeNumber();
  }
});

// Behavioural tests in the .test.ts counterpart
// src/events/__tests__/event-guards.test.ts
import { describe, expect, test } from "vitest";
import { isErrorEvent, isSuccessEvent } from "../event-guards";

describe("isSuccessEvent", () => {
  test("returns true for success events",  () => expect(isSuccessEvent({ type: "success", payload: "ok" })).toBe(true));
  test("returns false for error events",   () => expect(isSuccessEvent({ type: "error", code: 1, message: "x" })).toBe(false));
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Splitting type-level assertions into a separate `.test-d.ts` file keeps the behavioural test file clean but requires developers to maintain two files for the same unit. A practical compromise for smaller modules is to co-locate `expectTypeOf` calls inside the same `.test.ts` file using `import type` — the type assertions are elided at runtime and produce no overhead. The inferred type predicate feature (TS 5.5+) requires the compiler to be able to analyse the predicate function body; complex predicates with non-trivial control flow may still require an explicit `: x is T` annotation.

---

### 69. TDD for Vitest `vi.importActual` with Partial Module Mocking — Selectively Replacing Exports [official]

`vi.importActual<typeof import("./module")>("./module")` retrieves the real module implementation inside a `vi.mock` factory, enabling partial mocking: replace only the exports relevant to the test while delegating everything else to the real implementation. This is the correct TDD pattern when a module has both pure utility functions (which should remain real) and effectful functions (which should be mocked). Replacing the entire module with auto-factory mocks breaks tests that depend on the real utility functions; partial mocking preserves the real behaviour where it is not under test.

```typescript
// src/analytics/__tests__/event-tracker.test.ts
import { beforeEach, expect, test, vi } from "vitest";

// Partial mock: keep formatEventName real, mock only the network send
vi.mock("../analytics-client", async (importActual) => {
  const actual = await importActual<typeof import("../analytics-client")>();
  return {
    ...actual,                          // spread all real exports
    sendEvent: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: 200 }),  // replace only sendEvent
  };
});

import { formatEventName, sendEvent } from "../analytics-client";
import { EventTracker } from "../event-tracker";

beforeEach(() => vi.clearAllMocks());

test("tracker formats event name using real formatEventName before sending", async () => {
  const tracker = new EventTracker();
  await tracker.track("button_click", { elementId: "cta-signup" });

  // Real formatEventName converts snake_case to camelCase: "button_click" → "buttonClick"
  expect(sendEvent).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({ eventName: "buttonClick" })
  );
});

test("tracker attaches session ID from real sessionManager", async () => {
  const tracker = new EventTracker();
  await tracker.track("page_view", {});

  expect(sendEvent).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({ sessionId: expect.any(String) })
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Partial mocking creates a hybrid module that is neither fully real nor fully faked — this can make tests harder to reason about at a glance, because the reader must check the `vi.mock` factory to know which exports are real. Document the intention with a comment (`// keep real: ...`). Also note that `importActual` inside a `vi.mock` factory is asynchronous and requires the factory to be `async` — a synchronous factory that calls `importActual` will receive a Promise instead of the module object, which is a silent failure (the spread produces a Promise object with enumerable Promise methods, not the module exports).

---

### 70. TDD for Vitest `test.concurrent` with Fixture Isolation — Parallel Red-Green Cycles for Independent Tests [official]

`test.concurrent` (or `describe.concurrent`) instructs Vitest to run the marked tests in parallel within the same file. Combined with fixture scoping (`scope: "test"`), each concurrent test receives its own isolated instance of every fixture — database connections, HTTP clients, temporary directories — ensuring that parallel execution does not produce test interference. This pattern is valuable in integration TDD loops where each test provisions its own database row or API session: running them concurrently reduces wall-clock time from O(n) sequential to near O(1) parallel.

```typescript
// src/checkout/__tests__/checkout-flow.test.ts
import { describe, expect } from "vitest";
import { test as base } from "vitest";

// Each test gets its own isolated cart session
const test = base.extend<{ cartId: string }>({
  cartId: async ({}, use) => {
    const cart = await CartService.createEphemeralCart();
    await use(cart.id);
    await CartService.deleteCart(cart.id);  // cleanup after each test
  },
});

// concurrent: all tests run in parallel, each with its own cartId
describe.concurrent("Checkout flow — independent cart operations", () => {
  test("adding an item increments item count", async ({ cartId }) => {
    await CartService.addItem(cartId, { sku: "A1", qty: 2 });
    const cart = await CartService.getCart(cartId);
    expect(cart.itemCount).toBe(2);
  });

  test("applying a coupon reduces subtotal", async ({ cartId }) => {
    await CartService.addItem(cartId, { sku: "B2", qty: 1, price: 100 });
    await CartService.applyCoupon(cartId, "SAVE10");
    const cart = await CartService.getCart(cartId);
    expect(cart.subtotal).toBe(90);
  });

  test("removing all items empties the cart", async ({ cartId }) => {
    await CartService.addItem(cartId, { sku: "C3", qty: 1 });
    await CartService.clearCart(cartId);
    const cart = await CartService.getCart(cartId);
    expect(cart.itemCount).toBe(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.concurrent` requires that tests truly are independent — any shared mutable state (module-level counters, shared database sequences, singleton caches) will produce race conditions that manifest as intermittent failures rather than consistent ones. Before enabling concurrency, audit every fixture for hidden shared state. The most common violation is a module-level counter used for deterministic ID generation — it must be reset per fixture or replaced with a per-test counter to survive concurrent execution. Also note that `test.concurrent` inside a `describe.concurrent` block does not stack — the inner annotation is redundant but harmless.

---

### 71. TDD for Vitest `toHaveBeenCalledWith` Asymmetric Matchers — Partial Argument Matching in Spy Assertions [official]

Vitest's spy assertion `toHaveBeenCalledWith` accepts asymmetric matchers — `expect.any()`, `expect.objectContaining()`, `expect.stringMatching()`, `expect.arrayContaining()` — enabling partial argument assertion without over-specifying the exact call shape. In the Red phase, this allows writing a test that captures the essential contract ("the logger was called with the error code and message") without locking in volatile fields ("the timestamp, correlation ID, and host name"). Over-specified spy assertions are a primary cause of brittle tests that break on every refactor.

```typescript
// src/payments/__tests__/payment-processor.test.ts
import { beforeEach, describe, expect, test, vi } from "vitest";
import { PaymentProcessor } from "../payment-processor";
import { AuditLogger } from "../audit-logger";

vi.mock("../audit-logger");

describe("PaymentProcessor audit logging", () => {
  let processor: PaymentProcessor;

  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
    processor = new PaymentProcessor(new AuditLogger());
  });

  test("logs a PAYMENT_SUCCESS event with amount and currency on successful charge", async () => {
    await processor.charge({ amount: 2000, currency: "USD", customerId: "c1" });

    // Partial match: assert the contract, not the full log shape
    expect(AuditLogger.prototype.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({
        eventType:  "PAYMENT_SUCCESS",
        amount:     2000,
        currency:   "USD",
        // timestamp, correlationId, hostName are NOT asserted — they are volatile
      })
    );
  });

  test("logs a PAYMENT_FAILED event with error code on declined charge", async () => {
    vi.mocked(AuditLogger.prototype.log).mockImplementation(() => {});
    await expect(
      processor.charge({ amount: 99999999, currency: "USD", customerId: "c1" })
    ).rejects.toThrow();

    expect(AuditLogger.prototype.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({
        eventType:  "PAYMENT_FAILED",
        errorCode:  expect.stringMatching(/^DECLINE_/),
        amount:     expect.any(Number),
      })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Asymmetric matchers in spy assertions trade specificity for stability. The risk is under-specifying — if you only assert `eventType: "PAYMENT_SUCCESS"` but the production code logs `eventType: "PAYMENT_SUCESS"` (typo), the assertion fails as expected, but if the typo matches the matcher pattern it could pass. Always assert the minimum set of fields that constitute the observable contract, not just the fields that happen to be easy to assert. For critical audit trails (compliance, GDPR, financial), prefer fully-specified argument assertions even at the cost of some maintenance overhead.

---

### 72. TDD for TypeScript `Awaited<T>` Utility Type — Unwrapping Promise Types in Test Helper Declarations [official]

`Awaited<T>` (TypeScript 4.5+, but widely adopted with async/await patterns in 5.x+ codebases) recursively unwraps nested `Promise` types to their resolved value type. In TDD, it eliminates a class of test helper type declarations where developers manually write the resolved type of an async factory function. When the factory return type changes (a new field is added, a field is renamed), test helpers typed with `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof factory>>` update automatically — no manual sync required. This is the async counterpart of the Pattern 56 `ReturnType`/`Parameters` approach.

```typescript
// test/helpers/fixtures.ts
import { createUserWithProfile } from "../../src/users/user-factory";
import { createOrganisation }    from "../../src/orgs/org-factory";

// Awaited<ReturnType<...>> auto-syncs with the factory's resolved type
type UserWithProfile  = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createUserWithProfile>>;
type Organisation     = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createOrganisation>>;

// Builder for UserWithProfile — type stays in sync automatically
export function buildUserFixture(
  overrides: Partial<UserWithProfile> = {}
): Promise<UserWithProfile> {
  return createUserWithProfile({
    name:     "Test User",
    email:    "test@example.com",
    plan:     "free",
    verified: true,
    ...overrides,
  });
}

// In tests: the fixture type matches the production type exactly
// src/billing/__tests__/billing-service.test.ts
import { test, expect } from "vitest";
import { buildUserFixture } from "../../test/helpers/fixtures";
import { BillingService }   from "../billing-service";

test("upgrades user plan from free to pro", async () => {
  const user    = await buildUserFixture({ plan: "free" });
  const billing = new BillingService();

  const upgraded = await billing.upgradePlan(user, "pro");

  // upgraded type is also Awaited<ReturnType<...>>
  expect(upgraded.plan).toBe("pro");
  expect(upgraded.billingCycleStart).toBeInstanceOf(Date);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>` creates a tight coupling between the test helper type and the production factory function signature. If the factory is refactored to return a different type (e.g., from a plain object to a class instance), all test helpers typed with `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof factory>>` update automatically — which is the desired behaviour. However, if the factory is temporarily broken (returns `any` due to a `// @ts-ignore` comment or an incomplete implementation during TDD), the helper type degrades silently to `any`. Always keep the production factory fully typed; `Awaited<ReturnType<...>>` is only as precise as the source function's return type.

---

### 73. TDD for Vitest `context.annotate()` — Diagnostic Attachments for Failing Red-Phase Tests [official]

`context.annotate(message, { type, mimeType })` (Vitest 3.2+) attaches diagnostic metadata to a test case that is rendered by reporters on failure. In TDD, this enables the Red phase to produce maximally informative failure output: instead of a bare assertion diff, the test attaches the full request/response bodies, the rendered HTML, the database query plan, or a screenshot link. The annotation appears in the test report alongside the assertion failure, collapsing the debug cycle from "run → fail → manually inspect → re-run" to "run → fail → read annotation → fix."

```typescript
// src/api/__tests__/user-profile-api.test.ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { apiClient } from "../../test/helpers/api-client";

test("GET /users/:id returns a complete profile", async (ctx) => {
  const userId   = "user-001";
  const response = await apiClient.get(`/users/${userId}`);

  // Attach full response for diagnostic context on failure
  await ctx.annotate(
    JSON.stringify({ status: response.status, headers: response.headers, body: response.body }, null, 2),
    { type: "attachment", mimeType: "application/json" }
  );

  // RED assertions — all three must pass for Green
  expect(response.status).toBe(200);
  expect(response.body).toMatchObject({
    id:        userId,
    email:     expect.stringContaining("@"),
    createdAt: expect.any(String),
    profile: expect.objectContaining({
      displayName: expect.any(String),
      avatarUrl:   expect.stringMatching(/^https?:\/\//),
    }),
  });
});

test("GET /users/:id with invalid ID returns 404 with error body", async (ctx) => {
  const response = await apiClient.get("/users/nonexistent-id-xyz");

  await ctx.annotate(
    `Status: ${response.status}\nBody: ${JSON.stringify(response.body)}`,
    { type: "attachment", mimeType: "text/plain" }
  );

  expect(response.status).toBe(404);
  expect(response.body).toMatchObject({
    error:   "USER_NOT_FOUND",
    message: expect.any(String),
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Annotations are only rendered by reporters that support them — the default `dot` reporter discards annotations, while `verbose`, `html`, and `github-actions` reporters display them. Before adopting `context.annotate` team-wide, confirm your CI reporter renders annotations; otherwise the diagnostic information is collected but never surfaced. Also note that building the annotation value (e.g., serialising a large HTTP response) has a runtime cost that occurs even when the test passes — if the annotation value is expensive to compute, guard it with `if (process.env.VITEST_DEBUG)` to skip the serialisation in normal runs.

---

### 74. TDD for Vitest `sequence.groupOrder` — Controlling Multi-Project Test Execution Order [official]

`sequence.groupOrder: "parallel" | "sequential"` in `vitest.workspace.ts` controls whether projects within a workspace run concurrently or one-at-a-time. In TDD contexts with a monorepo, the default `parallel` mode can create resource contention when multiple projects share an external dependency (a single database instance, a fixed-port HTTP server, a shared Redis). Setting `groupOrder: "sequential"` for those projects serialises their execution, eliminating contention at the cost of total run time. Used with `sequence.concurrent: true` within each project, tests still run in parallel within a project while projects themselves are serialised.

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts — controlling project execution order
import { defineWorkspace } from "vitest/config";

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    test: {
      name:        "unit",
      root:        "./packages/core",
      environment: "node",
      sequence: {
        concurrent: true,     // tests within this project run in parallel
      },
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name:        "integration-api",
      root:        "./packages/api",
      environment: "node",
      // Uses a shared Postgres container — must not run with integration-workers
      sequence: {
        groupOrder: "sequential",   // serialise this project vs others in the group
        concurrent: false,          // within the project, also run sequentially
      },
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name:        "integration-workers",
      root:        "./packages/workers",
      environment: "node",
      sequence: {
        groupOrder: "sequential",   // same group as integration-api — runs after it
        concurrent: false,
      },
    },
  },
]);

// Run command: vitest --reporter=verbose
// Execution order: [unit] concurrently, then [integration-api], then [integration-workers]
```

**Tradeoff.** `sequence.groupOrder: "sequential"` increases total CI run time compared to `"parallel"` because projects no longer overlap. Measure the actual time cost before applying it broadly — often, making the shared resource support concurrent connections (a connection pool, a per-project database schema, isolated Redis keyspaces) eliminates the need for sequential ordering and is the better long-term investment. Use sequential ordering as a fast tactical fix during TDD spikes before the infrastructure isolation work is complete.

---

### 75. TDD for Vitest `--reporter=github-actions` — Inline CI Failure Annotations in the Red Phase [official]

The `github-actions` reporter (Vitest built-in) emits `::error file=...,line=...,col=...,title=...::` annotations directly in the GitHub Actions log, causing failing tests to appear as inline code annotations on the PR diff view and in the "Annotations" panel. In a TDD workflow, this means the Red-phase failure is visible directly in the PR — reviewers and the author see exactly which line contains the failing assertion without opening the full CI log. Combining the `github-actions` reporter with `verbose` as a fallback (for local runs) ensures both environments get appropriate output.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — environment-adaptive reporter configuration
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Use github-actions reporter in CI, verbose locally
    reporters: process.env.CI
      ? ["github-actions", "verbose"]
      : ["verbose"],

    // Ensure JSON report is also written for downstream tooling
    outputFile: process.env.CI
      ? { "json": ".vitest-results/results.json" }
      : undefined,

    coverage: {
      reporter:  process.env.CI ? ["json", "text-summary"] : ["text", "html"],
      reportsDirectory: ".vitest-results/coverage",
    },
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — consuming the Vitest github-actions reporter
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: "22" }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
        env:
          CI: "true"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: test-results
          path: .vitest-results/
```

**Tradeoff.** The `github-actions` reporter only works inside a GitHub Actions runner — running it locally produces `::error ...` lines in stdout that clutter the terminal. Always pair it with a local-friendly reporter (e.g., `["github-actions", "verbose"]` array form) so the output is readable in both environments. Note that the file path in the annotation must match the repository's file path relative to the workspace root — if your Vitest `root` is set to a subdirectory, verify that the emitted file paths include the subdirectory prefix, otherwise the GitHub UI will show "file not found" for the annotation.

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 46 Additions

204. **[community] `expect.schemaMatching` does NOT automatically import the schema library — if the test file imports Zod v4 (which uses the `zod/v4` import path) but the `schemaMatching` implementation internally calls `schema._parse()` using the v3 API shape, the matcher silently returns `false` because Zod v4's `_parse` method signature changed to `schema['~standard']['validate']`.** A developer migrates from Zod v3 to v4, updates all production code imports, and finds that `expect.schemaMatching(z.string())` now fails for valid strings without a clear error message. WHY this matters: the Standard Schema v1 protocol is the interop layer between Zod v4 and Vitest — if the Vitest version predates Standard Schema v1 support, the matcher falls back to a v3 code path that is incompatible with v4. Fix: ensure Vitest is at 4.1.0+ (which added Standard Schema v1 support) and Zod is at 3.24+ or 4.x (which implements the Standard Schema v1 interface via `schema['~standard']`).

205. **[community] `expect.soft` does not prevent the test from being reported as failed even when every `expect.soft` assertion happens to pass — if the test file has a single hard `expect()` call that fails after all soft assertions pass, Vitest reports the test as failed and includes the soft assertion results in the failure context, leading the developer to incorrectly diagnose the soft assertions as the cause.** A developer uses `expect.soft` for all field assertions in a transformation test, adds a final hard `expect(result).not.toBeNull()` guard, and finds the test output shows soft assertion failures even though all the soft assertions individually passed. WHY this matters: the developer spends time fixing fields that were already correct because the error context includes them. Fix: always read the failure output top-to-bottom — Vitest lists soft assertion results as context, not as the primary failure. The first non-context line in the failure report identifies the failing assertion; the soft-assertion summary below it is informational.

206. **[community] `vi.stubEnv` does not work for environment variables read via `import.meta.env` in Vite-based projects — Vite inlines `import.meta.env.X` at build time using `define` substitution, so there is no runtime `process.env` variable to stub; `vi.stubEnv` only affects `process.env` which is the Node.js global.** A developer stubs `vi.stubEnv("VITE_API_URL", "http://test-server")` expecting it to change the value of `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` seen by the module under test and discovers the module still uses the original build-time value. WHY this matters: the developer concludes that `vi.stubEnv` is broken rather than recognising the Vite-specific inlining behaviour. Fix: for Vite projects, use `vi.mock("./config", () => ({ API_URL: "http://test-server" }))` to mock the config module, or use `vitest.config.ts`'s `define` block to override `import.meta.env` values at test-build time.

207. **[community] Using `test.concurrent` with database fixtures that rely on `AUTO_INCREMENT` primary keys causes test ordering assumptions to fail — the first concurrent test to INSERT a row gets `id: 1`, but which test runs first is non-deterministic, so a test that asserts `expect(record.id).toBe(1)` passes locally (because it usually runs first) and fails in CI (where the scheduler is different).** A developer writes integration tests for a user registration flow, asserts that the first created user has `id: 1`, and observes intermittent CI failures that never reproduce locally. WHY this matters: concurrent execution changes which test "wins" the first INSERT, and deterministic ID assertions hide this assumption. Fix: never assert specific auto-increment ID values in tests; assert `expect(record.id).toBeGreaterThan(0)` or `expect(record.id).toEqual(expect.any(Number))`, and use stable identifiers (email, UUID, slug) for lookup assertions.

208. **[community] `vi.importActual` inside a `vi.mock` factory MUST be called with the exact same module specifier string as the `vi.mock` call — using a relative path in `vi.mock("../utils")` but an absolute path or a different alias in `vi.importActual("@/utils")` produces a second module evaluation rather than returning the same cached instance, causing the auto-spy replacement to apply only to the auto-factory copy while the partial spread receives an independent real instance with no spies applied.** A developer partially mocks a utility module by spreading `importActual` results and replacing one function with `vi.fn()`, then discovers that `expect(mockedFunction).toHaveBeenCalled()` always fails because the SUT imports the real module via a TypeScript path alias while the mock factory resolved a relative path. WHY this matters: the path alias resolution and the mock factory resolution go through different code paths in Vitest's module registry, producing two separate module instances — one mocked and one real. Fix: use the exact same module specifier in both `vi.mock(...)` and `await importActual<...>(...)`, matching whatever the SUT uses (either always relative, or always the alias, consistently).

209. **[community] `context.annotate()` in a concurrent test suite collects annotations per-test but the `ctx` object is not safely shareable — capturing `ctx` in a closure inside a concurrent `test` call and referencing it from an async callback after the test body returns throws a "context already cleaned up" error, because Vitest tears down the test context immediately after the test function's returned promise resolves.** A developer writes a concurrent integration test that fires an async background job and attempts to annotate the job result using `ctx.annotate` in a `.finally()` handler chained to the job promise — the `.finally()` runs after the test resolves, hitting the cleaned-up context. WHY this matters: the error message ("Cannot annotate after test completion") is not surfaced as a test failure — it appears as an unhandled rejection in the test runner output, making it hard to trace to the offending test. Fix: all `ctx.annotate()` calls must be awaited before the test function returns; restructure the test to `await` the background job inside the test body rather than in a post-resolve chain.

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### 76. TDD for Vitest Browser Mode — Component Testing with Real DOM Queries [official]

Vitest Browser Mode executes tests directly inside a real browser (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) via Playwright or WebdriverIO, eliminating the JSDOM approximation gap that causes subtle false-positives in unit tests for DOM-heavy code. In TDD, the Red phase is written against real browser globals (`window`, `document`, `ResizeObserver`, `IntersectionObserver`) that JSDOM either stubs imperfectly or omits entirely. Framework-specific render helpers (`vitest-browser-react`, `vitest-browser-vue`) integrate with the page locator API so that `render()` returns both the component wrapper and the `page` locator object, enabling accessible-query assertions immediately after render without additional setup.

```typescript
// src/components/__tests__/SearchInput.browser.test.tsx
import { render } from "vitest-browser-react";
import { page, userEvent } from "@vitest/browser/context";
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { SearchInput } from "../SearchInput";

test("SearchInput calls onSearch with trimmed value on Enter", async () => {
  const onSearch = vi.fn();

  // Renders inside the real browser DOM
  render(<SearchInput placeholder="Search…" onSearch={onSearch} />);

  const input = page.getByRole("textbox", { name: /search/i });

  // RED: fails until SearchInput trims leading/trailing spaces
  await userEvent.fill(input, "  hello world  ");
  await userEvent.keyboard("{Enter}");

  expect(onSearch).toHaveBeenCalledWith("hello world");
  expect(onSearch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
});

test("SearchInput clears value after submission", async () => {
  const onSearch = vi.fn();
  render(<SearchInput placeholder="Search…" onSearch={onSearch} />);

  const input = page.getByRole("textbox", { name: /search/i });
  await userEvent.fill(input, "query");
  await userEvent.keyboard("{Enter}");

  // RED: fails until SearchInput clears the field post-submit
  await expect.element(input).toHaveValue("");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Browser Mode tests are slower than JSDOM-based unit tests — each test file requires a browser page allocation (roughly 300–800ms overhead per file). Reserve Browser Mode for components that genuinely depend on layout, native form behaviour, accessibility APIs, or browser-specific globals. Pure data transformation or state management logic should remain in the faster JSDOM or `node` environment. Separate the two environments using project-level configuration in `vitest.workspace.ts` and distinct file naming conventions (e.g., `*.browser.test.tsx` vs `*.test.ts`).

### 77. TDD for Vitest `userEvent.setup()` — Stateful User Interaction Sessions [official]

`userEvent.setup()` creates a persistent user-event session that maintains keyboard modifier state (`Shift`, `Ctrl`, `Meta`) and pointer position across multiple interaction calls within the same test. The stateless `userEvent.click()` / `userEvent.type()` convenience methods reset state between calls, which makes them incorrect for multi-step interactions such as shift-click range selection, keyboard chord navigation, or clipboard sequences. In TDD, `userEvent.setup()` is the Red-phase tool for complex interaction contracts that require state continuity — the test is written against the expected accumulated behaviour first, then the component is implemented to satisfy it.

```typescript
// src/components/__tests__/MultiSelect.browser.test.tsx
import { render } from "vitest-browser-react";
import { userEvent } from "@vitest/browser/context";
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { MultiSelect } from "../MultiSelect";

test("shift-click selects a contiguous range of items", async () => {
  const onSelectionChange = vi.fn();
  render(
    <MultiSelect
      items={["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry", "Date", "Elderberry"]}
      onSelectionChange={onSelectionChange}
    />
  );

  // Setup preserves keyboard modifier state across interactions
  const user = userEvent.setup();

  const apple  = page.getByRole("option", { name: "Apple" });
  const cherry = page.getByRole("option", { name: "Cherry" });

  await user.click(apple);
  // Shift state is preserved in the session for the next click
  await user.keyboard("[ShiftLeft>]");
  await user.click(cherry);
  await user.keyboard("[/ShiftLeft]");

  // RED: fails until MultiSelect implements range selection
  expect(onSelectionChange).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith(
    expect.arrayContaining(["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"])
  );
  expect(onSelectionChange.mock.lastCall[0]).toHaveLength(3);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `userEvent.setup()` sessions maintain pointer position between calls — in Playwright and WebdriverIO providers, the pointer does not reset between tests. If a test that uses `user.hover()` is followed by another test, the second test starts with the pointer still over the element from the first test, potentially triggering `:hover` styles or `mouseenter` events unexpectedly. Always call `await userEvent.unhover(document.body)` in `afterEach` when any test in the file uses hover interactions. The stateless convenience functions do not have this problem because they reset per call.

### 78. TDD for Vitest `vi.mockObject()` — Deep Object Mocking Without Module Hoisting [official]

`vi.mockObject(object, options?)` (Vitest 3.2+) creates a deep mock of a plain object or class instance, replacing all methods with `vi.fn()` stubs while preserving the structural shape. Unlike `vi.mock("./module")` which must be hoisted to the top of the file and replaces an entire module, `vi.mockObject` is called inline and scoped to the variable it is assigned to — it does not require factory functions, does not interact with the module registry, and does not need to appear before imports. In TDD, this is the correct tool for mocking service objects, repository instances, or dependency-injected collaborators that are passed as constructor arguments rather than imported as modules.

```typescript
// src/orders/__tests__/order-processor.test.ts
import { expect, test, vi } from "vitest";
import { OrderProcessor }   from "../order-processor";
import { PaymentGateway }   from "../payment-gateway";
import { InventoryService } from "../inventory-service";

test("processor charges the gateway and decrements inventory on success", async () => {
  // Deep mock — all methods become vi.fn() stubs
  const gateway   = vi.mockObject(new PaymentGateway());
  const inventory = vi.mockObject(new InventoryService());

  gateway.charge.mockResolvedValue({ transactionId: "txn-001", status: "success" });
  inventory.reserve.mockResolvedValue({ reservationId: "res-001" });

  const processor = new OrderProcessor(gateway, inventory);
  const result    = await processor.process({ sku: "WIDGET", qty: 2, total: 4000 });

  // RED: fails until processor calls both collaborators correctly
  expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ amount: 4000, currency: "USD" });
  expect(inventory.reserve).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ sku: "WIDGET", qty: 2 });
  expect(result.status).toBe("confirmed");
});

test("processor rolls back inventory reservation if charge fails", async () => {
  const gateway   = vi.mockObject(new PaymentGateway());
  const inventory = vi.mockObject(new InventoryService());

  gateway.charge.mockRejectedValue(new Error("CARD_DECLINED"));
  inventory.reserve.mockResolvedValue({ reservationId: "res-002" });

  const processor = new OrderProcessor(gateway, inventory);
  await expect(processor.process({ sku: "WIDGET", qty: 1, total: 2000 }))
    .rejects.toThrow("CARD_DECLINED");

  // RED: fails until processor implements rollback on charge failure
  expect(inventory.release).toHaveBeenCalledWith("res-002");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.mockObject` mocks the object's own enumerable methods — it does not walk the prototype chain by default. If `PaymentGateway` stores its methods on the prototype (which is the standard ES class pattern), `vi.mockObject(new PaymentGateway())` will only mock the own-property methods. For prototype-based classes, combine `vi.mockObject` with `vi.spyOn` on the prototype, or use `vi.mock("./payment-gateway")` for the module-level approach. Always verify that the mocked methods are actually stubs by calling `vi.isMockFunction(gateway.charge)` in a debug test if behaviour is surprising.

### 79. TDD for Vitest `vi.mock()` with `{ spy: true }` — Module-Level Spying Without Replacing Behaviour [official]

`vi.mock("./module", { spy: true })` hoists a module spy that wraps every export in a `vi.fn()` proxy while forwarding all calls to the original implementation. This is the module-level analogue of `vi.spyOn`: the real code runs, the real return values are produced, but all calls are recorded and can be asserted with `toHaveBeenCalledWith`, `toHaveBeenCalledTimes`, and `toHaveReturnedWith`. In TDD, this pattern is valuable for verifying that a function is called with the correct arguments without needing to control what it returns — the production behaviour provides the Green-phase validation while the spy records the interaction contract.

```typescript
// src/analytics/__tests__/page-view-tracker.test.ts
import { expect, test, vi } from "vitest";
import { recordPageView } from "../analytics-client";
import { PageViewTracker } from "../page-view-tracker";

// Spy: real recordPageView runs; all calls are tracked
vi.mock("../analytics-client", { spy: true });

test("PageViewTracker sends page view with path and referrer", () => {
  const tracker = new PageViewTracker();

  // RED: fails until tracker calls recordPageView with these exact arguments
  tracker.track({ path: "/products", referrer: "https://google.com" });

  expect(recordPageView).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(recordPageView).toHaveBeenCalledWith({
    path:     "/products",
    referrer: "https://google.com",
    // timestamp is NOT asserted — volatile; use asymmetric matcher if needed
  });
});

test("PageViewTracker debounces rapid navigations within 300ms", () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  const tracker = new PageViewTracker();

  tracker.track({ path: "/a" });
  tracker.track({ path: "/b" });
  tracker.track({ path: "/c" });

  vi.advanceTimersByTime(350);

  // RED: only the last navigation should be recorded
  expect(recordPageView).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(recordPageView).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ path: "/c" }));
  vi.useRealTimers();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `{ spy: true }` spy-mocks cannot override return values unless you also call `vi.mocked(fn).mockReturnValue(...)` — at that point you are replacing the implementation and the "real code runs" benefit is lost. If tests need both real behaviour for some calls and controlled returns for others, combine a spy mock with `mockReturnValueOnce` for specific call positions. Also note that spy mocks are still hoisted to the top of the file like regular `vi.mock` calls — they interact with the module registry and the `{ spy: true }` option is processed at hoist time, not at `vi.mock` evaluation time.

### 80. TDD for Vitest `vi.setTimerTickMode()` — Automatic Timer Advancement Modes [official]

`vi.setTimerTickMode(mode)` (Vitest 4.1+) extends the fake timer system with two automatic advancement modes beyond the default `"manual"` mode. In `"nextTimerAsync"` mode, Vitest automatically advances the clock to the next scheduled timer after each macro-task, enabling tests to await promises that internally schedule timers without manual `advanceTimersByTime` calls. In `"interval"` mode, the clock automatically advances by a specified millisecond interval between ticks, useful for testing polling loops and retry mechanisms. These modes reduce the boilerplate of interleaving `vi.advanceTimersByTime` calls with `await` expressions in complex async timer tests.

```typescript
// src/polling/__tests__/status-poller.test.ts
import { afterEach, beforeEach, expect, test, vi } from "vitest";
import { StatusPoller } from "../status-poller";

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
});
afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
  vi.setTimerTickMode("manual"); // reset to default after each test
});

test("StatusPoller retries every 5s until max retries reached", async () => {
  // "interval" mode auto-advances 5s between each macro-task
  vi.setTimerTickMode("interval");
  vi.setTimerInterval(5_000);

  const fetchStatus = vi.fn()
    .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: "pending" })
    .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: "pending" })
    .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: "complete" });

  const poller = new StatusPoller(fetchStatus, { intervalMs: 5_000, maxRetries: 3 });

  // RED: fails until poller stops after 3 attempts and returns the final status
  const result = await poller.poll();

  expect(fetchStatus).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  expect(result.status).toBe("complete");
});

test("StatusPoller throws MaxRetriesExceeded after 3 pending responses", async () => {
  vi.setTimerTickMode("interval");
  vi.setTimerInterval(5_000);

  const fetchStatus = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: "pending" });
  const poller = new StatusPoller(fetchStatus, { intervalMs: 5_000, maxRetries: 3 });

  // RED: fails until poller throws when maxRetries is exhausted
  await expect(poller.poll()).rejects.toThrow("MaxRetriesExceeded");
  expect(fetchStatus).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `"interval"` and `"nextTimerAsync"` tick modes interact with `await` in non-obvious ways — the automatic advancement fires between macro-tasks, so an `await Promise.resolve()` inside the code under test will allow the tick to fire, but `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` may not if the zero-delay timer is processed before the tick. In practice, `"manual"` mode with explicit `advanceTimersByTimeAsync(n)` calls remains the most predictable approach for complex async sequences. Use the automatic modes only for simple polling and retry patterns where the timer schedule is uniform and well-understood.

### 81. TDD for Vitest `test.extend()` Builder Pattern — Chainable Fixture Composition with Type Inference [official]

The `.extend()` builder pattern (Vitest 4.1+) chains fixture definitions as method calls on the test object, each call returning a new test instance with accumulated fixture types automatically inferred. Unlike the `base.extend<Fixtures>({...})` single-call pattern, chaining multiple `.extend()` calls separates fixture concerns into independent, reusable declarations — a database fixture can live in one module, an HTTP client fixture in another, and a user-session fixture in a third, all composed at the test-file level without manual type intersection. TypeScript infers the full union of fixture types across all chained calls, so all fixtures are available in the final `test` function's callback with correct typing.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/db.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from "vitest";
import { createTestDatabase, TestDatabase } from "../helpers/test-database";

export const withDatabase = base.extend<{ db: TestDatabase }>({
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const db = await createTestDatabase();
    await use(db);
    await db.teardown();
  },
});

// test/fixtures/http.fixture.ts
import { withDatabase } from "./db.fixture";
import { createTestHttpClient, TestHttpClient } from "../helpers/test-http-client";

export const withHttp = withDatabase.extend<{ http: TestHttpClient }>({
  http: async ({ db }, use) => {
    // http fixture depends on db — resolved automatically
    const http = await createTestHttpClient({ databaseUrl: db.url });
    await use(http);
    await http.close();
  },
});

// src/users/__tests__/user-registration.test.ts
import { expect } from "vitest";
import { withHttp } from "../../test/fixtures/http.fixture";

// 'test' has both db and http typed correctly — no manual type intersection
const test = withHttp;

test("POST /users registers a new user and persists to the database", async ({ http, db }) => {
  // RED: fails until the endpoint creates the user record
  const response = await http.post("/users", { name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com" });

  expect(response.status).toBe(201);
  expect(response.body.id).toEqual(expect.any(String));

  const stored = await db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", ["alice@example.com"]);
  expect(stored.rows).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(stored.rows[0].name).toBe("Alice");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Deeply chained `.extend()` calls create implicit fixture dependency graphs — if `withHttp` depends on `withDatabase` which depends on `withConfig`, modifying `withConfig` ripples through all downstream fixtures. This is the intended design (like a DI container), but it means a broken base fixture causes failures across every test that chains from it, with error messages pointing to the top-level fixture rather than the root cause. Document fixture dependency chains with a comment graph at the top of each fixture file, and run fixture-only smoke tests that verify each layer in isolation before the full integration suite.

---

### 82. TDD for Vitest `test.override()` — Suite-Scoped Fixture Replacement [official]

`test.override(overrides)` (Vitest 4.1+, replaces deprecated `test.scoped()`) replaces fixture values for all tests within the enclosing `describe` block and its nested children, without affecting tests outside that block. This is the correct TDD pattern for a test file that has a default fixture configuration (e.g., a production-like database seed) but needs a subset of tests to run against a different configuration (e.g., an empty database or an error-state seed). The override is declared once at the top of the `describe` block rather than duplicated in each `test` call's inline override.

```typescript
// src/search/__tests__/search-service.test.ts
import { describe, expect } from "vitest";
import { test as base } from "vitest";

type SearchFixtures = {
  searchIndex: { documents: string[]; ready: boolean };
};

const test = base.extend<SearchFixtures>({
  searchIndex: async ({}, use) => {
    // Default: a populated index with sample documents
    const index = await createSearchIndex(["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]);
    await use({ documents: ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"], ready: true });
    await index.destroy();
  },
});

test("search returns matching documents from a populated index", async ({ searchIndex }) => {
  // Uses default fixture — populated index
  const results = await SearchService.query("beta", searchIndex);
  expect(results).toContain("beta");
});

describe("empty index behaviour", () => {
  // Override applies to all tests in this block only
  test.override({
    searchIndex: { documents: [], ready: true },
  });

  test("search returns empty array when index has no documents", async ({ searchIndex }) => {
    // RED: fails until SearchService handles empty index without throwing
    const results = await SearchService.query("anything", searchIndex);
    expect(results).toEqual([]);
  });

  test("search returns empty array for any query term", async ({ searchIndex }) => {
    const results = await SearchService.query("gamma", searchIndex);
    expect(results).toEqual([]);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.override()` must be called at the top level of a `describe` block — calling it inside a `test` callback or a `beforeEach` hook throws a runtime error. If you need per-test fixture variation, use the `test` function's inline fixture parameter instead: `test("name", { retry: 2 }, async ({ ... }) => { ... })`. Also note that `test.override()` replaces the fixture value entirely — it does not merge with the default fixture. If the fixture is an object with multiple fields and you only want to change one, provide the full replacement object with all required fields, or decompose the fixture into smaller granular fixtures that can be overridden independently.

---

### 83. TDD for Vitest Coverage Thresholds with `perFile` — Enforcing Per-File Coverage Floors [official]

Coverage threshold enforcement in Vitest can be applied globally (across all files combined) or per-file (each file individually must meet the threshold). In a TDD workflow, `perFile: true` is the stronger guarantee: a single file with zero coverage cannot hide behind high aggregate coverage from other files. This is especially valuable for enforcing the TDD discipline — a new file added without tests will cause CI to fail immediately rather than only when overall project coverage degrades below the global threshold. Negative threshold values (e.g., `lines: -5`) set a maximum uncovered-line count rather than a percentage, which is more stable as the codebase grows.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — per-file and glob-pattern threshold configuration
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      include:  ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"],
      exclude:  ["src/**/*.d.ts", "src/**/*.stories.tsx", "src/generated/**"],

      thresholds: {
        // Global floor: entire project must meet these
        lines:     80,
        functions: 80,
        branches:  70,
        statements: 80,

        // Per-file: every individual file must meet these (stricter)
        perFile: true,

        // Auto-update: raise thresholds automatically when coverage improves
        autoUpdate: true,

        // Critical path: higher bar for core business logic
        "src/core/**/*.ts": {
          lines:     95,
          functions: 95,
          branches:  90,
        },
        // Generated/config files: exempt from branch coverage requirement
        "src/config/*.ts": {
          lines:     70,
          branches:   0,
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `perFile: true` with strict thresholds causes false-positive CI failures for intentionally thin files — a re-export barrel file (`export * from "./module"`) may show 0% branch coverage because it has no branches. Always pair `perFile` thresholds with a well-tuned `exclude` list covering generated files, barrel exports, type-only files, and Storybook stories. Setting thresholds to negative values (`lines: -0` means zero uncovered lines allowed) is more expressive than `lines: 100` for critical core modules where a single untested line is a policy violation, not a percentage-rounding artefact.

---

### 84. TDD for Vitest `context.signal` — Cooperative Test Cancellation on Timeout [official]

`context.signal` is an `AbortSignal` attached to the test's execution context that becomes aborted when the test's timeout expires. In TDD, this enables writing integration tests for async workflows (HTTP streams, WebSocket connections, long-running database operations) that clean up cooperatively when the test runner times out, rather than leaving dangling connections or file handles. The signal can be passed to `fetch()`, Node.js `http.request()`, database query clients, and any other API that accepts an `AbortSignal`, making timeout cleanup a first-class concern in the test design rather than an afterthought.

```typescript
// src/streaming/__tests__/event-stream.test.ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { EventStreamClient } from "../event-stream-client";

test(
  "EventStreamClient receives and buffers events from a live stream",
  { timeout: 10_000 },
  async (ctx) => {
    const client = new EventStreamClient("https://api.example.com/events");
    const received: string[] = [];

    // Pass ctx.signal: client stops reading if the test times out
    const stream = await client.connect({ signal: ctx.signal });

    stream.on("event", (event: { type: string }) => {
      received.push(event.type);
    });

    // RED: fails until client correctly buffers the first 3 events
    await stream.waitForEvents(3, { signal: ctx.signal });

    expect(received).toHaveLength(3);
    expect(received.every(t => typeof t === "string")).toBe(true);

    // Graceful close — also respects signal if still connected
    await stream.close();
  }
);

test("EventStreamClient reconnects after network interruption", { timeout: 15_000 }, async (ctx) => {
  const client = new EventStreamClient("https://api.example.com/events");

  // signal propagates through the entire reconnect cycle
  const stream = await client.connect({ signal: ctx.signal });
  await stream.simulateNetworkInterruption();

  // RED: fails until client implements automatic reconnection
  await stream.waitForReconnect({ signal: ctx.signal });
  expect(stream.isConnected()).toBe(true);

  await stream.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `context.signal` is only aborted on timeout — it is NOT aborted when the test passes or fails normally. If a test completes in 100ms but you passed `ctx.signal` to a background process that is still running, the signal remains non-aborted and the process continues until the test runner's worker terminates. For proper resource cleanup on test completion (not just timeout), use `ctx.onTestFinished(() => resource.cleanup())` instead of relying on signal abort. Combine both: pass `ctx.signal` to the resource for timeout safety, and register an `onTestFinished` hook for normal-completion cleanup.

---

### 85. TDD for Vitest `test.beforeAll` on Extended Test Objects — Suite-Level Setup with Typed Fixtures [official]

`test.beforeAll(fn)` called on an extended test object (created via `test.extend()`) runs the setup function once before all tests in the file or `describe` block, with access to `file`-scoped and `worker`-scoped fixtures. Unlike the module-level `beforeAll` import from `vitest`, `test.beforeAll` inherits the extended fixture types — the callback receives the same typed fixture context as test callbacks. This enables a pattern where expensive once-per-file setup (spinning up a server, seeding a database schema, compiling a WASM module) is declared inside the fixture-typed test object rather than in a separate, untyped `beforeAll` block.

```typescript
// src/reports/__tests__/report-generator.test.ts
import { expect } from "vitest";
import { test as base } from "vitest";

type ReportFixtures = {
  reportEngine: ReportEngine;       // worker-scoped: shared across the worker
  templateCache: TemplateCache;     // file-scoped: reset between files
};

const test = base.extend<ReportFixtures>({
  reportEngine: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Expensive: compile WASM rendering engine once per worker
      const engine = await ReportEngine.compile("./wasm/renderer.wasm");
      await use(engine);
      engine.dispose();
    },
    { scope: "worker" },
  ],
  templateCache: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const cache = new TemplateCache();
      await use(cache);
      cache.clear();
    },
    { scope: "file" },
  ],
});

// Typed beforeAll — reportEngine and templateCache are available here
test.beforeAll(async ({ reportEngine, templateCache }) => {
  // Seed the template cache once for all tests in this file
  const templates = await loadTestTemplates("./fixtures/templates/");
  templates.forEach(t => templateCache.register(t));
});

test("generates a PDF invoice with all required sections", async ({ reportEngine, templateCache }) => {
  const template = templateCache.get("invoice-v2");
  const result = await reportEngine.render(template, { orderId: "ORD-001", total: 9900 });

  // RED: fails until renderer produces a valid PDF buffer with all sections
  expect(result.mimeType).toBe("application/pdf");
  expect(result.sections).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining(["header", "line-items", "totals", "footer"]));
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.beforeAll` on the extended test object only has access to `file`-scoped and `worker`-scoped fixtures — it cannot access `test`-scoped fixtures (which are per-test by definition). Attempting to use a `test`-scoped fixture in `test.beforeAll` will throw a runtime error. If the `beforeAll` setup requires a resource that would normally be test-scoped (e.g., a per-test database transaction), escalate its scope to `file` for this pattern to work. Document the scope escalation with a comment explaining why — accidental scope escalation is a common source of test cross-contamination.

### 86. TDD for TypeScript `NoInfer<T>` — Preventing Inference Leakage in Generic Test Fixtures [official]

`NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4+) prevents the type checker from widening the inferred type of a generic parameter by using the argument marked with `NoInfer` as an inference site. In TDD, this is valuable when writing generic fixture builder functions that accept a set of valid values and a default: without `NoInfer`, TypeScript widens the inferred union to include the default value even when it is not in the valid set, masking a bug in the test data. With `NoInfer` on the default parameter, the type is inferred only from the valid-values array, and the default must be a member of that inferred union or TypeScript emits a compile-time error — a Red signal that requires no test execution.

```typescript
// test/helpers/enum-fixture.ts

/**
 * Creates a fixture for a string-enum field with compile-time safety.
 * NoInfer prevents the defaultValue from widening the inferred union C.
 */
function createEnumFixture<C extends string>(
  validValues: readonly C[],
  defaultValue: NoInfer<C>
): { values: readonly C[]; default: C } {
  if (!validValues.includes(defaultValue)) {
    throw new Error(`Default "${defaultValue}" is not in valid values`);
  }
  return { values: validValues, default: defaultValue };
}

// ✅ Compiles: "pending" is in the array, C is inferred as "pending"|"confirmed"|"shipped"
const statusFixture = createEnumFixture(
  ["pending", "confirmed", "shipped"] as const,
  "pending"
);

// ❌ Type error at compile time: "cancelled" is not assignable to "pending"|"confirmed"|"shipped"
// const badFixture = createEnumFixture(
//   ["pending", "confirmed", "shipped"] as const,
//   "cancelled"  // TypeScript error — NoInfer prevents widening
// );

// In tests: use statusFixture.values for iteration, .default for single-value tests
// src/orders/__tests__/order-status.test.ts
import { describe, expect, test } from "vitest";
import { validateOrderStatus } from "../order-status";
import { statusFixture } from "../../test/helpers/fixtures";

describe("validateOrderStatus", () => {
  test.each(statusFixture.values)(
    "accepts valid status: %s",
    (status) => {
      expect(validateOrderStatus(status)).toBe(true);
    }
  );

  test("rejects unknown status", () => {
    // @ts-expect-error — deliberate invalid input test
    expect(validateOrderStatus("cancelled")).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `NoInfer<T>` is a compile-time constraint — it does not add any runtime validation. A `NoInfer`-guarded fixture builder that compiles correctly can still produce incorrect data if the `validValues` array itself is wrong (e.g., contains a value that is not actually valid in production). Always pair compile-time `NoInfer` guards with a runtime check (the `if (!validValues.includes(defaultValue))` guard in the example above) so that errors in the fixture definition are caught at test-initialisation time rather than during assertion. The compile-time check catches wrong types; the runtime check catches correct types with wrong values.
