### 87. TDD for Vitest Coverage `autoUpdate` — Ratchet-Style Threshold Progression [official]

`coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate: true` (Vitest) causes Vitest to automatically rewrite the threshold values in `vitest.config.ts` whenever the actual coverage exceeds the configured minimum. This implements a ratchet: coverage can only go up, never down. In a TDD workflow, this means the team does not need to manually bump threshold numbers as they write more tests — the config file self-documents the current coverage floor, and the CI gate ensures the floor is never regressed. Combined with the negative-value syntax (`lines: -5` meaning "no more than 5 uncovered lines"), autoUpdate provides a precise, file-size-stable coverage progression model.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — ratchet-style coverage configuration
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      include:  ["src/**/*.ts"],
      exclude:  ["src/**/*.d.ts", "src/generated/**", "src/**/__mocks__/**"],

      thresholds: {
        // These values are auto-bumped by Vitest when coverage improves
        // (do not hand-edit — let autoUpdate manage them)
        lines:      87,   // last auto-updated: 2026-05-10
        functions:  84,
        branches:   79,
        statements: 87,

        autoUpdate: true,

        // Negative value: maximum uncovered lines allowed in each file
        // More stable than percentages as file size grows
        "src/core/**/*.ts": {
          lines: -2,    // max 2 uncovered lines per core file
          branches: -1, // max 1 uncovered branch per core file
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `autoUpdate` modifies `vitest.config.ts` on disk during test runs — if the file is open in an editor, the editor may show a "file changed externally" prompt. More critically, if `autoUpdate` is enabled in a CI environment and the CI job has write access to the repository, the config file may be silently modified in the CI workspace without being committed, making the updated thresholds invisible in the next run. The intended workflow is: enable `autoUpdate` locally (in the watch loop), commit the bumped config, and keep `autoUpdate: false` (or absent) in CI-specific config overrides. Use separate `vitest.config.ci.ts` and `vitest.config.ts` files to separate the two concerns.

---

### 88. TDD for Vitest `expect.toSatisfy()` — Predicate-Based Assertions for Complex Invariants [official]

`expect(value).toSatisfy(predicate)` accepts a boolean-returning function and asserts that `predicate(value)` returns `true`. In TDD, this is the correct tool for assertions that cannot be expressed cleanly with structural matchers (`toMatchObject`, `toEqual`) — invariants like "all elements are sorted", "no two items share a key", "the total equals the sum of its parts", or "the result satisfies a domain rule too complex to express as a literal structure". Using `toSatisfy` with a named predicate function produces self-documenting failure messages and keeps the test readable when the assertion logic would otherwise require multi-line manual assertions.

```typescript
// src/pricing/__tests__/price-calculator.test.ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { calculateTieredPricing } from "../price-calculator";

// Named predicates — self-documenting in failure messages
const isSorted       = (arr: number[]) => arr.every((v, i) => i === 0 || arr[i - 1] <= v);
const hasNoDuplicates = (arr: string[]) => new Set(arr).size === arr.length;
const sumsTo         = (total: number) => (items: { price: number }[]) =>
  Math.abs(items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0) - total) < 0.01; // floating-point tolerance

test("calculateTieredPricing returns price tiers in ascending order", () => {
  const result = calculateTieredPricing({ basePrice: 1000, unitCount: 100 });

  // RED: fails until tiers are returned in ascending price order
  expect(result.tiers.map(t => t.pricePerUnit)).toSatisfy(isSorted);
});

test("calculateTieredPricing produces tiers with unique tier labels", () => {
  const result = calculateTieredPricing({ basePrice: 1000, unitCount: 100 });

  // RED: fails until tier labels are unique
  expect(result.tiers.map(t => t.label)).toSatisfy(hasNoDuplicates);
});

test("calculateTieredPricing line items sum to the invoice total", () => {
  const result = calculateTieredPricing({ basePrice: 500, unitCount: 50 });

  // RED: fails until line items correctly decompose the total
  expect(result.lineItems).toSatisfy(sumsTo(result.total));
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toSatisfy` predicate failures show "expected false to be truthy" rather than a meaningful diff — the predicate is a black box to the assertion engine. To improve failure messages, combine `toSatisfy` with `expect.soft()` and additional structural assertions that pinpoint the failure: assert `toSatisfy(isSorted)` for the contract, then assert specific element pairs with `toHaveProperty` for the diagnosis. Alternatively, use `expect.extend` to create a named custom matcher (`expect(arr).toBeSorted()`) that produces a diff-style failure message showing the out-of-order elements — the investment pays off for predicates used in 5+ test files.

---

### 89. TDD for Vitest `expect.extend()` — Domain-Specific Custom Matchers [official]

`expect.extend(matchers)` registers custom assertion functions that produce structured pass/fail results with custom failure messages. In TDD, domain-specific matchers encode business invariants once and reuse them across the test suite — rather than writing `expect(order.status).toBe("pending")` in thirty places and manually updating each when the status model changes, a `toBeInStatus(expected)` matcher encodes the assertion pattern, handles edge cases (null status, status history, transition validity), and produces a failure message that speaks the domain language. Custom matchers in TypeScript require an interface augmentation to be type-safe.

```typescript
// test/matchers/order-matchers.ts
import { expect } from "vitest";

interface OrderMatcherState {
  status: string;
  statusHistory: string[];
  lastTransitionAt: string | null;
}

expect.extend({
  toBeInStatus(received: OrderMatcherState, expected: string) {
    const pass = received.status === expected;
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `Expected order NOT to be in status "${expected}", but it was.\nHistory: ${received.statusHistory.join(" → ")}`
          : `Expected order to be in status "${expected}", but was "${received.status}".\nHistory: ${received.statusHistory.join(" → ")}\nLast transition: ${received.lastTransitionAt ?? "never"}`,
    };
  },

  toHaveTransitionedThrough(received: OrderMatcherState, ...statuses: string[]) {
    const historyStr = received.statusHistory.join(",");
    const pass = statuses.every(s => historyStr.includes(s));
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        `Expected status history [${received.statusHistory.join(", ")}] to include all of [${statuses.join(", ")}]`,
    };
  },
});

// TypeScript interface augmentation — required for type safety
declare module "vitest" {
  interface Assertion<R = any> {
    toBeInStatus(expected: string): R;
    toHaveTransitionedThrough(...statuses: string[]): R;
  }
}

// src/orders/__tests__/order-lifecycle.test.ts
import "../../test/matchers/order-matchers";
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { OrderService } from "../order-service";

test("order transitions through pending → confirmed → shipped on happy path", async () => {
  const order = await OrderService.create({ sku: "WIDGET", qty: 1 });
  await OrderService.confirm(order.id);
  await OrderService.ship(order.id);

  const current = await OrderService.get(order.id);

  // RED: domain-language assertions
  expect(current).toBeInStatus("shipped");
  expect(current).toHaveTransitionedThrough("pending", "confirmed", "shipped");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom matchers are shared infrastructure — a bug in a matcher can silently make many tests pass or fail incorrectly. Always write tests for custom matchers themselves (a `matcher.test.ts` file that verifies both the pass and fail branches of each matcher using `expect(fn).toThrow()` and `.not.toThrow()` patterns). Also note that the `declare module "vitest"` interface augmentation must be imported in every test file that uses the matcher — either import the matcher module directly or add it to `vitest.config.ts`'s `setupFiles` array so it is globally available without per-file imports.

---

### 90. TDD for Vitest `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` with Auto-Update — Snapshot-Driven API Contract Testing [official]

`expect(value).toMatchInlineSnapshot()` (empty parentheses) captures the current serialised value and writes it directly into the test file's source code on the first run. On subsequent runs it compares against the captured string. In TDD, the pattern is: write the test with empty `toMatchInlineSnapshot()`, run in watch mode, observe the captured value in the test file, verify it matches the intended API contract, then commit. The snapshot becomes the living specification of the API response shape. When the API evolves (new field added), the snapshot diff in the PR shows exactly what changed — making API contract regressions visible in code review rather than only in production.

```typescript
// src/api/__tests__/product-api.test.ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { createTestApp } from "../../test/helpers/test-app";

const app = createTestApp();

test("GET /products/:id returns the canonical product shape", async () => {
  const response = await app.inject({
    method: "GET",
    url:    "/products/prod-001",
  });

  // On first run (empty parentheses): Vitest writes the snapshot into this file
  // On subsequent runs: Vitest compares against the written snapshot
  expect(JSON.parse(response.body)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
    {
      "id": "prod-001",
      "name": "Widget Pro",
      "price": {
        "amount": 2999,
        "currency": "USD",
        "formatted": "$29.99",
      },
      "inventory": {
        "available": true,
        "quantity": expect.any(Number),
      },
      "createdAt": expect.any(String),
    }
  `);
});

test("GET /products/:id returns 404 shape for unknown products", async () => {
  const response = await app.inject({ method: "GET", url: "/products/nonexistent" });

  expect(JSON.parse(response.body)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
    {
      "error": "PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND",
      "message": "No product found with ID: nonexistent",
      "statusCode": 404,
    }
  `);
  expect(response.statusCode).toBe(404);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Inline snapshots embed the expected value directly in the test file — when the value is large (a 50-field API response, a deeply nested configuration object), the snapshot makes the test file difficult to read and the diff in code review becomes hard to parse. Limit inline snapshots to the essential contract fields; use `expect.any(Number)` and `expect.any(String)` for volatile or unimportant fields. For large responses, use file-based snapshots (`toMatchSnapshot()`) or a custom snapshot domain (Cycle 46 Pattern 67) that normalises and redacts the response to only the contract-relevant fields before snapshotting. Inline snapshots are ideal for API error shapes and small response objects (under ~20 fields).

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 47 Additions

210. **[community] Vitest Browser Mode tests that use `page.getByRole()` with the `name` option fail when the accessible name is computed from a `title` attribute on an SVG element rather than visible text — Vitest's locator uses the accessibility tree, and SVG `<title>` elements are reported as the accessible name only when the SVG has `role="img"` set explicitly; without the role, screen readers and the accessibility tree expose no name, so `getByRole("img", { name: /logo/ })` returns zero matches.** A developer writes a browser-mode test for a logo SVG, uses `getByRole("img", { name: /company logo/ })`, and finds the locator returns no element despite the SVG having `<title>Company Logo</title>`. WHY this matters: the JSDOM-based test with `@testing-library/dom` may pass because JSDOM's accessibility tree computation differs from the browser's native accessibility API. Fix: add `role="img"` and `aria-label="Company Logo"` to the SVG element directly, then assert `getByRole("img", { name: "Company Logo" })` — this also improves real accessibility for screen reader users.

211. **[community] `vi.mockObject()` does not mock methods inherited from a class prototype that were defined using the class field syntax (`method = () => {}`) — class fields are own properties on the instance, not on the prototype, so `vi.mockObject` correctly finds and mocks them; however, if the same class uses prototype methods for some exports and class fields for others, the developer may incorrectly assume all methods are prototype-based and apply `vi.spyOn(ClassName.prototype, "method")` which fails silently for class-field methods because the prototype does not have that property.** A developer attempts `vi.spyOn(Service.prototype, "fetchData")` on a class that defines `fetchData = async () => {}` as a class field, then finds the spy never records any calls because the spy is installed on the prototype while the instance's own `fetchData` property shadows it. WHY this matters: TypeScript compiles class fields to own properties in all modern targets, making this a widespread gotcha for any class authored in modern TypeScript. Fix: use `vi.spyOn(instance, "fetchData")` after creating the instance, targeting the own property; or use `vi.mockObject(new Service())` which correctly handles both prototype and own-property methods.

212. **[community] `coverage.thresholds.autoUpdate` modifies `vitest.config.ts` in-place using a heuristic AST rewrite that fails to preserve comments inside the `thresholds` block — any `// last auto-updated:` or `// do not edit` comments adjacent to threshold numbers are silently deleted by the autoUpdate rewrite.** A team uses autoUpdate to track when each threshold was last bumped by adding inline comments (`lines: 87, // bumped 2026-04-15`), runs the test suite, and finds all threshold comments have been stripped from the config file after autoUpdate rewrites it. WHY this matters: the team loses the audit trail of threshold progression that the comments were providing. Fix: store threshold progression history in a separate file (e.g., `coverage-history.json` or a CHANGELOG entry) rather than as inline comments in the config, since autoUpdate treats the threshold value as a bare number and discards surrounding comments. Alternatively, use `autoUpdate: false` and a separate script (`vitest --coverage --reporter=json | jq ...`) to extract and commit threshold updates manually.

213. **[community] `test.override()` silently no-ops when called inside a `beforeEach` hook or a `test` callback instead of at the top level of a `describe` block — rather than throwing an error, the override is registered but never applied, so all tests in the block continue using the default fixture values, making the developer believe the fixture is broken when in fact the override was mis-placed.** A developer migrates from the deprecated `test.scoped()` to `test.override()`, places the call inside `beforeEach` following the old mental model of `beforeEach`-based setup, and finds that all tests continue to receive the default fixture values without any error message indicating the override was ignored. WHY this matters: the silent no-op makes diagnosis difficult — the developer inspects the fixture implementation rather than the override placement. Fix: `test.override()` must appear as a bare statement at the top of the `describe` block body, at the same lexical level as `test(...)` and `describe(...)` calls; it cannot be nested inside any callback or hook.

214. **[community] Vitest `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` with `expect.any(Type)` asymmetric matchers inside the snapshot string works correctly when the snapshot is first auto-written by Vitest, but fails with a cryptic "received value does not match stored snapshot" error when the developer hand-edits the snapshot string to add `expect.any(Number)` for a volatile field — Vitest's inline snapshot comparison uses a serialisation round-trip that treats hand-written `expect.any(Number)` as a literal string, not as an asymmetric matcher instance.** A developer auto-generates an inline snapshot containing `"quantity": 42`, then edits it by hand to `"quantity": expect.any(Number)` to handle the volatile count, reruns the tests, and finds the snapshot fails because the comparison sees `expect.any(Number)` as the string `"expect.any(Number)"` rather than invoking the asymmetric matcher. WHY this matters: the auto-generated snapshot format looks similar to the asymmetric-matcher format used in `toMatchObject`, leading developers to assume they are interchangeable. Fix: for volatile fields in inline snapshots, use Vitest's snapshot property matching — call `toMatchObject(expect.objectContaining({ quantity: expect.any(Number) }))` for the volatile fields separately, and `toMatchInlineSnapshot(...)` for the stable structural fields only; do not mix asymmetric matchers into the snapshot string by hand.

### 91. Vitest Pool Selection as a TDD Feedback-Loop Knob [official]

Vitest supports three worker pool strategies — `forks` (default, most compatible), `threads` (faster for CPU-bound suites), and `vmThreads` (true VM isolation per file). During a TDD watch loop the dominant concern is re-run latency for a single changed file. Switching from `forks` to `threads` typically shaves 20–40 % off the per-file startup cost for medium-sized TypeScript projects. `vmThreads` is useful when modules carry module-level side effects that must be isolated, but it cannot be combined with `--no-isolate`, so it is the slowest option.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Switch from default 'forks' to 'threads' for faster TDD watch loop
    pool: "threads",

    // Optional: also disable per-file isolation if your codebase has no
    // module-level side effects — further reduces re-run cost
    isolate: false,

    // Limit max workers to avoid CPU thrashing on a dev laptop
    poolOptions: {
      threads: {
        minThreads: 1,
        maxThreads: 4,
      },
    },

    // During TDD: run only the file under development for fastest feedback
    // vitest watch --reporter=verbose src/domain/cart/cart-service.test.ts
  },
});

// TDD ergonomic tip: define a package.json script per domain area
// so `npm run tdd:cart` runs vitest watch scoped to that directory
// "scripts": {
//   "tdd:cart":    "vitest watch --pool=threads src/domain/cart",
//   "tdd:orders":  "vitest watch --pool=threads src/domain/orders",
//   "test":        "vitest run --pool=threads"
// }
```

**Tradeoff.** `pool: "threads"` uses `node:worker_threads` which shares the same process address space; modules that call `process.exit()` or mutate process globals can corrupt sibling tests. `pool: "forks"` uses `child_process.fork()` and is fully isolated at the OS level but pays the fork cost per file. For a TDD inner loop on a single file the difference is negligible — the isolation cost is amortised across the number of test files being watched. Only switch to `threads` after confirming your test suite has no process-global mutations.

---

### 92. `vi.withImplementation()` — Scoped Mock Override for Branching Logic TDD [official]

When a single test function needs to exercise two code paths that depend on a collaborator returning different values — for example, testing both the cache-hit and cache-miss branches in a single `describe` block — `vi.withImplementation()` provides a scoped override that restores the original mock after the callback returns. This eliminates the risk of a `mockReturnValueOnce` queue being accidentally consumed by the wrong assertion.

```typescript
// src/cache/__tests__/cache-aside.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import { CacheAsideLoader } from "../cache-aside-loader";
import { createFakeCache } from "../../test/fakes/fake-cache";
import { createFakeDataSource } from "../../test/fakes/fake-data-source";

describe("CacheAsideLoader", () => {
  it("returns cached value without hitting the data source on cache hit", async () => {
    const cache = createFakeCache();
    const dataSource = createFakeDataSource();
    const loader = new CacheAsideLoader(cache, dataSource);

    // Permanently mock cache.get to return a hit for this test
    vi.spyOn(cache, "get").mockResolvedValue({ id: "u1", name: "Alice" });

    const result = await loader.load("u1");

    expect(result).toEqual({ id: "u1", name: "Alice" });
    expect(dataSource.fetch).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  it("fetches from data source and populates cache on cache miss", async () => {
    const cache = createFakeCache();
    const dataSource = createFakeDataSource();
    const fetchSpy = vi.spyOn(dataSource, "fetch").mockResolvedValue({ id: "u2", name: "Bob" });
    const setSpy  = vi.spyOn(cache, "set");
    const loader  = new CacheAsideLoader(cache, dataSource);

    // Temporarily override cache.get to return null (miss), then restore
    const result = await vi.withImplementation(
      cache.get as ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>,
      () => Promise.resolve(null),
      async () => loader.load("u2"),
    );

    expect(result).toEqual({ id: "u2", name: "Bob" });
    expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith("u2");
    expect(setSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith("u2", { id: "u2", name: "Bob" });
    // cache.get is now restored to its original implementation
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.withImplementation()` accepts an async callback and awaits it, which means it is safe for async tests. However, if the callback throws, the original mock is still restored — this is the desired behaviour, but developers who rely on the spy being in a dirty state to diagnose a failure will find the post-throw state clean. Log the spy state inside the callback before the assertion when debugging. Also note that `vi.withImplementation()` targets a single mock function object, not an entire module — use `vi.mock()` with a factory for whole-module overrides.

---

### 93. `mock.settledResults` — Asserting Promise Resolution Order in TDD [official]

`MockInstance.mock.settledResults` is a parallel of `mock.results` but accumulates only after all in-flight Promises have resolved or rejected. In TDD scenarios that test retry logic, concurrency limits, or fan-out request aggregation, asserting on `settledResults` gives a deterministic view of every resolved and rejected value in order without needing to manually await each call.

```typescript
// src/infra/__tests__/batch-fetcher.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { BatchFetcher } from "../batch-fetcher";

describe("BatchFetcher", () => {
  let fetchFn: ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    fetchFn = vi.fn();
  });

  it("resolves all items and records results in submission order", async () => {
    // Arrange: set up three sequential responses
    fetchFn
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: 1, status: "ok" })
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: 2, status: "ok" })
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("timeout"));

    const batcher = new BatchFetcher(fetchFn);

    // Act: submit three IDs concurrently
    await batcher.fetchAll([1, 2, 3]);

    // Assert on settled results — typed as { type: 'fulfilled' | 'rejected', value?: T, reason?: unknown }
    expect(fetchFn.mock.settledResults).toHaveLength(3);

    expect(fetchFn.mock.settledResults[0]).toMatchObject({
      type: "fulfilled",
      value: { id: 1, status: "ok" },
    });
    expect(fetchFn.mock.settledResults[1]).toMatchObject({
      type: "fulfilled",
      value: { id: 2, status: "ok" },
    });
    expect(fetchFn.mock.settledResults[2]).toMatchObject({
      type: "rejected",
      reason: expect.objectContaining({ message: "timeout" }),
    });
  });

  it("exposes rejection reasons for partial-failure handling", async () => {
    fetchFn
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("404"))
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: 5 });

    const batcher = new BatchFetcher(fetchFn);
    await batcher.fetchAll([4, 5]);

    const rejections = fetchFn.mock.settledResults.filter(r => r.type === "rejected");
    expect(rejections).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(rejections[0].reason).toBeInstanceOf(Error);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `mock.settledResults` is only populated after the Promises produced by the mock have settled. If your production code never awaits the mock's return value (fire-and-forget), `settledResults` will be empty or partially populated at assertion time. You must ensure the test itself awaits or flushes all pending microtasks (use `await vi.runAllMicrotasksAsync()` or structure your production code to expose a `flush()` method for TDD purposes). Also, `settledResults` is ordered by settlement time, not submission order — for fan-out scenarios with variable latency, use controlled fake timers to determinise settlement order.

---

### 94. Vitest `experimental.fsModuleCache` — Persistent Transformation Cache for TDD Watch Mode [official]

Vitest's `experimental.fsModuleCache` option persists module transformation results (TypeScript transpilation, Vite plugin transforms) to the filesystem between watch-mode restarts. On a cold restart the cache is read from disk rather than recomputed, reducing the time-to-first-test from typically 3–8 s to under 1 s on projects with hundreds of modules. In a TDD workflow where the watch process is restarted frequently (after config changes, after crashes, at the start of each work session) this measurably tightens the Red-Green-Refactor feedback loop.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";
import tsconfigPaths from "vite-tsconfig-paths";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [tsconfigPaths()],
  test: {
    pool: "threads",
    experimental: {
      // Persist transformed modules to .vitest/cache on disk
      // Survives watch restarts; invalidated automatically on file change
      fsModuleCache: true,
    },
    // Pair with a scoped include to avoid caching unrelated test files
    include: ["src/**/*.{test,spec}.{ts,tsx}"],
    exclude: ["node_modules", "dist", "e2e/**"],
  },
});

// .gitignore — add the cache directory (auto-created by Vitest 5.0+)
// .vitest/

// package.json scripts for a TDD session that exploits the cache
// "scripts": {
//   "tdd": "vitest watch --experimental-fsModuleCache",
//   "tdd:warm": "vitest run && vitest watch"   // prime cache then enter watch
// }
```

**Tradeoff.** `fsModuleCache` is experimental and the on-disk format may change between Vitest minor versions, requiring a manual cache bust (`rm -rf .vitest/`). It is not beneficial for single-run CI pipelines (the cache would be cold every time unless the `.vitest/` directory is restored from a CI cache artifact). For local TDD loops on large projects the speed benefit is significant; for small projects with fewer than 50 modules the startup difference is negligible. Cache invalidation is file-content-based, so renaming or moving a module without changing its content may occasionally result in a stale cache entry — run `vitest run --clearCache` if watch mode shows unexpected behaviour after a file rename.

---

### 95. TDD for Discriminated Error Classes with `cause` Chain Verification [community]

TypeScript's `Error` subclassing, combined with the ES2022 `cause` option in the `Error` constructor, enables structured error hierarchies where each layer re-wraps the previous error. TDD-driven error design forces you to define the error contract (class name, `cause` chain, additional fields) in the test before writing the implementation, ensuring that calling code can reliably `instanceof`-check and extract structured error data rather than parsing error message strings.

```typescript
// src/payments/errors.ts (skeleton — TDD drives its shape)
export class PaymentGatewayError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public readonly code: string,
    message: string,
    options?: ErrorOptions,
  ) {
    super(message, options);
    this.name = "PaymentGatewayError";
  }
}

export class NetworkError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string, options?: ErrorOptions) {
    super(message, options);
    this.name = "NetworkError";
  }
}

// src/payments/__tests__/payment-processor.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import { PaymentProcessor }   from "../payment-processor";
import { PaymentGatewayError, NetworkError } from "../errors";
import { createFakeGateway }   from "../../test/fakes/fake-gateway";

describe("PaymentProcessor", () => {
  it("wraps a gateway network failure in PaymentGatewayError preserving the cause", async () => {
    const networkErr = new NetworkError("ECONNREFUSED", { cause: undefined });
    const gateway = createFakeGateway();
    vi.spyOn(gateway, "charge").mockRejectedValue(networkErr);

    const processor = new PaymentProcessor(gateway);

    // RED: define the error contract before implementation exists
    await expect(processor.charge({ amount: 1000, currency: "USD" }))
      .rejects.toSatisfy((err: unknown) => {
        return (
          err instanceof PaymentGatewayError &&
          err.code === "GATEWAY_UNAVAILABLE" &&
          err.cause instanceof NetworkError &&
          err.cause.message === "ECONNREFUSED"
        );
      });
  });

  it("throws PaymentGatewayError with DECLINED code on gateway decline response", async () => {
    const gateway = createFakeGateway();
    vi.spyOn(gateway, "charge").mockResolvedValue({ status: "declined", reason: "insufficient_funds" });

    const processor = new PaymentProcessor(gateway);

    await expect(processor.charge({ amount: 1000, currency: "USD" }))
      .rejects.toMatchObject({
        name:    "PaymentGatewayError",
        code:    "DECLINED",
        message: expect.stringContaining("insufficient_funds"),
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `expect.toSatisfy()` with an inline predicate produces concise Red-phase code but generates poor failure messages — when the assertion fails, Vitest prints `received value did not satisfy the predicate` without showing which property was wrong. For production test suites, replace the `toSatisfy` predicate with a custom domain matcher (see Pattern 89) that produces structured failure output listing which property mismatched. The `cause` chain verification is especially valuable in observability contexts: error monitoring tools (Sentry, Datadog) can traverse the `cause` chain, so TDD-driven error design directly improves production debuggability.

---

### 96. Vitest Test Sharding for CI Parallelism — TDD at Scale [official]

As a TDD codebase grows, the full test suite may take minutes even in parallel. Vitest's built-in `--shard` flag splits the test file list across N machines without any external test orchestrator. Combined with the `--reporter=blob` output and `--merge-reports` consolidation step, the full suite result is reconstructed from shards for a single combined coverage report. In a GitHub Actions matrix job, sharding allows a 400-file test suite to complete in the same time as a 100-file suite on a single runner.

```typescript
// .github/workflows/ci.yml (relevant excerpt)
// strategy:
//   matrix:
//     shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
// steps:
//   - run: npx vitest run --reporter=blob --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
//   - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
//     with:
//       name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shard }}
//       path: .vitest-reports/

// vitest.config.ts — configure blob output directory
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    pool: "threads",
    // Blob reporter emits a binary results file per shard
    // The merge step re-reads all blobs and writes the final HTML/JSON report
    reporters: process.env.CI ? ["blob"] : ["verbose"],
    outputFile: {
      blob: ".vitest-reports/results.blob",
    },
    // Coverage per-shard — merged in the consolidation step
    coverage: {
      enabled:  !!process.env.CI,
      provider: "v8",
      reporter: ["json"],
    },
  },
});

// Merge step (runs after all matrix jobs):
// npx vitest merge-reports .vitest-reports/
// This produces the combined HTML report and final coverage summary
```

**Tradeoff.** Sharding splits by file, not by test case count or estimated duration. A suite with 3 slow integration-test files and 397 fast unit-test files will have highly unbalanced shards — one shard finishes in 30 s while another runs for 5 min. Mitigate by grouping slow tests into a dedicated project (`vitest.config.integration.ts`) and running it as a separate unsharded job. Use `--shard` only for the large pool of fast unit tests where duration variance per file is small. Also, sharding requires each shard to independently resolve modules, so module-level globalSetup work is repeated per shard — ensure `globalSetup` is fast or idempotent.

---

### 97. `vi.mock()` with `importOriginal()` — Partial Module Mock for Minimal Seams [official]

When a module exports five functions and a test only needs to mock one, replacing the entire module with a factory loses the real implementations of the other four and creates maintenance burden when the module evolves. `importOriginal()` inside a `vi.mock()` factory spreads the real module into the mock object so only the targeted export is overridden. This is the canonical "minimal seam" pattern for module mocking in Vitest.

```typescript
// src/analytics/__tests__/event-tracker.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";

// Partially mock the analytics SDK:
// keep real `formatEvent` and `validateEvent`; mock only `sendToEndpoint`
vi.mock("../analytics-sdk", async (importOriginal) => {
  const real = await importOriginal<typeof import("../analytics-sdk")>();
  return {
    ...real,
    // Override only the network call — keep all pure helpers real
    sendToEndpoint: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: 200, ok: true }),
  };
});

import { EventTracker }    from "../event-tracker";
import { sendToEndpoint }  from "../analytics-sdk";

describe("EventTracker", () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it("sends a formatted purchase event to the endpoint", async () => {
    const tracker = new EventTracker({ userId: "u1", sessionId: "s1" });

    await tracker.trackPurchase({ sku: "WIDGET", amount: 2999 });

    expect(sendToEndpoint).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendToEndpoint).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({
        eventType: "purchase",
        userId:    "u1",
        payload:   expect.objectContaining({ sku: "WIDGET", amount: 2999 }),
      }),
    );
  });

  it("does not send the event when the amount is zero (business rule)", async () => {
    const tracker = new EventTracker({ userId: "u2", sessionId: "s2" });
    await tracker.trackPurchase({ sku: "FREEBIE", amount: 0 });
    expect(sendToEndpoint).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `importOriginal()` executes the real module during the mock factory — any module-level side effects (HTTP calls, file reads, `console.warn` output) will fire. If the real module has problematic side effects at module scope, you cannot safely use `importOriginal()`; you must fully replace the module. Also, `vi.mock()` is hoisted to the top of the file by Vitest's Babel/Vite transform, which means the mock factory runs before any `import` statements in the test file. The `importOriginal()` async import inside the factory is the idiomatic way to access the real module from that hoisted position.

---

### 98. Sequential Mock Queues with `mockImplementationOnce` — Testing Retry and Fallback Logic [official]

Production code that retries failed operations, falls back to secondary systems, or consumes items from a queue produces a sequence of calls to the same collaborator with different expected results. Vitest's `mockImplementationOnce()`, `mockReturnValueOnce()`, and `mockRejectedValueOnce()` methods build an ordered queue on the mock — each successive call pops the next queued behaviour. When the queue is exhausted, the mock falls back to its persistent `mockImplementation()` (or returns `undefined` if none is set).

```typescript
// src/resilience/__tests__/retry-fetcher.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { RetryFetcher } from "../retry-fetcher";

describe("RetryFetcher — three-attempt retry with exponential backoff", () => {
  it("succeeds on the third attempt after two transient failures", async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();

    const fetchFn = vi.fn()
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("503 Service Unavailable"))  // attempt 1
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("503 Service Unavailable"))  // attempt 2
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ data: "success" });                  // attempt 3

    const fetcher = new RetryFetcher(fetchFn, {
      maxAttempts: 3,
      baseDelayMs: 100,
    });

    const resultPromise = fetcher.fetch("/api/resource");

    // Advance fake timers through the exponential backoff delays
    await vi.runAllTimersAsync();
    const result = await resultPromise;

    expect(result).toEqual({ data: "success" });
    expect(fetchFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });

  it("throws after exhausting all retry attempts", async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();

    const fetchFn = vi.fn()
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("timeout"))
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("timeout"))
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("timeout"));

    const fetcher = new RetryFetcher(fetchFn, { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 50 });
    const resultPromise = fetcher.fetch("/api/failing");

    await vi.runAllTimersAsync();

    await expect(resultPromise).rejects.toThrow("timeout");
    expect(fetchFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });

  afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());
});
```

**Tradeoff.** A long queue of `mockRejectedValueOnce` + `mockResolvedValueOnce` calls in a single test encodes a specific call sequence in the test setup; if the production code changes the retry count the test fails at the "wrong" call rather than at the assertion, producing a confusing error. Make the queue length match the production retry count explicitly — extract it as a named constant shared between production code and the test. Also, the queue falls through to `mockImplementation()` after exhaustion; forgetting to set a fallback means the fourth call returns `undefined`, which may silently pass assertions that should fail. Explicitly set `.mockRejectedValue(new Error("unexpected extra call"))` as the fallback to catch unexpected over-retrying.

---

### 99. `fileParallelism: false` — Serialised Watch Mode for Startup-Bound TDD Suites [official]

Some test suites spin up expensive process-level resources (a database connection pool, a gRPC server, a browser instance) in `globalSetup`. Running files in parallel causes multiple files to race on those resources, increasing memory pressure and producing flaky tests. `fileParallelism: false` serialises file execution so that at most one test file runs at a time, eliminating the contention. This is a deliberate trade of throughput for determinism — valuable in a TDD loop where determinism outweighs raw speed.

```typescript
// vitest.config.integration.ts — separate config for resource-heavy integration tests
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    include: ["src/**/*.integration.test.ts"],

    // Run integration test files one at a time to avoid resource contention
    fileParallelism: false,

    // Use forks pool so each file gets a fresh child process
    pool: "forks",

    // Allow more time per test — integration tests are inherently slower
    testTimeout: 30_000,
    hookTimeout: 30_000,

    globalSetup: ["./test/global-setup-integration.ts"],
    setupFiles: ["./test/setup-integration.ts"],

    // Verbose reporter helps locate the slow file when running serially
    reporters: ["verbose"],
  },
});

// package.json
// "test:integration": "vitest run --config vitest.config.integration.ts"
// "tdd:integration":  "vitest watch --config vitest.config.integration.ts --fileParallelism=false"
```

**Tradeoff.** `fileParallelism: false` makes total suite duration proportional to the sum of file durations rather than the maximum. A 20-file integration suite where each file takes 5 s will now complete in ~100 s instead of ~10 s on a 4-core machine. Only apply `fileParallelism: false` to the integration project; keep the unit-test project parallel. Profile first: if your integration suite already runs in a single file or the shared resource is stateless and supports concurrent connections, the contention may not exist and parallelism is safe.

---

### 100. `vi.stubEnv()` and `vi.stubGlobal()` — Deterministic Environment in TDD [official]

Tests that depend on environment variables or global browser/Node APIs are vulnerable to the CI environment's actual values, making test results non-deterministic across machines. `vi.stubEnv()` overrides a specific `process.env` key and restores it automatically when `unstubAllEnvs()` is called (or automatically per test if `unstubEnvs: true` is set in config). `vi.stubGlobal()` does the same for global objects. Both methods enable Red-phase tests to assert on code that reads environment configuration without modifying the real environment.

```typescript
// src/config/__tests__/app-config.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from "vitest";
import { loadAppConfig } from "../app-config";

// Auto-restore all environment stubs after each test
afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllEnvs();
  vi.unstubAllGlobals();
});

describe("loadAppConfig", () => {
  it("reads the API base URL from APP_API_URL env var", () => {
    vi.stubEnv("APP_API_URL", "https://api.staging.example.com");
    vi.stubEnv("NODE_ENV", "production");

    const config = loadAppConfig();

    expect(config.apiBaseUrl).toBe("https://api.staging.example.com");
    expect(config.isProduction).toBe(true);
  });

  it("falls back to localhost when APP_API_URL is not set", () => {
    // Ensure the var is absent — stubEnv with undefined removes it
    vi.stubEnv("APP_API_URL", undefined as unknown as string);
    vi.stubEnv("NODE_ENV", "development");

    const config = loadAppConfig();

    expect(config.apiBaseUrl).toBe("http://localhost:3000");
    expect(config.isProduction).toBe(false);
  });

  it("reads feature flags from a global __FEATURE_FLAGS__ object", () => {
    vi.stubGlobal("__FEATURE_FLAGS__", {
      newCheckoutFlow: true,
      darkMode:        false,
    });

    const config = loadAppConfig();

    expect(config.features.newCheckoutFlow).toBe(true);
    expect(config.features.darkMode).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.stubEnv()` calls `process.env[key] = value` internally; it does not fork the environment. If tested code caches `process.env.SOME_KEY` in a module-level `const` at import time, stubbing after import has no effect — the cached value is used instead. TDD forces you to discover this anti-pattern in the Red phase (the test fails even after stubbing). Fix: always read environment variables lazily inside functions, not at module scope. The `unstubAllEnvs()` call in `afterEach` is critical — if it is omitted, a stub set in one test leaks into all subsequent tests in the same worker, producing order-dependent failures that are extremely hard to diagnose.

---

### 101. `resolve.alias` Test Seams — Fake-by-Default Infrastructure Injection [community]

Path aliases (`@/`, `#/`, `~/`) configured in `tsconfig.json` must be mirrored in Vitest's `resolve.alias` (or via the `vite-tsconfig-paths` plugin) or the test runner will fail with `Cannot find module '@/...'`. In TDD the alias is also a seam: you can remap a path alias in test config to point to a fake/stub module for an entire project without touching individual test files, enabling a "fake-by-default" injection strategy for infrastructure modules.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — mirror tsconfig paths AND add test-seam aliases
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";
import { resolve }      from "path";

export default defineConfig({
  resolve: {
    alias: {
      // Mirror tsconfig.json paths
      "@/": resolve(__dirname, "src/"),

      // In test environment only: remap the email transport to an in-memory fake
      // This ensures no test accidentally sends a real email
      "@/infra/email-transport": resolve(__dirname, "src/test/fakes/fake-email-transport.ts"),

      // Remap the payment gateway to a controllable fake
      "@/infra/payment-gateway": resolve(__dirname, "src/test/fakes/fake-payment-gateway.ts"),
    },
  },
  test: {
    include: ["src/**/*.test.ts"],
    // Override the alias for integration tests that need the real transport
    // Use a separate vitest.config.integration.ts with alias overrides
  },
});

// src/test/fakes/fake-email-transport.ts
// Implements the same interface as the real EmailTransport
// but stores sent messages in memory for assertion
export class FakeEmailTransport {
  public sent: Array<{ to: string; subject: string; body: string }> = [];

  async send(options: { to: string; subject: string; body: string }): Promise<void> {
    this.sent.push(options);
  }

  lastEmailTo(address: string) {
    return this.sent.filter(e => e.to === address).at(-1);
  }
}

export const emailTransport = new FakeEmailTransport();
```

**Tradeoff.** Global alias remapping applies to every test file in the project. If some tests need the real implementation (e.g., an integration test that verifies the actual email SMTP handshake), a single `vitest.config.ts` alias override is too coarse. Use a second Vitest config file for integration tests with different alias mappings. Also, `vite-tsconfig-paths` auto-reads paths from `tsconfig.json` but does not support the test-seam override pattern above — for test-seam aliases, use `resolve.alias` in `vitest.config.ts` directly and remove `vite-tsconfig-paths` from the test config.

---

### 102. TDD with `test.todo()` as a Design Placeholder — Backlog-Driven Red Phase [official]

`test.todo("description")` marks a test as intentionally unwritten — it appears in the Vitest output as a pending item with a distinct symbol, is counted in the suite summary, and never fails. In a TDD workflow, `test.todo()` externalises the backlog of known test cases at design time: during API design you enumerate all the cases you intend to test (error paths, boundary conditions, happy paths) as `test.todo()` entries before writing any code. This makes the scope of the implementation explicit, prevents scope creep, and gives the team a visible indicator of incomplete specification.

```typescript
// src/auth/__tests__/token-validator.test.ts
// Written at design time — before any production code exists
import { describe, it, expect, test } from "vitest";
import { validateToken } from "../token-validator";

describe("validateToken", () => {
  // ------ Implemented cases ------
  it("returns { valid: true, userId } for a well-formed unexpired JWT", () => {
    const result = validateToken("eyJ...valid.token");
    expect(result).toMatchObject({ valid: true, userId: "u1" });
  });

  // ------ Backlog: known cases to implement next (drive the next Red-Green cycle) ------
  test.todo("returns { valid: false, reason: 'expired' } for an expired token");
  test.todo("returns { valid: false, reason: 'malformed' } for a non-JWT string");
  test.todo("returns { valid: false, reason: 'wrong-audience' } when aud claim does not match");
  test.todo("returns { valid: false, reason: 'algorithm-mismatch' } for RS256 when HS256 expected");
  test.todo("throws InvalidKeyError when the JWKS endpoint is unreachable");
  test.todo("caches JWKS keys and does not refetch within the TTL");
  test.todo("refetches JWKS keys after the TTL expires");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.todo()` does not accept a test callback — if you accidentally pass one (i.e., write `test.todo("desc", () => {...})`), Vitest ignores the callback silently. Use `test.skip("desc", () => {...})` when you want to write the test body but temporarily skip it; use `test.todo("desc")` only for genuinely unwritten tests. In CI, `test.todo()` entries do not cause the suite to fail, which means a team can accumulate an unbounded backlog of todos without any pipeline pressure. Set a policy: `test.todo()` entries must be converted to real tests before a feature branch is merged, enforced by a lint rule (`no-test-todo` custom ESLint rule) or a CI step that counts todos and fails above a threshold.

---

### 103. Vitest `.concurrent` Tests with `context.expect` — Parallel Case Execution Without Assertion Pollution [official]

By default, using the module-level `expect` inside a `test.concurrent()` callback can attribute assertion failures to the wrong test in the report because concurrent tests share the module-level `expect` context. The fix is to destructure `expect` from the test context (first argument), which gives each concurrent test its own reporter-linked assertion instance. This pattern is valuable in TDD when you have a matrix of independent, data-driven cases that can validly execute in parallel.

```typescript
// src/pricing/__tests__/discount-calculator.concurrent.test.ts
import { describe, test } from "vitest";
import { calculateDiscount } from "../discount-calculator";

// All cases run in parallel — each gets its own context.expect
describe("calculateDiscount — concurrent case matrix", () => {
  test.concurrent("applies 10% discount for SILVER tier", async ({ expect }) => {
    const result = calculateDiscount({ price: 100, tier: "SILVER" });
    expect(result).toBe(90);
  });

  test.concurrent("applies 20% discount for GOLD tier", async ({ expect }) => {
    const result = calculateDiscount({ price: 100, tier: "GOLD" });
    expect(result).toBe(80);
  });

  test.concurrent("applies 30% discount for PLATINUM tier", async ({ expect }) => {
    const result = calculateDiscount({ price: 100, tier: "PLATINUM" });
    expect(result).toBe(70);
  });

  test.concurrent("returns original price for unknown tier", async ({ expect }) => {
    const result = calculateDiscount({ price: 100, tier: "UNKNOWN" as any });
    expect(result).toBe(100);
  });

  test.concurrent("handles zero price correctly", async ({ expect }) => {
    const result = calculateDiscount({ price: 0, tier: "GOLD" });
    expect(result).toBe(0);
  });

  test.concurrent("floors sub-cent results to avoid floating-point drift", async ({ expect }) => {
    const result = calculateDiscount({ price: 1, tier: "SILVER" });
    expect(result).toBe(0.9);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.concurrent` parallelises within the same worker thread (Promises, not OS threads), so CPU-bound computations do not actually speed up — only I/O-bound and async-sleeping tests benefit from concurrency. For pure synchronous functions like `calculateDiscount` above, the concurrent form produces no speed benefit; it just demonstrates the pattern. Use `test.concurrent` for cases that have async I/O (DB queries, HTTP calls to fakes) or that call `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()`. Also, `test.concurrent` inside a `describe.concurrent` block makes all tests in the block concurrent; use `test.concurrent` selectively inside a regular `describe` to opt individual cases in.

---

### 104. `mock.invocationCallOrder` — Asserting Cross-Mock Execution Sequence [official]

`mock.invocationCallOrder` is a numeric array where each element is a monotonically increasing global call counter. When two mocks are called during the same test, comparing their `invocationCallOrder` values tells you which mock was called first, enabling strict ordering assertions. This is essential for TDD of event-sourced systems, middleware pipelines, and observer chains where the sequence of side effects is part of the contract.

```typescript
// src/middleware/__tests__/pipeline.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import { createMiddlewarePipeline } from "../middleware-pipeline";

describe("MiddlewarePipeline — execution order", () => {
  it("executes middleware in registration order before the handler", async () => {
    const authMiddleware      = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    const loggingMiddleware   = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    const rateLimitMiddleware = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    const handler             = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: 200 });

    const pipeline = createMiddlewarePipeline()
      .use(authMiddleware)
      .use(loggingMiddleware)
      .use(rateLimitMiddleware)
      .handle(handler);

    await pipeline.execute({ method: "GET", path: "/api/users" });

    // Assert each ran exactly once
    expect(authMiddleware).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(loggingMiddleware).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(rateLimitMiddleware).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(handler).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();

    // Assert strict execution sequence via global invocation counters
    const [authOrder]    = authMiddleware.mock.invocationCallOrder;
    const [logOrder]     = loggingMiddleware.mock.invocationCallOrder;
    const [rateOrder]    = rateLimitMiddleware.mock.invocationCallOrder;
    const [handlerOrder] = handler.mock.invocationCallOrder;

    expect(authOrder).toBeLessThan(logOrder);
    expect(logOrder).toBeLessThan(rateOrder);
    expect(rateOrder).toBeLessThan(handlerOrder);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `invocationCallOrder` values are global within the Vitest worker, not local to the test. They reset between test files but not between tests within the same file unless you call `vi.clearAllMocks()` in `beforeEach`. If you forget to clear, the absolute counter values drift, making assertions like `expect(authOrder).toBe(1)` fragile. Always assert relative ordering (`authOrder < logOrder`) rather than absolute values. For complex pipelines with branching, combine `invocationCallOrder` with `mock.calls` argument inspection to verify that each middleware received the same request context object (reference equality via `toBe`).

---

### 105. TDD for Module-Level Class Fields vs Prototype Methods — Spy Placement Discipline [community]

TypeScript compiles class field syntax (`method = () => {}`) to own-property assignments in the constructor, not to prototype methods. This means `vi.spyOn(MyClass.prototype, "method")` silently fails (the spy is placed on the prototype but the instance's own property shadows it), and `vi.spyOn(instance, "method")` is the correct target. TDD forces this discovery in the Red phase when the spy records zero calls despite the method clearly being invoked. Writing the test first and watching it fail for this reason produces a concrete learning moment that prevents the prototype-spy anti-pattern from propagating.

```typescript
// src/notifications/notification-service.ts
export class NotificationService {
  // Class field syntax — compiled to own property, NOT on prototype
  send = async (message: string, recipient: string): Promise<void> => {
    await fetch("/api/notify", {
      method: "POST",
      body:   JSON.stringify({ message, recipient }),
    });
  };

  // Prototype method syntax — available on NotificationService.prototype
  formatMessage(template: string, vars: Record<string, string>): string {
    return template.replace(/\{\{(\w+)\}\}/g, (_, k) => vars[k] ?? "");
  }
}

// src/notifications/__tests__/notification-service.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { NotificationService } from "../notification-service";

describe("NotificationService", () => {
  let service: NotificationService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    service = new NotificationService();
  });

  it("calls send with formatted message on notifyUser()", async () => {
    // CORRECT: spy on the instance's own 'send' property (class field)
    const sendSpy = vi.spyOn(service, "send").mockResolvedValue(undefined);

    // WRONG (silently fails): vi.spyOn(NotificationService.prototype, "send")
    // because 'send' is an own property on each instance, not on the prototype

    await service.notifyUser("u1", "Hello {{name}}!", { name: "Alice" });

    expect(sendSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith("Hello Alice!", "u1");
  });

  it("formats the message using prototype method — spy on prototype is correct here", () => {
    // CORRECT: formatMessage IS on the prototype
    const formatSpy = vi.spyOn(NotificationService.prototype, "formatMessage");

    service.formatMessage("Hi {{name}}", { name: "Bob" });

    expect(formatSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith("Hi {{name}}", { name: "Bob" });
    formatSpy.mockRestore();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The correct spy placement depends on whether the method is a class field or a prototype method — information that requires reading the class definition. In large codebases with inconsistent conventions (some classes use fields, some use prototype methods), developers spend time diagnosing "spy called 0 times" failures. Standardise on one convention per layer: prefer prototype methods for service classes (spyable on the prototype) and class fields only for React event handler callbacks (where the `this` binding behaviour of class fields is genuinely useful). Document the convention in your coding standards and enforce it with an ESLint rule (`class-methods-use-this` or a custom rule).

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 48 Additions

215. **[community] Vitest `pool: "threads"` causes intermittent test failures when test code uses `process.chdir()` or mutations to `process.env` without cleanup — worker threads share the `process` object across all test files running in the same thread, so a `process.chdir()` call in file A's `afterAll` that fails to restore the original directory leaves the working directory wrong for file B, causing `fs.readFileSync("./fixtures/data.json")` calls in file B to throw `ENOENT` with no obvious connection to file A.** The failures are intermittent because the file execution order within a thread depends on module load timing. WHY this matters: switching from `pool: "forks"` (the default) to `pool: "threads"` for performance exposes latent process-mutation bugs that `forks` hides through OS-level isolation; a team that adds `pool: "threads"` and sees new intermittent CI failures should look for `process.chdir`, `process.env` mutations without cleanup, and global object mutations in `afterAll` hooks. Fix: restore all process mutations in `afterAll`, use `vi.stubEnv()` for env variables (which auto-restores), and never use `process.chdir()` in tests — construct absolute paths instead.

216. **[community] `vi.mock()` factory functions that use `async/await` inside the factory cause the module mock to be applied after the first import of the mocked module completes when using static `import` statements at the top of the test file — the async factory is awaited lazily, so the first `import` resolves against the un-mocked real module, and only subsequent dynamic `import()` calls within the test body receive the mocked version.** A developer writes `vi.mock("./db", async () => ({ connect: vi.fn() }))` and then imports `db` at the top of the file with a static `import`, finds that `db.connect` is the real function (not a mock), and concludes vi.mock is broken. WHY this matters: `vi.mock()` is hoisted to the top of the file by Vitest's Vite transform, but an async factory cannot synchronously resolve the mock before the static imports are processed. Fix: use a synchronous factory whenever possible (`vi.mock("./db", () => ({ connect: vi.fn() }))`), or use `vi.doMock()` (not hoisted) combined with `await import()` inside the test body to control exactly when the mocked version is loaded.

217. **[community] Vitest's `coverage.thresholds` checks run after the test suite finishes and emit a non-zero exit code when thresholds are not met, but the exit code is `1` for both test failures and threshold failures — CI systems that gate on exit code alone cannot distinguish "tests failed" from "coverage fell below threshold", causing coverage threshold violations to appear as test failures in the CI dashboard with no actionable test output.** A team sets `coverage.thresholds.lines: 90` and a developer's PR drops line coverage to 88 %; the CI job fails with exit code 1, the dashboard shows "X tests failed", and the developer investigates test failures that do not exist. WHY this matters: the misleading dashboard entry wastes investigation time and erodes trust in the CI signal. Fix: run coverage in a separate CI step (`vitest run --coverage`) from the test step (`vitest run`) so that the two failure modes produce failures in different named jobs; the coverage job's failure message will clearly include the threshold text ("Coverage for lines (88%) does not meet global threshold (90%)") visible in the job log without confusion with test failures.

218. **[community] `test.todo()` accepts only a string description and no callback — if a developer writes `test.todo("should handle X", async () => { expect... })`, Vitest silently drops the callback and marks the test as todo rather than running it, producing a false sense that the test is pending when it is actually never executed and the implementation it was meant to verify ships untested.** A developer prototypes a test, marks it `test.todo()` intending to "come back to it", accidentally leaves the callback in place, and the CI suite passes with the todo counted as pending — the production code path the callback would have caught is never tested. WHY this matters: the silent callback drop is indistinguishable from an intentional `test.todo()` with no body, so code review is the only safeguard. Fix: use `test.skip("desc", async () => {...})` when the test has a body and you want to temporarily disable it (Vitest will warn on skipped tests); reserve `test.todo("desc")` for genuinely unwritten tests with no body.

219. **[community] `mock.invocationCallOrder` values are global across the entire test file for the duration of the worker's lifetime — calling `vi.clearAllMocks()` in `beforeEach` resets `mock.calls` and `mock.results` but does NOT reset `invocationCallOrder`, so the counter continues monotonically increasing across every test in the file; any test that asserts `invocationCallOrder[0] === 1` (assuming it is the first call in the whole file) will pass only in the first test and fail in all subsequent tests.** A developer adds a guard assertion `expect(authMiddleware.mock.invocationCallOrder[0]).toBe(1)` to verify the middleware was the very first thing called, finds it passes when the test runs alone but fails when the full file runs. WHY this matters: the failure is invisible in `--watch` when you run only the single file after a change, but breaks in CI where the full suite runs. Fix: always assert relative ordering between mocks (`expect(aOrder).toBeLessThan(bOrder)`) rather than absolute values; if you need absolute-value assertions, create the mock inside the test body (not in `beforeEach`) so the counter is at least consistent within the test even if not equal to 1.
