### 136. Partial Module Mock with `importOriginal` — Override Only What You Need [official]

When `vi.mock()` provides a factory, every export that is not explicitly returned from the factory becomes `undefined` in the test. The correct pattern for partial module mocks is to call `vi.importActual` (or use the `importOriginal` parameter available in the factory signature) to spread the real module exports and override only the target function. This preserves utility exports, type guards, and constants that the code under test depends on, preventing cryptic `TypeError: X is not a function` failures caused by silently undefined exports.

```typescript
// src/services/__tests__/order-service.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { processOrder } from "../order-service";

// importOriginal preserves all real exports; only generateOrderId is replaced
vi.mock("../order-utils", async (importOriginal) => {
  const real = await importOriginal<typeof import("../order-utils")>();
  return {
    ...real,
    generateOrderId: vi.fn().mockReturnValue("ORDER-TEST-001"),
  };
});

describe("processOrder", () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it("uses the generated order ID in the persisted record", async () => {
    const result = await processOrder({ productId: "P1", quantity: 2 });
    expect(result.orderId).toBe("ORDER-TEST-001");
  });

  it("still validates order quantity via real validateOrderQuantity", async () => {
    // Real validateOrderQuantity (not mocked) should reject quantity 0
    await expect(processOrder({ productId: "P1", quantity: 0 })).rejects.toThrow("Invalid quantity");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `importOriginal` makes the test correctly isolated at the function level rather than the module level, but the test now depends on the real implementations of all non-overridden exports. If those real exports have side effects (e.g., initiating a DB connection on import), they will execute. The escape hatch is to mock those side-effectful paths explicitly, or to separate them into their own modules so that the utility module being partially mocked has no import-time side effects.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 137. `vi.hoisted()` — Lift Mock State Above Module Hoisting [official]

Vitest's `vi.mock()` call is syntactically hoisted to the top of the compiled file by the transform pipeline, above all `import` and `const` declarations. Any variable declared at module scope is not yet assigned when the mock factory executes — it captures the temporal dead zone value (`undefined`). `vi.hoisted()` accepts a factory function that runs at the same hoisted position as `vi.mock()`, allowing mock functions to be created before the factory runs and then referenced both inside the factory and in test assertions.

```typescript
// src/auth/__tests__/token-refresh.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";

// vi.hoisted lifts these declarations to run before vi.mock factories
const { mockRefresh, mockRevoke } = vi.hoisted(() => ({
  mockRefresh: vi.fn<() => Promise<string>>(),
  mockRevoke: vi.fn<() => Promise<void>>(),
}));

vi.mock("../token-client", () => ({
  TokenClient: vi.fn().mockImplementation(() => ({
    refresh: mockRefresh,
    revoke: mockRevoke,
  })),
}));

import { ensureValidToken } from "../token-refresh";

describe("ensureValidToken", () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
    mockRefresh.mockResolvedValue("new-access-token-abc123");
  });

  it("refreshes expired tokens and returns the new token", async () => {
    const result = await ensureValidToken({ token: "expired", expiresAt: 0 });
    expect(mockRefresh).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(result).toBe("new-access-token-abc123");
  });

  it("does not refresh valid tokens", async () => {
    const future = Date.now() + 60_000;
    const result = await ensureValidToken({ token: "valid", expiresAt: future });
    expect(mockRefresh).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
    expect(result).toBe("valid");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.hoisted()` solves a real hoisting problem that is otherwise confusing and produces no useful error message. The downside is that it is a Vitest-specific API with no Jest equivalent — migrating test files that use it to Jest requires refactoring to inline `jest.fn()` declarations inside `jest.mock()` factory closures. Treat `vi.hoisted()` as the idiomatic Vitest pattern and document the hoisting reason in a comment so future maintainers understand why the unusual structure exists.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 138. Coverage Thresholds as TDD Contracts — Enforce Minimum Confidence Levels [official]

Jest and Vitest both support per-directory and per-file coverage thresholds that fail the test run when coverage drops below a specified percentage. In a TDD workflow, thresholds function as executable team contracts: they prevent new production code from being merged without a corresponding test that exercises it. The power of per-directory thresholds is that business-critical modules (payment processing, authentication) can have higher thresholds (90%+) than lower-risk infrastructure glue code (50%+).

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      // Global minimum: CI fails if any dimension drops below these values
      thresholds: {
        statements: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 80,
        lines: 80,
        // Per-module overrides for high-criticality code
        "src/payments/**": {
          statements: 95,
          branches: 90,
          functions: 95,
          lines: 95,
        },
        "src/auth/**": {
          statements: 90,
          branches: 85,
          functions: 90,
          lines: 90,
        },
        // Lower threshold for generated/boilerplate code
        "src/generated/**": {
          statements: 30,
          branches: 20,
          functions: 30,
          lines: 30,
        },
      },
      // Ensure uncovered files (never imported by tests) still appear in report
      include: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"],
      exclude: ["src/**/*.d.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts", "src/**/index.ts"],
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Thresholds create a forcing function for TDD discipline, but they incentivise writing tests that merely execute code paths (raising line coverage) rather than tests that assert meaningful behaviour (which is what TDD actually produces). A test that calls a function and asserts nothing still raises coverage to 100%. Pair thresholds with mutation testing (Stryker) to distinguish coverage-driven tests from behaviour-asserting tests — mutation scores expose tests that visit code without verifying its output.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 139. Inline Snapshot TDD — Specification as Living Documentation [official]

`toMatchInlineSnapshot()` embeds the serialised expected output directly in the test source file, next to the assertion. In a TDD workflow, this pattern works in reverse from the usual "write assertion, see failure, write code" loop: write the test with an empty snapshot argument (`toMatchInlineSnapshot()`), run the test once in update mode (Vitest writes the snapshot into the source file), inspect the written snapshot as the specification, then refactor the production code knowing the snapshot acts as a regression guard. This is particularly useful for serialisers, formatters, and API response shapers.

```typescript
// src/formatters/__tests__/invoice-formatter.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { formatInvoice } from "../invoice-formatter";

describe("formatInvoice", () => {
  it("formats a standard invoice with line items and totals", () => {
    const invoice = {
      id: "INV-2026-001",
      customer: "Acme Corp",
      items: [
        { description: "Widget A", qty: 10, unitPrice: 9.99 },
        { description: "Widget B", qty: 5, unitPrice: 24.99 },
      ],
      taxRate: 0.2,
    };

    // On first run with no argument, Vitest writes the output here
    expect(formatInvoice(invoice)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
      "INV-2026-001 | Acme Corp
      ─────────────────────────
      Widget A       10 × £9.99   = £99.90
      Widget B        5 × £24.99  = £124.95
      ─────────────────────────
      Subtotal:  £224.85
      Tax (20%):  £44.97
      Total:     £269.82"
    `);
  });

  it("renders a zero-item invoice without crashing", () => {
    const empty = { id: "INV-2026-002", customer: "Test", items: [], taxRate: 0 };
    expect(formatInvoice(empty)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
      "INV-2026-002 | Test
      ─────────────────────────
      (no items)
      ─────────────────────────
      Subtotal:  £0.00
      Tax (0%):   £0.00
      Total:      £0.00"
    `);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Inline snapshots keep the expected value visible without jumping to a separate `__snapshots__` file, which is excellent for review in PRs — reviewers can see both the test intent and the expected output in a single diff hunk. The downside is that inline snapshots bloat test files for complex outputs (multi-KB JSON). Use inline snapshots for human-readable formatted output (text, small JSON objects, HTML snippets) and file-based snapshots (`toMatchFileSnapshot`) for large or binary serialisations. Never use snapshots as a substitute for specific behavioural assertions — they test output stability, not semantic correctness.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 140. Consumer-Driven Contract Testing with Pact — TDD for Distributed System Boundaries [community]

Consumer-Driven Contract (CDC) testing applies the TDD principle to inter-service contracts: the consumer team writes tests expressing what they expect from a provider API, those expectations are packaged as a machine-readable "pact" contract file, and the provider team runs its own test suite against the pact to verify compliance. In a TDD workflow, the consumer writes the contract before the provider endpoint exists (Red), the provider implements the endpoint to satisfy the contract (Green), and both teams refactor independently without breaking the contract (Refactor).

```typescript
// consumer/src/__tests__/product-api.pact.test.ts
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from "@pact-foundation/pact";
import { ProductApiClient } from "../product-api-client";
import path from "path";

const { like, eachLike } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: "checkout-service",
  provider: "product-catalog-service",
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), "pacts"),
});

describe("ProductApiClient — pact contract", () => {
  it("GET /products/:id returns a product with required fields", async () => {
    await provider
      .given("product P1 exists")
      .uponReceiving("a request for product P1")
      .withRequest({ method: "GET", path: "/products/P1" })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: {
          id: like("P1"),
          name: like("Widget"),
          priceCents: like(999),
          inStock: like(true),
          categories: eachLike("electronics"),
        },
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const client = new ProductApiClient(mockServer.url);
        const product = await client.getProduct("P1");
        expect(product.id).toBe("P1");
        expect(typeof product.priceCents).toBe("number");
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** CDC testing via Pact requires both teams to adopt the Pact toolchain and a shared broker (Pact Broker or PactFlow) for contract storage and provider verification. This infrastructure overhead is significant for small teams or monorepos where the "services" are collocated. The payoff is massive for genuinely distributed microservice architectures where a breaking API change previously required a full integration environment to detect. For monorepos, consider using shared TypeScript interface types enforced by `satisfies` as a lighter-weight contract mechanism before adopting a full Pact workflow.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### 141. Sociable Unit Tests — Testing Clusters of Collaborating Units [community]

The solitary/sociable distinction (from Martin Fowler's practical test pyramid) determines whether collaborating classes are mocked or used for real. Solitary unit tests mock all collaborators; sociable unit tests use real implementations for in-process collaborators and only mock at infrastructure boundaries (databases, HTTP, file system). In a TDD workflow, sociable tests drive the design of the collaboration contracts between units without requiring a full integration environment — they are faster than integration tests but verify more realistic interaction patterns than solitary mocks.

```typescript
// src/checkout/__tests__/checkout-flow.sociable.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { CheckoutOrchestrator } from "../checkout-orchestrator";
import { CartService } from "../../cart/cart-service"; // REAL — in-process collaborator
import { PricingEngine } from "../../pricing/pricing-engine"; // REAL — pure business logic
import { OrderRepository } from "../order-repository"; // MOCKED — infrastructure boundary

// Only mock the infrastructure boundary, not in-process business logic
vi.mock("../order-repository");

describe("CheckoutOrchestrator — sociable test", () => {
  let orchestrator: CheckoutOrchestrator;
  let mockRepo: ReturnType<typeof vi.mocked<OrderRepository>>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    const cart = new CartService(); // Real CartService
    const pricing = new PricingEngine(); // Real PricingEngine
    mockRepo = vi.mocked(new OrderRepository());
    mockRepo.save.mockResolvedValue({ orderId: "ORD-001" });

    orchestrator = new CheckoutOrchestrator(cart, pricing, mockRepo);
  });

  it("calculates the correct total including applied discount codes", async () => {
    const result = await orchestrator.checkout({
      items: [{ productId: "P1", qty: 2, unitPrice: 50_00 }],
      discountCode: "SAVE10",
    });

    // Real PricingEngine and CartService ran; only repo was mocked
    expect(result.totalCents).toBe(90_00); // 100.00 - 10%
    expect(mockRepo.save).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ totalCents: 90_00 })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Sociable tests provide stronger confidence than solitary tests because they exercise the real interaction between collaborating classes, surfacing integration bugs that mocks hide (e.g., a CartService that returns items in a different order than PricingEngine expects). The cost is that a failure in a sociable test can be caused by any of the real collaborators, making diagnosis slower. Use sociable tests to specify the observable output of a cluster of classes; use solitary unit tests to specify each class's individual contract with its mocked collaborators.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### 142. `moduleNameMapper` Path Alias Resolution — Eliminating `../../../../` in Test Imports [official]

Jest's `moduleNameMapper` and Vitest's `resolve.alias` both map path alias prefixes (e.g., `@/`, `#/`) to absolute directories. Configuring these in the test tool to match the TypeScript compiler's `paths` configuration eliminates fragile relative import chains in test files, makes module refactoring cheaper (only the alias target changes, not every import), and ensures the test execution environment resolves modules identically to the TypeScript compiler. Mismatches between `paths` and `moduleNameMapper` are a common source of `Cannot find module` errors that only manifest in tests, not in TypeScript compilation.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — alias configuration matching tsconfig.json paths
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";
import path from "path";

export default defineConfig({
  resolve: {
    alias: {
      "@": path.resolve(__dirname, "src"),
      "@shared": path.resolve(__dirname, "src/shared"),
      "@testing": path.resolve(__dirname, "src/__test-utils__"),
    },
  },
  test: {
    environment: "node",
  },
});

// tsconfig.json must match exactly:
// "paths": {
//   "@/*": ["src/*"],
//   "@shared/*": ["src/shared/*"],
//   "@testing/*": ["src/__test-utils__/*"]
// }

// Usage in test files — clean, refactor-safe imports
// import { createTestUser } from "@testing/factories/user";
// import { validateEmail } from "@shared/validators/email";
// instead of: import { createTestUser } from "../../../__test-utils__/factories/user";
```

**Tradeoff.** Alias configuration in `vitest.config.ts` (or `jest.config.ts`) must be kept manually in sync with `tsconfig.json` `paths`. TypeScript 6.0 deprecated `baseUrl` as a path resolution mechanism, meaning projects must now use `paths` or `#/` subpath imports (Node.js package.json `imports` field) instead. For new TypeScript 6.0+ projects, prefer `#/` subpath imports over `@/` aliases — they are resolved natively by Node.js and TypeScript without any configuration duplication between `tsconfig.json` and the test runner config.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 143. `globalSetup` + `inject` — Sharing Expensive Setup Across Test Worker Processes [official]

Vitest's `globalSetup` module runs once per test run in the main process, making it the correct place for expensive one-time setup (starting a test database, launching a mock HTTP server). Values produced by `globalSetup` can be passed to test workers via its return value and consumed in tests via the `inject()` function (Vitest 1.3+). This replaces the fragile `process.env` mutation pattern and avoids the `test.runIf()` evaluation-order bug where env vars set in `globalSetup` are not visible at module-parse time in test workers.

```typescript
// test/global-setup.ts
import { startTestDatabase } from "./test-db";

export async function setup() {
  const db = await startTestDatabase();
  // Return value is serialised and available via inject() in test files
  return {
    databaseUrl: db.connectionString,
    databasePort: db.port,
  };
}

export async function teardown() {
  await stopTestDatabase();
}

// vitest.config.ts
// test: { globalSetup: ["./test/global-setup.ts"] }

// src/users/__tests__/user-repository.integration.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll } from "vitest";
import { inject } from "vitest";
import { createUserRepository } from "../user-repository";

describe("UserRepository — integration", () => {
  let repo: ReturnType<typeof createUserRepository>;

  beforeAll(() => {
    const dbUrl = inject("databaseUrl"); // Typed via GlobalSetupContext augmentation
    repo = createUserRepository(dbUrl);
  });

  it("persists and retrieves a user by email", async () => {
    const user = await repo.create({ email: "test@example.com", name: "Test" });
    const fetched = await repo.findByEmail("test@example.com");
    expect(fetched?.id).toBe(user.id);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `globalSetup` runs in a separate process from test workers, which means the setup function cannot share in-memory state (class instances, mock objects) with test files — only serialisable values (strings, numbers, plain objects) can be passed via `inject`. For sharing non-serialisable resources, use `setupFiles` (which run in each worker's module scope) rather than `globalSetup`. `globalSetup` is strictly for bootstrapping external infrastructure that must exist before any test worker starts, not for creating shared in-memory objects.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 144. `transformIgnorePatterns` — Unblocking ESM-Only npm Packages in Jest [official]

Jest's default `transformIgnorePatterns` excludes everything under `node_modules` from Babel/TypeScript transformation, which breaks tests when dependencies ship native ES modules (ESM-only packages like `chalk`, `nanoid`, `uuid` v9+, and many modern utilities). The fix is a negative lookahead that excludes specific ESM packages from the ignore pattern, allowing Jest to transform them. Vitest handles ESM natively and does not require this workaround, but Jest projects on Node 18/20 frequently hit this exact issue during dependency upgrades.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "jest";

export default defineConfig({
  preset: "ts-jest",
  testEnvironment: "node",
  // Default pattern breaks ESM packages — override with a negative lookahead
  transformIgnorePatterns: [
    // Transform everything in node_modules EXCEPT these ESM-only packages
    "/node_modules/(?!(nanoid|uuid|chalk|@sindresorhus|execa|p-limit|got)/)",
  ],
  // Alternative for projects with many ESM dependencies:
  // transform: { "^.+\\.[tj]sx?$": ["ts-jest", { useESM: true }] },
  // extensionsToTreatAsEsm: [".ts"],
  moduleNameMapper: {
    // ESM-style .js extensions in imports resolve to TypeScript source
    "^(\\.{1,2}/.*)\\.js$": "$1",
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Maintaining a manual list of ESM packages in `transformIgnorePatterns` requires updates every time a new ESM-only dependency is added, which is easy to miss and produces a confusing `SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement in a module` failure rather than a clear "package needs transformation" error. Projects experiencing this pain repeatedly should consider migrating to Vitest (which has native ESM support) or switching to `--experimental-vm-modules` Jest mode with a full ESM TypeScript configuration. The negative-lookahead pattern is a tactical fix, not a strategic solution.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 145. Mock Reset Discipline — `clearMocks`, `resetMocks`, `restoreMocks` Semantics [official]

Vitest and Jest offer three distinct mock reset levels that are frequently confused. `clearMocks` clears recorded calls, instances, and results without resetting implementation. `resetMocks` does everything `clearMocks` does plus removes any custom implementation set via `mockImplementation`, returning the mock to a no-op state. `restoreMocks` does everything `resetMocks` does plus restores `vi.spyOn` spies to their original (real) implementation. Using the wrong level causes subtle cross-test contamination: a test that sets a `mockReturnValue` will affect subsequent tests if only `clearMocks` is configured, because the implementation survives the clear.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — recommended configuration for TDD projects
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // restoreMocks is the safest: clears + resets + restores spies
    // Equivalent to calling vi.restoreAllMocks() in beforeEach globally
    restoreMocks: true,
    // DO NOT also set resetMocks: true — restoreMocks subsumes it
    // DO NOT also set clearMocks: true — restoreMocks subsumes it
  },
});

// src/__tests__/mock-levels.test.ts — demonstrating the difference
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import * as mathUtils from "../math-utils";

describe("mock level semantics", () => {
  it("clearMocks: preserves implementation between tests", () => {
    const spy = vi.spyOn(mathUtils, "add").mockReturnValue(999);
    expect(mathUtils.add(1, 2)).toBe(999); // Custom implementation active
    vi.clearAllMocks();
    expect(mathUtils.add(1, 2)).toBe(999); // STILL 999 — implementation survives clear
  });

  it("restoreMocks: implementation is gone after restore", () => {
    const spy = vi.spyOn(mathUtils, "add").mockReturnValue(999);
    expect(mathUtils.add(1, 2)).toBe(999);
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
    expect(mathUtils.add(1, 2)).toBe(3); // Back to real implementation
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Setting `restoreMocks: true` globally is the safest TDD configuration because it prevents all three categories of cross-test contamination. The cost is that any spy whose original implementation was a side-effect-producing function will resume producing those side effects after restoration — a test that relies on a spy being in a "reset but still mocked" state between tests must explicitly re-spy in each test or in `beforeEach`. This is rarely a problem in well-isolated TDD suites but can require refactoring when migrating legacy test files that relied on `clearMocks`-only behaviour.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 146. Test Environment Docblock Override — Per-File `jsdom` vs `node` [official]

Both Jest and Vitest default to a `node` test environment, but UI component tests typically require a `jsdom` environment for `document`, `window`, and DOM APIs. Rather than running an entire project with `jsdom` (which adds overhead to server-side tests that don't need it), the environment can be overridden per-file using a `@vitest-environment` docblock comment. This preserves fast `node`-environment execution for service tests while enabling the correct environment for component tests, with no configuration file changes required.

```typescript
// src/components/__tests__/dropdown.test.ts
// @vitest-environment jsdom
// (Jest equivalent: @jest-environment jsdom)

import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";
import { Dropdown } from "../dropdown";

describe("Dropdown component", () => {
  let container: HTMLElement;

  beforeEach(() => {
    container = document.createElement("div");
    document.body.appendChild(container);
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    document.body.removeChild(container);
  });

  it("renders closed by default", () => {
    const dropdown = new Dropdown(container, {
      options: ["Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"],
      placeholder: "Select an option",
    });
    dropdown.mount();

    expect(container.querySelector(".dropdown-menu")).toBeNull();
    expect(container.querySelector(".dropdown-trigger")?.textContent).toBe("Select an option");
  });

  it("opens the menu on trigger click", () => {
    const dropdown = new Dropdown(container, { options: ["Alpha", "Beta"] });
    dropdown.mount();

    const trigger = container.querySelector<HTMLElement>(".dropdown-trigger")!;
    trigger.click();

    expect(container.querySelector(".dropdown-menu")).not.toBeNull();
    expect(container.querySelectorAll(".dropdown-option")).toHaveLength(2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Per-file environment docblocks require every developer to know to add the comment when creating UI test files — it is easy to forget, and the resulting error (`document is not defined`) is clear but requires knowledge of the override mechanism to fix quickly. For projects where all tests require `jsdom`, set `testEnvironment: "jsdom"` globally and use `@vitest-environment node` on the (fewer) server-side test files instead. The per-file override is most valuable in mixed-codebase projects (Next.js, SvelteKit) where server and client code coexist and have genuinely different environment requirements.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 147. Test Pyramid Layer Discipline — Duplicating Tests Across Layers Destroys Confidence [community]

The test pyramid (unit → integration → e2e) works only when each layer tests something unique. A common anti-pattern is to write the same logical assertion at all three levels: a unit test mocks the database, an integration test hits a test database, and an e2e test navigates to a page — all three asserting the same "user with email X exists" fact. This duplication inflates the test suite size and run time without increasing confidence; worse, it creates a maintenance problem where changing business logic requires updating three identical assertions in three separate test files.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: same assertion duplicated across layers
// unit: expect(repository.findByEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith("a@b.com")
// integration: expect(await db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email=?", ["a@b.com"])).not.toBeNull()
// e2e: expect(page.getByText("a@b.com")).toBeVisible()

// CORRECT: each layer tests what only that layer can test

// unit test — tests the SERVICE LOGIC, not the database
it("returns null for unknown emails (service logic)", async () => {
  mockRepo.findByEmail.mockResolvedValue(null);
  const result = await userService.findByEmail("unknown@example.com");
  expect(result).toBeNull();
  expect(mockRepo.findByEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith("unknown@example.com");
});

// integration test — tests the REPOSITORY QUERY, not the service
it("repository returns null when email is absent from DB", async () => {
  const repo = new UserRepository(testDb);
  const result = await repo.findByEmail("nobody@example.com");
  expect(result).toBeNull(); // Tests the SQL query logic, not the service
});

// e2e test — tests the USER-VISIBLE FLOW, not the data layer
it("login page shows error for unknown email (e2e)", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/login");
  await page.fill('[name="email"]', "nobody@example.com");
  await page.fill('[name="password"]', "anything");
  await page.click('[type="submit"]');
  await expect(page.getByText("Invalid credentials")).toBeVisible();
  // Does NOT assert database state — that belongs to integration tests
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Enforcing pyramid layer discipline requires explicit team agreement on what each layer "owns." The temptation to write a quick integration test for every unit-test scenario is strong because integration tests "feel more real." The discipline pays off in CI speed (unit tests run in seconds; integration and e2e tests run in minutes) and in localised failures — when a unit test fails you know the business logic changed; when an integration test fails you know the data layer changed; when an e2e test fails you know the user-facing flow changed.

**Tag:** [community]

---

### 148. `setupFiles` vs `setupFilesAfterFramework` — Global Test Utilities Placement [official]

Jest's `setupFiles` (Vitest equivalent: `setupFiles`) run before the test framework (Jest, Vitest) is installed in the worker, meaning `expect`, `describe`, `it`, and `vi` are not yet available. `setupFilesAfterFramework` (Jest: `setupFilesAfterFramework`, Vitest: `setupFiles` runs after internal init) runs after the framework is ready. Custom matchers registered via `expect.extend`, global mocks applied via `vi.mock`, and `@testing-library/jest-dom` matchers must be registered in the after-framework setup file, not the before-framework one, or they will not be applied to the test execution context.

```typescript
// test/setup.ts — setupFilesAfterFramework equivalent (loaded after Vitest framework)
import "@testing-library/jest-dom"; // Custom matchers: toBeInTheDocument, toBeVisible, etc.
import { expect, beforeEach, vi } from "vitest";
import { customMatchers } from "./custom-matchers";

// Register project-wide custom matchers
expect.extend(customMatchers);

// Global beforeEach: reset any globally-shared state
beforeEach(() => {
  // Reset MSW request handlers to defaults before each test
  // (actual reset handled by the MSW setup file, this is illustrative)
});

// test/env-setup.ts — setupFiles (runs BEFORE framework, for polyfills only)
// This file can NOT use describe/it/expect/vi
import "fake-indexeddb/auto"; // Polyfill IndexedDB for Node.js environments
import { TextEncoder, TextDecoder } from "util";

// Polyfill globals that jsdom doesn't provide
Object.defineProperty(global, "TextEncoder", { value: TextEncoder });
Object.defineProperty(global, "TextDecoder", { value: TextDecoder });
```

**Tradeoff.** Many developers use a single `setupFilesAfterFramework` file for everything (polyfills, custom matchers, global mocks), which works correctly but conflates two concerns. Separating polyfill installation (pre-framework) from custom matcher registration (post-framework) makes the setup intent clearer and prevents accidental use of framework APIs in the polyfill file. The risk of splitting into two files is that the execution order must be understood — polyfills first, then framework registration.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 149. `expect.extend` — Domain-Specific Matchers as First-Class TDD Vocabulary [official]

Custom matchers registered via `expect.extend` allow test authors to express domain-specific assertions as named, readable predicates rather than sequences of primitive assertions. A custom matcher both improves test readability (the failure message says "expected PaymentResult to be successful, but it was declined with code INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS") and acts as a reusable specification for what "successful" means for a given domain type. Writing the custom matcher before the domain type implementation is itself a TDD act — it forces the team to agree on the observable contract before writing code.

```typescript
// test/matchers/payment-matchers.ts
import { expect } from "vitest";

interface PaymentResult {
  status: "success" | "declined" | "pending";
  code?: string;
  transactionId?: string;
  amountCents: number;
}

expect.extend({
  toBeSuccessfulPayment(received: PaymentResult) {
    const pass =
      received.status === "success" &&
      typeof received.transactionId === "string" &&
      received.transactionId.length > 0;

    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `Expected payment NOT to be successful, but status=${received.status} transactionId=${received.transactionId}`
          : `Expected payment to be successful, but status=${received.status} code=${received.code ?? "none"} transactionId=${received.transactionId ?? "absent"}`,
    };
  },

  toBeDeclinedWithCode(received: PaymentResult, expectedCode: string) {
    const pass = received.status === "declined" && received.code === expectedCode;
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `Expected payment NOT to be declined with ${expectedCode}`
          : `Expected payment to be declined with code=${expectedCode}, but status=${received.status} code=${received.code ?? "none"}`,
    };
  },
});

// Usage in tests — domain-readable, failure messages include context
it("declines payments from sanctioned countries", async () => {
  const result = await processPayment({ country: "XX", amountCents: 5000 });
  expect(result).toBeDeclinedWithCode("SANCTIONED_COUNTRY");
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom matchers require TypeScript interface augmentation (`interface Assertion<R>` extension in a `.d.ts` file) to provide type-checking for the custom assertion names — without augmentation, `expect(x).toBeSuccessfulPayment()` produces a TypeScript error even though it works at runtime. This augmentation boilerplate is a one-time cost per matcher file. The payoff is a vocabulary of domain matchers that makes test code read like business requirements, which is particularly valuable when non-engineers review test output in CI logs.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### 150. V8 vs Istanbul Coverage Provider Selection — Trade-offs for TDD Feedback Speed [official]

Vitest supports two coverage instrumentation backends: `v8` (using Node.js/V8's native coverage API) and `istanbul` (compile-time instrumentation). V8 requires no pre-transpilation pass, making it faster to start and less memory-intensive, and it runs coverage collection in the same process as the tests. Istanbul instruments source code before execution, produces more accurate branch coverage for complex TypeScript patterns (type narrowing, conditional types), and works across all JavaScript runtimes including browsers. The choice affects the speed of the TDD red-green loop when coverage is enabled.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — V8 provider: fastest for TDD inner loop
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      // V8 ignores specific code via inline comments (esbuild @preserve required):
      // /* v8 ignore next -- @preserve */ (single line)
      // /* v8 ignore start -- @preserve */ ... /* v8 ignore stop -- @preserve */
      reporter: ["text", "html", "lcov"],
    },
  },
});

// vitest.config.ts — Istanbul provider: most accurate for complex TypeScript
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "istanbul",
      // Istanbul ignores via standard comments (no @preserve needed):
      // /* istanbul ignore next */
      // /* istanbul ignore if */
      // /* istanbul ignore else */
      reporter: ["text", "html", "lcov"],
      // Istanbul requires @vitest/coverage-istanbul package
    },
  },
});

// Inline ignore annotation for a defensive code path (V8 provider):
function divide(a: number, b: number): number {
  /* v8 ignore next -- @preserve */
  if (b === 0) throw new Error("Division by zero");
  return a / b;
}
```

**Tradeoff.** V8 coverage is the right default for most TDD projects because the fast startup makes it practical to run with coverage enabled during development (`vitest --coverage --watch`). Istanbul should be selected when precise branch coverage reporting is required for compliance reporting or when the codebase uses complex TypeScript control-flow patterns that V8 misreports. A common hybrid: use V8 in watch mode (TDD inner loop) and Istanbul in CI (coverage gate enforcement), configured via separate `vitest.config.dev.ts` and `vitest.config.ci.ts` files.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Real-World Gotchas [community] — Cycle 51 Additions

231. **[community] `vi.mock()` with `importOriginal` (or `vi.importActual` inside the factory) must be called with `await` because the factory is an `async` function — omitting `await` causes the spread `...real` to operate on a pending `Promise` object rather than the resolved module, silently replacing every re-exported value with `undefined` in the test, and the failure manifests as `TypeError: X is not a function` for any function that was supposed to be preserved from the real module.** A developer adds `const real = vi.importActual("../utils")` (without `await`) inside a `vi.mock` factory, spreads `...real` over the mock return, then wonders why every non-overridden export is `undefined` — the `Promise` object's own enumerable properties (`then`, `catch`, `finally`) are spread instead of the module's actual exports. WHY this matters: JavaScript silently spreads a `Promise` without error, so the symptom is downstream `TypeError` failures that are far removed from the `vi.mock` call that caused them. Fix: always `await vi.importActual()` inside factory functions and mark the factory as `async`: `vi.mock("../mod", async (importOriginal) => { const real = await importOriginal(); return { ...real, myFn: vi.fn() }; })`.

232. **[community] Jest's `moduleNameMapper` patterns are evaluated in declaration order, and a broad pattern placed before a narrow pattern will shadow it — a mapping for `"^@/(.*)": "<rootDir>/src/$1"` listed before `"^@/auth/(.*)": "<rootDir>/src/auth-v2/$1"` will always match `@/auth/login` with the first rule, routing it to `src/auth/login` instead of the intended `src/auth-v2/login`, and no error is thrown because both paths exist.** A team migrates their auth module to `src/auth-v2/` and adds a specific alias to `moduleNameMapper` but puts it after the existing catch-all `@/` alias; all auth imports still resolve to the old path, causing tests to pass against stale implementations while the real application uses the new ones. WHY this matters: the silent success is the most dangerous outcome — tests pass, CI is green, but tests and production code are testing different implementations. Fix: always place narrow (more specific) patterns before broad (catch-all) patterns in `moduleNameMapper`; or use TypeScript path aliases with `subpath imports` (`#/`) which are resolved by Node.js before any mapper can intercept them.

233. **[community] Vitest's `globalSetup` return value (used with `inject()` in test files) must be a plain JSON-serialisable object — returning a `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, class instance, or any value with a prototype other than `Object.prototype` silently results in `inject("key")` returning `undefined` in the test worker, because the return value is serialised through `JSON.stringify`/`JSON.parse` during the inter-process handoff between the main process and the worker processes.** A developer returns `{ dbInstance: new DatabasePool(url) }` from `globalSetup` intending to share a pool across all tests, then calls `inject("dbInstance")` expecting the pool object but receives `undefined` — the pool was stringified to `{}` during transfer. WHY this matters: the loss of the `dbInstance` does not throw; `inject()` returns `undefined` silently, and the first database call in the test fails with a confusing null-dereference error rather than an "inject returned undefined" error. Fix: return only serialisable values from `globalSetup` (strings for connection URLs, numbers for ports); construct resource objects from those values inside `setupFiles` (which run in each worker's process scope) or `beforeAll` blocks.

234. **[community] Snapshot files committed to version control with Windows-style CRLF line endings will cause all snapshot assertions to fail on Unix CI runners because the snapshot serialiser normalises line endings to LF before comparing — a snapshot written on Windows with CRLF line endings will never match the LF-normalised comparison string, causing every snapshot test to fail on Linux CI even though the snapshots are logically identical.** A developer on Windows creates inline snapshots in watch mode, the Vitest snapshot writer inserts CRLF-terminated strings into the source file (matching the file's existing line endings), and the CI pipeline on Ubuntu fails every snapshot assertion with a diff that shows only invisible `\r` characters. WHY this matters: the diff in the CI log shows the snapshot failure but the `\r` characters are often invisible in the browser-based CI log viewer, making the root cause extremely difficult to diagnose. Fix: add `* text=auto eol=lf` to the project's `.gitattributes` file to enforce LF normalisations on commit; or add `--snapshot-options.normalizeLineEndings=lf` to the Vitest config; run `git add --renormalize .` after adding the `.gitattributes` rule to fix existing committed files.

235. **[community] `expect.extend` custom matchers defined in TypeScript must also augment the Vitest/Jest `Assertion` interface in a `.d.ts` file to avoid TypeScript errors on the custom matcher call sites — but the augmentation must use the correct interface name for the version of Vitest in use: Vitest 3.2 renamed the matcher type from per-context `Assertion<R>` to the unified `Matchers<R>` interface, so projects upgrading from Vitest 3.1 to 3.2+ will have augmentation in the old `Assertion<R>` form that TypeScript silently ignores, leaving custom matcher call sites with `Property 'toBeSuccessfulPayment' does not exist on type 'Assertion<PaymentResult>'` compile errors even though the matcher works at runtime.** A team upgrades Vitest from 3.1 to 3.2, runs `npm test`, sees no failures, then runs `tsc --noEmit` and discovers 47 new TypeScript errors all of the form "property does not exist on type 'Assertion'" — the runtime tests still pass because the matcher is registered, but TypeScript does not accept the calls because the augmentation targets the removed `Assertion<R>` interface. WHY this matters: test files without strict TypeScript checking (e.g., with `skipLibCheck: true`) will not surface this regression until a developer adds a new custom matcher call and sees the error — the existing custom matcher call sites were already accepted before the upgrade and TypeScript only rechecks call sites that change. Fix: update all augmentation files from `interface Assertion<R> { toBeSuccessfulPayment(): R; }` to `interface Matchers<R> { toBeSuccessfulPayment(): R; }` (the unified form introduced in Vitest 3.2), then run `tsc --noEmit` to confirm all 47 errors are resolved.
